AI.motivation: Robots in real-world environments must perform complex, long-horizon, multi-step bimanual tasks rather than isolated single actions. Existing manipulation datasets cannot adequately support this: single-arm datasets, despite reaching hundreds of thousands of trajectories, usually provide only one high-level instruction per episode, and the rare bimanual datasets that do label subtasks annotate only a fraction of their total hours. This leaves a gap in dense, subtask-level supervision needed for long-horizon bimanual learning.
AI.method: The authors introduce FineART, a densely annotated bimanual manipulation dataset comprising 40,543 episodes, 1,718 hours, and 533,913 subtasks across 151 tasks. Building on it, they propose FineART-VLA, a vision-language-action policy that predicts its own next subtask, and use this subtask-prediction objective during mid-training. They also evaluate step-by-step human subtask guidance and fine-tune the policy on a new robot to assess data efficiency and zero-shot transfer.
AI.result: Mid-training with self-predicted subtasks yields substantial gains: success on a spatial disambiguation task rises from 32.0% to 100.0%, and step-by-step human subtask guidance improves success on an unseen long-horizon task from 16.0% to 76.0%. After minimal fine-tuning on a new robot, the policy requires one-tenth the data of baselines without mid-training and generalizes zero-shot to completely unseen tasks on the new hardware.
AI.conclusion: Dense subtask-level annotation in bimanual manipulation data, combined with a VLA policy that self-predicts its next subtask during mid-training, substantially improves long-horizon task success, data efficiency, and zero-shot generalization to new hardware and unseen tasks. The full dataset, model weights, and training code are open-sourced.

title: Right Words, Wrong Moment: A Clinician-Grounded Analysis of Distress in 19,930 Conversations between Young People and ChatGPT
summary: Young people increasingly turn to General-Purpose Conversational Agents (GPCAs), such as ChatGPT, in moments of distress. We examine young adults' (ages 18-25) experiences using ChatGPT. We first collected 19,930 ChatGPT conversations and survey data from 158 young adults. We then selected five example conversations reflecting user distress. Finally, we asked ten clinicians to review those five conversations. We found distressed participants reported greater emotional engagement with ChatGPT and greater behavioral change from using it than their peers. When they turned to ChatGPT in moments of acute distress, ChatGPT was quick to give overly dramatic responses and excessive action-oriented suggestions. Clinicians endorsed ChatGPT's availability and much of its wording, but identified seven process failures, such as prematurely jumping to solutions. We translated clinicians' feedback into design guidelines following three stages: 1) asking about safety, 2) de-escalating intensity to restore emotional regulation, and 3) exploring concerns without agreeing with them.

AI.tldr: Young adults in distress engage more emotionally with ChatGPT and change behavior more, but ChatGPT responds with overly dramatic and action-oriented suggestions; clinicians identified seven process failures, translated into three-stage design guidelines.
AI.motivation: Young people increasingly turn to General-Purpose Conversational Agents (GPCAs) like ChatGPT during moments of distress, yet little is known about how young adults actually experience these interactions and whether the responses are clinically appropriate.
AI.method: Collected 19,930 ChatGPT conversations and survey data from 158 young adults (ages 18-25); selected five example conversations reflecting user distress; had ten clinicians review those five conversations.
AI.result: Distressed participants reported greater emotional engagement with ChatGPT and greater behavioral change than peers. In acute distress, ChatGPT gave overly dramatic responses and excessive action-oriented suggestions. Clinicians endorsed ChatGPT's availability and much of its wording but identified seven process failures, e.g., prematurely jumping to solutions.
AI.conclusion: Clinician feedback was translated into design guidelines across three stages: 1) asking about safety, 2) de-escalating intensity to restore emotional regulation, and 3) exploring concerns without agreeing with them.

title: Losing the name before the box: measuring and repairing what narrow fine-tuning costs a detector outside its deployment vocabulary
comment: 25 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary material (69 pages) is included as an ancillary file. Submitted to the International Journal of Computer Vision
summary: A detector pretrained on a broad corpus is fine-tuned on a narrow domain, its in-domain accuracy improves, and it ships. We ask what happens meanwhile to its coverage of objects the vocabulary never names, which in obstacle detection and inspection carry the risk. No in-domain test set holds an example of one. We give a longitudinal protocol: one pretrained checkpoint against its own fine-tuned descendants. It tracks held-out top-$K$ proposal coverage $C_τ$: of categories pretraining covered and the vocabulary omits, the share of boxes a detector's top $K$ regions still cover. The quantity is the open-world proposal literature's; the longitudinal reading is not. $C_τ$ falls while in-domain accuracy rises, on four architectures and three domains, by $5.12$ to $63.35$ points on boxes above $1024$ px$^2$. No in-domain number identifies the fall, and neither does detection average precision, which charges a missed and a misnamed box alike. On the one architecture scoring both, adaptation costs $87\%$ of the AP against a fifth of the coverage, and the naming goes first at all six depths of its freeze ladder, every run. What breaks is structured: three architectures sharing no pretraining run agree on which categories lose coverage, and those a model never learned do not lose any. A repair follows and needs no training: mixing a quarter of the pretrained state back, normalisation statistics included, raises coverage on every cell swept for at most $2.47$ points of in-domain accuracy. Seeing it costs one extra evaluation pass.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning a pretrained detector on a narrow domain improves in-domain accuracy but silently degrades coverage of pretraining categories the target vocabulary omits; this open-world coverage loss is quantifiable via a longitudinal top-$K$ proposal metric and can be largely repaired by weight interpolation with no extra training.
AI.motivation: In obstacle detection and inspection, detectors are routinely fine-tuned from broad pretraining to narrow domains and shipped, yet no in-domain test set contains examples of objects the target vocabulary never names. The risk is that these unnamed-but-learned categories lose coverage during adaptation, and standard in-domain accuracy cannot reveal it.
AI.method: A longitudinal protocol comparing one pretrained checkpoint against its own fine-tuned descendants. It tracks held-out top-$K$ proposal coverage $C_\tau$: among pretraining-covered categories omitted by the vocabulary, the fraction of boxes still covered by the detector's top $K$ regions. The metric is borrowed from open-world proposal literature, but its longitudinal reading is new. Experiments span four architectures and three domains, with analysis of detection AP, a freeze-depth ladder, cross-run category agreement, and a training-free repair that mixes pretrained state (including normalisation statistics) back into the fine-tuned model.
AI.result: $C_\tau$ drops while in-domain accuracy rises across four architectures and three domains, by $5.12$ to $63.35$ points on boxes above $1024$ px$^2$. No in-domain metric identifies the decline, nor does detection AP, which penalises missed and misnamed boxes equally. On the architecture scoring both, adaptation costs $87\%$ of AP but only about a fifth of coverage, and naming is lost first at all six depths of its freeze ladder in every run. The failure is structured: three architectures with independent pretraining agree on which categories lose coverage, and categories never learned lose none. Mixing a quarter of the pretrained state back (normalisation statistics included) raises coverage in every swept cell for at most $2.47$ points of in-domain accuracy, costing one extra evaluation pass.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning silently trades away coverage of unnamed pretraining categories, a failure invisible to in-domain accuracy and detection AP. The loss is systematic and category-structured rather than random, and it can be substantially mitigated post hoc by training-free weight mixing with pretrained parameters, offering a practical safeguard for open-world deployment.

title: SAGE: A Statistical Acceptance Gate for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly self-evolve by editing a persistent skill document that encodes their workflow, tool-use rules, and decision logic. This loop has two steps, an optimizer that proposes a candidate edit and a gate that accepts or rejects it. Prior work has concentrated on the optimizer, while the gate still follows a naive rule that keeps any edit which improves an aggregate validation score. We show that this rule fails in two ways. First, it admits permanent regressions, since an edit can raise the average while breaking items the skill already solves. Second, it is vulnerable to the Optimizer's Curse, since the best observed score on a finite and noisy validation set is upward biased. To solve the above two limitations, we propose a statistical acceptance gate for self-evolving agents (SAGE). Compared with previous work, SAGE has two contributions. First, SAGE proposes a per-item paired comparison that evaluates the current skill and the edited skill on identical validation items, which exposes regressions that an aggregate score hides and penalizes them asymmetrically. Second, SAGE also employs a one-sided paired test that commits an edit only when its wins are statistically reliable against its losses, and it abstains otherwise. SAGE is a conservative refinement of the standard gate that recovers the baseline exactly at a boundary setting. It commits only a subset of the baseline's edits, filtering out those whose gains are unreliable or purchased by breaking already-solved items. Across five benchmarks and four backbone LLMs under an equal-budget protocol, SAGE lowers the regression rate in 19 of 20 settings and matches the baseline in the remaining one, for example from 36.5% to 0% on LiveMath and from 42.8% to 0% on OfficeQA with DeepSeek-V4. SAGE also attains the highest final score in all 20 settings, raising LiveMath from 34.15 to 48.78.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAGE, a statistical acceptance gate for LLM-based self-evolving agents that replaces the naive aggregate-score gate with per-item paired comparison and a one-sided paired significance test, eliminating permanent regressions and mitigating the Optimizer's Curse.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving LLM agents iteratively edit a persistent skill document via an optimizer plus an acceptance gate, but prior work neglects the gate. The naive gate keeps any edit that improves an aggregate validation score, which (1) admits permanent regressions because averages can rise while previously solved items break, and (2) suffers from the Optimizer's Curse, since the best observed score on a finite, noisy validation set is upward biased.
AI.method: SAGE introduces two mechanisms: (1) a per-item paired comparison that evaluates the current and edited skills on identical validation items, exposing and asymmetrically penalizing regressions hidden by aggregate scores; and (2) a one-sided paired significance test that accepts an edit only when its wins are statistically reliable against its losses, otherwise abstaining. SAGE is a conservative refinement of the standard gate, recovering the baseline exactly at a boundary setting.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks and four backbone LLMs under an equal-budget protocol, SAGE reduces the regression rate in 19 of 20 settings and matches the baseline in the remaining one (e.g., 36.5% to 0% on LiveMath and 42.8% to 0% on OfficeQA with DeepSeek-V4), while attaining the highest final score in all 20 settings (LiveMath: 34.15 to 48.78).
AI.conclusion: Treating the acceptance gate as a statistical decision problem rather than a naive threshold yields substantial gains: SAGE commits only a reliable subset of baseline edits, filtering out those whose gains are unreliable or bought by breaking already-solved items, improving both regression robustness and final performance.

title: World4Scorer: Outcome-Grounded World Modeling for Autonomous Driving
comment: 28 pages, 14 figures, 13 tables. Project page: https://guobapei.github.io/World4Scorer/
summary: Autonomous driving requires choosing a safe and efficient plan as surrounding traffic evolves. Generate-and-select planners propose multiple trajectories and score them for execution, and they have outperformed representative direct-prediction baselines on NAVSIM. Their scorer must compare plans that were never executed. Driving logs record the future of only the executed trajectory, so matching the logged future can leave predictions for the alternatives unconstrained; a simulator, in contrast, can label the outcome of every candidate. We introduce World4Scorer, which builds the scorer as a trajectory-conditioned JEPA-style predictor: it predicts a state for each candidate and reads the candidate's scores from that state. Simulator outcome labels supervise the states of all candidates, and the observed future of the executed trajectory anchors the predictor to real scene evolution. Because one predictor produces every candidate's state, the anchor can constrain shared parameters used to score unexecuted plans, while the future itself is needed only during training. Generated candidates mostly score well, so a scene-matched bank adds low-scoring plans to the outcome supervision; framewise choices can conflict, so inertial re-ranking keeps consecutive selections consistent. World4Scorer achieves state-of-the-art NAVSIM-v2 performance and a strong adapted-system result on closed-loop Bench2Drive. With the LeWM world model and planning budget fixed, outcome-based scoring also improves manipulation planning on the OGBench-Cube benchmark.

AI.tldr: World4Scorer builds a trajectory-conditioned JEPA-style scorer that predicts a per-candidate state, supervised by simulator outcome labels and anchored by the logged executed future, achieving SOTA NAVSIM-v2, strong Bench2Drive, and improved OGBench-Cube manipulation planning.
AI.motivation: Generate-and-select planners must score candidate trajectories never actually driven, but driving logs only record the executed trajectory's future, leaving alternative plans' outcomes unconstrained. A simulator can label every candidate's outcome, motivating the need to exploit simulator-outcome supervision while still anchoring predictions to real logged scene evolution.
AI.method: World4Scorer formulates the scorer as a trajectory-conditioned JEPA-style predictor: it predicts a state for each candidate and reads that candidate's scores from the state. Simulator outcome labels supervise all candidate states, while the executed trajectory's observed future anchors the predictor to real scene evolution. Since one shared predictor produces every candidate's state, the anchor constrains the shared parameters used to score unexecuted plans, and the future is needed only at training. A scene-matched bank adds low-scoring plans to the outcome supervision, and inertial re-ranking enforces consistency across consecutive framewise selections.
AI.result: World4Scorer achieves state-of-the-art NAVSIM-v2 performance and a strong adapted-system result on closed-loop Bench2Drive. With the LeWM world model and a fixed planning budget, outcome-based scoring also improves manipulation planning on OGBench-Cube.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-conditioned, outcome-supervised scoring with a logged-future anchor and consistency mechanisms yields a robust generate-and-select scorer, transferring effectively from driving benchmarks to manipulation planning.

title: PowerZooJax: A JAX-based Power System Benchmark for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Power system operation is a safety-critical sequential decision-making problem, making it a natural testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). However, existing RL environments for power systems are often narrow in scope and computationally limited by CPU-based simulation workflows, making large-scale evaluation difficult. We introduce PowerZooJax, a JAX-based benchmark suite for RL in power system operation. It provides five constrained Markov decision process tasks spanning generation, transmission, distribution, distributed energy resources, and data center microgrid. By rewriting power flow, economic dispatch, market clearing, and device dynamics as JAX computation graphs, PowerZooJax keeps the entire training and evaluation loop on the GPU. Experiments show substantial speedups over CPU-based simulations and demonstrate standardized evaluation of policy returns, safety violations, and out-of-distribution stress conditions. Our open-source benchmark is available at: https://github.com/powerzoojax/PowerZooJax.

AI.tldr: PowerZooJax is a JAX-based GPU-accelerated benchmark suite for reinforcement learning in power system operation, offering five constrained MDP tasks and standardized evaluation of returns, safety violations, and out-of-distribution stress.
AI.motivation: Power system operation is a safety-critical sequential decision-making problem and a natural RL testbed, but existing RL environments for power systems are narrow in scope and limited by CPU-based simulation workflows, hindering large-scale evaluation.
AI.method: The authors rewrite power flow, economic dispatch, market clearing, and device dynamics as JAX computation graphs, keeping the entire training and evaluation loop on the GPU, and package five constrained MDP tasks spanning generation, transmission, distribution, distributed energy resources, and data center microgrid.
AI.result: Experiments show substantial speedups over CPU-based simulations and demonstrate standardized evaluation of policy returns, safety violations, and out-of-distribution stress conditions.
AI.conclusion: PowerZooJax provides a broad, GPU-accelerated, open-source benchmark (available at https://github.com/powerzoojax/PowerZooJax) that enables large-scale, standardized evaluation of RL policies for safety-critical power system operation.

title: Staircase Policy: Streaming Inference for World-Action Models with Large Action Chunks
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by conditioning action generation on predicted future observations, but future prediction adds further inference overhead to already expensive iterative action generation. Action chunking can amortize this cost over multiple actions, yet performance degrades over long execution horizons because later actions remain conditioned on stale observations. We introduce STAIRCASE POLICY, a streaming inference and training framework that turns a flow-matching VLA into a JEPA-style WAM and partitions a large action chunk into sub-chunks at staggered denoising stages. Near-term actions are executed as soon as they become available, while later actions continue to be refined. At each sub-chunk boundary, the future latent is re-predicted from the latest observation and used to update all unexecuted actions, enabling long-horizon execution without repeated full policy inference. The resulting future-prediction error can further serve as a signal for adaptive chunking. S-WAM achieves 97.7% on LIBERO and 87.9% on LIBERO-Plus, and improves performance across multiple policy backbones and real-robot tasks. It reaches 292.7 executed actions per second, $3.62\times$ the throughput of conventional execution at comparable accuracy, while reducing time-to-first-action from 123.6 to 73.3 ms. With additional inference optimizations, throughput further increases to 642.9 actions per second.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Staircase Policy (S-WAM), a streaming inference and training framework that turns a flow-matching VLA model into a JEPA-style World-Action Model, partitioning action chunks into staggered denoising sub-chunks for efficient long-horizon robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: World-Action Models condition action generation on predicted future observations, improving manipulation but adding inference overhead to already expensive iterative action generation. Action chunking can amortize this cost, yet performance degrades over long horizons because later actions remain conditioned on stale observations.
AI.method: The framework converts a flow-matching VLA into a JEPA-style WAM and splits a large action chunk into sub-chunks at staggered denoising stages. Near-term actions are executed as soon as available while later actions continue to be refined. At each sub-chunk boundary, the future latent is re-predicted from the latest observation and used to update all unexecuted actions, enabling long-horizon execution without repeated full policy inference. Future-prediction error also serves as a signal for adaptive chunking.
AI.result: S-WAM achieves 97.7% on LIBERO and 87.9% on LIBERO-Plus, improves performance across multiple policy backbones and real-robot tasks, reaches 292.7 executed actions per second (3.62x the throughput of conventional execution at comparable accuracy), reduces time-to-first-action from 123.6 to 73.3 ms, and with additional inference optimizations reaches 642.9 actions per second.
AI.conclusion: Staircase Policy provides a streaming framework that resolves the staleness-efficiency tradeoff in action chunking for World-Action Models, delivering high accuracy, substantially higher throughput, and lower latency while generalizing across backbones and real-robot settings.

title: GeoWind2Plan: Mission-Time 3D Urban Wind Prediction for Energy-Efficient UAV Planning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). 31 pages. Code and dataset: https://github.com/DUAL-Xiao/GeoWind2Plan/
summary: In urban low-altitude flight, buildings reshape ambient wind into spatially varying 3D flow, making unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) energy depend on local wind exposure as well as path length. However, building-resolved wind information is rarely available when a mission must be planned. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) can produce high-fidelity urban flow fields, but each simulation is tied to a fixed inflow boundary condition and can take hours to days, which is incompatible with urban UAV missions that typically last minutes to tens of minutes. We present GeoWind2Plan, a geometry-to-wind-to-planning framework for mission-time 3D urban wind prediction and energy-efficient UAV planning. Given only a background wind vector, 3D building geometry, and a start-goal pair, GeoWind2Plan transforms the building geometry into a reference-wind frame, predicts mission-relevant 3D wind patches with a localized geometry-conditioned neural operator, stitches them into a queryable local wind field, and optimizes a feasible 3D path and speed profile using a physically grounded UAV energy model. Rather than pursuing CFD-perfect reconstruction, GeoWind2Plan targets decision-useful wind prediction: trajectories are planned with predicted wind and evaluated under high-fidelity CFD wind. Across held-out urban domains, wind speeds, and mission wind-angle regimes, GeoWind2Plan performs corridor-localized wind inference in about 3 seconds, compared with roughly 8 hours for CFD. Under CFD evaluation, trajectories planned with GeoWind2Plan reduce energy by 6.9%, 12.7%, and 4.5% in tailwind, headwind, and crosswind missions relative to wind-agnostic planning, recovering 87.9%, 85.7%, and 75.0% of CFD-reference savings. These results show that fast, corridor-localized 3D urban wind prediction can make wind-aware UAV energy planning practical at mission time.

AI.tldr: GeoWind2Plan is a geometry-to-wind-to-planning framework that predicts mission-relevant 3D urban wind in ~3 s (vs ~8 h for CFD) and enables wind-aware UAV energy-efficient planning, cutting energy by up to 12.7% and recovering most CFD-reference savings.
AI.motivation: In urban low-altitude flight, buildings reshape ambient wind into spatially varying 3D flow, so UAV energy depends on local wind exposure, not just path length. Building-resolved wind data is usually unavailable at mission time, and CFD is high-fidelity but tied to fixed inflow conditions and takes hours to days—too slow for missions lasting minutes to tens of minutes.
AI.method: Given a background wind vector, 3D building geometry, and a start-goal pair, GeoWind2Plan: (1) transforms building geometry into a reference-wind frame, (2) predicts mission-relevant 3D wind patches via a localized geometry-conditioned neural operator, (3) stitches patches into a queryable local wind field, and (4) optimizes a feasible 3D path and speed profile using a physically grounded UAV energy model. It targets decision-useful wind prediction rather than CFD-perfect reconstruction.
AI.result: Across held-out urban domains, wind speeds, and mission wind-angle regimes, corridor-localized wind inference takes ~3 s versus ~8 h for CFD. Under CFD evaluation, trajectories planned with GeoWind2Plan reduce energy by 6.9% (tailwind), 12.7% (headwind), and 4.5% (crosswind) versus wind-agnostic planning, recovering 87.9%, 85.7%, and 75.0% of CFD-reference savings.
AI.conclusion: Fast, corridor-localized 3D urban wind prediction makes wind-aware UAV energy planning practical at mission time.

title: DQ-MPCC: Dual-Quaternion MPCC for Quadrotor Racing
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
summary: Quadrotor racing demands aggressive attitude and progress control while passing through every gate, and conventional quadrotor MPCC formulations state the prediction model in inertial coordinates and the attitude error in the body frame. We present a Dual-Quaternion Model Predictive Contouring Control (DQ-MPCC) for quadrotor racing in which the pose is a unit dual quaternion and the contouring errors are projected onto the tangent space of the dual quaternion manifold, expressed in the desired body frame: the same rigid-body dynamics as the conventional model, in unified pose-twist coordinates in the body frame. We compare DQ-MPCC against a baseline MPCC through Monte Carlo software-in-the-loop simulations and real-world racing on an eight-gate circuit of 11x4.5x3.65 m. With the same gains in simulation and hardware, DQ-MPCC keeps every crossing of its completed flights within the prescribed geometric margin, whereas the baseline exceeds it, its median worst-gate offset growing by 71.5% sim-to-real against a 10.1% decrease for DQ-MPCC. Among the configurations that keep every simulated gate crossing within the geometric margin, DQ-MPCC also reduces the minimum lap time by 6.7%, and by 10.5% in the real-world flights, while running onboard at 100 Hz.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Dual-Quaternion Model Predictive Contouring Control (DQ-MPCC) for quadrotor racing, expressing pose as a unit dual quaternion with contouring errors projected onto the manifold tangent space in the desired body frame, and demonstrates improved gate-crossing accuracy and lap times over a baseline MPCC in both simulation and real-world flights.
AI.motivation: Quadrotor racing requires aggressive attitude and progress control while passing through every gate. Conventional MPCC formulations define the prediction model in inertial coordinates and the attitude error in the body frame, which is suboptimal for enforcing geometric gate-crossing margins.
AI.method: The authors formulate a Dual-Quaternion MPCC in which the pose is a unit dual quaternion, the contouring errors are projected onto the tangent space of the dual quaternion manifold and expressed in the desired body frame, and the rigid-body dynamics are the same as the conventional model but in unified pose-twist coordinates in the body frame. The method is evaluated against a baseline MPCC via Monte Carlo software-in-the-loop simulations and real-world racing on an eight-gate circuit of 11x4.5x3.65 m.
AI.result: With identical gains in simulation and hardware, DQ-MPCC keeps every gate crossing of completed flights within the prescribed geometric margin, whereas the baseline exceeds it; the baseline's median worst-gate offset grows by 71.5% sim-to-real versus a 10.1% decrease for DQ-MPCC. Among configurations keeping every simulated gate crossing within the margin, DQ-MPCC reduces minimum lap time by 6.7% (simulation) and 10.5% (real-world), while running onboard at 100 Hz.
AI.conclusion: DQ-MPCC improves gate-crossing geometric accuracy and reduces lap time compared with conventional MPCC, with better sim-to-real robustness, and is computationally feasible for onboard execution at 100 Hz.

title: Mirror-Score: Calibrated, Inference-only Scoring Exposes the Limits of Sequence-compatibility Ranking in D-peptide Design
summary: D-peptides combine protease resistance with high target specificity, but computational design of D-peptide binders remains immature. Mirror-Peptidizer introduced an in silico mirror-image screening pipeline using target reflection, backbone generation, and ProteinMPNN sequence design, but its raw ProteinMPNN negative log-likelihood (NLL) ranking was not validated against measured affinities, and only 4 of 9 tested MDM2 designs bound detectably. We introduce Mirror-Score, a calibrated, inference-only scoring framework for heterochiral D-peptide/L-protein complexes, and a public benchmark of 31 crystal complexes across four target families, including 18 with literature-verified affinities. Raw ProteinMPNN NLL is not a valid affinity ranker: its pooled Spearman correlation with affinity is 0.19, and correlations reverse between MDM2/CHIP (+0.62) and gp41 (-0.70). We therefore evaluate Boltz-2 mirror-space cofolding confidence. For the complete viral-entry family (7 structures representing 3 peptides), interface predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) achieves structure-level leave-one-out Spearman rho = 0.90 (p = 0.006) and correctly orders all three peptides by affinity, whereas NLL fails (structure-level rho = 0.18). Because only three independent chemotypes are represented, this result indicates directional consistency rather than a statistically validated predictor. Cross-family calibration does not transfer at current sample sizes, supporting family-matched calibration as the practical deployment mode. We also specify a prospective design protocol for the antimicrobial-resistance targets LasR and LecB from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, including mirrored structures, ligand-derived hotspot maps, diffusion-model-ready inputs, and Mirror-Score ranking. Code, benchmark data, structures, and analysis scripts are openly available at https://github.com/Jiadalee/Mirror-Score.

AI.tldr: Mirror-Score introduces a calibrated, inference-only scoring framework for heterochiral D-peptide/L-protein complexes, plus a public benchmark of 31 crystal complexes. Raw ProteinMPNN NLL is shown to be an invalid affinity ranker, while Boltz-2 mirror-space cofolding confidence (interface pLDDT) achieves structure-level Spearman rho = 0.90 for the viral-entry family, though cross-family calibration does not transfer.
AI.motivation: D-peptides offer protease resistance and high target specificity, but computational design of D-peptide binders remains immature. The prior Mirror-Peptidizer pipeline relied on raw ProteinMPNN NLL ranking that was never validated against measured affinities, and only 4 of 9 tested MDM2 designs bound detectably, highlighting the need for a validated scoring approach.
AI.method: The authors build Mirror-Score, a calibrated inference-only scoring framework for heterochiral D-peptide/L-protein complexes, together with a public benchmark of 31 crystal complexes spanning four target families (18 with literature-verified affinities). They assess raw ProteinMPNN NLL as an affinity ranker and evaluate Boltz-2 mirror-space cofolding confidence, specifically interface pLDDT, using structure-level leave-one-out Spearman correlation. They also specify a prospective design protocol for LasR and LecB.
AI.result: Raw ProteinMPNN NLL proved an invalid affinity ranker: pooled Spearman correlation 0.19, with reversed correlations between MDM2/CHIP (+0.62) and gp41 (-0.70). For the viral-entry family (7 structures, 3 peptides), interface pLDDT achieved structure-level leave-one-out Spearman rho = 0.90 (p = 0.006) and correctly ordered all three peptides, whereas NLL failed (rho = 0.18). Cross-family calibration did not transfer at current sample sizes.
AI.conclusion: Boltz-2 mirror-space interface pLDDT shows directional consistency as an affinity indicator for the viral-entry family, but with only three independent chemotypes it is not yet a statistically validated predictor. Family-matched calibration is recommended as the practical deployment mode, and a prospective protocol for LasR and LecB is provided; all code, data, structures, and scripts are openly available.

title: Closed-Form Cartesian Forward Kinetostatics for Spatial Multi-Segment Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots
summary: Forward kinetostatics of spatial tendon-driven continuum robots typically requires a nonlinear equilibrium solve for each actuation input. This paper develops a force-to-Cartesian-configuration model with a closed-form solution in quadratures for spatial multi-segment robots under tendon actuation. The Cartesian backbone centerline and accumulated material twist serve as generalized coordinates, from which the strain measures and tendon geometry are derived. Variational equilibrium yields explicit axial and bending relations and establishes zero equilibrium material twist within the proposed model for admissible longitudinal non-helical routing. The solution is propagated segment by segment without an iterative equilibrium solve, while retaining axial deformation, spatially varying axial and bending stiffnesses and tendon-routing diameter, and segment-dependent tendon participation. Numerical comparisons with a full-strain geometric variable-strain model (GVS) yield maximum length-normalized tip-position discrepancies of 8.91 x 10^-6 and 1.01 x 10^-5 for the single- and three-segment robots, respectively. Mean evaluation times of 1.52 μs and 2.94 μs, with corresponding speedups of approximately 1864x and 3348x over the baseline, demonstrate the computational advantage of the explicit force-to-configuration mapping in the reported benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a closed-form, non-iterative force-to-Cartesian-configuration model for spatial multi-segment tendon-driven continuum robots, achieving microsecond-level evaluation with near-negligible error versus a full-strain baseline.
AI.motivation: Forward kinetostatics of spatial tendon-driven continuum robots conventionally requires a nonlinear equilibrium solve for each actuation input, which is computationally expensive and unsuitable for fast, repeated force-to-configuration evaluation.
AI.method: The Cartesian backbone centerline and accumulated material twist are used as generalized coordinates, from which strain measures and tendon geometry are derived. Variational equilibrium yields explicit axial and bending relations and proves zero equilibrium material twist for admissible longitudinal non-helical routing. The solution is propagated segment by segment without an iterative equilibrium solve, retaining axial deformation, spatially varying axial and bending stiffnesses and tendon-routing diameter, and segment-dependent tendon participation.
AI.result: Compared with a full-strain geometric variable-strain (GVS) model, maximum length-normalized tip-position discrepancies are 8.91 x 10^-6 and 1.01 x 10^-5 for single- and three-segment robots. Mean evaluation times are 1.52 μs and 2.94 μs, corresponding to speedups of approximately 1864x and 3348x over the baseline.
AI.conclusion: The explicit force-to-configuration mapping provides a closed-form quadrature solution that eliminates the iterative equilibrium solve, demonstrating a substantial computational advantage while maintaining accuracy relative to the baseline model.

title: SMat-Attention: Structured Long-Context Sequence Modeling
summary: Long-context sequence models face a fundamental tradeoff: softmax attention uses flexible token-level interactions at quadratic cost, whereas linear attention obtains linear-time training and constant-time decoding by compressing history into a fixed-size state. In this work, we ask whether we can connect these regimes through a tunable notion of structure. To this end, we introduce Structured Matrix Attention (SMat-Attention) via a family of causal masks with structured long-range routing whose row supports have VC-dimension $d$. In our construction, $d=1$ recovers the standard causal mask, and increasing $d$ permits richer subset-routing patterns. We give chunkwise forward and backward algorithms to enable hardware-efficiency. For sequences of length $T$, the hard-routing construction takes $O(T^{2-3/d}+T)$ work, despite the mask being dense, for our prescribed family. In fixed-horizon streaming, decoding after the distant prefix takes constant time per token using $O(T^{1-1/d})$ cached states. SMat-Attention therefore makes VC-dimension an explicit knob governing access-pattern complexity, prefill cost, and decoding memory. Empirically, subset-routing and rule-assisted multi-key retrieval experiments illustrate the masks' routing expressiveness. Extensions to Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet using learned routing with top-$k$ query reads retain subquadratic prefill, improve recall accuracy over the backbones in several settings, and achieve comparable small-scale language-modeling performance.

AI.tldr: SMat-Attention introduces structured causal masks with VC-dimension $d$ to interpolate between softmax attention ($d=1$, quadratic) and linear attention, achieving subquadratic prefill and constant-time decoding.
AI.motivation: Softmax attention offers flexible token-level interactions but at quadratic cost, while linear attention trains in linear time and decodes in constant time by compressing history into a fixed-size state. The paper seeks a principled way to connect these regimes through a tunable notion of structure.
AI.method: The authors propose Structured Matrix Attention (SMat-Attention), built on a family of causal masks with structured long-range routing whose row supports have VC-dimension $d$. Setting $d=1$ recovers the standard causal mask; larger $d$ enables richer subset-routing. They design chunkwise forward and backward algorithms for hardware efficiency, and extend the approach to Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet via learned routing with top-$k$ query reads.
AI.result: For length-$T$ sequences, the hard-routing construction requires $O(T^{2-3/d}+T)$ work despite a dense mask. In fixed-horizon streaming, decoding after the distant prefix costs constant time per token with $O(T^{1-1/d})$ cached states. Subset-routing and rule-assisted multi-key retrieval experiments show routing expressiveness; extensions retain subquadratic prefill, improve recall accuracy over backbones in several settings, and match small-scale language-modeling performance.
AI.conclusion: VC-dimension serves as an explicit knob governing access-pattern complexity, prefill cost, and decoding memory, offering a tunable continuum between softmax and linear attention.

title: LIBERO-MAX: Do Robot Policies Adapt When the World Changes?
summary: Robots must often continue a task after a target moves, the viewpoint shifts, or an obstacle appears, even though their earlier observations and committed actions reflect the previous scene. Many simulation robustness benchmarks fix external conditions at reset, leaving this temporal challenge underexamined. We introduce LIBERO-MAX, a benchmark of 8,000 paired cases spanning eight types of changes to geometry, observations, appearance, clutter, and paths. Each pair compares task execution with and without a mid-task event, holding the task, initial state, policy seed, and pre-event action sequence fixed. This controlled comparison distinguishes event-associated regressions from failures already present without the change. Across fourteen current VLA, hybrid, and world-action policies, events reduce success by 11.0-25.7 percentage points. Event profiles reveal shared vulnerabilities to geometry and observation changes, while policy-family rankings interleave. Camera controls show that robustness reflects both competence under the changed conditions and the trajectory from which they are encountered; varying query cadence does not eliminate the gap. Together, the paired protocol and temporal diagnostics establish LIBERO-MAX as a reproducible testbed for diagnosing failures under mid-execution changes and measuring progress toward robot policies that remain effective as the world changes.

AI.tldr: LIBERO-MAX is a new benchmark of 8,000 paired cases that diagnoses how robot manipulation policies fail when events change the scene mid-execution, revealing 11.0-25.7 pp success drops across fourteen policies.
AI.motivation: Robots must continue tasks after a target moves, the viewpoint shifts, or an obstacle appears, even though prior observations and committed actions reflect the old scene. Existing simulation robustness benchmarks typically fix external conditions at reset, leaving this temporal, mid-execution challenge underexamined.
AI.method: The authors build LIBERO-MAX: 8,000 paired cases spanning eight change types across geometry, observations, appearance, clutter, and paths. Each pair compares execution with and without a mid-task event while holding task, initial state, policy seed, and pre-event action sequence fixed. This controlled pairing separates event-associated regressions from pre-existing failures. They evaluate fourteen current VLA, hybrid, and world-action policies, and run camera-control and query-cadence analyses.
AI.result: Mid-task events reduce success by 11.0-25.7 percentage points across all fourteen policies. Event profiles show shared vulnerabilities to geometry and observation changes, while policy-family rankings interleave. Camera controls indicate robustness depends both on competence under changed conditions and on the trajectory from which they are encountered; varying query cadence does not close the gap.
AI.conclusion: The paired protocol and temporal diagnostics make LIBERO-MAX a reproducible testbed for diagnosing failures under mid-execution changes and for measuring progress toward robot policies that remain effective as the world changes.

title: LongCat-DeepResearch Technical Report
summary: We present LongCat-DeepResearch, a deep research system that combines an enhanced LongCat model with a multi-agent workflow for producing comprehensive, evidence-grounded reports. The workflow separates global planning from detailed investigation and coordinates revision at the section level. Multiple planning agents first explore external sources and refine an actionable research plan, termed ResearchSpec. Research agents then investigate and draft their assigned sections in parallel, gathering additional evidence in separate contexts as their analyses develop. Once the sections are assembled, global review guides targeted local revisions, reducing reliance on repeated full-report rewriting. This workflow also supports the construction of research tasks and trajectories for the mid-training and post-training of LongCat's general-purpose models. LongCat-DeepResearch achieves 55.25 on DeepResearchBench, 51.35 on DeepResearchBench II, and 79.83 on ResearchRubrics. On an in-house benchmark, it scores 76.04, ranking second among four compared systems. Development-set analyses show benefits from combining planning perspectives, while further planning refinement has mixed effects. Additional editing improves average automatic readability preference across two benchmarks, with different trends on each.

AI.tldr: LongCat-DeepResearch is a deep research system coupling an enhanced LongCat model with a multi-agent workflow (global planning, parallel section investigation, section-level revision) that produces evidence-grounded reports and doubles as a data engine for model training, scoring 55.25/51.35/79.83 on DeepResearchBench, DeepResearchBench II, and ResearchRubrics.
AI.motivation: Comprehensive report generation requires both broad global planning and deep local investigation; monolithic single-pass generation struggles with evidence grounding and forces costly repeated full-report rewriting.
AI.method: A multi-agent workflow: planning agents explore external sources and produce an actionable ResearchSpec; research agents then investigate and draft assigned sections in parallel, gathering evidence in separate contexts; assembled sections undergo global review that guides targeted local/section-level revisions. The same workflow generates research tasks and trajectories for mid-training and post-training of LongCat models.
AI.result: 55.25 on DeepResearchBench, 51.35 on DeepResearchBench II, 79.83 on ResearchRubrics; 76.04 on an in-house benchmark (2nd of 4 systems). Development-set analyses: combining planning perspectives helps; further planning refinement has mixed effects; additional editing raises average automatic readability preference across two benchmarks with differing per-benchmark trends.
AI.conclusion: Separating global planning from parallel, context-isolated section investigation with section-level revision yields strong, evidence-grounded report generation and serves as an effective trajectory source for training LongCat's general-purpose models, though planning refinement and editing gains are task-dependent.

title: Distilling Privileged Control Barrier Functions into RGB-Only Safety Filters for Dynamic Visual Navigation
summary: RGB-only end-to-end visual navigation policies remain vulnerable to collisions in real-world dynamic environments, motivating a dedicated safety layer. Existing visual Control Barrier Function (CBF) approaches seek to provide safety from RGB observations, but often rely on real-time rendering or explicit scene reconstruction and are primarily designed for static scenes, limiting their practicality for onboard deployment. We propose a teacher-student visual distillation framework that transfers the safety behavior of a privileged CBF teacher to an RGB-only student filter for dynamic environments. The student maps a short RGB history, robot velocity, and a nominal control action directly to a safe action, while the teacher uses ground-truth robot and obstacle states in a real-to-sim dynamic Gaussian Splatting environment. To reduce the teacher-student information gap, the teacher constructs safety constraints only from obstacles observable within the student's RGB history. It also accounts for obstacle-velocity uncertainty to improve robustness to motion variations, while action augmentation exposes the student to diverse safe and unsafe nominal actions to better capture the safety boundary. At deployment, the student requires only RGB observations and robot velocity, without explicit 3D reconstruction or online rendering. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms visual CBF baselines and improves the safety of RGB-based navigation policies under dynamic obstacle motion. Project page: https://syeon-yoo.github.io/distill-cbf-site/.

AI.tldr: A teacher-student visual distillation framework transfers a privileged CBF teacher's safety behavior to an RGB-only student filter for dynamic environments, avoiding 3D reconstruction or online rendering at deployment.
AI.motivation: RGB-only end-to-end visual navigation policies remain vulnerable to collisions in real-world dynamic environments, motivating a dedicated safety layer. Existing visual Control Barrier Function (CBF) approaches often rely on real-time rendering or explicit scene reconstruction and are primarily designed for static scenes, limiting onboard practicality.
AI.method: A teacher-student visual distillation framework transfers the safety behavior of a privileged CBF teacher to an RGB-only student filter. The teacher uses ground-truth robot and obstacle states in a real-to-sim dynamic Gaussian Splatting environment, and constructs safety constraints only from obstacles observable within the student's RGB history to reduce the teacher-student information gap. It also accounts for obstacle-velocity uncertainty for robustness to motion variations. The student maps a short RGB history, robot velocity, and a nominal control action directly to a safe action. Action augmentation exposes the student to diverse safe and unsafe nominal actions to better capture the safety boundary.
AI.result: Experiments show the proposed method outperforms visual CBF baselines and improves the safety of RGB-based navigation policies under dynamic obstacle motion. At deployment, the student requires only RGB observations and robot velocity, without explicit 3D reconstruction or online rendering.
AI.conclusion: The proposed teacher-student visual distillation framework provides a practical onboard safety layer for RGB-based navigation in dynamic environments, achieving improved safety over visual CBF baselines while removing the need for 3D reconstruction or online rendering.

title: A Polyphonic Conception of AI Understanding
summary: When a doctor, a judge, or an engineer must decide whether to trust an AI model's output, they cannot avoid asking what the model understands. Purely mathematical or statistical descriptions struggle to distinguish trustworthy from untrustworthy outputs without reintroducing the question of AI understanding in all but name. Yet the question is ill-framed as it stands, because the inherited concept operates within a monophonic paradigm: the idea that a cognitive system's understanding of something must be localised to a single mechanism underpinning all the capacities conferred by such understanding. Drawing on a wide range of mechanistic evidence, we show that LLMs are pervasively polyphonic: outputs emerge from coalitions of parallel mechanisms of uneven reliability, which variously complement, duplicate, or drown out one another, with several coalitions sufficing for a task without any one being indispensable. Polyphony not only complicates attributions of understanding, but renders monophonic inference patterns hazardous. In response, we develop a conception of understanding fit for polyphonic AI. It centres on sound circuitry that is reliably and correctly recruited and in control of outputs. Attributions of understanding thereby become tractable claims about internal organisation, and can do the work of guiding trust in AI.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that LLMs are "polyphonic": their outputs arise from coalitions of parallel, unevenly reliable mechanisms rather than a single locus of understanding. This makes monophonic attributions of understanding hazardous, so the authors propose a reconceived, polyphonic notion of understanding centered on sound, reliably recruited, output-controlling circuitry to guide trust in AI.
AI.motivation: Practitioners such as doctors, judges, and engineers need to judge whether to trust AI outputs, which implicitly requires assessing what the model understands. Purely mathematical or statistical accounts cannot distinguish trustworthy from untrustworthy outputs without covertly reintroducing the notion of understanding. However, the inherited concept of understanding is ill-framed because it assumes a monophonic paradigm: that understanding must be localized to a single mechanism underpinning all conferred capacities.
AI.method: Drawing on a wide range of mechanistic evidence, the authors argue that LLMs are pervasively polyphonic—outputs emerge from coalitions of parallel mechanisms of uneven reliability that complement, duplicate, or drown out one another, with multiple coalitions sufficing for a task and none indispensable. Building on this, they develop a reconceived conception of understanding suited to polyphonic AI.
AI.result: The analysis shows that polyphony complicates attributions of understanding and renders monophonic inference patterns hazardous. The proposed alternative conception centers on sound circuitry that is reliably and correctly recruited and in control of outputs.
AI.conclusion: Under the polyphonic conception, attributions of understanding become tractable claims about internal organization rather than murky holistic judgments, enabling them to do real work in guiding warranted trust in AI systems.

title: Trajectory-Level Mode Guidance for Controllable Diffusion-Based Multi-Robot Motion Planning
summary: Motion planning often admits multiple feasible solutions, making multimodal generation valuable, particularly for flexible multi-robot coordination. Diffusion models naturally learn such trajectory distributions, yet incorporating coarse and partial trajectory priors without restricting generation remains challenging. Such priors indicate a desirable region of the solution space rather than a single solution, motivating conditioned generation that preserves multimodality. In this paper, we guide trajectory generation in the clean trajectory space and progressively incorporate trajectory priors with a timestep-dependent guidance strength. At each reverse diffusion step, the reconstructed clean trajectory provides a unified space for integrating planning costs and partial trajectory priors. Planning costs are incorporated through gradient-based refinement, while the partial prior is progressively injected at the corresponding noise levels with decreasing guidance strength. This guides generation toward the prior in early stages while gradually releasing the constraint to preserve the inherent multimodality of the diffusion model. The framework naturally extends to multi-robot planning by incorporating inter-robot collision costs. Experiments on single- and multi-robot planning tasks demonstrate controllable trajectory synthesis, diverse feasible solutions, and safe multi-agent coordination.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a diffusion-based motion planning framework that guides trajectory generation in the clean trajectory space, progressively injecting partial trajectory priors with decreasing, timestep-dependent strength to preserve multimodality while satisfying planning costs, and extends to multi-robot coordination via inter-robot collision costs.
AI.motivation: Motion planning typically admits multiple feasible solutions, so multimodal generation is valuable, especially for flexible multi-robot coordination. Diffusion models naturally capture such trajectory distributions, but incorporating coarse and partial trajectory priors without collapsing generation to a single mode is challenging. Such priors specify a desirable region of the solution space rather than one solution, motivating conditioned generation that retains multimodality.
AI.method: Guidance is performed in the clean trajectory space, where the reconstructed clean trajectory at each reverse diffusion step serves as a unified space for integrating planning costs and partial priors. Planning costs enter via gradient-based refinement, while the partial prior is progressively injected at corresponding noise levels with decreasing guidance strength. This steers generation toward the prior in early stages and gradually relaxes the constraint later to preserve the diffusion model's inherent multimodality. The framework extends to multi-robot planning by adding inter-robot collision costs.
AI.result: Experiments on single- and multi-robot planning tasks show controllable trajectory synthesis, diverse feasible solutions, and safe multi-agent coordination.
AI.conclusion: Guiding generation in clean trajectory space with progressively decreasing prior strength enables controllable, multimodal, and prior-informed trajectory synthesis, and the same formulation scales naturally to safe multi-robot coordination through collision costs.

title: GeoOutageBench: Benchmarking Ambiguity-aware, Ontology-grounded Geospatiotemporal KGQA for Multimodal Power Outage and Resilience Analysis
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Advances in Geographic Information Systems (SIGSPATIAL '26), November 3-6, 2026, Riverside, CA, USA
summary: We introduce GeoOutageBench, a benchmark for assessing LLM-based geospatiotemporal KGQA for multimodal outage and resilience analysis. Unlike existing KGQA benchmarks for Web knowledge, GeoOutageBench considers a spatiotemporal KG that integrates visual, textual, and structured data from outage records, remote sensing, weather observations, storm and power events, geographic entities, and domain ontologies. It provides a competency query taxonomy at different difficulty levels from spatiotemporal containment and proximity, spatiotemporal co-occurrence analysis, multimodal evidence, to hypothetical evaluation. Over multimodal KG and query classes, GeoOutageBench provides user-configurable evaluation of three important, highly coherent yet less studied tasks: (1) LLMs' understanding for ambiguous geospatiotemporal questions in terms of NL to SPARQL interpretation, (2) query-driven assessment of ontology utility, and (3) answer accuracy of multimodal KGQA retrieval. GeoOutageBench provides a design principle and foundation for assessing LLM-KG systems that support real-world infrastructure resilience analysis. Our benchmark, source code, data, results, and other documentation are available at https://github.com/UCF-SAGE/GeoOutageBench.

AI.tldr: GeoOutageBench is a new benchmark for evaluating LLM-based geospatiotemporal knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in multimodal outage and resilience analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing KGQA benchmarks focus on Web knowledge and lack support for multimodal, spatiotemporal, real-world infrastructure resilience analysis. There is a need for a benchmark that assesses LLM-KG systems on outage and resilience tasks integrating visual, textual, and structured data.
AI.method: The benchmark constructs a spatiotemporal KG integrating visual, textual, and structured data from outage records, remote sensing, weather observations, storm and power events, geographic entities, and domain ontologies. It provides a competency query taxonomy at multiple difficulty levels: spatiotemporal containment and proximity, spatiotemporal co-occurrence analysis, multimodal evidence, and hypothetical evaluation. It supports user-configurable evaluation of three tasks: NL-to-SPARQL interpretation for ambiguous geospatiotemporal questions, query-driven ontology utility assessment, and answer accuracy of multimodal KGQA retrieval.
AI.result: GeoOutageBench enables multimodal KG and query-class evaluation across three understudied, highly coherent tasks, offering configurable assessment of LLM performance on geospatiotemporal KGQA.
AI.conclusion: GeoOutageBench provides a design principle and foundation for assessing LLM-KG systems supporting real-world infrastructure resilience analysis. Benchmark, source code, data, results, and documentation are available at https://github.com/UCF-SAGE/GeoOutageBench.

title: Asymmetric Scout-Worker Reconnaissance for Route Validation in Unknown Environments
summary: This paper studies asymmetric scout-worker reconnaissance in unknown environments, where a small, agile autonomous scout explores routes for a larger worker robot that must visit an ordered sequence of goal locations. Because the scout has a smaller footprint and greater mobility, a scout-traversable route may be infeasible for the worker; worker feasibility must therefore be inferred from scout observations. This setting is not explicitly addressed by existing exploration and replanning methods, which typically assume a single traversability model and seek optimal paths for the same robot performing the exploration. We introduce a symbiotic scout-based framework that exploits the scout's superior mobility to explore only the portions of the unknown environment needed to identify worker-feasible path segments connecting the ordered goals. Evaluations in simulated and real-world settings demonstrate that the proposed approach validates feasible routes, repairs blocked segments with validated worker-feasible detours, and substantially reduces scout travel compared to baseline exploration and planning methods. A real-world indoor deployment further demonstrates the scout navigating narrow corridors to identify a worker-feasible route.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a symbiotic scout-based framework for asymmetric scout-worker reconnaissance, where a small agile scout explores unknown environments to infer worker-feasible routes connecting an ordered sequence of goals, exploiting the scout's superior mobility while minimizing scout travel.
AI.motivation: Existing exploration and replanning methods assume a single traversability model and seek optimal paths for the same robot performing exploration. They do not address settings where a scout with a smaller footprint and greater mobility must infer feasibility for a larger, less mobile worker robot along an ordered goal sequence.
AI.method: A symbiotic scout-based framework is introduced that leverages the scout's superior mobility to explore only the portions of the unknown environment necessary to identify worker-feasible path segments connecting the ordered goals. Worker feasibility is inferred from scout observations, accounting for the fact that scout-traversable routes may be infeasible for the worker. The framework validates feasible routes and repairs blocked segments with validated worker-feasible detours.
AI.result: Evaluations in simulated and real-world settings show the approach validates feasible routes, repairs blocked segments with validated worker-feasible detours, and substantially reduces scout travel compared to baseline exploration and planning methods. A real-world indoor deployment demonstrates the scout navigating narrow corridors to identify a worker-feasible route.
AI.conclusion: The symbiotic scout-based framework effectively addresses asymmetric scout-worker reconnaissance by exploiting differential mobility, enabling efficient identification of worker-feasible routes for an ordered goal sequence while reducing exploration cost relative to baseline methods.

title: An Exact Generate - Transform Decomposition of Small-LLM Team Scaling Across Orchestration Architectures
summary:
Replacing one LLM agent with a collaborating team can raise accuracy, but whether scaling the team helps, and which architecture to scale, is unclear. Sweeping eight agent orchestration architectures across five instruction-tuned 7-9B models, five short-answer benchmarks, and an executable-code benchmark up to 30 calls, we find that the returns to team scaling are sharply task-dependent: from three to thirty calls accuracy rises by up to 17 points on the two arithmetic word-problem benchmarks (GSM8K, GSMHard) but by at most four on ARC, GPQA, and MMLU, for every architecture, a split the usual task-averaged number conceals. Proposer-Critic captures the arithmetic gains, scaling steepest and, in aggregate, surpassing every other architecture at the largest budget (item-clustered intervals exclude zero), though it ranks among the weakest elsewhere, and no architecture wins across tasks.
  We explain these trajectories with an exact generate-transform decomposition. Partitioning any workflow into proposal coverage and a downstream transform, any accuracy change splits exactly into an extensive coverage dividend and an intensive transformation change. The decomposition diagnoses each task: arithmetic offers coverage headroom that a critic-guided transform converts, whereas the multiple-choice benchmarks either saturate in coverage or fail to convert it, and on open-ended code generative recovery nearly vanishes so accuracy tracks coverage. At equal call budgets token cost still varies 2.1x. Extra calls therefore create candidate opportunity that only some architectures, on some tasks, convert. Team scaling is a task- and architecture-specific bet, not a uniform lever.

AI.tldr: Scaling LLM agent teams yields sharply task-dependent returns: accuracy gains from 3 to 30 calls reach 17 points on arithmetic word problems but ≤4 points on ARC, GPQA, and MMLU, across all eight orchestration architectures. The authors introduce an exact generate-transform decomposition separating an extensive coverage dividend from an intensive transformation change, showing the difference lies in whether tasks offer convertible coverage headroom rather than in architecture alone, while token cost at equal call budgets varies 2.1x.
AI.motivation: Collaborating LLM agent teams can improve accuracy over a single agent, but it is unclear whether adding more agents/calls helps, which orchestration architecture should be scaled, and on which tasks. Task-averaged accuracy hides this heterogeneity, so a principled account of when and why team scaling pays off is needed before treating it as a general-purpose lever.
AI.method: The authors sweep eight agent orchestration architectures across five instruction-tuned 7–9B models, five short-answer benchmarks, and an executable-code benchmark, with budgets up to 30 calls, and compare accuracy trajectories. They then derive an exact generate-transform decomposition: any workflow is partitioned into proposal coverage and a downstream transform, so any accuracy change splits exactly into an extensive coverage dividend and an intensive transformation change.
AI.result: Returns to team scaling are sharply task-dependent. From 3 to 30 calls, accuracy rises by up to 17 points on GSM8K and GSMHard but by at most four points on ARC, GPQA, and MMLU, for every architecture. Proposer-Critic captures the arithmetic gains, scales steepest, and in aggregate surpasses every other architecture at the largest budget (item-clustered intervals exclude zero), yet ranks among the weakest elsewhere, and no architecture wins across tasks. The decomposition diagnoses each task: arithmetic offers coverage headroom a critic-guided transform converts, whereas multiple-choice benchmarks either saturate in coverage or fail to convert it, and on open-ended code generative recovery nearly vanishes so accuracy tracks coverage. At equal call budgets token cost still varies 2.1x.
AI.conclusion: Extra calls create candidate opportunity that only some architectures, on some tasks, can convert into accuracy. Team scaling is a task- and architecture-specific bet rather than a uniform lever; practitioners should match architecture and budget to the coverage headroom and transform convertibility of the target task, and account for token cost differences at equal call budgets.

title: Reactive Real-Time Flow Policies via Asynchronous Distribution Alignment
summary: Generalist robot policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) have achieved remarkable generalization, but their inference delays can conflict with the demands of real-time control. Asynchronous execution avoids pauses between action chunks by predicting the next sequence of actions while the robot carries out the previous one. In this paper, we study whether asynchronous execution produces the same action distribution as the original VLA. We find that, for non-Markovian demonstrations, asynchronous execution can produce a fundamentally different action distribution, which can limit the policy's reactivity. In our method, we seek to restore this reactivity by aligning the asynchronously produced action distribution with that of the original VLA through two complementary mechanisms. First, Recursive Flow-Field Distillation trains the asynchronous policy using the VLA's action-generation flow. We characterize the learned distribution theoretically and show experimentally that our asynchronous policy can generate nearly the full range of actions the original VLA would produce, while existing asynchronous methods recover only a fraction of that range. Second, Propose-Resolve prepares multiple action sequences asynchronously and uses the latest observation to select among them based on a lightweight approximation of their likelihood under the VLA's action distribution. Our resulting method matches the original VLA's success on LIBERO and retains about 80% of its success on RoboMimic, about 30 percentage points more than existing asynchronous methods.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how asynchronous execution changes the action distribution of VLAs and proposes Recursive Flow-Field Distillation plus Propose-Resolve to restore reactivity, matching VLA success on LIBERO and retaining ~80% on RoboMimic.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action models generalize well but their inference delays conflict with real-time robot control. Asynchronous execution removes pauses between action chunks, yet prior work had not examined whether it preserves the original VLA's action distribution. The authors find that for non-Markovian demonstrations asynchronous execution shifts the action distribution, reducing policy reactivity.
AI.method: Two complementary mechanisms: (1) Recursive Flow-Field Distillation, which trains the asynchronous policy using the VLA's action-generation flow, with a theoretical characterization of the learned distribution; (2) Propose-Resolve, which asynchronously prepares multiple action sequences and selects among them using the latest observation via a lightweight approximation of their likelihood under the VLA's action distribution.
AI.result: The asynchronous policy can generate nearly the full range of actions the original VLA would produce, whereas existing asynchronous methods recover only a fraction. The method matches the original VLA's success on LIBERO and retains about 80% of its success on RoboMimic, roughly 30 percentage points above existing asynchronous methods.
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous execution can fundamentally alter VLA action distributions for non-Markovian demonstrations, but aligning the asynchronous distribution with the original VLA via flow-field distillation and likelihood-based selection restores reactivity and substantially closes the success gap.

title: The Layer Mystery of VLA: An Information-Theoretical Analysis of VLA Latent Interface
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies connect a pretrained vision-language backbone to an action head through a latent interface, but which backbone layers this interface should expose remains unclear. We study single-layer selection and multi-layer fusion for frozen backbones across three pretrained models and two manipulation benchmarks, LIBERO and CALVIN, with three policy-training seeds per configuration. Across three fusion mechanisms and three layer-subset strategies, 47 of 54 configurations underperform the best observed single-layer policy. Our stastical analysis further confirms that fusion's advantage is very limited. However, the best layer varies substantially across backbones and benchmarks, making layer selection consequential and exhaustive policy sweeps expensive. We further derive a reweighting equivalence between the proposed information-bottleneck objectives for action-conditioned InfoNCE and action prediction, motivating InfoNCE as a proxy for layer quality. Empirically, InfoNCE provides the most consistent positive association with policy success among four evaluated proxies. Selecting the layer with the highest InfoNCE score requires 9-33 times less GPU compute than exhaustive policy sweeps and reduces mean selection regret from 17.89 percentage points for deepest-layer selection to 3.71 points across six settings. Its mean regret is close to the 3.28-3.50 points achieved by fixed-layer heuristics optimized retrospectively using all six oracle sweeps, without requiring closed-loop evaluations during selection.

AI.tldr: This paper studies which vision-language backbone layers a VLA policy's latent interface should expose, finds multi-layer fusion rarely beats the best single layer, and shows that selecting the highest-InfoNCE layer is a cheap, near-oracle proxy for layer quality.
AI.motivation: The latent interface in vision-language-action (VLA) policies determines which backbone layers feed the action head, but it is unclear whether to expose one layer or fuse several. Layer choice is consequential, yet exhaustive policy sweeps are computationally expensive, so a cheap and reliable selection criterion is needed.
AI.method: The authors benchmark single-layer selection versus multi-layer fusion over frozen backbones using three pretrained models, two manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO and CALVIN), and three policy-training seeds per configuration, spanning three fusion mechanisms and three layer-subset strategies. They also derive a reweighting equivalence between information-bottleneck objectives for action-conditioned InfoNCE and action prediction, motivating InfoNCE as a proxy for layer quality, and compare it against four evaluated proxies.
AI.result: 47 of 54 fusion configurations underperform the best observed single-layer policy, and statistical analysis confirms fusion's advantage is very limited. The best layer varies substantially across backbones and benchmarks. Among four proxies, InfoNCE shows the most consistent positive association with policy success; selecting the highest-InfoNCE layer needs 9-33x less GPU compute than exhaustive sweeps and cuts mean selection regret from 17.89 percentage points (deepest-layer selection) to 3.71 points across six settings, close to the 3.28-3.50 points of retrospectively optimized fixed-layer heuristics.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer fusion offers little benefit over selecting the single best backbone layer, and the optimal layer is highly backbone- and benchmark-dependent. InfoNCE is a cheap, effective proxy for layer quality, achieving near-oracle layer selection without closed-loop evaluations.

title: Planning Oriented 3D Scene Completion via Coupled TUDF Occupancy Representation Learning from Partial Observations
summary: Partial observability remains a fundamental challenge in robotic navigation, where limited sensor coverage and occlusions leave large portions of the environment unobserved. Existing scene completion methods primarily focus on improving incomplete mapping or reconstructing partially observed 3D structures, but rarely investigate how scene completion can be designed to benefit downstream tasks such as path planning. In this work, we propose a path-planning-oriented 3D scene completion framework that moves beyond pure occupancy modeling toward a coupled geometric formulation. Specifically, given partial LiDAR observations as input, the proposed framework jointly predicts completed Truncated Unsigned Distance Field (TUDF)-based continuous geometric representations and voxel-wise occupancy maps. This coupled representation allows the network to better reason about obstacle boundaries and free-space geometry. To fully exploit the synergy between the two representations, we introduce a bidirectionally coupled learning scheme, where TUDF features provide dense geometric guidance to improve occupancy reconstruction, while occupancy features in turn offer complementary structural constraints that refine distance-field estimation. Consequently, the proposed network directly predicts complete occupancy and TUDF representations, allowing seamless integration of TUDF into trajectory planning without post-processing. Extensive experiments on unseen environments demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves both geometric reconstruction quality and downstream planning performance.

AI.tldr: A path-planning-oriented 3D scene completion framework jointly predicts continuous TUDF geometry and voxel occupancy from partial LiDAR, coupled via a bidirectionally coupled learning scheme that improves both reconstruction and downstream planning.
AI.motivation: Partial observability is a fundamental challenge in robotic navigation, as limited sensor coverage and occlusions leave much of the environment unobserved. Existing scene completion methods mainly target better incomplete mapping or partial 3D reconstruction, and rarely examine how scene completion can be designed to benefit downstream tasks like path planning.
AI.method: The framework takes partial LiDAR observations as input and jointly predicts completed TUDF-based continuous geometric representations and voxel-wise occupancy maps, moving beyond pure occupancy modeling to a coupled geometric formulation. A bidirectionally coupled learning scheme is introduced: TUDF features provide dense geometric guidance to improve occupancy reconstruction, while occupancy features supply complementary structural constraints that refine distance-field estimation. The network directly predicts complete occupancy and TUDF representations, enabling seamless TUDF integration into trajectory planning without post-processing.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on unseen environments show that the proposed method consistently improves both geometric reconstruction quality and downstream planning performance.
AI.conclusion: Coupling continuous TUDF geometry with voxel occupancy through bidirectional learning yields a scene completion representation tailored for path planning, outperforming prior approaches on both reconstruction and planning under partial observability.

title: AdaST: Adaptive Coupling for Spatial-Temporal Forecasting
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (main conference). Code: https://github.com/LzyFischer/AdaST
summary: Spatial-temporal (ST) forecasting underpins many real-world systems such as traffic, climate, and energy networks. While existing methods implicitly assume strong spatiotemporal coupling, we observe that real-world ST data exhibits distinct coupling regimes, ranging from temporal-dominated and spatial-dominated to strongly coupled patterns. This mismatch causes current models to suffer from spurious dependencies and degraded performance when one correlation dominates. To overcome this limitation, we aim to dynamically modulate spatial and temporal modeling based on the data's inherent coupling structure. However, three key challenges exist: unknown coupling structure, heterogeneous coupling dynamics, and suboptimal spatial modeling. We propose AdaST, an adaptive ST forecasting framework that tackles these challenges through a decompose-recompose paradigm. AdaST factorizes inputs into components capturing different coupling patterns using heterogeneity-aware experts. Each component is processed by role-aligned modules, and a correlation-informed adaptive recomposer integrates them for final prediction. Extensive experiments confirm that AdaST significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the necessity of an adaptive approach.

AI.tldr: AdaST is an adaptive spatial-temporal forecasting framework that dynamically modulates spatial and temporal modeling according to the data's inherent coupling regime, via a decompose-recompose paradigm, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing ST forecasting methods implicitly assume strong spatiotemporal coupling.
