However, real-world ST data exhibits distinct coupling regimes (temporal-dominated, spatial-dominated, strongly coupled). This mismatch causes current models to suffer from spurious dependencies and degraded performance when one correlation dominates, motivating the need to dynamically modulate spatial and temporal modeling based on the data's inherent coupling structure.
AI.method: AdaST employs a decompose-recompose paradigm. It factorizes inputs into components capturing different coupling patterns using heterogeneity-aware experts. Each component is processed by role-aligned modules, and a correlation-informed adaptive recomposer integrates them for final prediction. The design targets three challenges: unknown coupling structure, heterogeneous coupling dynamics, and suboptimal spatial modeling.
AI.result: Extensive experiments confirm that AdaST significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: The results validate the necessity of an adaptive approach to spatial-temporal forecasting, showing that dynamically aligning modeling with the inherent coupling structure yields superior performance.

title: Learning to Explore Hidden Kinematics for Articulated Object Manipulation
summary: The kinematics of an articulated object is often ambiguous from vision alone. Interaction resolves the ambiguity, and active perception methods exploit this by searching for the single action that most sharpens a belief over the kinematic parameters at each step. Such greedy search cannot be extended over a horizon without forward models of the contact and inertial dynamics, which are themselves unknown. We instead amortize action selection into training. We maintain a belief distribution over joint type and parameters, initialized from a generative prior and updated by Bayesian filtering on the observed part motion. To condition the policy on this belief, we render it as a per-point articulation flow field, the motion that the current posterior predicts for every point on the object. Carrying the inductive bias of articulated motion, this representation generalizes better than a latent encoding of the belief or flow tracked from observation. We train the policy with reinforcement learning, rewarding the entropy that each interaction removes from the posterior, so that informative exploration becomes learned behavior rather than a search at every step. Our method outperforms previous approaches across door and drawer manipulation on the PartManip benchmark, and reaches 61.7% success on ArticuRiddle, a new dataset of objects whose appearance implies the wrong articulation, against 44.4% for the best previous method. Project Website: https://hiddenkinematics.github.io/

AI.tldr: The paper amortizes active perception for articulated object manipulation by training an RL policy whose observation is a belief rendered as a per-point articulation flow field, rewarding entropy reduction, outperforming prior methods on PartManip and a new ArticuRiddle benchmark.
AI.motivation: Articulated object kinematics are ambiguous from vision alone; interaction disambiguates them. Greedy active perception that picks the single most informative action each step cannot be extended over a horizon because forward models of contact and inertial dynamics are unknown.
AI.method: Maintain a belief distribution over joint type and parameters, initialized from a generative prior and updated via Bayesian filtering on observed part motion. Condition the policy on this belief by rendering it as a per-point articulation flow field—the motion the posterior predicts for every point. Train the policy with reinforcement learning, rewarding the entropy each interaction removes from the posterior, so informative exploration is learned rather than searched.
AI.result: The flow-field belief representation, carrying the inductive bias of articulated motion, generalizes better than a latent encoding of the belief or flow tracked from observation. The method outperforms previous approaches on door and drawer manipulation on PartManip and reaches 61.7% success on ArticuRiddle (objects whose appearance implies the wrong articulation) versus 44.4% for the best prior method.
AI.conclusion: Amortizing action selection into training, with belief rendered as an articulation flow field and entropy-reduction rewards, yields an effective learned active perception policy for articulated object manipulation.

title: Memory Is a Derivation: The Distributed-Evidence Paradox in Long-Term Agents
summary: Long-running LLM agents compress past interactions into persistent memories that may be reused as premises for later tasks. This creates a distinct derivation problem: whether the memory actually follows from what the interaction history supports. Relevant evidence may be scattered across earlier interactions, while compression can introduce relations or event status that the history never established. A valid memory may therefore appear unsupported because its citations omit relevant evidence, while individually supported facts may be composed into a stronger statement the history never established. We characterize this problem through three coupled requirements: (1) Evidence scope; (2) Compositional validity; (3) Admission reliability. We therefore ask whether the interaction history available at write time supports what enters persistent memory. We introduce DerivAudit, a framework for auditing whether a memory is actually supported by the history available when it was written. The audit separates three questions: whether supporting evidence lies beyond writer-provided citations, whether the composed memory introduces unsupported meaning, and how write-time admission decisions affect later memory use. Across two natural memory corpora, audits using broader pre-write history recover support for nearly 60% of memories that appear unsupported from citations alone, while 17-21% remain unsupported after expansion. Yet broader evidence does not by itself make admission reliable: unsupported memories are still frequently admitted across verification models, and evidence expansion alone worsens it on two backbones.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and formalizes the "derivation problem" in long-running LLM agents: persistent memories may not actually follow from the interaction history that supports them, due to omitted evidence, unsupported composition, and unreliable admission. It introduces DerivAudit, a framework auditing memory validity via three requirements (Evidence scope, Compositional validity, Admission reliability), and finds that broader pre-write history recovers support for ~60% of seemingly unsupported memories, yet 17-21% remain unsupported, with admission still unreliable.
AI.motivation: Long-running LLM agents compress past interactions into persistent memories reused as premises for later tasks. This creates a derivation problem: memories may not follow from the supporting interaction history because relevant evidence is scattered and compression can introduce relations or event status never established. A valid memory may look unsupported when citations omit evidence, while individually supported facts can be composed into stronger statements the history never established.
AI.method: The authors characterize the problem through three coupled requirements—(1) Evidence scope, (2) Compositional validity, and (3) Admission reliability—and frame it as asking whether the interaction history available at write time supports what enters persistent memory. They introduce DerivAudit, a framework that audits whether a memory is supported by the write-time history, separating three questions: whether supporting evidence lies beyond writer-provided citations, whether the composed memory introduces unsupported meaning, and how write-time admission decisions affect later memory use.
AI.result: Across two natural memory corpora, audits using broader pre-write history recover support for nearly 60% of memories that appear unsupported from citations alone, while 17-21% remain unsupported after expansion. Broader evidence alone does not ensure reliable admission: unsupported memories are still frequently admitted across verification models, and evidence expansion alone worsens admission on two backbones.
AI.conclusion: Memory validity in long-running LLM agents depends on whether write-time history supports what is admitted into persistent memory, not merely on cited evidence. Wider pre-write history recovers much apparent unsupport but leaves a persistent unsupported fraction, and evidence expansion alone can degrade admission reliability—indicating that admission reliability must be addressed separately from evidence scope.

title: A robust single-sensing-element tactile sensor for concurrent pressure and tackiness detection with real-time signal decoupling capability
summary: Integrating tackiness sensation into the artificial skin of humanoid robots significantly enhances their cognitive and operational capabilities. However existing tactile sensors face challenges in decoupling of the multimodal signal and stability. Here we present a surface-soft tactile sensor that incorporates a Hall effect sensor and a soft magnetic composite within a robust elastic framework. The sensor surface indents under pressure and bulges prominently when retracted from sticky surfaces dynamically altering the Hall sensor-magnet distance. This generates whole-process-traceable and baseline-separated signals enabling real-time differentiation between pressure and pull-off force. This single-sensing-element design facilitates bimodal sensing at the same contact spot while eliminate stress cross-talk enhancing both accuracy and sensitivity. The fusion of a robust framework and magneto-mechanical sensing mechanism equips the sensor with exceptional reliability and excellent signal baseline stability. This tactile sensor holds substantial potential for advancing robotic capabilities in evaluating adhesive properties monitoring rubber aging precisely handling lightweight objects and cognizing natural objects surface characteristics.

AI.tldr: A surface-soft tactile sensor combining a Hall effect sensor with a soft magnetic composite in a robust elastic framework achieves real-time, cross-talk-free decoupling of pressure and pull-off (tackiness) forces in a single sensing element.
AI.motivation: Endowing humanoid robot artificial skin with tackiness sensation would greatly enhance cognitive and operational abilities, but existing tactile sensors struggle with decoupling multimodal signals and maintaining stability.
AI.method: The sensor embeds a Hall effect sensor and a soft magnetic composite within a robust elastic framework. The surface indents under pressure and bulges when retracted from sticky surfaces, dynamically changing the Hall sensor-to-magnet distance. This produces whole-process-traceable, baseline-separated signals that allow real-time differentiation of pressure versus pull-off force within a single sensing element at the same contact spot, eliminating stress cross-talk.
AI.result: The single-element design enables bimodal sensing at one contact spot with no stress cross-talk, improving accuracy and sensitivity. The combination of a robust framework and magneto-mechanical mechanism yields exceptional reliability and excellent signal baseline stability.
AI.conclusion: The sensor shows strong potential for advancing robotic capabilities in evaluating adhesive properties, monitoring rubber aging, precisely handling lightweight objects, and recognizing natural object surface characteristics.

title: More Features Are Not More Evidence: Limits of Training-Free Human Activity Recognition with Jev
summary: General-purpose models promise sensor-based decisions without training a task-specific classifier, which could reduce the dependence of Human Activity Recognition (HAR) on labeled data. Yet it remains unclear whether such models can directly interpret deterministic descriptions of physical sensor signals well enough to replace or complement trained HAR models. We study this question using Jev, a fixed general-purpose probabilistic decision model, on 1,800 class-balanced accelerometer windows from WISDM, UCI341, and PAMAP2. Jev receives no labeled examples, retrieval context, or HAR-specific parameter updates. We evaluate three deterministic sensor representations and compare 5,400 Jev decisions with a generative baseline and three supervised HAR models. Jev remains far below supervised recognition, with its strongest representation reaching macro-F1 of 0.038, 0.118, and 0.089 across the three datasets, compared with 0.686 to 0.907 for the supervised models. More numerical features do not improve Jev. Instead, they reduce recognition on all three datasets, while augmenting the same numerical evidence with a deterministic semantic rendering partially recovers performance, although the experiment does not isolate semantics from the accompanying serialization and redundancy changes. Jev is fast and inexpensive to query, but its probabilities are not reliably calibrated for recognition. A post-hoc fusion analysis finds a small improvement on WISDM that does not replicate on UCI341 or PAMAP2. These results show that training-free sensor decisions depend not only on the information available in the signal, but also on whether the model can use the representation through which that information is exposed. The sensor-to-model interface should therefore be treated as part of the model evaluation rather than as a neutral preprocessing step.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether a fixed general-purpose probabilistic model (Jev) can make training-free sensor decisions for Human Activity Recognition, finding it remains far below supervised models and is sensitive to how sensor signals are represented at the model interface.
AI.motivation: General-purpose models promise sensor-based decisions without training task-specific classifiers, potentially reducing HAR's dependence on labeled data. However, it is unclear whether such models can directly interpret deterministic descriptions of physical sensor signals well enough to replace or complement trained HAR models.
AI.method: Using Jev, a fixed general-purpose probabilistic decision model, the authors test 1,800 class-balanced accelerometer windows from WISDM, UCI341, and PAMAP2. Jev receives no labeled examples, retrieval context, or HAR-specific parameter updates. They evaluate three deterministic sensor representations, compare 5,400 Jev decisions against a generative baseline and three supervised HAR models, and conduct a post-hoc fusion analysis.
AI.result: Jev remains far below supervised recognition, with its strongest representation reaching macro-F1 of 0.038, 0.118, and 0.089 across the three datasets, versus 0.686–0.907 for supervised models. More numerical features reduce recognition on all three datasets, while adding a deterministic semantic rendering partially recovers performance, though semantics are not isolated from serialization and redundancy changes. Jev is fast and inexpensive to query, but its probabilities are not reliably calibrated. Post-hoc fusion yields a small improvement on WISDM that does not replicate on UCI341 or PAMAP2.
AI.conclusion: Training-free sensor decisions depend not only on the information available in the signal but also on whether the model can use the representation through which that information is exposed. The sensor-to-model interface should therefore be treated as part of model evaluation rather than as a neutral preprocessing step.

title: Riemannian Splat Regression Models for Learning Time Fields on Arbitrary Riemannian Manifolds
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, Spotlight Paper at IEEE/RSJ IROS Workshop on Geometric Representations in Robotics
summary: Motion planning on arbitrary Riemannian manifolds is an important and difficult problem that frustrates typical planning methods for Euclidean spaces. In particular, motion planning methods that approximate optimal time-to-go functions with neural networks, e.g., Neural Time Fields (NTFields), cannot be directly applied without using ad-hoc coordinate projections into higher dimensions. Using these methods directly without such projections is desirable, as it promises to provide the lowest-possible-runtime method for obtaining optimal plans on high-dimensional manifolds while using minimal model capacity. In this work, we develop a model that requires no coordinate projection and can learn arbitrary functions on Riemannian manifolds by combining splat regression models with splats defined by wrapped Gaussian distributions. We successfully apply this model for learning arrival time fields on several Riemannian manifolds, and we compare the accuracy and model size of this approach with multi-layer perceptrons adapted to work on each manifold individually.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a coordinate-projection-free model combining splat regression with wrapped Gaussian splats to learn arbitrary functions on Riemannian manifolds, and applies it to learn arrival time (time-to-go) fields for motion planning, comparing accuracy and model size against manifold-adapted MLPs.
AI.motivation: Motion planning on arbitrary Riemannian manifolds is important but difficult, since Euclidean planning methods do not transfer directly. Neural time-to-go approaches such as NTFields cannot be applied without ad-hoc coordinate projections into higher dimensions. Such projections are undesirable because avoiding them promises the lowest-possible runtime for optimal plans on high-dimensional manifolds with minimal model capacity.
AI.method: The authors develop a model requiring no coordinate projection that learns arbitrary functions on Riemannian manifolds by combining splat regression models with splats defined by wrapped Gaussian distributions.
AI.result: The model successfully learns arrival time fields on several Riemannian manifolds. Its accuracy and model size are compared with multi-layer perceptrons adapted to work on each manifold individually.
AI.conclusion: The proposed projection-free splat regression approach enables learning of functions such as arrival time fields directly on Riemannian manifolds, and is evaluated against manifold-specific MLP baselines in terms of accuracy and model size.

title: Principled Thoughts for Latent Recursive LLM Systems
summary: Large language models can reason in continuous space instead of decoded text, by recurring on their own hidden states or by passing those states between agents, while training supervises only the Cross-Entropy (CE) of the final decoded answer and does not constrain the thought. Theoretical and empirical analyses establish and confirm four failures of CE-only training that lead to a lower probability of the correct answer such as collapsing thoughts across distinct questions and retaining irrelevant information. We introduce REST (REpresentation-Supervised Thoughts), a training objective that turns four properties of a valid thought representation (causality, minimality, separability, and stability) into differentiable losses added to CE. We instantiate it in latent single-agent and multi-agent systems, without architectural changes or added parameters at inference. Across 7 benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, medicine, and code generation, with the same training data, compute, and latent budget, REST increases accuracy over CE-only training across agent settings and model sizes by up to 7.5 percentage points and convergence on a final answer by 30\%. Furthermore, REST thoughts encode more of what is required to achieve the correct answer, and decoding them better recovers the intended output of the agent, which makes latent communication easier to interpret. Project Website: https://fard-lab.github.io/REST

AI.tldr: REST supervises the latent thought representations of LLM reasoning (beyond CE loss) using four differentiable properties—causality, minimality, separability, stability—yielding up to +7.5 pp accuracy and 30% faster convergence over CE-only training in single- and multi-agent latent systems.
AI.motivation: LLMs can reason in continuous space via hidden states or inter-agent state passing, but training supervises only the CE of the final decoded answer and never constrains the thought. CE-only training exhibits four failures (e.g., collapsing thoughts across distinct questions, retaining irrelevant information) that reduce the probability of the correct answer, motivating direct supervision of the thought representation.
AI.method: REST (REpresentation-Supervised Thoughts) converts four properties of a valid thought representation—causality, minimality, separability, stability—into differentiable losses added to CE. It is instantiated in latent single-agent and multi-agent systems with no architectural changes and no extra inference parameters.
AI.result: Across 7 benchmarks (mathematics, science, medicine, code generation), under identical data, compute, and latent budget, REST improves accuracy over CE-only training across agent settings and model sizes by up to 7.5 percentage points and final-answer convergence by 30%. REST thoughts encode more of the information required for the correct answer and decode better to the agent's intended output, easing latent-communication interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Supervising latent thought representations with the four representation properties is an effective, architecture-agnostic complement to CE training, improving both accuracy and interpretability of latent reasoning and communication.

title: EquivDP3: A SIM(3)-Invariant Point-Cloud Encoder for Data-Efficient Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. A shorter version has been submitted to ICASSP 2027
summary: Visuomotor policies for humanoid loco-manipulation must generalize across object poses and lighting from only a handful of demonstrations. 3D Diffusion Policy (DP3) conditions a diffusion-based action generator on point-cloud features, but its PointNet-style encoder has no built-in equivariance to the rotations, translations, and scalings (SIM(3)) that manipulation tasks respect. EquiBot closed this gap for wheeled manipulators with a SIM(3)-equivariant Vector Neuron Network (VNN) encoder. We extend this to a substantially more complex embodiment, the 43-joint Unitree G1 humanoid, and propose EquivDP3: a two-stage policy where a high-level diffusion planner with a SIM(3)-equivariant VNN encoder emits 6 Hz whole-body command chunks, executed at 50 Hz by a frozen, pre-trained RL locomotion policy and a differential inverse-kinematics module for the arms, trained end-to-end by behavior cloning. Across two simulated IsaacLab benchmarks and four non-equivariant baselines (5-100 demonstrations, in- and out-of-distribution), EquivDP3's advantage concentrates in the low-data regime: at 5-10 demonstrations it reaches 67.1% success versus 38.2-52.4% for the baselines, while by 50-100 all encoders converge (74.3-85.2%) and the ordering is no longer meaningful. A proprioception-only control confirms this gap is genuinely perceptual: with the point cloud removed, success drops to 31% vs. 60% (EquivDP3) at 5 demonstrations and 78% vs. 99% at 10, but vanishes by 50-100, showing the high-data plateau reflects a benchmark ceiling, not five encoders learning the same invariance. The encoder costs only 0.8 ms of extra latency per action chunk over the PointNet encoder it replaces. Baking geometric symmetry into a hierarchical diffusion policy's perception backbone is a practical, nearly free way to improve data efficiency for humanoid loco-manipulation when demonstrations are scarce.

AI.tldr: EquivDP3 adds a SIM(3)-equivariant VNN encoder to a hierarchical diffusion policy for a 43-joint humanoid, boosting low-data loco-manipulation success to 67.1% at 5-10 demos (vs. 38.2-52.4% baselines) at only 0.8 ms extra latency.
AI.motivation: Humanoid loco-manipulation visuomotor policies must generalize across object poses and lighting from only a handful of demonstrations. While 3D Diffusion Policy (DP3) conditions a diffusion action generator on point-cloud features, its PointNet-style encoder lacks built-in equivariance to the rotations, translations, and scalings (SIM(3)) that manipulation tasks respect. EquiBot addressed this for wheeled manipulators via a SIM(3)-equivariant Vector Neuron Network (VNN) encoder, but extending such equivariance to a far more complex embodiment remains unexplored.
AI.method: The authors propose EquivDP3, a two-stage policy for the 43-joint Unitree G1 humanoid. A high-level diffusion planner with a SIM(3)-equivariant VNN encoder emits 6 Hz whole-body command chunks; these are executed at 50 Hz by a frozen, pre-trained RL locomotion policy and a differential inverse-kinematics module for the arms. The system is trained end-to-end by behavior cloning. Evaluation spans two simulated IsaacLab benchmarks and four non-equivariant baselines across 5-100 demonstrations in-and out-of-distribution, plus a proprioception-only control to isolate perceptual contributions.
AI.result: At 5-10 demonstrations, EquivDP3 reaches 67.1% success versus 38.2-52.4% for baselines; by 50-100 demonstrations all encoders converge (74.3-85.2%) and ordering is no longer meaningful. The proprioception-only control confirms the gap is genuinely perceptual: removing the point cloud drops success to 31% vs. 60% (EquivDP3) at 5 demos and 78% vs. 99% at 10, but the gap vanishes at 50-100 demos, indicating the high-data plateau reflects a benchmark ceiling rather than shared learned invariance. The encoder adds only 0.8 ms latency per action chunk over the replaced PointNet encoder.
AI.conclusion: Baking geometric symmetry into the perception backbone of a hierarchical diffusion policy is a practical, nearly free way to improve data efficiency for humanoid loco-manipulation when demonstrations are scarce. The equivariance advantage is concentrated in the low-data regime and reflects genuinely improved perceptual generalization.

title: FigAct: Turning Scientific Figures into Active Canvases for Explanation
summary: Scientific figures are designed to communicate information visually, yet MLLMs typically explain them by translating their visual content back into text. This requires readers to manually map the resulting explanations back to the figure. Inspired by how people present visual information, we introduce FigAct, a framework that transforms static scientific figures into question-conditioned visual presentations by acting directly on their existing graphical elements. Like a human presenter, FigAct generates a sequence of short narrations, grounds each narration in the corresponding visual evidence, and applies visual actions to guide the viewer's attention. We develop a hierarchical search strategy for efficient element localization, reducing token usage by approximately 40$\times$. We further train FigAct-8B using three task-specific rewards for grounding accuracy, search efficiency, and rendering quality. We further build a human-verified benchmark from figures in real-world scientific papers to evaluate the ability of MLLMs to generate grounded visual explanations. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of FigAct and show that treating scientific figures as presentation canvases makes explanations clearer and easier to follow.

AI.tldr: FigAct transforms static scientific figures into question-conditioned visual presentations by acting on existing graphical elements—generating grounded narrations with visual attention cues—using a hierarchical search strategy (~40x token reduction) and training FigAct-8B with task-specific rewards.
AI.motivation: MLLMs typically explain scientific figures by translating visual content back into text, forcing readers to manually map explanations back to the figure. Inspired by human presentation, the authors want explanations that act directly on the figure's graphical elements.
AI.method: FigAct generates a sequence of short narrations, grounds each in corresponding visual evidence, and applies visual actions to guide viewer attention. A hierarchical search strategy enables efficient element localization, reducing token usage ~40x. FigAct-8B is trained with three task-specific rewards for grounding accuracy, search efficiency, and rendering quality.
AI.result: A human-verified benchmark built from real-world scientific paper figures evaluates MLLMs' ability to generate grounded visual explanations. Results demonstrate FigAct's effectiveness in producing clearer and easier-to-follow explanations.
AI.conclusion: Treating scientific figures as presentation canvases improves explanation clarity and comprehensibility, validating the FigAct framework.

title: Inferring Soil Friction Angle from Robot Foot-Ground Force Histories: A Bayesian Inverse Approach to Proprioceptive Soil Sensing
summary: Foot-ground interaction signals recorded by quadruped robots may enable spatially distributed, in situ characterization of soil strength. As a first step, we test whether the internal friction angle $φ$ of cohesionless soil can be identified from the force history of a simplified rotating leg. A two-dimensional continuum model implemented with the material point method, benchmarked against measured rotating-leg force histories, generates the training data, and two Gaussian-process surrogates support Bayesian inversion of the full histories. In matched-model experiments, the framework recovers 14 off-grid friction angles with a median absolute error of approximately $0.1^\circ$ (maximum $\sim 0.7^\circ$); the reported credible intervals contain the true value in every case. These results establish that $φ$ is identifiable when the forward model is correctly specified, and support further development of proprioceptive soil sensing for spatially variable terrain, with applications from physics-grounded world models for robot training to post-wildfire slope assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the internal friction angle of cohesionless soil can be accurately identified from the force history of a simplified rotating quadruped leg, using MPM-simulated training data and Gaussian-process surrogates for Bayesian inversion.
AI.motivation: Foot-ground interaction signals from quadruped robots could enable spatially distributed, in situ soil strength characterization, but it is first necessary to establish whether soil parameters such as the internal friction angle are identifiable from leg force histories.
AI.method: A 2D continuum model implemented with the material point method, benchmarked against measured rotating-leg force histories, generates training data. Two Gaussian-process surrogates then support Bayesian inversion of the full force histories to infer the internal friction angle φ of cohesionless soil.
AI.result: In matched-model experiments, the framework recovers 14 off-grid friction angles with a median absolute error of about 0.1° (maximum ~0.7°), and the reported credible intervals contain the true value in every case.
AI.conclusion: φ is identifiable when the forward model is correctly specified, supporting further development of proprioceptive soil sensing for spatially variable terrain, with applications from physics-grounded world models for robot training to post-wildfire slope assessment.

title: An Empirical Study and Assessment of EU AI Act Compliance Checkers
summary: The EU AI Act introduces extensive compliance requirements for organizations that develop, deploy, or integrate AI systems. Many of these requirements are directly relevant to security and privacy, while also addressing closely related issues such as data governance, transparency, accuracy, and robustness. However, stakeholders such as small-to-medium businesses and individual developers often lack the legal expertise required to interpret these obligations and translate them into engineering and governance practices. This disconnect creates challenges for implementing the EU AI Act and may lead to missing safeguards or misdirected development and deployment efforts. To address this, various automated EU AI Act compliance checkers (AIACCs) have emerged, claiming to streamline compliance assessments and provide practical guidance. In this paper, we present the first empirical study and assessment of AIACCs. We characterize 12 mainstream AIACCs across multiple dimensions, evaluate their legal coverage and alignment, and analyze checker-generated compliance reports for structure, determinacy, and actionability. We find that the quality of AIACCs varies significantly and that they currently can only serve as early-stage orientation tools. Specifically, we observe inconsistent interaction modes and user-friendliness, a tendency to overly simplify or omit key obligations, and a failure to provide determinate, actionable guidance. As a result, reliance on the current generation of AIACCs may foster a false sense of compliance. With our study, we provide a critical baseline of the current AIACC landscape. We further offer design principles for the implementation of more reliable compliance-support tools.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first empirical study and assessment of 12 automated EU AI Act compliance checkers (AIACCs), finding wide variation in quality, oversimplified or omitted obligations, and non-determinate, non-actionable guidance, concluding that current AIACCs only serve as early-stage orientation tools and risk fostering a false sense of compliance.
AI.motivation: The EU AI Act imposes extensive compliance requirements directly relevant to security, privacy, data governance, transparency, accuracy, and robustness. Stakeholders such as small-to-medium businesses and individual developers often lack the legal expertise to interpret these obligations and translate them into engineering and governance practices, creating a disconnect that may lead to missing safeguards or misdirected development and deployment efforts. Automated EU AI Act compliance checkers (AIACCs) have emerged claiming to streamline compliance assessments and provide practical guidance, yet no empirical assessment of these tools exists.
AI.method: The first empirical study and assessment of AIACCs. The authors characterize 12 mainstream AIACCs across multiple dimensions, evaluate their legal coverage and alignment with the EU AI Act, and analyze checker-generated compliance reports for structure, determinacy, and actionability.
AI.result: The quality of AIACCs varies significantly. The study observes inconsistent interaction modes and user-friendliness, a tendency to overly simplify or omit key obligations, and a failure to provide determinate, actionable guidance. Consequently, AIACCs currently can only serve as early-stage orientation tools.
AI.conclusion: Reliance on the current generation of AIACCs may foster a false sense of compliance. The study provides a critical baseline of the current AIACC landscape and offers design principles for implementing more reliable compliance-support tools.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Vision-Language-Action Models via Reinforced Fine Tuning
summary: We study reinforcement learning (RL) methods for cooperative multi-agent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. This problem is challenging because VLAs are pretrained on large-scale single-agent data and therefore lack the fine-grained coordination skills required for inter-robot collaboration. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on multi-robot demonstrations partially bridges this gap, but its performance is bounded by the demonstration data and cannot improve from its own experience. We present a three-stage reinforced fine-tuning (RFT) pipeline for multi-agent VLAs. First, initialization-aware data collection sweeps over initial configurations and invokes human demonstrations only when the pretrained VLA repeatedly fails, yielding robustness to initialization shift with reduced human cost. Second, offline credit-filtered tuning assigns credit to individual agents and fine-tunes on per-agent trajectories with positive advantage rather than on entire joint rollouts. Third, we find existing online RL for VLAs are less effective for hard multi-agent tasks, which we attribute to noisy co-exploration and unstable updates. We instead use online latent-space fine tuning, which freeze the VLA and perform RL in its latent noise space. We evaluate our multi-agent VLA with both $π_0$ and $π_{0.5}$ backbones across 11 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboFactory and real-world manipulation with two Franka robots. Our multi-agent VLA improves the average success rate by $+23.1\%$, $+16.4\%$, and $+44\%$ on RoboTwin, RoboFactory, and real-world tasks, respectively. Code available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/mavla_rft-2BC0/.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a three-stage reinforced fine-tuning (RFT) pipeline for cooperative multi-agent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, combining initialization-aware data collection, offline credit-filtered tuning, and online latent-space fine-tuning. It improves average success rates by +23.1% (RoboTwin), +16.4% (RoboFactory), and +44% (real-world) over baselines.
AI.motivation: Pretrained VLAs are trained on large-scale single-agent data and lack fine-grained coordination skills for inter-robot collaboration. While supervised fine-tuning on multi-robot demonstrations partially bridges this gap, its performance is bounded by demonstration data and cannot improve from the agent's own experience, motivating an RL-based approach.
AI.method: A three-stage RFT pipeline: (1) initialization-aware data collection that sweeps initial configurations and invokes human demonstrations only when the pretrained VLA repeatedly fails, reducing human cost while handling initialization shift; (2) offline credit-filtered tuning that assigns credit to individual agents and fine-tunes on per-agent trajectories with positive advantage instead of full joint rollouts; (3) online latent-space fine-tuning that freezes the VLA and performs RL in its latent noise space, addressing noisy co-exploration and unstable updates in existing online RL for VLAs on hard multi-agent tasks.
AI.result: Evaluated with π0 and π0.5 backbones across 11 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboFactory, and real-world manipulation with two Franka robots. The multi-agent VLA improves average success rate by +23.1% on RoboTwin, +16.4% on RoboFactory, and +44% on real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed three-stage RFT pipeline effectively adapts pretrained single-agent VLAs for cooperative multi-agent manipulation, achieving substantial success-rate gains across simulated and real-world benchmarks.

title: MERID: Multimodal Exploration via Recursive Self-Improvement Agents for Major Depression Analysis
summary: Major depressive disorder (MDD) severely impacts daily activities and quality of life. Detecting MDD involves multimodal data, such as interview recordings and sensor measurements. This is particularly challenging, as these heterogeneous modalities often demand distinct, customized prediction pipelines. Existing efforts to address this challenge have explored both manually engineered multimodal architectures and agent-assisted pipeline development. Despite their progress, it remains challenging to autonomously revise pipelines based on experimental feedback and carry verified improvements forward into subsequent designs. To this end, we propose Multimodal Exploration via Recursive Self-Improvement Agents for Major Depression Analysis (MERID). The framework develops depression pipelines through experience-based recursive self-improvement (RSI). Grounded State Construction (GSC) grounds experience by aligning multimodal records with subject-level depression targets. Coupled Pipeline Exploration (CPE) jointly modifies representations, fusion, and predictors to build successor pipelines for classification and severity estimation. Evidence-Guided Evolution (EGE) guides revisions through feedback and verifies gains under uncertainty in small depression cohorts before inheritance. Extensive experiments on depression benchmarks show that MERID achieves the best results on multiple tasks compared with multimodal and agent-based baselines. Further analysis highlights the value of acoustic and linguistic cues for depression detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/DiscoAILab/MERID

AI.tldr: MERID is a recursive self-improvement agent framework that autonomously constructs and evolves multimodal pipelines for major depressive disorder detection and severity estimation, achieving state-of-the-art results on depression benchmarks.
AI.motivation: MDD severely impacts daily life, and detecting it requires heterogeneous multimodal data (interview recordings, sensor measurements) that typically demand distinct, customized prediction pipelines. Existing manually engineered multimodal architectures and agent-assisted pipeline development struggle to autonomously revise pipelines based on experimental feedback and to carry verified improvements forward into subsequent designs.
AI.method: MERID develops depression pipelines through experience-based recursive self-improvement (RSI), comprising three components: Grounded State Construction (GSC), which grounds experience by aligning multimodal records with subject-level depression targets; Coupled Pipeline Exploration (CPE), which jointly modifies representations, fusion, and predictors to build successor pipelines for classification and severity estimation; and Evidence-Guided Evolution (EGE), which guides revisions via feedback and verifies gains under uncertainty in small depression cohorts before inheritance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on depression benchmarks show that MERID achieves the best results on multiple tasks compared with multimodal and agent-based baselines. Further analysis highlights the value of acoustic and linguistic cues for depression detection.
AI.conclusion: MERID demonstrates that recursive self-improvement with grounded experience, coupled pipeline exploration, and evidence-guided evolution enables effective autonomous multimodal pipeline development for MDD analysis, with acoustic and linguistic cues proving particularly informative. Code is available at https://github.com/DiscoAILab/MERID.

title: Simple Agentic Memory for Generalist Robot Policies
summary: Visual-memory systems commonly retain or compress past observations. Robot control additionally requires interaction-derived state that no individual frame may explicitly represent, such as persistent identity relations, accumulated progress, or ordered procedures. We introduce Simple Agentic Robot Memory (SimpleARM), a training-free memory layer for frozen generalist robot policies. From the task instruction, SimpleARM specifies what to monitor; frozen perceptual tools maintain compact typed state online; structured access retrieves that state only when a proposed subgoal depends on history; and current-view grounding resolves recalled entities before execution. We evaluate SimpleARM on RoboMME, a benchmark of memory-dependent robot manipulation tasks that require history information no longer available in the current observation. Across all 16 tasks and three policy seeds, SimpleARM achieves 67.17% mean success, compared with 44.51% for the strongest non-oracle baseline. Matched ablations show mechanism specificity: removing relation, reference, progress, or route state produces large losses where the affected state is retrieved for control, while largely sparing other tasks. These results support a state-based view of robot memory: effective memory for control is not simply retained visual history, but compact task-relevant state derived from the interaction history.

AI.tldr: SimpleARM is a training-free memory layer for frozen generalist robot policies that maintains compact typed state derived from interaction history and retrieves it only when a proposed subgoal depends on history, achieving 67.17% mean success on the RoboMME benchmark versus 44.51% for the strongest non-oracle baseline.
AI.motivation: Visual-memory systems typically retain or compress past observations, but robot control requires interaction-derived state that no individual frame may explicitly represent, such as persistent identity relations, accumulated progress, or ordered procedures. Existing memory approaches, based on retained visual history, are insufficient for these control-relevant states.
AI.method: SimpleARM is a training-free memory layer built on frozen generalist robot policies. From the task instruction, it specifies what to monitor; frozen perceptual tools maintain compact typed state online; structured access retrieves that state only when a proposed subgoal depends on history; and current-view grounding resolves recalled entities before execution.
AI.result: Evaluated on RoboMME, a benchmark of memory-dependent robot manipulation tasks requiring history information no longer available in the current observation. Across all 16 tasks and three policy seeds, SimpleARM achieves 67.17% mean success versus 44.51% for the strongest non-oracle baseline. Matched ablations show mechanism specificity: removing relation, reference, progress, or route state produces large losses where the affected state is retrieved for control, while largely sparing other tasks.
AI.conclusion: Results support a state-based view of robot memory: effective memory for control is not simply retained visual history, but compact task-relevant state derived from the interaction history.

title: ChronoSRL: Temporal Geometry for Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning
summary: A goal that is close in space can be far away in time. Obstacles, terrain, and the agent's own capabilities determine how long it takes to get there. Yet, critics in contrastive and survival reinforcement learning do not measure the distances in their representation space in units of time. We therefore introduce ChronoSRL, which gives the critic's embeddings an explicit temporal geometry. The distance between state-action and goal embeddings is trained to match the time that the agent takes to reach the goal (goal-reaching time), while goals that were not reached, and goals from other trajectories, are pushed at least one discount horizon away. Furthermore, reaching a goal quickly once does not mean that reaching it is reliable in general, so the policy should not follow the temporal distance directly. Instead, we build on survival reinforcement learning and predict from our temporal embeddings not only the full distribution of goal-reaching times but also the time spent near the goal. Thereby, the policy is trained to favor actions that reach the goal sooner and more reliably and that keep the agent near it. ChronoSRL learns faster and reaches higher performance than contrastive, action-chunked contrastive, and survival reinforcement learning baselines on seven standard locomotion and navigation benchmarks, even with much smaller networks. To test the limits of self-supervised reinforcement learning, we introduce velocity tracking, goal-position reaching, and box climbing tasks with a quadruped robot in a realistic sim-to-real locomotion setup, and show how the shaping terms that are typical for robotics can be naturally incorporated into our framework. ChronoSRL is the only one of the tested self-supervised reinforcement learning methods that learns to stay at the commanded velocities and goal positions, and climbs the highest boxes.

AI.tldr: ChronoSRL gives the critic's embeddings an explicit temporal geometry, where distances match goal-reaching time, and predicts both the distribution of reaching times and time spent near the goal to train a more reliable and efficient policy.
AI.motivation: Critics in contrastive and survival reinforcement learning do not measure distances in their representation space in units of time, even though obstacles, terrain, and agent capabilities determine how long it takes to reach a goal. A goal close in space can be far in time. Measuring representation distances directly in units of time would provide a more meaningful metric for goal-reaching behavior.
AI.method: ChronoSRL gives the critic's embeddings an explicit temporal geometry by training the distance between state-action and goal embeddings to match the agent's goal-reaching time. Goals that were not reached, and goals from other trajectories, are pushed at least one discount horizon away. Building on survival reinforcement learning, it predicts from the temporal embeddings not only the full distribution of goal-reaching times but also the time spent near the goal, so the policy favors actions that reach the goal sooner and more reliably and that keep the agent near it.
AI.result: ChronoSRL learns faster and reaches higher performance than contrastive, action-chunked contrastive, and survival reinforcement learning baselines on seven standard locomotion and navigation benchmarks, even with much smaller networks. On new velocity tracking, goal-position reaching, and box climbing tasks with a quadruped robot in a realistic sim-to-real locomotion setup, ChronoSRL is the only tested self-supervised RL method that learns to stay at the commanded velocities and goal positions, and that climbs the highest boxes.
AI.conclusion: Measuring distances in representation space in units of time, rather than space, provides a useful temporal geometry for the critic. Because reaching a goal quickly once does not imply reliable general reaching, the policy should not follow temporal distance directly; instead, predicting both goal-reaching time distributions and time spent near the goal yields policies that reach goals sooner and more reliably. This framework also naturally incorporates shaping terms typical for robotics, and enables self-supervised RL to handle challenging quadruped sim-to-real tasks.

title: HACo: Learning Haptic Active Compliance for Force-Aware Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich dexterous manipulation requires policies that translate physical feedback into motion commands while regulating interaction loads across evolving multi-contact interactions. This requires haptic observations of contact state and action supervision showing how commands should adapt. Existing policies often overlook complementary fingertip tactile and joint-torque feedback, while common action targets either encode excessive loading or omit motion constrained by the object. We introduce HACo, a Haptic Active Compliance policy that learns force-regulating actions directly from haptic feedback. Compliance-regulated teleoperation converts operator inputs into controller-executable compliant actions that preserve motion intent while regulating loads. HACo learns these actions directly, using command-state discrepancy as auxiliary compliant-intent supervision. It combines local fingertip tactile responses with joint-torque feedback capturing load transmission through the articulated hand, including contacts beyond tactile coverage. A Compliance Grounding Module uses gated haptic cross-attention to ground action generation in the evolving haptic state, enabling closed-loop force regulation without explicit online contact modeling. We evaluate HACo on a real-world benchmark covering multi-contact friction, tangential interaction, fragile curved-surface contact, rotational torque, and deformable-object manipulation. Across 20 trials per task, HACo achieves an 83% mean success rate, compared with 35% for the strongest evaluated baseline. These results demonstrate active compliance across diverse force-sensitive dexterous manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: HACo is a haptic active compliance policy that learns force-regulating dexterous manipulation actions directly from complementary fingertip tactile and joint-torque feedback, achieving 83% mean success across five real-world force-sensitive tasks versus 35% for the best baseline.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich dexterous manipulation requires policies that convert physical feedback into motion commands while regulating interaction loads across evolving multi-contact interactions. This demands haptic observation of contact state and action supervision indicating how commands should adapt. Existing policies overlook complementary fingertip tactile and joint-torque feedback, and common action targets either encode excessive loading or omit object-constrained motion.
AI.method: Compliance-regulated teleoperation converts operator inputs into controller-executable compliant actions that preserve motion intent while regulating loads. HACo learns these actions directly, using command-state discrepancy as auxiliary compliant-intent supervision. It fuses local fingertip tactile responses with joint-torque feedback capturing load transmission through the articulated hand, including contacts beyond tactile coverage. A Compliance Grounding Module uses gated haptic cross-attention to ground action generation in the evolving haptic state, enabling closed-loop force regulation without explicit online contact modeling.
AI.result: Evaluated on a real-world benchmark covering multi-contact friction, tangential interaction, fragile curved-surface contact, rotational torque, and deformable-object manipulation. Across 20 trials per task, HACo achieves 83% mean success rate, compared with 35% for the strongest evaluated baseline.
AI.conclusion: HACo demonstrates active compliance across diverse force-sensitive dexterous manipulation tasks, validating direct learning of force-regulating actions from combined tactile and joint-torque haptic feedback.

title: CoRe: Co-Evolving Reward Models for Mitigating Latent Reward Hacking in Video Diffusion Models
summary: Latent reward models (LRMs) enable efficient alignment of video diffusion models by scoring intermediate states directly in latent space. However, we find that optimizing against a fixed latent reward rapidly leads to latent reward hacking: the predicted reward stays high while perceptual and motion quality deteriorate. Our analysis identifies distributional escape as the central cause: within a few hundred updates, the generator moves beyond the reward model's training support, where its scores no longer reflect video quality. Based on this insight, we introduce CoRe, a co-evolving reward framework that treats latent-space alignment as a dynamic interaction between the generator and the reward model. Rather than optimizing against a stationary proxy, CoRe continually refits the reward model on the generator's current samples while anchoring it to real-video preferences, so the generator cannot gain reward by drifting away from the data. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, experiments show that CoRe consistently improves generation quality over both the pretrained model and prior alignment methods, while avoiding the quality collapse of fixed-reward optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies latent reward hacking caused by distributional escape in latent reward models (LRMs) for video diffusion alignment, and proposes CoRe, a co-evolving reward framework that continually refits the reward model on the generator's current samples while anchoring to real-video preferences.
AI.motivation: Latent reward models enable efficient alignment of video diffusion models by scoring intermediate states in latent space, but optimizing against a fixed latent reward rapidly leads to latent reward hacking: predicted reward stays high while perceptual and motion quality deteriorate. The authors identify distributional escape as the central cause—within a few hundred updates the generator moves beyond the reward model's training support, where scores no longer reflect video quality.
AI.method: CoRe is a co-evolving reward framework that treats latent-space alignment as a dynamic interaction between generator and reward model. Instead of optimizing against a stationary proxy, it continually refits the reward model on the generator's current samples while anchoring it to real-video preferences, preventing the generator from gaining reward by drifting away from the data distribution.
AI.result: On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, experiments show that CoRe consistently improves generation quality over both the pretrained model and prior alignment methods, while avoiding the quality collapse characteristic of fixed-reward optimization.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving the reward model with the generator and anchoring it to real-video preferences mitigates latent reward hacking and distributional escape, yielding more effective alignment of video diffusion models.

title: Executor-aware Candidate Selection via a Feasibility Certificate
summary:
Modular robotic systems often separate motion planning from a downstream executor that enforces state-dependent hard constraints. A candidate that is geometrically valid may therefore be incompatible with the executor's available command set. We present a certificate-based candidate-selection framework that constructs a command witness from the executor hard set at predicted rollout states and verifies it against the original constraints, without changing candidate generation, ranking, or the executor.
  Across 5,085 geometry-valid numerical evaluations on two robot models, 795 admitted no executor-feasible command. The certificate is sufficient but conservative: none of the 795 was certified, while 7.09\% of reference-feasible cases remained uncertified. In controlled FR3 and fixed-base RB-Y1 simulations, certificate admission frequently changed candidate selection, and a post-hoc exact linear-programming (LP) admission baseline revealed platform-dependent conservatism. Relative to geometry-based selection, certificate admission was associated with lower planner-command coverage and higher nominal tracking error, without a consistent advantage in reached-state interaction reserve. A planner-generated MoveIt/OMPL study further evaluates the same admission rule on externally generated candidate pools.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a certificate-based candidate-selection framework that builds a command witness from an executor's hard constraint set at predicted rollout states and verifies it against the original constraints, without altering candidate generation, ranking, or the executor.
AI.motivation: In modular robotic systems, motion planning and downstream execution are often decoupled, so a geometrically valid candidate may still be incompatible with the executor's available command set. This gap motivates a method to test whether a candidate can actually be realized by the executor before selection.
AI.method: The framework constructs a command witness from the executor hard set at predicted rollout states and verifies it against the original constraints, leaving candidate generation, ranking, and the executor unchanged. It is evaluated across 5,085 geometry-valid numerical evaluations on two robot models, with controlled FR3 and fixed-base RB-Y1 simulations, a post-hoc exact linear-programming (LP) admission baseline, and a planner-generated MoveIt/OMPL study on externally generated candidate pools.
AI.result: Of the 5,085 evaluations, 795 admitted no executor-feasible command. The certificate proved sufficient but conservative: none of the 795 infeasible cases was certified, while 7.09% of reference-feasible cases remained uncertified. Certificate admission frequently changed candidate selection, and the LP baseline revealed platform-dependent conservatism. Relative to geometry-based selection, certificate admission was associated with lower planner-command coverage and higher nominal tracking error, with no consistent advantage in reached-state interaction reserve.
AI.conclusion: The certificate reliably excludes executor-infeasible candidates but is conservative, leaving some feasible cases uncertified. Its impact on selection is platform-dependent, and it does not consistently improve downstream performance over geometry-based selection, suggesting a trade-off between feasibility assurance and practical execution quality.

title: Towards Mitigating Deceptive Safety Alignment in Large Reasoning Models
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are commonly trained with reinforcement learning (RL) to improve their generation of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before producing final answers. However, RL rewards are typically assigned based on final answers, providing little or no direct supervision over intermediate reasoning. This can lead to deceptive safety alignment, where the reasoning trace and final answer convey inconsistent safety signals. To systematically investigate this phenomenon, we introduce DSAR (Deceptive Safety Alignment Rate), a metric that jointly assesses reasoning traces and final answers to quantify their safety inconsistency. Across multiple LRMs and benchmarks, we find that deceptive safety alignment is pervasive under standard prompting conditions and is substantially amplified under prefilling attacks. We further provide a hidden representation analysis showing that models exhibit stronger safety discrimination at the final-answer stage than during intermediate reasoning. To close this gap, we propose SARA (Safety-Aware Reasoning Alignment), an RL-based method that rewards both safety-aware reasoning and safe final answers, encouraging early harmful intent recognition and enforcing reasoning-answer consistency. Experiments show that SARA significantly mitigates deceptive safety alignment under both standard and adversarial settings while preserving helpfulness and utility. Code is available at https://github.com/xzhou98/SARA.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DSAR to measure deceptive safety alignment in LRMs (safety inconsistency between reasoning traces and final answers), shows it is pervasive and amplified by prefilling attacks, and proposes SARA, an RL method rewarding both safe reasoning and safe answers to close this gap.
AI.motivation: LRMs are RL-trained for chain-of-thought reasoning, but rewards based on final answers give little supervision over intermediate reasoning. This can produce deceptive safety alignment, where reasoning trace and final answer convey inconsistent safety signals—an under-investigated risk.
AI.method: The authors propose DSAR (Deceptive Safety Alignment Rate), a metric jointly assessing reasoning traces and final answers to quantify safety inconsistency, and perform hidden representation analysis across multiple LRMs and benchmarks. They then propose SARA (Safety-Aware Reasoning Alignment), an RL-based method that rewards both safety-aware reasoning and safe final answers to encourage early harmful intent recognition and reasoning-answer consistency.
AI.result: Deceptive safety alignment is pervasive under standard prompting and substantially amplified under prefilling attacks. Models show stronger safety discrimination at the final-answer stage than during intermediate reasoning. SARA significantly mitigates deceptive safety alignment under both standard and adversarial settings while preserving helpfulness and utility.
AI.conclusion: Final-answer-only RL rewards leave intermediate reasoning under-supervised, enabling deceptive safety alignment. Jointly rewarding safety-aware reasoning and safe answers (SARA) effectively reduces this inconsistency without sacrificing helpfulness or utility, supported by hidden representation evidence.

title: OTRetarget: Joint Robot and Object Motion Retargeting via Optimal Transport
summary: Transferring human motion to humanoid robots requires adapting the demonstrated motion to the robot morphology while preserving interactions with the environment. This is particularly challenging for loco-manipulation tasks, where contacts with the ground and manipulated objects must remain consistent despite differences in body proportions. Yet, skeletal motion alone does not fully describe these interactions, and fixing object trajectories limits the adaptation to a new embodiment. In this paper, we introduce OTR ETARGET, a unified approach to jointly retarget robot and multi-object motion from human demonstrations. Our approach represents surface interactions through signed distances, closest surface points, and relative directions, and uses entropic optimal transport to transfer these quantities across human, robot, and object geometries. We incorporate the resulting interaction targets into a constrained inverse kinematics formulation that balances contact preservation with motion style and jointly optimizes robot and object poses at each frame. This formulation accommodates robot-object and object-object interactions without rescaling the scene or the demonstration. We validate the proposed approach on OMOMO, where it achieves a robot- object interaction Jaccard score of 87% and a depth error of 8.7 mm, compared with 28% and 29.3 mm for OmniRetarget. Finally, we demonstrate transfer to a physical G1 humanoid using whole-body policies trained with reinforcement learning on the retargeted references, across motions including two-handed box pick-and-place onto a table.

AI.tldr: OTR ETARGET jointly retargets humanoid robot and multi-object motion from human demonstrations using entropic optimal transport over surface-interaction descriptors, integrated into a constrained IK that preserves contacts without scene rescaling.
AI.motivation: Transferring human motion to humanoid robots must adapt to robot morphology while preserving environmental interactions. Loco-manipulation is especially hard because ground and object contacts must stay consistent under differing body proportions. Skeletal motion alone insufficiently describes these interactions, and fixing object trajectories restricts adaptation to new embodiments.
AI.method: The approach represents surface interactions via signed distances, closest surface points, and relative directions, and uses entropic optimal transport to transfer these quantities across human, robot, and object geometries. These interaction targets feed a constrained inverse kinematics formulation that balances contact preservation with motion style and jointly optimizes robot and object poses per frame, supporting robot-object and object-object interactions without rescaling the scene or demonstration.
AI.result: On OMOMO, it achieves a robot-object interaction Jaccard score of 87% and depth error of 8.7 mm, versus 28% and 29.3 mm for OmniRetarget. Transfer to a physical G1 humanoid is demonstrated using whole-body RL policies trained on the retargeted references, including two-handed box pick-and-place onto a table.
AI.conclusion: Joint robot-and-object retargeting via optimal transport of surface-interaction descriptors yields accurate, contact-consistent loco-manipulation references that transfer effectively to a physical humanoid robot.

title: OTROPE: Optimal Transport-based Robust Off-policy Evaluation for Large Language Models
summary: Reliable evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is essential for their development and deployment, yet is often costly, risky, and difficult to perform safely online. We study off-policy evaluation for LLMs, where limited human-labeled data from a behavior model are used to evaluate a newer target LLM. This setting is challenging because labels are scarce, behavior--target distribution shift is common, and response likelihoods are often unavailable for black-box LLMs. We propose the Optimal Transport-based Robust Off-Policy Evaluation (OTROPE), a likelihood-free evaluation that performs distributional correction in a semantic space via optimal transport to align labeled behavior-policy samples with unlabeled target-policy samples. OTROPE combines corrected human-labeled residuals with proxy predictors, yielding a doubly robust-style evaluation without behavior-policy modeling or density-ratio estimation. We theoretically characterize why baseline evaluators fail under LLM distribution shift, and establish consistency and convergence rates for OTROPE when either the reweighted behavior distribution or the proxy predictor converges. Experiments on synthetic and real LLM evaluation tasks show that OTROPE consistently outperforms baselines while enabling ensembles of weaker LLM evaluators to approach and sometimes surpass stronger evaluators. Code is available at https://github.com/LinerXiang/OTROPE.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OTROPE, a likelihood-free, optimal-transport-based robust off-policy evaluation method for LLMs that performs distributional correction in semantic space to align labeled behavior-policy samples with unlabeled target-policy samples, achieving doubly robust-style evaluation without behavior-policy modeling.
AI.motivation: Reliable LLM evaluation is costly, risky, and hard to perform safely online. In off-policy evaluation, limited human-labeled data from a behavior model must evaluate a newer target LLM, but this is challenging due to scarce labels, behavior-target distribution shift, and unavailable response likelihoods for black-box LLMs.
AI.method: OTROPE (Optimal Transport-based Robust Off-Policy Evaluation) performs likelihood-free evaluation, conducting distributional correction in a semantic space via optimal transport to align labeled behavior-policy samples with unlabeled target-policy samples. It combines corrected human-labeled residuals with proxy predictors, yielding a doubly robust-style evaluation without behavior-policy modeling or density-ratio estimation.
AI.result: The authors theoretically characterize why baseline evaluators fail under LLM distribution shift, and establish consistency and convergence rates for OTROPE when either the reweighted behavior distribution or the proxy predictor converges. Experiments on synthetic and real LLM evaluation tasks show OTROPE consistently outperforms baselines and enables ensembles of weaker LLM evaluators to approach and sometimes surpass stronger evaluators.
AI.conclusion: OTROPE provides a robust, likelihood-free off-policy evaluation framework for LLMs, addressing distribution shift and label scarcity while enabling effective ensemble evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/LinerXiang/OTROPE.

title: RoboChrono: A Real Robot Benchmark for Streaming Task Understanding
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures. Project website: https://continuity3.github.io/robochrono/ ; Code: https://github.com/mfan-res/ROBOCHRONO ; Datasets: https://huggingface.co/datasets/gimai/RC-Tianji and https://huggingface.co/datasets/gimai/RC-GIM
summary: Understanding ongoing robot manipulation requires models to interpret visual observations in relation to interaction history and task progress. We introduce RoboChrono, a benchmark for streaming task understanding comprising 39 scenarios and 34,713 evaluation instances, constructed from real robot executions and complementary bare-hand human recordings. The benchmark evaluates seven tasks grouped into recognition, alignment, and temporal grounding, covering action understanding and anticipation, visual correspondence, temporal ordering, and action localization. Zero-shot evaluation of 18 vision-language models reveals substantial differences across tasks. GPT-6-Astra achieves 98.3% accuracy on Frame Matching but 68.3% on Frame Ordering, while RynnBrain1.1-122B-A10B exhibits a larger gap, reaching 95.4% and 32.9%, respectively. Input ablations on matched questions with five open-weight models further reveal distinct dependencies on visual evidence: removing visual observations reduces Current Action Recognition accuracy by 22.1 percentage points, whereas Next Action Prediction decreases by only 0.7 points. These findings show that strong visual matching does not consistently coincide with strong temporal ordering, and suggest that next-action prediction can be supported by task and action priors even when visual evidence is unavailable. RoboChrono provides a diagnostic setting for examining these differences, highlighting the need for capability-specific evaluation beyond aggregate scores when assessing task understanding in robot manipulation.

AI.tldr: RoboChrono is a new streaming task-understanding benchmark of 39 scenarios and 34,713 instances built from real robot and bare-hand human recordings, evaluating seven recognition, alignment, and temporal-grounding tasks; zero-shot tests of 18 VLMs reveal large capability gaps (e.g., strong frame matching but weak temporal ordering) and distinct reliance on visual evidence.
AI.motivation: Understanding ongoing robot manipulation requires models to interpret visual observations jointly with interaction history and task progress, but existing evaluation does not diagnose how well models perform these distinct streaming capabilities. The paper argues that aggregate scores hide capability-specific differences, motivating a dedicated diagnostic benchmark.
AI.method: The authors construct RoboChrono from real robot executions plus complementary bare-hand human recordings, yielding 39 scenarios and 34,713 evaluation instances. Seven tasks are grouped into three categories: recognition, alignment, and temporal grounding, spanning action understanding and anticipation, visual correspondence, temporal ordering, and action localization. They run zero-shot evaluation of 18 vision-language models and, additionally, input ablations on matched questions with five open-weight models to probe dependence on visual evidence.
AI.result: Zero-shot evaluation shows substantial cross-task differences. GPT-6-Astra reaches 98.3% on Frame Matching but 68.3% on Frame Ordering; RynnBrain1.1-122B-A10B shows a larger gap at 95.4% and 32.9%. Input ablations reveal distinct visual dependencies: removing visual observations drops Current Action Recognition accuracy by 22.1 percentage points, while Next Action Prediction falls only 0.7 points.
AI.conclusion: Strong visual matching does not consistently coincide with strong temporal ordering, and next-action prediction can be supported by task and action priors even without visual evidence. RoboChrono offers a diagnostic setting for examining these differences and highlights the need for capability-specific evaluation beyond aggregate scores when assessing task understanding in robot manipulation.

title: From Surfaces to Volumes: Registered Geometry for Protein Representation Learning
summary: Existing protein geometry models typically represent molecular surfaces using local geometric features such as sampled points, normals, and curvature. While effective for capturing exposed molecular shape, these representations do not explicitly model the volumetric organization beneath the surface or provide a consistent coordinate system for residue-wise volumetric structure. We introduce Protein-TetSphere, a registered residue-wise volumetric representation for proteins. Each protein chain is tetrahedralized to obtain local volumetric regions associated with individual residues, which are then registered to a shared fixed-topology tetrahedral reference and represented in a common Laplacian basis. This registration establishes consistent volumetric coordinates across residues, enabling local three-dimensional deformation to be integrated with surface and chemical information in a multimodal protein representation. We evaluate Protein-TetSphere on ligand-binding pocket classification, protein--protein interface prediction, and de novo protein binder design. Across the three tasks, Protein-TetSphere improves ligand-binding pocket balanced accuracy from $0.795$ to $0.826$, Pinder-Pair/Site AUROC from $0.914/0.852$ to $0.932/0.866$, and binder-design success from $14.95\%$ to $19.90\%$ on the BoltzGen Challenge Set and from $27.62\%$ to $32.19\%$ at the ProtDBench backbone level. These results show that registered volumetric geometry provides complementary spatial information beyond molecular surfaces across protein recognition, interaction, and design.

AI.tldr: Protein-TetSphere introduces a registered residue-wise volumetric representation for proteins, tetrahedralizing each chain into local volumetric regions per residue and mapping them to a shared fixed-topology tetrahedral reference in a common Laplacian basis, improving performance on binding-pocket classification, interface prediction, and binder design.
AI.motivation: Existing protein geometry models represent molecular surfaces via local features (points, normals, curvature). These capture exposed shape but fail to explicitly model volumetric organization beneath the surface and lack a consistent coordinate system for residue-wise volumetric structure.
AI.method: Each protein chain is tetrahedralized to obtain local volumetric regions associated with individual residues. These regions are registered to a shared fixed-topology tetrahedral reference and represented in a common Laplacian basis, establishing consistent volumetric coordinates across residues. This yields a multimodal representation integrating local 3D deformation with surface and chemical information.
AI.result: On ligand-binding pocket classification, balanced accuracy improves from 0.795 to 0.826; on Pinder-Pair/Site, AUROC improves from 0.914/0.852 to 0.932/0.866; on binder design, success improves from 14.95% to 19.90% (BoltzGen Challenge Set) and from 27.62% to 32.19% (ProtDBench backbone level).
AI.conclusion: Registered volumetric geometry provides complementary spatial information beyond molecular surfaces, benefiting protein recognition, interaction, and design tasks.

title: Foundation-Model-Guided Topology-Aware Semantic Risk Fields for Manipulation
summary: Robot motion planning in everyday environments must satisfy hard geometric constraints while accounting for context-dependent semantic risk. We present a foundation-model-guided, topology-aware semantic risk field that extends manipulation safety beyond collision avoidance. For each manipulated-object/scene-object pair, a foundation model provides six directional risk weights and a pair-specific spatial decay scale. The method combines these priors with voxelized 3D scene geometry using topology-aware shielding and geodesic spatial decay. A GPU-parallel backend batches object-level distance and risk computations to construct a dense 3D field that serves as a modular cost for downstream motion planning. We evaluate the field's shielding behavior under full and partial barriers and compare its 3D workspace representation with a pixel-wise semantic-prior baseline. Across three household simulation scenarios, trajectories optimized with the proposed field have lower semantic exposure than collision-only trajectories under the same geometric constraints. We also evaluate the computational practicality and reliability of the supporting pipeline. Together, these results support the proposed field as a practical topology-aware semantic cost representation for manipulation planning beyond collision avoidance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a foundation-model-guided, topology-aware semantic risk field that combines semantic priors with voxelized 3D geometry to produce a modular cost for manipulation motion planning, reducing semantic exposure beyond collision avoidance.
AI.motivation: Robot motion planning in everyday environments must satisfy hard geometric constraints while also accounting for context-dependent semantic risk, meaning safety should go beyond mere collision avoidance.
AI.method: For each manipulated-object/scene-object pair, a foundation model supplies six directional risk weights and a pair-specific spatial decay scale. These priors are fused with voxelized 3D scene geometry using topology-aware shielding and geodesic spatial decay, and a GPU-parallel backend batches object-level distance and risk computations to build a dense 3D field serving as a modular planning cost.
