AI.motivation: As agents orchestrate tools and reason over long contexts, larger LLM capabilities open indirect prompt injection surfaces. An attacker may not need to insert a complete malicious instruction if the agent can reconstruct the objective from incomplete fragments spread across a long context; existing safety evaluations overlook this reconstruction-based threat.
AI.method: AdaLCPI splits an attack objective into incomplete fragments, embeds them in external content retrieved via the agent's tools, and adds a reconstruction cue prompting the agent to combine them. It iteratively refines fragments and cue with OpenEvolve using graded scoring and natural-language execution feedback from the target agent.
AI.result: AdaLCPI attains 61.4% macro-average attack success rate, outperforming Trojan Hippo-style (32.8%) and AgentVigil (30.0%) adaptive baselines.
AI.conclusion: Long-context fragmentation combined with adaptive search is a potent indirect prompt injection strategy, so safety evaluations should test whether agents remain robust when harmful objectives must be reconstructed from incomplete fragments.

title: Adversarially Robust Geometric Safety Certificates for Nonholonomic Robots Against Maneuvering Obstacles
summary: Safe navigation against obstacles that can actively maneuver within bounded capabilities remains challenging: robust control barrier function methods typically treat obstacle actions as generic disturbances, while differential-game approaches are computationally expensive for online navigation. We propose an adversarially robust geometric certificate that accounts for the worst-case effect of admissible obstacle maneuvers directly in the safe-set geometry through a closed-form contraction of the certificate parameters. The construction exploits a structural property of line-of-sight (LoS) certificates: the robot and obstacle actions enter the certificate through a common state-dependent geometric gain. This gain cancels in the worst-case comparison, reducing the differential game to a direct comparison between obstacle maneuvering capability and the weaker of the robot's longitudinal and steering authorities. Instantiated on the parabolic certificate, the construction yields Adversarially Robust Dynamic Parabolic Control Barrier Functions (AR-DPCBF), for which we establish sufficient conditions for forward invariance of the contracted safe set against all admissible obstacle maneuvers under kinematic bicycle dynamics with bounded inputs. When the obstacle capability is unknown, a sliding-window estimator supplies a high-probability upper bound, allowing the guarantee to be retained with the corresponding coverage probability. We further formulate soft and buffered variants to recover feasibility in dense environments. Simulations across obstacle capabilities, densities, and capability mismatch show substantial reductions in barrier violations and collisions and demonstrate that pointwise robustification of the barrier derivative cannot substitute for contraction of its geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adversarially robust geometric certificate (AR-DPCBF) that accounts for worst-case obstacle maneuvers via a closed-form contraction of control barrier function parameters, exploiting a structural cancellation property of line-of-sight certificates.
AI.motivation: Safe navigation around actively maneuvering obstacles is difficult: robust control barrier function (CBF) methods treat obstacle actions merely as generic disturbances, losing structure, while differential-game approaches are too computationally expensive for online navigation. A gap exists for a method that is both computationally tractable and formally robust to worst-case admissible obstacle maneuvers.
AI.method: The authors construct an adversarially robust geometric certificate using a closed-form contraction of certificate parameters. The construction exploits a structural property of line-of-sight (LoS) certificates: robot and obstacle actions enter through a common state-dependent geometric gain that cancels in the worst-case comparison, reducing the differential game to a comparison between obstacle maneuvering capability and the weaker of the robot's longitudinal and steering authorities. Instantiated on the parabolic certificate, this yields Adversarially Robust Dynamic Parabolic Control Barrier Functions (AR-DPCBF). Sufficient conditions for forward invariance of the contracted safe set are established under kinematic bicycle dynamics with bounded inputs. For unknown obstacle capability, a sliding-window estimator provides a high-probability upper bound, retaining the guarantee with corresponding coverage probability. Soft and buffered variants are formulated to recover feasibility in dense environments.
AI.result: Simulations across varying obstacle capabilities, densities, and capability mismatch show substantial reductions in barrier violations and collisions. The results demonstrate that pointwise robustification of the barrier derivative cannot substitute for contraction of its geometry.
AI.conclusion: The adversarial geometric contraction provides a tractable, formally robust safe-navigation certificate against worst-case admissible obstacle maneuvers, with extendable guarantees under unknown obstacle capability and practical variants for dense settings.

title: SafeCoEvo: Co-Evolving Safety Harnesses and Guards for LLM Agents at Test-Time
summary: LLM agents deployed in real-world environments continually encounter new tasks and safety risks, while execution feedback typically becomes available only after each task is completed. However, existing self-evolving approaches commonly rely on multiple rounds of optimization over fixed and repeatedly accessible task distributions, fundamentally differing from test-time adaptation in real-world deployment, where only experience accumulated from past tasks can be used to improve safety decisions on future unseen tasks. To address this limitation, we propose SafeCoEvo, a test-time Harness-Guard co-evolution framework for LLM agent safety that enables the external safety system to continually adapt from accumulated runtime experience. SafeCoEvo jointly improves two complementary safety capabilities at different timescales: S-Harness rapidly externalizes recent runtime experience into updatable explicit safety knowledge that can promptly influence subsequent tasks, while GuardVPO internalizes accumulated runtime safety experience over a longer timescale into parametric risk-judgment capabilities. By combining short-term rapid adaptation with long-term capability consolidation, SafeCoEvo continually improves the agent's safety capabilities, reducing the unsafe outcome rate by 10.05% while improving the task success rate by 12.15% over the strongest baseline, thereby achieving simultaneous gains in safety and task utility.

AI.tldr: SafeCoEvo is a test-time harness-guard co-evolution framework that lets an LLM agent's external safety system continuously adapt using experience from past tasks to safeguard future unseen tasks, cutting unsafe outcomes by 10.05% and raising task success by 12.15%.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in real-world deployment keep meeting new tasks and safety risks, yet execution feedback only arrives after a task finishes. Existing self-evolving methods assume fixed, repeatedly accessible task distributions and need multiple optimization rounds, which does not match real deployment where only accrued past experience is available. This mismatch motivates a test-time adaptation approach for safety decisions on unseen future tasks.
AI.method: SafeCoEvo jointly evolves two complementary safety capabilities across different timescales. S-Harness rapidly externalizes recent runtime experience into updatable explicit safety knowledge that promptly influences subsequent tasks. GuardVPO internalizes accumulated runtime safety experience over a longer timescale into parametric risk-judgment capabilities. Combining short-term rapid adaptation with long-term capability consolidation yields continual improvement of agent safety.
AI.result: Compared with the strongest baseline, SafeCoEvo reduces the unsafe outcome rate by 10.05% and improves the task success rate by 12.15%, achieving simultaneous gains in safety and task utility.
AI.conclusion: SafeCoEvo addresses test-time safety adaptation for LLM agents by co-evolving an explicit knowledge harness and a parametric guard, demonstrating that short-term adaptation and long-term consolidation can jointly improve both safety and task performance under real-world deployment conditions.

title: ReF-HIL: Shaping the Critic around Human Action Neighborhoods for Efficient Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Shaoyin Luo and Song Wang contributed equally to this work
summary: Human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (HIL-RL) offers a promising route to efficient training of robotic manipulation policies by combining autonomous learning with human demonstrations and online corrections. However, insufficient use of successful human experience in value learning prolongs costly real-world training, while persistent imitation penalties can limit value-driven policy improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ReF-HIL, an efficient HIL-RL framework that uses human guidance to accelerate the learning process. Human-Reference-Guided Value Shaping learns an independent value reference from successful human experience to guide online value learning, while incorporating local corrective feedback. A Human Action Fence defines a learned human-action neighborhood, allowing value-driven optimization for better performance without imitation penalties inside while constraining policy and value updates outside. Experiments on five diverse and challenging real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improved overall learning efficiency and higher success rates compared with the evaluated baselines. Specifically, ReF-HIL reaches 90% autonomous success in only 18-63 minutes of active training and achieves final success rates of 91.7-100%. These results highlight the potential of human-guided reinforcement learning to acquire reliable manipulation skills efficiently in the real world. Project website: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ReF-HIL-7762/

AI.tldr: ReF-HIL is a human-in-the-loop RL framework that leverages successful human experience for value learning and uses a learned "human-action neighborhood" to balance value-driven improvement with imitation constraints, achieving fast, high-success real-world robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing human-in-the-loop RL for robotic manipulation underutilizes successful human experience in value learning, prolonging costly real-world training, while persistent imitation penalties can restrict value-driven policy improvement.
AI.method: ReF-HIL combines two components: (1) Human-Reference-Guided Value Shaping, which learns an independent value reference from successful human experience to guide online value learning while incorporating local corrective feedback; and (2) a Human Action Fence, which defines a learned human-action neighborhood enabling value-driven optimization without imitation penalties inside the neighborhood while constraining policy and value updates outside it.
AI.result: On five diverse, challenging real-world manipulation tasks, ReF-HIL improves overall learning efficiency and success rates over evaluated baselines, reaching 90% autonomous success within only 18-63 minutes of active training and attaining final success rates of 91.7-100%.
AI.conclusion: Human-guided reinforcement learning can efficiently acquire reliable manipulation skills in the real world, demonstrating the practicality of better exploiting human experience and mitigating imitation-penalty limitations.

title: MemEvo: Automatic Discovery of Streaming Video Memory Mechanisms
summary: Query-agnostic streaming video understanding requires vision-language models to continuously compress an indefinitely growing visual stream into a bounded memory before future queries are known. The performance depends critically on the memory mechanism--what observations to preserve, how to represent and consolidate them, and what information to retrieve when a query eventually arrives. Rather than designing a single memory architecture by hand, we formulate memory design as a search problem over executable memory programs. We introduce a lightweight domain-specific language that expresses memory mechanisms through structured primitives for representation, admission, retention, consolidation, budgeting, and retrieval, while enforcing causal and bounded-memory constraints. Although structured, the derived program space remains large and contains heterogeneous, conditionally dependent design choices whose effects can only be assessed via downstream execution. We therefore propose MemEvo, an LLM-driven auto-research framework that uses pretrained LLM as a semantics-aware proposal model to iteratively generate and refine candidate memory programs based on accumulated experimental feedback. At runtime, a deterministic evaluation pipeline validates and evaluates each candidate, while the underlying vision-language model remains frozen throughout discovery. We finally produce a training-free, bounded-memory mechanism. Extensive experiments on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench demonstrate strong streaming video understanding performance together with substantial context and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates the design of memory mechanisms for query-agnostic streaming video understanding as a search problem over executable memory programs, and proposes MemEvo, an LLM-driven auto-research framework that discovers a training-free, bounded-memory mechanism with strong performance and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Query-agnostic streaming video understanding requires vision-language models to compress an indefinitely growing visual stream into a bounded memory before future queries are known. Performance depends critically on the memory mechanism (what to preserve, how to represent/consolidate, and what to retrieve), yet hand-designing a single memory architecture is limiting.
AI.method: The authors cast memory design as a search problem over executable memory programs. They introduce a lightweight domain-specific language expressing memory mechanisms via structured primitives for representation, admission, retention, consolidation, budgeting, and retrieval, under causal and bounded-memory constraints. To navigate the large, heterogeneous, conditionally dependent program space, they propose MemEvo, an LLM-driven auto-research framework using a pretrained LLM as a semantics-aware proposal model that iteratively generates and refines candidate memory programs from experimental feedback. A deterministic evaluation pipeline validates and evaluates each candidate while the underlying VLM stays frozen.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench demonstrate strong streaming video understanding performance together with substantial context and inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The work yields a training-free, bounded-memory mechanism discovered automatically, showing that framing memory design as program search with an LLM-driven auto-research loop is an effective alternative to manual architecture design for streaming video understanding.

title: CoRe-VLA: Preserving Cross-View Coordination in VLAs under Camera Shifts
summary: VLAs combine pretrained vision-language representations with action generation to enable language-guided control across diverse tasks, becoming a mainstream paradigm in embodied intelligence. However, multiple studies have reported VLA's substantial declines in task success under camera shifts, revealing a key vulnerability that limits reliable deployment. To address this vulnerability, existing methods collect paired observations of the same scene from different viewpoints to fine-tune the VLA or train visual adaptation modules. Unfortunately, they require additional data collection and VLA training costs. In this paper, we first identify \emph{cross-view coordination breakdown} under external camera shifts: the robot may rely too heavily on wrist-view cues and consequently execute subtasks in the wrong order when losing global view. Motivated by this, we propose CoRe-VLA, a plug-and-play framework requiring neither additional multi-view data collection nor VLA fine-tuning, which can incorporate with exsiting VLAs. It reconstructs a scene point cloud and renders the observation from the VLA's training viewpoint to restore cross-view coordination. In CoRe-VLA, Render-to-Camera (R2C) Restoration reduces rendering-induced visual degradation, while Execution-Trajectory-Conditioned Alignment (ETCA) reduces robot idle time and mitigates motion conflicts during asynchronous execution. Experiments on 5 real-robot tasks, LIBERO-100 and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate CoRe-VLA substantially improves task success across mainstream VLAs under camera shifts. For example, CoRe-VLA raises PI0.5's success rate from 13.3% to 83.3% at a 1.6m camera shift in real-robot environment.

AI.tldr: CoRe-VLA is a plug-and-play framework that restores cross-view coordination in Vision-Language-Action models under camera shifts by reconstructing a scene point cloud and re-rendering observations from the VLA's training viewpoint, without extra multi-view data collection or VLA fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: VLAs are a mainstream paradigm in embodied intelligence, but task success declines substantially under camera shifts, limiting reliable deployment. Existing remedies require collecting paired multi-view observations and fine-tuning the VLA or training visual adaptation modules, which incurs additional data collection and training costs.
AI.method: The paper identifies cross-view coordination breakdown under external camera shifts, where the robot over-relies on wrist-view cues and executes subtasks in the wrong order upon losing the global view. It proposes CoRe-VLA, a plug-and-play framework incorporating existing VLAs. It reconstructs a scene point cloud and renders the observation from the VLA's training viewpoint. Render-to-Camera (R2C) Restoration reduces rendering-induced visual degradation, and Execution-Trajectory-Conditioned Alignment (ETCA) reduces robot idle time and mitigates motion conflicts during asynchronous execution.
AI.result: Experiments on 5 real-robot tasks, LIBERO-100 and LIBERO-Plus show substantial success-rate improvements across mainstream VLAs under camera shifts. For instance, CoRe-VLA raises PI0.5's success rate from 13.3% to 83.3% at a 1.6m camera shift in a real-robot environment.
AI.conclusion: CoRe-VLA effectively restores cross-view coordination and improves VLA robustness to camera shifts without extra multi-view data or VLA fine-tuning, offering a practical, plug-and-play solution for reliable deployment.

title: Transformers Stop Thinking Too Early, and a Tiny LoRA Fixes It
summary: Pretrained transformers use little of their depth to follow references in context. Thirteen base models reliably follow only 1.4-3.6 lines, and extra pretrained loops add little. A task-trained rank-8 LoRA at one early layer extends this computation with all model weights frozen. Qwen3-8B improves from 15.5% to 99% exact accuracy on 24-line chains; a longer-trained LoRA reaches 50 lines. Ouro-1.4B reaches 60 lines after four loops and at least 160 after eight. The LoRA starts a relay: program lines pass on their chain identity through a short range of middle layers. Frozen heads read progressively further up the chain, and removing parent-line attention stops the relay. A frozen-model measurement locates the last useful intervention layer within tolerance in three of four held-out models. Task-specific LoRAs also improve MuSiQue. Default answers therefore understate the computation accessible through a tiny edit. Code and an interactive demo are available at https://lunamos.github.io/stop-thinking-too-early/

AI.tldr: Pretrained transformers barely use their depth for in-context reference chains (base models follow only 1.4-3.6 lines). A task-trained rank-8 LoRA on one early layer, with all base weights frozen, extends this to 24-50 lines in Qwen3-8B and 60-160 lines in Ouro-1.4B via a mid-layer "relay" mechanism.
AI.motivation: Pretrained transformers appear to use little of their depth when following references in context, and extra pretrained loops add little. The authors aim to show that default answers understate the computation accessible through a tiny edit, prompting the question of why depth is underused and whether a minimal modification can unlock it.
AI.method: They train a task-specific rank-8 LoRA at one early layer while freezing all model weights. They experiment on Qwen3-8B and Ouro-1.4B (with recurrent loops) on exact-accuracy reference-chain tasks (24 to 50-line chains), plus MuSiQue. They analyze the mechanism via parent-line attention removal, frozen-head probing, and a frozen-model measurement that localizes the last useful intervention layer.
AI.result: Thirteen base models reliably follow only 1.4-3.6 lines. Qwen3-8B improves from 15.5% to 99% exact accuracy on 24-line chains; a longer-trained LoRA reaches 50 lines. Ouro-1.4B reaches 60 lines after four loops and at least 160 after eight. The LoRA starts a relay where program lines pass on their chain identity through a short range of middle layers; frozen heads read progressively further up the chain, and removing parent-line attention stops the relay. The frozen-model measurement locates the last useful intervention layer within tolerance in three of four held-out models. Task-specific LoRAs also improve MuSiQue.
AI.conclusion: A tiny rank-8 LoRA edit can substantially unlock latent in-context reference-following computation, with a reproducible relay mechanism and a transferable layer-localization measurement. Default answers therefore understate the computation accessible through a minimal edit. Code and an interactive demo are available.

title: Disentangling Spurious Correlations in Vision-Language-Action Models via Predicting Domain-Invariant Latent Lookahead
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026. Project website: https://dill-vla.github.io/
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models remain brittle under visual distribution shifts, often relying on spurious correlations tied to domain-specific factors rather than task-relevant structure. We propose Domain-Invariant Latent Lookahead (DILL), a representation-learning framework that mitigates shortcut learning in VLA policies. Our key idea is to supervise policies with domain-invariant future latents learned from domain-transformed trajectory data. A Task-Domain Encoder is trained with contrastive objectives and Gaussian disentanglement regularization to separate task-relevant structure from domain-specific visual variation. The learned encoder then provides future latents for VLA policy learning through lookahead prediction and domain disentanglement, encouraging the policy to focus on task-relevant structure rather than incidental visual factors. Counterfactual task-view evaluations show that DILL reduces shortcut reliance, while LIBERO-Plus evaluations demonstrate improved visual robustness, with 69.1% average success, 11.4 percentage points above the strongest baseline. Real-world manipulation experiments further support DILL's applicability beyond controlled simulation. Complementary latent-space diagnostics show that these behavioral gains are accompanied by representations that better preserve task-consistent structure while suppressing domain-specific variation. Our project page is available at https://dill-vla.github.io/.

AI.tldr: DILL is a representation-learning framework that mitigates shortcut learning in Vision-Language-Action policies by supervising them with domain-invariant future latents, improving visual robustness and real-world manipulation performance.
AI.motivation: VLA models remain brittle under visual distribution shifts, often relying on spurious correlations tied to domain-specific factors rather than task-relevant structure.
AI.method: DILL supervises VLA policies with domain-invariant future latents learned from domain-transformed trajectory data. A Task-Domain Encoder is trained with contrastive objectives and Gaussian disentanglement regularization to separate task-relevant structure from domain-specific visual variation. The encoder provides future latents via lookahead prediction and domain disentanglement.
AI.result: Counterfactual task-view evaluations show reduced shortcut reliance. LIBERO-Plus evaluations achieve 69.1% average success, 11.4 percentage points above the strongest baseline. Real-world manipulation experiments support applicability beyond simulation, and latent-space diagnostics show representations preserving task-consistent structure while suppressing domain-specific variation.
AI.conclusion: DILL effectively reduces shortcut learning in VLA policies, improving visual robustness and generalization in both simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.

title: SAKI: Maximal-Coupling-Routed Teacher Supervision for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) reduces train-test state mismatch by training a student on its own generated trajectories, but weak students may visit teacher-misaligned prefixes where supervision is less representative. We introduce SAKI (Supervision Allocation with KL-constrained Interpolation), which combines a KL-constrained teacher-guided rollout with maximal coupling and reuses realized accept/correction events to route token-level supervision. Accepted positions retain sampled-token reverse-KL supervision, while correction positions receive direct supervision on the teacher's highest-probability token. Under maximal coupling, the correction probability is exactly TV(p_t, q_t), so the same trust-region radius controls rollout deviation and upper-bounds intervention and specialized-supervision frequency. We further implement an engine-resident speculative verifier that preserves the exact-q trajectory distribution and coupling semantics while improving matched-workload rollout throughput by 4.22x. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SAKI improves the matched teacher-guided baseline in Mean@8 and Pass@8 for both 1.7B and 0.6B students. Placement controls and fixed-prefix analysis further support correction-triggered routing as a conflict-adaptive supervision signal.

AI.tldr: SAKI combines KL-constrained teacher-guided rollouts with maximal coupling to route token-level supervision, retaining sampled-token reverse-KL on accepted positions and teacher-top-token supervision on correction positions, yielding a controllable intervention budget and improved math reasoning distillation.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation reduces train-test state mismatch by training a student on its own trajectories, but weak students may reach teacher-misaligned prefixes where supervision is unrepresentative. The paper aims to allocate supervision adaptively where student and teacher distributions conflict.
AI.method: SAKI (Supervision Allocation with KL-constrained Interpolation): (1) a KL-constrained teacher-guided rollout using maximal coupling; (2) reuse of realized accept/correction events to route supervision — accepted positions keep sampled-token reverse-KL supervision, correction positions get direct supervision on teacher's argmax token; (3) theoretical result that correction probability equals TV(p_t, q_t), so one trust-region radius bounds rollout deviation, interventions, and specialized-supervision frequency; (4) an engine-resident speculative verifier preserving exact-q trajectory distribution and coupling semantics, giving 4.22x matched-workload rollout throughput.
AI.result: On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SAKI improves the matched teacher-guided baseline in Mean@8 and Pass@8 for both 1.7B and 0.6B students. Placement controls and fixed-prefix analysis support correction-triggered routing as a conflict-adaptive supervision signal. The speculative verifier achieves 4.22x throughput improvement while preserving exact trajectory distribution.
AI.conclusion: Correction-triggered token-level routing, grounded in maximal coupling and controlled by a single KL radius, provides an effective conflict-adaptive supervision signal for on-policy distillation, improving reasoning performance across model scales with efficient rollout implementation.

title: EgoHumanoid-V2: Human-to-Humanoid Transfer of Coordinated Whole-Body Skills for Loco-Manipulation
summary: Human demonstrations capture diverse scenes and rich whole-body skills without requiring robot teleoperation. Prior work on egocentric transfer has emphasized scene generalization in loco-manipulation under decoupled control, leaving direct transfer of coordinated whole-body skills less explored. We present EgoHumanoid-V2, the first egocentric human-to-humanoid skill transfer framework for coordinated whole-body loco-manipulation. At its core, coarse-to-fine action alignment combines kinematic reference correction with dynamics-aware refinement. It improves end-effector pose accuracy while preserving whole-body coordination. We also use robot-arm rendering and training-time image augmentation to reduce the visual embodiment gap and improve viewpoint robustness. On four real-world tasks, vision-language-action (VLA) policies trained on aligned human data show zero-shot skill transfer without target-task robot demonstrations. Task scores are comparable to those of policies trained on teleoperation data at a lower collection cost. These results support human data as direct skill supervision.

AI.tldr: EgoHumanoid-V2 is the first egocentric human-to-humanoid framework for coordinated whole-body loco-manipulation, using coarse-to-fine action alignment and visual embodiment-gap reduction to enable zero-shot skill transfer from human data to VLA policies.
AI.motivation: Human demonstrations offer diverse scenes and rich whole-body skills without needing robot teleoperation, but prior egocentric transfer work focused only on scene generalization in loco-manipulation under decoupled control. Direct transfer of coordinated whole-body skills remained underexplored.
AI.method: The framework applies coarse-to-fine action alignment: kinematic reference correction followed by dynamics-aware refinement, improving end-effector pose accuracy while preserving whole-body coordination. It also uses robot-arm rendering and training-time image augmentation to reduce the visual embodiment gap and boost viewpoint robustness.
AI.result: On four real-world tasks, VLA policies trained on aligned human data achieved zero-shot skill transfer without target-task robot demonstrations. Task scores were comparable to policies trained on teleoperation data, at a lower collection cost.
AI.conclusion: The results support human data as direct skill supervision for humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation, validating egocentric human-to-humanoid transfer as a viable and cost-effective alternative to teleoperation.

title: Multi-Channel Mitigation of Source-Trust Shortcuts in Fact-Checking RL Agents
summary: Retrieval-augmented fact-checkers often receive a reliability label, such as HIGH or LOW trust, for each evidence source. These labels should adjust the model's confidence and its decision to search for more evidence, while the verdict should follow the evidence content. We introduce TrustSwap, a counterfactual test that swaps, lowers, or removes source labels while keeping every evidence text fixed, and measures its three output channels (the verdict, the confidence, and the search decision) separately. Across untrained and RL-trained models at two scales, three datasets, and two prompts, confidence and search respond to the labels as intended in 49 of 50 comparisons, yet a label change alone alters 4-23% of confident verdicts for Qwen3 models and up to 50% for an existing RL-trained fact-checker. Standard GRPO fine-tuning amplifies this shortcut at 8B in all six settings. To reduce it, we propose trust-swap augmentation (TSA), which trains GRPO on each claim with both its original and its label-swapped evidence under the same gold verdict. At 4B, TSA lowers the verdict flip rate by 7-35% (relative) in four of six settings, keeps accuracy and the intended confidence and search responses, outperforms reward-based alternatives in the main setting, and carries over to an unseen label-removal perturbation. An added consistency reward helps on the trained-on swap but not on unseen perturbations. At 8B, TSA's effect is not detectable, which makes scale the main open question.

AI.tldr: TrustSwap is a counterfactual test showing that fact-checkers can be biased by source reliability labels: changing labels alone flips many verdicts, and GRPO fine-tuning amplifies this shortcut; trust-swap augmentation (TSA) mitigates it at 4B but not at 8B.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented fact-checkers receive reliability labels (e.g., HIGH/LOW trust) for each evidence source. These labels should only modulate the model's confidence and search decisions, while the verdict should be determined by evidence content. This work investigates whether models improperly let such labels influence the verdict itself — a reliability-label shortcut.
AI.method: TrustSwap is a counterfactual test that swaps, lowers, or removes source labels while keeping evidence text fixed, and measures three output channels separately: verdict, confidence, and search decision. Evaluation spans untrained and RL-trained models at two scales, three datasets, and two prompts. To mitigate the shortcut, the authors propose trust-swap augmentation (TSA), which trains GRPO on each claim with both its original and label-swapped evidence under the same gold verdict. A consistency reward variant is also tested.
AI.result: Confidence and search respond appropriately to labels in 49 of 50 comparisons, but label changes alone flip 4-23% of confident verdicts for Qwen3 models and up to 50% for an existing RL-trained fact-checker. Standard GRPO fine-tuning amplifies the shortcut at 8B in all six settings. TSA at 4B reduces the verdict flip rate by 7-35% (relative) in four of six settings, preserves accuracy and intended confidence/search responses, outperforms reward-based alternatives, and generalizes to unseen label removal. The consistency reward helps only on the trained-on swap, not on unseen perturbations. At 8B, TSA's effect is not detectable.
AI.conclusion: Source reliability labels act as a shortcut affecting verdicts, and GRPO training can amplify it. TSA mitigates the shortcut at 4B while maintaining accuracy and intended label-conditioned behavior, but scale is a critical factor since TSA's benefit vanishes at 8B. The main open question is why scale modulates the effectiveness of the mitigation.

title: Recovering the View: Benchmarking Physical Active Vision for Occlusion Recovery in Robotic Manipulation
summary: Physical active vision allows robots to change their viewpoint when task-relevant observations become unreliable, yet existing manipulation benchmarks provide limited support for studying how policies recover from occlusion during execution. We introduce BAVO-Bench (Bimanual Active Vision under Occlusion), a bimanual active-vision benchmark that systematically controls external visibility through Clean, Stage Occlusion, and Random-time Occlusion conditions, enabling evaluation of both manipulation performance and active visual recovery. Building on this setting, we present A-FAR (Active Future-Aware Recovery), an active-vision policy for joint viewpoint and manipulation control. A-FAR represents moving-camera observations in a unified robot-centric 3D frame and distills relational structure together with its future evolution from a pretrained 4D model, providing the policy with future-aware geometric guidance without requiring future observations at deployment. Experiments across multiple manipulation tasks show that A-FAR improves robustness to both structured and temporally shifted occlusions while maintaining strong performance under clean observations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BAVO-Bench, a bimanual active-vision benchmark with controlled occlusion conditions, and A-FAR, a future-aware active-vision policy that improves robustness to occlusion while maintaining clean-observation performance.
AI.motivation: Robots with physical active vision can change viewpoints when task-relevant observations become unreliable, but existing manipulation benchmarks offer limited support for studying how policies recover from occlusion during execution.
AI.method: The paper proposes BAVO-Bench, which systematically controls external visibility via Clean, Stage Occlusion, and Random-time Occlusion conditions to evaluate manipulation and active visual recovery. It also presents A-FAR, which represents moving-camera observations in a unified robot-centric 3D frame and distills relational structure and its future evolution from a pretrained 4D model, enabling future-aware geometric guidance without future observations at deployment.
AI.result: Across multiple manipulation tasks, A-FAR improves robustness to both structured and temporally shifted occlusions while maintaining strong performance under clean observations.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a benchmark and policy framework for bimanual active vision under occlusion, demonstrating that future-aware geometric guidance supports effective visual recovery and robust manipulation.

title: Neural Structural Reasoner: A Brain-inspired Architecture for Reasoning over Structured Knowledge
summary: Structural reasoning, the ability to recognize and make inferences over the relational structure between objects and concepts, is a hallmark of human cognition, yet prevailing methods often collapse relational topology into flat embeddings, cannot discover hidden structure and lack interpretability. We introduce Neural Structural Reasoner (NSR), a brain-inspired network that preserves relational structure directly in the connectivity and dynamics of coupled neuronal populations. NSR draws inspiration from three biological mechanisms: multi-layered architecture for encoding hierarchical knowledge, stable representations of entity and concepts, and path integration for input-driven state inference. At query time, NSR parallelizes computation over candidate relational structures and leverages confidence-weighted scores to perform link prediction. Across standard knowledge-graph benchmarks, NSR achieves competitive accuracy without leading on every dataset, and has lower reported training times than several neural baselines. Because reasoning is implemented through sequences of human-readable neuron activations, NSR affords native interpretability by tracking intermediate inference steps. The model further extracts latent relational hierarchies and compositional rules, demonstrating the brain-inspired architecture as an effective, efficient, and highly interpretable substrate for structural reasoning.

AI.tldr: NSR is a brain-inspired network that encodes relational structure directly in the connectivity and dynamics of coupled neuronal populations, achieving competitive link-prediction accuracy with lower training times and native interpretability.
AI.motivation: Structural reasoning is fundamental to human cognition, but prevailing methods collapse relational topology into flat embeddings, cannot discover hidden structure, and lack interpretability.
AI.method: NSR preserves relational structure in the connectivity and dynamics of coupled neuronal populations, drawing on three biological mechanisms: a multi-layered architecture for hierarchical knowledge, stable entity/concept representations, and path integration for input-driven state inference. At query time it parallelizes computation over candidate relational structures and uses confidence-weighted scores for link prediction.
AI.result: On standard knowledge-graph benchmarks, NSR attains competitive accuracy (without leading on every dataset) and lower reported training times than several neural baselines. Its human-readable neuron activations yield native interpretability via traceable intermediate inference steps, and it extracts latent relational hierarchies and compositional rules.
AI.conclusion: The brain-inspired architecture proves to be an effective, efficient, and highly interpretable substrate for structural reasoning.

title: Remember What You Did: Action-History Memory with Dual-Expert Denoising for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have driven rapid progress in robotic manipulation, demonstrating strong fine-grained control and promising performance on long-horizon tasks. However, many existing VLAs lack explicit access to interaction history, making them vulnerable to perceptual aliasing: similar current observations and robot states at different task stages may induce action ambiguity and lower success rate. Existing methods incorporate temporal or progress cues through feature conditioning, action-prior modification, or sampling guidance. However, methods that jointly fine-tune memory modules and the base VLA incur additional policy-training costs, motivating the separation of trainable history-conditioned steering from frozen base-policy refinement. We propose ActMem-VLA, a dual-expert handover architecture that augments a frozen, fine-tuned VLA with a memory plugin comprising a Mamba-based memory module and a lightweight PreAction Expert (PAE). Specifically, Mamba encodes executed-action history into memory that conditions PAE alongside current context. With these inputs, PAE steers task progression during early, high-noise denoising, then passes the partially denoised action to the frozen Action Expert (AE) to refine action details during the remaining low-noise steps. The fine-tuned base VLA remains frozen throughout training, while only the Mamba module and PAE are jointly optimized. On LIBERO-Mem, ActMem-VLA achieves 80.8\% average success across all ten tasks, compared with 65.2\% for $π_{0.5}$ and 49.5\% for MemoryVLA, while introducing only 3.45\% additional parameters. Across four real-world tasks, it improves the average success rate over $π_{0.5}$ by 28.8\%.

AI.tldr: ActMem-VLA augments a frozen, fine-tuned VLA with a trainable memory plugin (Mamba memory + PreAction Expert), achieving state-of-the-art results on memory-dependent manipulation tasks with minimal parameter overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models lack explicit access to interaction history, causing perceptual aliasing where similar observations at different task stages lead to action ambiguity and reduced success rates. Prior memory/progress-cue methods face high joint policy-training costs, motivating separation of trainable history-conditioned steering from frozen base-policy refinement.
AI.method: ActMem-VLA is a dual-expert handover architecture combining a frozen, fine-tuned VLA with a memory plugin. A Mamba-based module encodes executed-action history into memory that conditions a lightweight PreAction Expert (PAE) along with current context. PAE steers task progression during early high-noise denoising, then hands the partially denoised action to the frozen Action Expert (AE) for refinement over the remaining low-noise steps. Only the Mamba module and PAE are optimized; the base VLA stays frozen.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Mem, ActMem-VLA reaches 80.8% average success across all ten tasks vs. 65.2% for π0.5 and 49.5% for MemoryVLA, adding only 3.45% extra parameters. On four real-world tasks, it improves average success over π0.5 by 28.8%.
AI.conclusion: Separating trainable, history-conditioned steering (Mamba memory + PAE) from a frozen base policy effectively resolves perceptual aliasing in VLAs, yielding large success-rate gains on memory-dependent manipulation at negligible parameter cost.

title: DualTrack: Synchronized speech-gesture generation via symmetric coupling of pretrained priors
summary: Joint speech-gesture synthesis must coordinate two modalities despite limited paired data. Existing approaches often lack bidirectional interaction, have limited language coverage, or simplify body and finger representations. We present DualTrack, which couples pretrained speech and motion priors on a shared 12.5 Hz timeline. Causal adapters exchange previous-packet information, while current-state fusion coordinates the streams before they separately complete sixteen-codebook packets. We evaluate 43 BEAT2 recordings in four languages, with speakers held out from joint training and validation. On the shared English/Spanish inputs, without speech or motion prefixes, DualTrack achieves lower word error rate and full-motion Fréchet Gesture Distance, higher beat consistency and speech naturalness than the evaluated GELINA baseline.

AI.tldr: DualTrack couples pretrained speech and motion priors on a shared 12.5 Hz timeline using causal adapters and current-state fusion, achieving improved joint speech-gesture synthesis.
AI.motivation: Joint speech-gesture synthesis requires coordinating two modalities despite limited paired data, and existing approaches lack bidirectional interaction, have limited language coverage, or oversimplify body and finger representations.
AI.method: DualTrack couples pretrained speech and motion priors on a shared 12.5 Hz timeline. Causal adapters exchange previous-packet information, and current-state fusion coordinates the streams before they separately complete sixteen-codebook packets.
AI.result: Evaluated on 43 BEAT2 recordings in four languages with speakers held out from joint training and validation, DualTrack on shared English/Spanish inputs without speech or motion prefixes achieves lower word error rate and full-motion Fréchet Gesture Distance, higher beat consistency, and higher speech naturalness than the GELINA baseline.
AI.conclusion: DualTrack demonstrates that coupling pretrained unimodal priors with bidirectional cross-modal interaction enables more effective joint speech-gesture synthesis.

title: Battery-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Aggressive Quadrotor Flight
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ICRA 2027. Supplementary video: https://youtu.be/-JTRXvstFAo
summary: Agile flight tasks such as drone racing and pursuit-evasion require strong acceleration and precise turns, but the available thrust changes as the battery discharges and voltage drops under load. Conservative command limits make this variation easier to tolerate, at the cost of unused performance. We investigate how learned controllers can use that additional thrust while retaining the flight controller's voltage compensation and rate control. Our training simulator couples an identified load-transient battery model to rotor dynamics and firmware saturation. The feedforward policy receives filtered voltage during both training and deployment. Controlled ablations distinguish the benefit of a larger thrust-command range from that of voltage information. On a 38 g Crazyflie Brushless, the resulting policy reduces circle tracking error by 49% relative to stock-authority RL at 3.84 m/s, while preserving easy-task precision. Mean 20-lap race time decreases from 106.22 s to 95.24 s. Compared with a voltage-blind policy with the same increased authority, hardware error and race time are lower by 15.3% and 4.5%, respectively. In simulation, replacing the policy's voltage input with a recording from a different battery condition worsens hard-circle tracking, with a smaller, voltage-dependent effect in racing. Together, these results show where a simple voltage input complements existing actuator compensation in aggressive learned flight.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how learned controllers can exploit battery-voltage-dependent thrust headroom while retaining existing voltage compensation and rate control, showing that feeding filtered voltage to a feedforward RL policy improves aggressive quadrotor flight.
AI.motivation: Agile flight tasks like drone racing and pursuit-evasion need strong acceleration and precise turns, but available thrust varies as the battery discharges and voltage sags under load. Conventional conservative command limits tolerate this variation at the cost of unused performance. The authors aim to let learned controllers use that extra thrust without discarding the flight controller's voltage compensation and rate control.
AI.method: A training simulator couples an identified load-transient battery model to rotor dynamics and firmware saturation. The feedforward policy receives filtered voltage during both training and deployment. Controlled ablations separate the benefit of a larger thrust-command range from that of voltage information. Hardware experiments use a 38 g Crazyflie Brushless, plus simulation studies replacing the voltage input with a recording from a different battery condition.
AI.result: The policy reduces circle tracking error by 49% versus stock-authority RL at 3.84 m/s while preserving easy-task precision; mean 20-lap race time drops from 106.22 s to 95.24 s. Compared with a voltage-blind policy using the same increased authority, hardware error and race time are lower by 15.3% and 4.5%. In simulation, mismatched voltage input worsens hard-circle tracking, with a smaller, voltage-dependent effect in racing.
AI.conclusion: A simple filtered voltage input complements existing actuator compensation in aggressive learned flight, enabling greater use of available thrust on hard tasks without sacrificing precision on easy ones.

title: Semantic Projection for Continual Self-Evolution of Language Agents
summary: Language-model agents increasingly rely on persistent natural-language skills to adapt beyond their frozen model parameters. When a shared skill is repeatedly revised from a non-stationary, heterogeneous task stream, however, improvements for new tasks can overwrite procedures needed for earlier ones. In continual learning, Orthogonal Gradient Descent (OGD) addresses analogous interference by projecting a new-task gradient onto a subspace that locally preserves prior predictions. Natural-language skill revisions, however, have neither gradients nor a canonical vector space in which such a projection can be performed. We introduce \emph{Semantic-Scope Projected Evolution} (SSPE), which transfers the functional principle of gradient projection from parameter space to behavior space. SSPE treats an unconstrained skill revision as a proposed update, identifies acquired capabilities with which it may interfere, and uses the observed gains and regressions to construct a compatible revision rather than merely rejecting the update. This enables one shared skill to evolve across latent and recurring task contexts without exposing semantic domain identities to the evolution model. Across controlled synthetic streams and heterogeneous real-agent benchmarks, SSPE improves final cross-domain competence and mitigates forgetting relative to strong skill-evolution baselines. The evolved skill also retains the strongest average performance after transfer to a different executor model. These results establish semantic projection as a promising principle for stable and adaptive self evolution of language agents.

AI.tldr: SSPE transfers orthogonal gradient descent's projection principle from parameter space to behavior space, enabling a shared natural-language skill to evolve across a non-stationary task stream without overwriting earlier capabilities.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents rely on persistent natural-language skills to adapt beyond frozen parameters. When such a shared skill is repeatedly revised from a non-stationary, heterogeneous task stream, gains on new tasks can overwrite procedures needed for earlier ones. Orthogonal Gradient Descent mitigates analogous interference in continual learning by projecting new-task gradients onto a subspace preserving prior predictions, but natural-language skill revisions have neither gradients nor a canonical vector space for such projection.
AI.method: Semantic-Scope Projected Evolution (SSPE) transfers the functional principle of gradient projection from parameter space to behavior space. It treats an unconstrained skill revision as a proposed update, identifies acquired capabilities with which it may interfere, and uses observed gains and regressions to construct a compatible revision rather than merely rejecting the update. This allows one shared skill to evolve across latent and recurring task contexts without exposing semantic domain identities to the evolution model.
AI.result: Across controlled synthetic streams and heterogeneous real-agent benchmarks, SSPE improves final cross-domain competence and mitigates forgetting relative to strong skill-evolution baselines. The evolved skill also retains the strongest average performance after transfer to a different executor model.
AI.conclusion: Semantic projection is established as a promising principle for stable and adaptive self-evolution of language agents.

title: Taming VLAs under Robot Execution Errors: Self-Compensation and Stress Testing
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies often fail when a robot's executed motion deviates from their commanded action. Such execution errors arise from the robot's mechanics and operating conditions, such as wear and payload changes. We propose self-compensating VLA, a deployment-time adaptation method that enables a VLA policy to pre-compensate for the robot's execution errors when generating commands. Without task rewards or labels, it updates the policy online using the residual between the action commanded by a VLA and the motion executed by the robot. To stress-test VLA robustness across execution conditions that are impractical to cover with physical robots alone, we introduce RoboStress, a controlled simulation benchmark. It combines established joint-level models of friction, backlash, compliance, and gravity-compensation error into seven deployment scenarios whose execution errors depend on the robot's state and motion history. On RoboStress, self-compensating VLA achieves higher average task success than both the base policies and methods that build in robustness during training. On two physical robot arms with different usage histories, it raises the average task success rate by more than 30 percentage points on each arm, and the gains extend to objects not seen in the task demonstrations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes self-compensating VLA, a deployment-time online adaptation method that uses the residual between commanded and executed actions to pre-compensate robot execution errors, and introduces RoboStress, a simulation benchmark of seven deployment scenarios modeling friction, backlash, compliance, and gravity-compensation error. It outperforms base policies and training-time robustness methods in simulation, and improves real-robot task success by over 30 percentage points on two arms.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action policies often fail when the robot's executed motion deviates from the commanded action. These execution errors stem from robot mechanics and operating conditions, such as wear and payload changes, which the policy does not account for.
AI.method: Self-compensating VLA updates the policy online at deployment time, without task rewards or labels, using the residual between the action commanded by the VLA and the motion actually executed by the robot, so that the policy pre-compensates for execution errors when generating commands. To evaluate robustness across execution conditions impractical to cover with physical robots alone, the authors build RoboStress, a controlled simulation benchmark combining established joint-level models of friction, backlash, compliance, and gravity-compensation error into seven deployment scenarios whose execution errors depend on robot state and motion history.
AI.result: On RoboStress, self-compensating VLA achieves higher average task success than base policies and methods that build in robustness during training. On two physical robot arms with different usage histories, it raises average task success by more than 30 percentage points on each arm, with gains generalizing to objects unseen in the task demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: Deployment-time residual-based self-compensation is an effective way to make VLA policies robust to execution errors arising from robot mechanics and operating conditions, improving both simulated and real-world task success, including generalization to unseen objects.

title: Distilling Agentic Systems: A Roadmap across Models, Artifacts, and Harnesses
summary: Modern agents increasingly rely on memories, tools, and execution logic, so their competence extends beyond model parameters. This shift exposes a limitation of conventional knowledge distillation, which asks how a student model imitates a teacher model. We define Agent Distillation as the persistent transfer of task-solving knowledge from a teacher agent to a student agent. Our study organizes the field by where transferred knowledge is retained: within the model, as artifacts, through the execution harness, or across substrates. This perspective separates transfer evidence from its outcome and clarifies how knowledge moves between agent components. We develop an evaluation framework that relates retention to causal contribution and deployed utility. Together, these contributions establish a foundation for the reliable, maintainable, and safe development of increasingly complex agentic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper defines "Agent Distillation" as the persistent transfer of task-solving knowledge between agents, and organizes the field by where the transferred knowledge is retained.
AI.motivation: Modern agents' competence depends not only on model parameters but also on memories, tools, and execution logic. This exposes limits of conventional knowledge distillation (student imitating teacher), motivating a broader framing of knowledge transfer across agent components.
AI.method: The authors define Agent Distillation and provide a taxonomy/positioning organizing the field by where transferred knowledge is retained: within the model, as artifacts, through the execution harness, or across substrates. They also develop an evaluation framework relating retention to causal contribution and deployed utility.
AI.result: The framework separates transfer evidence from its outcome and clarifies how knowledge moves between agent components, offering an organizing lens and evaluation criteria.
AI.conclusion: These contributions establish a foundation for reliable, maintainable, and safe development of increasingly complex agentic systems.

title: DROM: A Language-Guided Diffusion Framework for Multi-Skill Robotic Manipulation
summary: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse, long-horizon tasks from limited demonstrations remains a fundamental challenge in robotics. We present DROM, a language-guided diffusion framework that enables robots to learn, represent, and compose multiple manipulation skills within a single generative policy. DROM leverages Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) to augment a small set of expert demonstrations into expressive multi-skill datasets, substantially reducing data collection while improving spatial generalization beyond the demonstrated workspace. Building upon Motion Planning Diffusion (MPD), we extend the diffusion architecture to support language-conditioned multi-skill trajectory generation through cross-attention, allowing a single model to generate skill-consistent motions for a diverse set of manipulation primitives, including orientation-sensitive behaviors that are difficult to design using conventional motion planning or hard-coded controllers. For long-horizon manipulation, a large language model decomposes high-level operator requests into executable sequences of skills, enabling natural language interaction and autonomous task execution. We validate DROM on a Franka Emika Panda robot, a FANUC CRX25ia robot, and in MuJoCo simulation across a wide range of manipulation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that DROM outperforms Motion Planning Diffusion and Behavior Cloning baselines, achieves robust multi-skill generalization, and composes learned skills to reliably execute long-horizon manipulation tasks from natural language instructions using only a limited number of human demonstrations. Datasets, simulation environments, and more at https://github.com/automation-robotics-machines/drom.

AI.tldr: DROM is a language-guided diffusion framework that learns, represents, and composes multiple manipulation skills in a single generative policy using limited demonstrations, validated across real robots and simulation.
AI.motivation: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse, long-horizon tasks from limited demonstrations remains a fundamental challenge in robotics. Existing approaches struggle with data efficiency, spatial generalization, orientation-sensitive behaviors, and skill composition.
AI.method: DROM leverages Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) to augment a small set of expert demonstrations into expressive multi-skill datasets. Building on Motion Planning Diffusion (MPD), it extends the diffusion architecture with cross-attention for language-conditioned multi-skill trajectory generation. For long-horizon tasks, a large language model decomposes high-level operator requests into executable skill sequences.
AI.result: Validated on a Franka Emika Panda robot, a FANUC CRX25ia robot, and in MuJoCo simulation, DROM outperforms Motion Planning Diffusion and Behavior Cloning baselines, achieving robust multi-skill generalization and reliable long-horizon task execution from natural language instructions with only a limited number of human demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: DROM enables data-efficient, language-guided acquisition and composition of multiple manipulation skills within a single generative policy, supporting natural language interaction and autonomous long-horizon task execution.

title: RankBuffer: Efficient Ranking-Based Rewards for Open-Ended Generation
summary: Open-ended generation lacks canonical answers, making pointwise rewards difficult to calibrate for group-based reinforcement learning. Directly ranking same-query rollouts provides a more suitable relative reward signal, but existing ranking-based reward methods can incur substantial judging cost. We introduce RankBuffer, which maintains an ordered, query-specific buffer of previously judged responses as a reusable quality scale. Each rollout is first inserted into an anchor interval through an independent coarse judgment, after which only rollouts assigned to the same interval undergo local fine ranking. The resulting complete order is converted into bounded rank rewards, while boundary expansion, local refinement, and inactive-anchor pruning adapt the buffer as the policy evolves. Across four open-ended benchmarks, RankBuffer consistently outperforms all pointwise baselines. It also achieves nearly on-par performance with the strongest ranking-based reward baseline while substantially reducing judging cost. Ablations demonstrate the importance of both local fine ranking and anchor response content, while buffer analyses show that rollout-derived anchors progressively extend and refine the covered quality scale. These results establish response reuse as an effective approach to efficient relative reward construction.

AI.tldr: RankBuffer constructs relative rewards for group-based RL by reusing previously judged responses as a query-specific ordered quality scale, enabling efficient ranking-based rewards.
AI.motivation: Open-ended generation lacks canonical answers, so pointwise rewards are hard to calibrate; ranking same-query rollouts provides a better relative signal but existing ranking methods incur high judging cost.
AI.method: RankBuffer maintains an ordered, query-specific buffer of previously judged responses. Each rollout is inserted into an anchor interval via coarse judgment; only rollouts in the same interval undergo local fine ranking. The complete order yields bounded rank rewards, and boundary expansion, local refinement, and inactive-anchor pruning adapt the buffer as the policy evolves.
AI.result: Across four open-ended benchmarks, RankBuffer consistently outperforms all pointwise baselines and matches the strongest ranking-based baseline with substantially lower judging cost. Ablations confirm the value of local fine ranking and anchor content; buffer analyses show rollout-derived anchors progressively extend and refine the covered quality scale.
AI.conclusion: Response reuse is an effective approach for constructing efficient relative rewards in group-based reinforcement learning.

title: Encore: Few-Shot Agentic Discovery of Manipulation Strategies
summary: Coding agents can now write, run, and debug programs with little human help. Robot tasks, however, are usually specified by a sentence that leaves out how to grasp, in what order to make contact, and what the result should look like, and an agent given only the sentence must find these details by trial and error. We introduce ENCORE, which gives the agent a few demonstrations as evidence to read rather than as training data. A deterministic builder distills each demonstration into a pack of multi-view keyframes, gripper events, frame strips, and the full trajectory. A coding agent studies the pack, writes a policy program against a fixed perception and action API, refines it iteratively over a few development rollouts, and freezes it before a sealed evaluation that never reveals the success signal. On LIBERO-PRO, the agent's first program already succeeds in half of the perturbed tasks with demonstrations and in one task without them, and the frozen programs outperform the strongest prior agentic system run with the same language model (96.3% against 89.3%). On RoboDojo tasks whose instructions leave the goal unstated, no program succeeds without demonstrations. ENCORE also runs on a real bimanual robot, learning cube handover and cup inversion from five demonstrations each.

AI.tldr: ENCORE enables a coding agent to solve robot tasks by reading a few demonstrations as evidence (multi-view keyframes, gripper events, frame strips, trajectories) rather than training on them, writing a policy program against a fixed API, then freezing it for sealed evaluation.
AI.motivation: Robot tasks are underspecified by a single sentence—grasp, contact order, and success criteria are omitted—so an agent must discover these by trial and error. Demonstrations are typically used as training data, but the authors instead want to use them as readable evidence for a coding agent.
AI.method: A deterministic builder distills each demonstration into a pack of multi-view keyframes, gripper events, frame strips, and the full trajectory. A coding agent studies the pack, writes a policy program against a fixed perception and action API, refines it iteratively over a few development rollouts, and freezes it before a sealed evaluation that never reveals the success signal.
AI.result: On LIBERO-PRO, the first program succeeds in half of the perturbed tasks with demonstrations and one task without them; frozen programs reach 96.3% versus 89.3% for the strongest prior agentic system with the same language model. On RoboDojo tasks with unstated goals, no program succeeds without demonstrations. ENCORE also works on a real bimanual robot, learning cube handover and cup inversion from five demonstrations each.
AI.conclusion: Treating demonstrations as evidence for program synthesis, rather than training data, lets a coding agent produce effective frozen robot policies, outperforming prior agentic systems and transferring to real bimanual hardware.

title: FineSID: Scalable and Efficient Semantic Identifier Learning for Generative Recommendation
summary: A critical prerequisite of generative recommendation is designing semantic identifiers (SIDs) that are both scalable to large item sets and efficiently learnable. Existing SID learning methods fundamentally rely on Top-1 hard assignment during vector quantization. While heuristic strategies -- such as clustering-based initialization or forced post-hoc collision resolution -- can artificially inflate codebook coverage, they often disrupt end-to-end semantic alignment and fail to address the underlying optimization bottleneck: sparse gradient propagation. In standard Top-1 assignment, gradients concentrate on a narrow subset of frequently selected codewords, leaving the majority inherently under-trained and causing severe SID collisions. To overcome this limitation natively without relying on complex initialization priors, we propose FineSID, a unified quantization framework that moves beyond Top-1 assignment by enabling fine-grained gradient propagation across the entire codebook. Instead of updating only a single selected codeword, FineSID distributes learning signals to all codewords in a soft, differentiable manner. This design promotes globally balanced codebook optimization while strictly preserving semantic consistency, effectively alleviating SID collisions and stabilizing training in large, high-dimensional codebooks. Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that FineSID is robust to initialization configurations and consistently improves both codebook utilization and recommendation accuracy. Our work provides a principled, initialization-agnostic solution for semantic identifier learning, advancing the practicality of generative recommendation.

AI.tldr: FineSID replaces Top-1 hard assignment in SID quantization with soft, differentiable gradient propagation across the entire codebook, achieving initialization-agnostic, collision-reduced, and more accurate generative recommendation.
AI.motivation: Generative recommendation requires semantic identifiers (SIDs) that scale to large item sets and are efficiently learnable. Existing SID learning relies on Top-1 hard assignment during vector quantization, which propagates sparse gradients concentrated on a few frequently selected codewords. This leaves most codewords under-trained and causes severe SID collisions. Heuristic fixes (clustering-based initialization, post-hoc collision resolution) inflate codebook coverage artificially, disrupt end-to-end semantic alignment, and do not solve the underlying optimization bottleneck.
AI.method: FineSID is a unified quantization framework that moves beyond Top-1 assignment. Rather than updating only the single selected codeword, it distributes learning signals to all codewords in a soft, differentiable manner, enabling fine-grained gradient propagation across the whole codebook. This promotes globally balanced codebook optimization while preserving semantic consistency, thereby alleviating SID collisions and stabilizing training for large, high-dimensional codebooks without complex initialization priors.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks show that FineSID is robust to initialization configurations and consistently improves both codebook utilization and recommendation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: FineSID offers a principled, initialization-agnostic solution for semantic identifier learning, advancing the practicality of generative recommendation.

title: Towards Spatial Perception for Heterogeneous Robot Collaboration in Subterranean Mining Environments
summary: The autonomous extraction of deep mineral deposits in abandoned underground mines is fundamentally a multi-agent integration problem. No single platform simultaneously offers the mobility to traverse kilometers of degraded drifts and the sensing payload required to characterize an ore body. This article presents the onboard perception pipeline that bridges two heterogeneous agents within the PERSEPHONE autonomous mining mission. Which consist of a lightweight Explorer robot that maps an unknown mine and generates a 3D scene graph of inspection targets, by running a zero-shot, vision-language semantic segmentation stack that detects mineral deposits directly from natural-language prompts. The map and the graph are then handed to a second Inspector robot, which carries an advanced sensing payload and uses them to plan close-range inspection viewpoints. We detail the complete pipeline, with emphasis on the geometric abstraction that turns raw detections into actionable inspection targets, spanning per-view bounding-box generation, cross-view box merging, plane fitting, and polygon extraction, and we report an extensive field validation in a subterranean test facility and in an active magnesite mine, covering both iron-vein and magnesite mineralization under realistic, perceptually degraded conditions.

AI.tldr: This article presents PERSEPHONE's onboard perception pipeline that couples a lightweight Explorer robot for vision-language deposit detection and 3D scene-graph mapping with a sensor-rich Inspector robot for close-range inspection planning, validated in an underground test facility and an active magnesite mine.
AI.motivation: Autonomous extraction of deep mineral deposits in abandoned underground mines is a multi-agent integration problem: no single platform offers both the mobility to traverse kilometers of degraded drifts and the sensing payload needed to characterize an ore body. Heterogeneous agents must therefore be bridged, but a perception pipeline that converts one agent's exploration output into actionable targets for another is lacking.
AI.method: Two heterogeneous agents are coupled. The lightweight Explorer robot maps an unknown mine and builds a 3D scene graph of inspection targets using a zero-shot, vision-language semantic segmentation stack that detects mineral deposits directly from natural-language prompts. The map and graph are handed to a second, sensor-rich Inspector robot, which plans close-range inspection viewpoints. The geometric abstraction converting raw detections into actionable targets spans per-view bounding-box generation, cross-view box merging, plane fitting, and polygon extraction.
AI.result: Extensive field validation was conducted in a subterranean test facility and in an active magnesite mine, covering both iron-vein and magnesite mineralization under realistic, perceptually degraded conditions.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline enables heterogeneous multi-agent cooperation for autonomous deep-mineral exploration, with zero-shot vision-language detection feeding a geometrically abstracted target representation that supports downstream close-range inspection planning in degraded underground environments.

title: FairDiff: Mitigating the Self-Reinforcing Matthew Effect in Diffusion Recommender Models
summary: While the "Matthew Effect" and filter bubbles are widely recognized outcome-level biases in recommender systems, we reveal that Diffusion Recommender Models (DRMs) uniquely compound this issue through their generative dynamics. Rather than merely inheriting data imbalances, DRMs trigger a self-reinforcing amplification of popularity bias. We identify that this phenomenon is driven by two compounding mechanisms. First, while optimization loss is universally dominated by high-frequency items across recommenders, DRMs suffer from a unique structural prior mismatch during generation. Because the forward terminal distribution of long-tailed data deviates significantly from the standard Gaussian prior, reverse sampling trajectories inherently collapse toward high-density popular items, fundamentally suppressing niche item generation. To dismantle this self-reinforcing loop, we propose FairDiff, a plug-and-play fairness-aware diffusion framework. To overcome the popularity-dominated loss, we introduce Popularity Condition Guidance (PCG). Rather than altering the training objective, PCG acts as an inference-time distributional reweighting mechanism, mathematically reshaping the score-based gradient field to penalize high-popularity regions and guide trajectories toward niche semantics. Furthermore, we design a Semantic Calibration (SC) Module to bridge the prior mismatch, aligning the forward and reverse distributions via one-step optimal transport. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that FairDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance while effectively mitigating the self-reinforcing Matthew Effect, highlighting its value as a general framework for DRMs.

AI.tldr: Diffusion Recommender Models (DRMs) uniquely amplify popularity bias via a self-reinforcing loop driven by popularity-dominated loss and a structural prior mismatch; FairDiff, a plug-and-play framework combining inference-time Popularity Condition Guidance and a Semantic Calibration module, mitigates this bias while achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: The Matthew Effect and filter bubbles are well-known outcome-level biases in recommender systems, but the authors argue DRMs do more than inherit data imbalance: their generative dynamics actively compound the problem through self-reinforcing popularity amplification. Two mechanisms are identified: (1) although loss is universally dominated by high-frequency items across recommenders, DRMs suffer a unique structural prior mismatch—long-tailed data's forward terminal distribution deviates from the standard Gaussian prior, so reverse sampling collapses toward high-density popular items; (2) this suppresses niche item generation. The goal is to break this self-reinforcing loop.
AI.method: FairDiff is a plug-and-play, fairness-aware diffusion framework with two components. Popularity Condition Guidance (PCG) is an inference-time distributional reweighting mechanism that, without altering the training objective, mathematically reshapes the score-based gradient field to penalize high-popularity regions and steer sampling trajectories toward niche semantics. A Semantic Calibration (SC) module bridges the prior mismatch by aligning forward and reverse distributions via one-step optimal transport.
AI.result: Comprehensive evaluations show that FairDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance while effectively mitigating the self-reinforcing Matthew Effect.
AI.conclusion: FairDiff highlights its value as a general framework for DRMs, addressing a generative-dynamics-level bias rather than only an outcome-level one.

title: FP2: Equipping Robotic Foundation Models with Force Control
summary: Robotic foundation models (RFMs) are increasingly capable of general-purpose manipulation, yet reliable physical interaction remains challenging in contact-rich settings. We present FP2, a lightweight downstream interface that equips task-adapted RFMs with explicit force control while preserving their action-generation capability. FP2 adopts an action-regulation decomposition: the task-adapted RFM serves as a foundation policy responsible for task-level action generation, while a high-frequency force control policy focuses solely on interaction regulation. To condition force regulation on the ongoing manipulation, FP2 compresses foundation-policy contextual representations and combines them with wrench and proprioceptive histories to predict structured force-control parameters. We evaluate FP2 with four RFM backbones across four real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks.
