FP2 consistently improves task performance and force regulation quality over the corresponding foundation policies, while comparing favorably with representative force-aware and force-control baselines. Ablations further show that foundation-policy context and physical feedback are complementary for effective force regulation, while preserving foundation-policy action generation improves both efficiency and novel-object generalization. Project website: http://force-policy.github.io/fp2

AI.tldr: FP2 is a lightweight downstream interface that adds explicit force control to task-adapted robotic foundation models while preserving their action-generation ability, improving contact-rich manipulation performance and force regulation across four RFM backbones and four real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Robotic foundation models (RFMs) are increasingly capable of general-purpose manipulation, but reliable physical interaction remains challenging in contact-rich settings, where explicit force control is typically lacking.
AI.method: FP2 adopts an action-regulation decomposition: the task-adapted RFM acts as a foundation policy generating task-level actions, while a high-frequency force control policy handles interaction regulation. It compresses foundation-policy contextual representations and combines them with wrench and proprioceptive histories to predict structured force-control parameters, conditioning force regulation on the ongoing manipulation.
AI.result: Evaluated with four RFM backbones on four real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, FP2 consistently improves task performance and force regulation quality over the corresponding foundation policies, and compares favorably with representative force-aware and force-control baselines. Ablations show foundation-policy context and physical feedback are complementary, and preserving foundation-policy action generation improves efficiency and novel-object generalization.
AI.conclusion: FP2 provides a lightweight, effective interface that equips task-adapted RFMs with explicit force control without sacrificing their action-generation capability, yielding consistent gains in contact-rich manipulation.

title: MLToolBench: Learning Tool-Augmented Agents for Machine Learning Development
summary: Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents have made substantial progress, but learning through ML experimentation remains costly in time and computation. Synthetic environments reduce these costs while introducing variations in data and experimental settings that require task-specific diagnosis. Access to diagnostic tools alone does not ensure that agents learn when to use them or how to act on their findings. We introduce ToolMLBench, a suite of executable tools for data inspection, code verification, and experiment diagnosis, together with an SFT and RL pipeline for learning their use. Diagnostic calls acquire evidence whose value depends on subsequent decisions, so final outcomes provide limited guidance on which calls to reinforce. We address this challenge with SPICE, which measures how privileged context changes the likelihood of a sampled tool action and uses this difference as a turn-level reward alongside the final outcome. We train on 80 synthetic tasks and evaluate on 25 in-domain and 10 out-of-domain tasks. Providing tool interfaces and descriptions alone yields inconsistent gains across unadapted models. With the same diagnostic interface, our training pipeline raises in-domain success from 24.8% to 52.4% for Qwen3-8B and from 35.6% to 69.2% for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. The latter also improves from 31% to 48% out-of-domain, supporting learned diagnostic tool use on held-out sources and targets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ToolMLBench, a suite of executable diagnostic tools (data inspection, code verification, experiment diagnosis) for ML engineering agents, and SPICE, a turn-level reward that measures how privileged context changes the likelihood of a sampled tool action. Combining SFT and RL with SPICE substantially raises task success for several LLMs.
AI.motivation: Learning through ML experimentation is costly in time and computation, motivating synthetic environments. But such environments introduce variations in data and experimental settings that require task-specific diagnosis. Merely giving agents access to diagnostic tools does not guarantee they learn when to use them or how to act on their findings, and final-outcome rewards give limited guidance on which diagnostic calls to reinforce because a call's value depends on subsequent decisions.
AI.method: ToolMLBench: a suite of executable tools for data inspection, code verification, and experiment diagnosis, paired with an SFT and RL training pipeline. The core technique, SPICE, measures how privileged context changes the likelihood of a sampled tool action and uses that difference as a turn-level reward alongside the final outcome reward. Training spans 80 synthetic tasks; evaluation covers 25 in-domain and 10 out-of-domain tasks.
AI.result: Providing tool interfaces and descriptions alone yields inconsistent gains across unadapted models. With the same diagnostic interface, the training pipeline raises in-domain success from 24.8% to 52.4% for Qwen3-8B and from 35.6% to 69.2% for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. The 35B model also improves out-of-domain from 31% to 48%.
AI.conclusion: Turn-level privileged-context rewards (SPICE) enable MLE agents to learn effective diagnostic tool use, yielding large in-domain gains and transferring to held-out sources and targets in out-of-domain settings.

title: Anisotropic Representations Improve Planning in JEPA World Models
summary: Latent world models learn action-conditioned dynamics in representation space and often score candidate actions by Euclidean distance to a goal representation. Joint training typically regularizes the representation to prevent collapse, but the resulting representation geometry also determines how terminal errors are weighted during planning. We show that accurate prediction and noncollapsed representations do not guarantee a task-aligned latent planning cost: isotropic Gaussian regularization can induce a geometry that ranks feasible outcomes differently from the task cost. To address this mismatch, we introduce AnisoWM with $Λ$Reg, which replaces the fixed isotropic Gaussian target with a learnable diagonal covariance under fixed-trace and anisotropy constraints. The prediction objective, predictor architecture, and Euclidean planner remain unchanged; the target is used only during training. Our analysis characterizes the prediction-driven allocation of target variance, its dependence on the training distribution, and the conditions under which the induced metric reduces planning regret. Across four visual control environments, AnisoWM improves planning success over LeWorldModel in all four. Its latent planning cost also shows better agreement with task outcomes. Project website: https://rkdrn79.github.io/AnisoWM-page/

AI.tldr: AnisoWM replaces the fixed isotropic Gaussian regularizer in latent world models with a learnable diagonal covariance (ΛReg), reshaping latent geometry so that Euclidean planning cost better aligns with task outcomes, improving success across four visual control environments.
AI.motivation: Latent world models plan by scoring candidate actions via Euclidean distance to a goal representation, so the representation geometry induced by joint-training regularization directly determines how terminal errors are weighted during planning. The authors show that accurate prediction and non-collapsed representations are insufficient: isotropic Gaussian regularization can produce a geometry whose ranking of feasible outcomes disagrees with the true task cost.
AI.method: AnisoWM introduces ΛReg, replacing the fixed isotropic Gaussian target with a learnable diagonal covariance subject to fixed-trace and anisotropy constraints. The prediction objective, predictor architecture, and Euclidean planner are left unchanged; the modified target is used only during training. The paper analyzes the prediction-driven allocation of target variance, its dependence on the training distribution, and conditions under which the induced metric reduces planning regret.
AI.result: Across four visual control environments, AnisoWM improves planning success over LeWorldModel in all four, and its latent planning cost shows better agreement with task outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Task-aligned latent planning cost is not guaranteed by accurate prediction and non-collapsed representations; explicitly shaping the regularization target's covariance is an effective, minimal modification for better aligning latent geometry with task cost.

title: JudgeProfile: Understanding and Steering Subjectivity in LLM Judges
summary: LLM judges are inherently subjective, often favoring different responses in pairwise comparison when neither option is objectively wrong. To study this subjectivity, we introduce JudgeProfile, a framework that dissects LLM evaluation into perception (how a judge compares two responses across specific attributes like clarity, correctness, and detail) and prioritization (how much each attribute influences the final choice). We curate SubjectiveSet, a dataset of 50,013 response pairs from 17 public data sources, evaluated by 21 LLM judges across 87 attributes. We find a hidden consensus in perception: judges frequently agree on attribute judgments even when their overall choices diverge. Building on this separation, we first characterize each judge's prioritization using attribute weights estimated from its own overall choices. These weights differ across judges even when estimated from the same attribute judgments. We then learn new weights from reference labels to adapt their decisions to a target evaluation standard. Reweighting perceived attributes improves average held-out agreement with reference labels from 66.48% to 71.97%, outperforming fine-tuning and rubric prompting. Our findings show that understanding and steering the subjectivity of LLM judges requires attention not only to what they perceive, but also to how they prioritize it.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces JudgeProfile, a framework separating LLM judge evaluation into perception (attribute-level comparisons) and prioritization (attribute weighting), showing that judges largely agree on perception but diverge in prioritization, and that learning reference-based weights improves alignment with target standards.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are inherently subjective and often favor different responses in pairwise comparisons when neither option is objectively wrong. Prior work treats judge disagreement as a monolithic problem, lacking a principled decomposition of where the subjectivity originates and how to steer it toward a desired evaluation standard.
AI.method: The authors propose JudgeProfile, which dissects LLM evaluation into perception (how a judge compares two responses across attributes such as clarity, correctness, and detail) and prioritization (how much each attribute influences the final choice). They curate SubjectiveSet, comprising 50,013 response pairs from 17 public data sources, evaluated by 21 LLM judges across 87 attributes. Judge-specific prioritization is characterized via attribute weights estimated from each judge's own overall choices, and new weights are learned from reference labels to adapt decisions to a target evaluation standard.
AI.result: Judges exhibit a hidden consensus in perception: they frequently agree on attribute-level judgments even when their overall choices diverge. Prioritization weights differ across judges even when estimated from identical attribute judgments. Learning new weights from reference labels raises average held-out agreement with reference labels from 66.48% to 71.97%, outperforming fine-tuning and rubric prompting.
AI.conclusion: Understanding and steering the subjectivity of LLM judges requires attention not only to what they perceive but also to how they prioritize it. Separating perception from prioritization provides an effective, lightweight mechanism for aligning judge decisions with a target evaluation standard.

title: Surgical Master Console Using General-Purpose Robot Arms and a Separable Articulated Distal Interface: Porcine In-Vivo Evaluation
summary: High-performance surgical master consoles offer intuitive articulated manipulation but are expensive and difficult to reproduce, while accessible commercial haptic devices lack built-in interfaces for surgical wrist articulation and continuous grasp. We present a laparoscopic master in which general-purpose robot manipulators provide the programmable base and surgical-specific interaction is concentrated in a separable distal adapter. Each 6-DoF arm carries a custom 2-DoF direct-drive wrist, continuous grasp sensing, and clutch-based workspace management; the complete bimanual hardware costs approximately US$5,500, below common bimanual commercial haptic references. To support sustained hand-guided use, we characterize current scaling, gravity, and break-away friction and use them for posture-dependent gravity compensation and motion-gated assistance, reducing continuous actuation and thermal loading. A common master state drives either Isaac Sim or an RCM-constrained dual-FR3 platform. Master-state publication to FR3 target update adds at most 8 ms, and tip tracking shows 0.31-0.66 mm mean delay-aligned residuals. In a porcine cholecystectomy experiment, five common operator-side metrics and hand/tip-speed distributions were compared descriptively with human in-vivo telemetry from 120 clinical Versius recordings of 99 cholecystectomy procedures; no interruption originated from the master console, and no abnormal clinical signs were recorded during the 7-day postoperative observation period. These results demonstrate a surgical master built from general-purpose robot arms with surgical-specific interaction concentrated in a separable distal interface.

AI.tldr: A laparoscopic surgical master console built from low-cost general-purpose 6-DoF robot arms plus a separable custom 2-DoF wrist adapter with continuous grasp sensing, costing ~US$5,500, achieving sub-millisecond-level tip tracking (0.31-0.66 mm residuals) and validated in simulation, an RCM-constrained dual-FR3 platform, and a porcine cholecystectomy.
AI.motivation: High-performance surgical master consoles offer intuitive articulated manipulation but are expensive and hard to reproduce, while accessible commercial haptic devices lack built-in interfaces for surgical wrist articulation and continuous grasp. There is a need for a low-cost, reproducible master console that retains surgical-specific interaction capabilities.
AI.method: The authors build a laparoscopic master from general-purpose robot manipulators providing the programmable base, with surgical-specific interaction concentrated in a separable distal adapter. Each 6-DoF arm carries a custom 2-DoF direct-drive wrist, continuous grasp sensing, and clutch-based workspace management. They characterize current scaling, gravity, and break-away friction to enable posture-dependent gravity compensation and motion-gated assistance. A common master state drives either Isaac Sim or an RCM-constrained dual-FR3 platform. Evaluation includes latency measurement (master-state publication to FR3 target update), tip tracking residuals, and a porcine cholecystectomy experiment compared descriptively against human in-vivo telemetry from 120 clinical recordings of 99 cholecystectomy procedures.
AI.result: The complete bimanual hardware costs approximately US$5,500, below common bimanual commercial haptic references. Master-state publication to FR3 target update adds at most 8 ms, and tip tracking shows 0.31-0.66 mm mean delay-aligned residuals. In the porcine cholecystectomy, five common operator-side metrics and hand/tip-speed distributions were compared with human in-vivo telemetry; no interruption originated from the master console, and no abnormal clinical signs were recorded during the 7-day postoperative observation period.
AI.conclusion: A surgical master console can be built from general-purpose robot arms with surgical-specific interaction concentrated in a separable distal interface, delivering low cost, adequate tracking fidelity, and safe operation in a preclinical porcine study.

title: Can AI Scientists Change Their Minds? Prior-Evidence Conflict in Synthetic Universes
summary: Can a scientific agent distinguish a law it inferred from evidence from one it merely recognizes? We introduce Synthetic Universes, a controlled benchmark that pairs canonical famous worlds with matched twisted twins governed by nearby noncanonical mechanisms. We evaluate each reported law twice: by executing it on held-out continuations and transfer settings, and by independently checking whether it recovers the generating mechanism. In the current checkpoint of a pre-specified 60-cell study, 22 trials were graded and one additional run ended in infrastructure failure. Among 20 twin trials, 8 pass predictive verification while 5 recover the generator. The dissociation is bidirectional: six parsable outputs predict successfully while missing the mechanism, whereas three recover the mechanism but fail predictive rollout. Drag exhibits the first pattern (5/5 predictive pass, 1/5 mechanism recovery); Gravity exhibits the second (1/5 predictive pass, 4/5 mechanism recovery). Because matched famous controls, the corrected identifiability sweep, and the Evidence Ladder remain incomplete, we do not claim a confirmatory causal prior-conflict effect. Instead, the completed runs establish a narrower verification result: predictive adequacy and mechanism recovery are distinct scientific claims and require distinct tests.

AI.tldr: Predictive success and mechanism recovery are dissociable: a scientific agent can produce a law that forecasts well without recovering the true generating mechanism, and vice versa.
AI.motivation: To determine whether a scientific agent can distinguish a law it genuinely inferred from evidence from one it merely recognizes (e.g., a memorized famous law applied to a superficially similar noncanonical world).
AI.method: Synthetic Universes: a controlled benchmark pairing canonical famous worlds with matched "twisted twins" governed by nearby noncanonical mechanisms. Each reported law is evaluated twice — by executing it on held-out continuations and transfer settings (predictive verification), and by independently checking whether it recovers the generating mechanism (mechanism recovery). Pre-specified 60-cell study; 22 trials graded, 1 run lost to infrastructure failure.
AI.result: Among 20 twin trials, 8 pass predictive verification while 5 recover the generator. Dissociation is bidirectional: 6 parsable outputs predict successfully but miss the mechanism; 3 recover the mechanism but fail predictive rollout. Drag shows the first pattern (5/5 predictive pass, 1/5 mechanism recovery); Gravity shows the second (1/5 predictive pass, 4/5 mechanism recovery).
AI.conclusion: No confirmatory causal prior-conflict effect is claimed, since matched famous controls, the corrected identifiability sweep, and the Evidence Ladder are incomplete. The completed runs establish a narrower verification result: predictive adequacy and mechanism recovery are distinct scientific claims requiring distinct tests.

title: Contact-Adaptive Robotic Ultrasound Probe Control for Tissue Exploration and Continuous Task-Relevant Visualization Using Robot-Free Image-Motion Demonstration
summary: Robotic ultrasound commonly targets standardized views, predefined scanning protocols, or expert-scan reproduction. We target a different role: while a clinician performs the primary procedure, a robotic assistant maintains a clinician-selected view so that changing tissue remains observable. We present contact-adaptive robotic ultrasound monitoring derived from robot-free demonstrations. Sonologger clamps a six-axis inertial sensor to the clinician-operated probe and records synchronized ultrasound and probe-frame relative rotations without a robot, camera, or tracker. Rather than imitating trajectories, the recordings measure which probe axis and sign the clinician uses to correct an image offset. A measured image latency is removed before still-move-still segmentation yields relative-rotation labels; translation is excluded from control because of inertial drift. These measurements parameterize the Demonstration-Informed Image-Motion Controller (DIMC), an interpretable, non-learned controller combined with beam-axis force regulation and an independent safety supervisor with 5 N forced retreat. On a dynamic bladder phantom, DIMC acquired and held a task-relevant view in 7 of 7 blind, pose-paired trials versus 1 of 7 for a static hold (McNemar p = 0.031), and retained the view during syringe-driven hydro-distension while the supervisor bounded the force excursion. The framework offers an operational representation of ultrasound context for contact-adaptive intraoperative monitoring; clinical validation remains future work.

AI.tldr: Sonologger records clinician probe motions with a clamped six-axis IMU, deriving relative-rotation labels that parameterize DIMC, a non-learned controller for contact-adaptive robotic ultrasound monitoring, achieving 7/7 view-holding versus 1/7 static in phantom trials.
AI.motivation: Robotic ultrasound typically targets standardized views, predefined protocols, or reproduction of expert scans. This work instead addresses a different role: while a clinician performs the primary procedure, a robotic assistant should maintain a clinician-selected view so that changing tissue remains observable.
AI.method: Sonologger clamps a six-axis inertial sensor to the clinician-operated probe and records synchronized ultrasound and probe-frame relative rotations without robot, camera, or tracker. The recordings, rather than imitating trajectories, measure which probe axis and sign the clinician uses to correct an image offset. A measured image latency is removed before still-move-still segmentation yields relative-rotation labels, while translation is excluded from control due to inertial drift. These measurements parameterize the Demonstration-Informed Image-Motion Controller (DIMC), an interpretable, non-learned controller combined with beam-axis force regulation and an independent safety supervisor featuring 5 N forced retreat.
AI.result: On a dynamic bladder phantom, DIMC acquired and held a task-relevant view in 7 of 7 blind, pose-paired trials, versus 1 of 7 for a static hold (McNemar p = 0.031). It also retained the view during syringe-driven hydro-distension while the supervisor bounded the force excursion.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an operational representation of ultrasound context for contact-adaptive intraoperative monitoring. Clinical validation remains future work.

title: Can Agents Design Libraries for Agents?
comment: 26 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/SprocketLab/librarydesignbench
summary: Agents increasingly build on code written by other agents, and they reimplement rather than reuse, growing the codebases later agents must work in. To measure how well agents design libraries for other agents, we introduce LibraryDesignBench, a two-phase benchmark in which an agent implements a full-featured library from a specification that defines required capabilities and potential use cases without prescribing the design. We evaluate the library through the correctness and simplicity of programs written by three user agents from different model families. The benchmark spans 242 expert-validated programming problems across 15 library-design tasks in four languages. On eleven of the fifteen tasks, agent designers reproduce the abstractions of the human-written production library. Downstream agents adopt agent- and human-written libraries alike but underuse them, reimplementing capabilities the library already provides. Our failure analysis finds that downstream agents write extra code mainly because agent-written libraries are rigid or hard to use, not because capabilities are missing. We also experiment with giving designers more prescriptive, agent-first guidance and having them test their library with subagents; this improves downstream scores and yields simpler programs. LibraryDesignBench provides both a testbed for evaluating library-design practices for agent users and an initial design baseline that improves downstream reuse.

AI.tldr: LibraryDesignBench, a two-phase benchmark spanning 242 problems across 15 library-design tasks in four languages, measures how well agents design libraries for other agents. Agent designers often reproduce human abstractions, but downstream agents underuse libraries—reimplementing existing capabilities mainly because libraries are rigid or hard to use; prescriptive agent-first guidance and subagent testing improve downstream reuse.
AI.motivation: Agents increasingly build on code written by other agents, and they tend to reimplement rather than reuse, causing codebases to grow. This raises the question of how well agent-designed libraries serve downstream agent users, which was previously unmeasured.
AI.method: A two-phase benchmark: in phase one, an agent implements a full-featured library from a specification defining required capabilities and use cases without prescribing design; in phase two, the library is evaluated via the correctness and simplicity of programs written by three user agents from different model families. It covers 242 expert-validated problems across 15 tasks in four languages. Additional experiments give designers more prescriptive, agent-first guidance and have them test their library with subagents.
AI.result: On eleven of fifteen tasks, agent designers reproduce the abstractions of the human-written production library. Downstream agents adopt agent- and human-written libraries alike but underuse them, reimplementing capabilities the library already provides. Failure analysis finds downstream agents write extra code mainly because agent-written libraries are rigid or hard to use, not because capabilities are missing. Prescriptive agent-first guidance and subagent testing improve downstream scores and yield simpler programs.
AI.conclusion: LibraryDesignBench provides both a testbed for evaluating library-design practices for agent users and an initial design baseline that improves downstream reuse.

title: Waggle-Dance-Inspired Multi-UAV Recruitment with RGB and Synthetic Event Vision
summary: The honeybee waggle dance motivates a communication mechanism in which one agent's motion guides the subsequent work of other agents. For aerial robots, realizing this mechanism requires a link from observed movement to a complete message, local task selection, and execution. This paper presents a MuJoCo system for comparing RGB and synthetic event vision within that link. One performer broadcasts six-bit task offers to one to three observers, each of which independently decodes both offers before selecting a task. The RGB receiver extracts trajectories using sparse optical flow; the event receiver uses only local event support and packet timing. Both use a common motion alphabet and explicit null delimiters. Because event silence does not establish target visibility, the event version includes a physical acquisition motion and continuity-qualified null confirmation. In the nominal three-observer case, each version produced 12 complete message receptions, six completed work units, and reassignment after withdrawal of a depleted task. Six paired functional cases produced the same message and work counts; an additional event-stream dropout case preserved inactivity of the affected observer. Replaying 42,060,633 recorded synthetic events reproduced all 12 event-message payloads and completion timestamps. Total nominal mission time was 493.80 s for RGB and 517.40 s for events, with the difference dominated by the event acquisition schedule. These fixed simulation results establish functional feasibility across two receiver implementations, rather than a sensor-performance advantage or hardware validation.

AI.tldr: This paper builds a MuJoCo simulation in which a "honeybee waggle dance"-inspired communication link lets aerial robots turn observed motion into complete task messages, and compares RGB versus synthetic event-vision receivers across multi-observer task-selection missions.
AI.motivation: The waggle dance suggests a mechanism where one agent's motion guides other agents' work. Applying this to aerial robots requires linking observed movement to a full message, local task selection, and execution. The paper aims to test whether two different vision front-ends (RGB and event) can realize that link within such a system.
AI.method: A MuJoCo system is used to compare RGB and synthetic event vision in the observation-to-message link. One performer broadcasts six-bit task offers to one to three observers, each independently decoding both offers before selecting a task. The RGB receiver extracts trajectories using sparse optical flow; the event receiver relies only on local event support and packet timing. Both share a common motion alphabet and explicit null delimiters. Because event silence cannot establish target visibility, the event version adds a physical acquisition motion and continuity-qualified null confirmation. Results are evaluated via nominal runs, paired functional cases, an event-stream dropout case, and event replay.
AI.result: In the nominal three-observer case, each version produced 12 complete message receptions, six completed work units, and reassignment after withdrawal of a depleted task. Six paired functional cases yielded the same message and work counts; an extra event-stream dropout case preserved inactivity of the affected observer. Replaying 42,060,633 recorded synthetic events reproduced all 12 event-message payloads and completion timestamps. Total nominal mission time was 493.80 s for RGB and 517.40 s for events, with the difference dominated by the event acquisition schedule.
AI.conclusion: The fixed simulation results establish functional feasibility for both receiver implementations in the waggle-dance-inspired communication link. They do not demonstrate a sensor-performance advantage or provide hardware validation.

title: BiFE: Search-Efficient Discovery of CPU-Only Branching Policies via LLM-based Bi-Fidelity Evolution
summary: In branch-and-bound (B&B) for mixed-integer linear programming (MILP), branching variable selection critically impacts efficiency. Existing neural branching policies often require GPU inference, while CPU-efficient symbolic expressions lack the representational capacity for complex logic. Large Language Model (LLM)-generated code provides a flexible search space for designing lightweight branching rules with diverse algorithmic logic. To discover effective rules within LLM-based evolutionary frameworks, a core challenge arises: full B&B evaluation on real instances is prohibitively expensive, whereas offline imitation learning suffers from distribution shift. To address this, we introduce a Bi-Fidelity Evolutionary framework (BiFE). It employs low-fidelity imitation scores as a rapid pre-screener and selectively applies high-fidelity on-instance evaluation only to elite candidates, effectively balancing search efficiency with performance reliability. Experiments validate both the search efficiency of BiFE and the competitiveness of its discovered rules, which outperform the SCIP solver and other baselines on CPUs, and even surpass certain GPU-based neural policies.

AI.tldr: BiFE, a bi-fidelity evolutionary framework, discovers lightweight CPU-friendly branching rules via LLM-generated code, using low-fidelity imitation screening plus selective high-fidelity B&B evaluation to outperform SCIP and some GPU neural policies.
AI.motivation: Branching variable selection is critical to B&B efficiency in MILP. Existing neural branching policies need GPU inference, while CPU-efficient symbolic rules lack representational capacity for complex logic. LLM-generated code offers a flexible search space for lightweight branching rules, but discovering effective rules is hard: full B&B evaluation on real instances is prohibitively expensive, and offline imitation learning suffers from distribution shift.
AI.method: A Bi-Fidelity Evolutionary framework (BiFE) that searches over LLM-generated branching-rule code. It uses low-fidelity imitation scores as a fast pre-screener to filter candidates, then applies high-fidelity on-instance B&B evaluation selectively only to elite candidates, balancing search efficiency and performance reliability.
AI.result: Experiments validate BiFE's search efficiency and the competitiveness of its discovered rules, which outperform the SCIP solver and other baselines on CPUs, and even surpass certain GPU-based neural policies.
AI.conclusion: A bi-fidelity evolutionary search over LLM-generated code can efficiently discover lightweight branching rules that run efficiently on CPUs and are competitive with or superior to existing symbolic baselines and some GPU-based neural branching policies.

title: Learning Social Navigation from Internet Videos in the Policy State Space
summary: Training robust social-navigation policies requires simulators with diverse scene layouts, terrain, and human motion, but constructing such environments and specifying pedestrian behavior is costly. We propose an efficient pipeline that converts ordinary monocular walking videos directly into closed-loop social-navigation training environments in the policy's state space. Our key observation is that local social navigation primarily depends on two types of information: where the robot can traverse and how nearby pedestrians move. We therefore represent the static scene as a metric traversability map, which can be rigidly transformed under counterfactual robot motion, while directly replaying the pedestrian trajectories recovered from the video over time. This abstraction allows us to define the forward dynamics directly in the policy's state space and efficiently simulate counterfactual robot states without reconstructing or rendering photorealistic observations. The resulting policy achieves 81.2% success in the independent Arena benchmark, compared with 75.0% for the strongest baseline, and succeeds in 19/20 real-robot trials without policy fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an efficient pipeline converting ordinary monocular walking videos into closed-loop social-navigation training environments directly in the policy's state space, avoiding photorealistic reconstruction. It represents static scenes as metric traversability maps (rigidly transformable under counterfactual robot motion) and replays recovered pedestrian trajectories over time. The resulting policy achieves 81.2% success on the Arena benchmark (vs. 75.0% for the strongest baseline) and succeeds in 19/20 real-robot trials without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Training robust social-navigation policies requires simulators with diverse scene layouts, terrain, and human motion, but constructing such environments and specifying pedestrian behavior is costly. There is a need for an efficient, low-cost way to obtain diverse closed-loop training environments.
AI.method: The key observation is that local social navigation depends primarily on two information types: where the robot can traverse and how nearby pedestrians move. The static scene is represented as a metric traversability map that can be rigidly transformed under counterfactual robot motion, while pedestrian trajectories recovered from the video are directly replayed over time. This abstraction defines forward dynamics directly in the policy's state space, enabling efficient simulation of counterfactual robot states without reconstructing or rendering photorealistic observations.
AI.result: The resulting policy achieves 81.2% success in the independent Arena benchmark, compared with 75.0% for the strongest baseline, and succeeds in 19/20 real-robot trials without policy fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Ordinary monocular walking videos can be efficiently converted into closed-loop social-navigation training environments within the policy's state space, yielding policies that outperform the strongest baseline and transfer to real robots without fine-tuning.

title: Distinguish or Homogenize: Last-Chance Policy Identification and Risk-Budgeted Recovery under Irreversible Resource Depletion
summary: Under irreversible resource depletion, an agent can spend resources to distinguish among latent fault models, or to change the system state so that the remaining models admit a common acceptable continuation--at which point further diagnosis becomes unnecessary. This distinguish-or-homogenize principle identifies a path that existing frameworks for identification, planning, and diagnosis do not make explicit: prior formulations treat the mapping from fault models to acceptable policies as a given, whereas LCPI makes it a function of the agent's own actions. We formalize this principle through Last-Chance Policy Identification (LCPI), where correctness is evaluated at the state the agent reaches rather than at the initial state. The Last Identifiable Margin (LIM) marks the feasibility boundary between distinguishing and homogenizing. For deterministic diagnostic graphs we provide the Exact-LIM recursion; for noisy finite-horizon recovery we propose Risk-Budgeted Compatibility Planning (RBCP), which searches a compatibility-aware frontier under a hard worst-case failure constraint. Across incident recovery on abstract microservice topologies and latent-damage navigation in MiniGrid, RBCP improves risk-feasible recovery while satisfying the failure budget. A sham control--cost-matched actions that preserve model incompatibility--eliminates the gain entirely, confirming that the benefit comes from changing which policies are acceptable for which models, not from extra search or additional budget.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the "distinguish-or-homogenize" principle for acting under irreversible resource depletion, formalized as Last-Chance Policy Identification (LCPI), where correctness is judged at the reached state rather than the initial state. It defines the Last Identifiable Margin (LIM) as the boundary between distinguishing fault models and homogenizing them, provides the Exact-LIM recursion for deterministic diagnostic graphs, and proposes Risk-Budgeted Compatibility Planning (RBCP) for noisy finite-horizon recovery under a hard worst-case failure constraint. RBCP improves risk-feasible recovery in microservice incident scenarios and MiniGrid latent-damage navigation, with a sham control confirming gains stem from altering policy-model compatibility rather than extra search or budget.
AI.motivation: Existing frameworks for identification, planning, and diagnosis treat the mapping from fault models to acceptable policies as fixed, and evaluate correctness at the initial state. This misses a key option available under irreversible resource depletion: instead of spending resources to distinguish latent fault models, an agent can act to change the system state so that remaining models share a common acceptable continuation, making further diagnosis unnecessary. The paper aims to make this "distinguish-or-homogenize" choice explicit and formalize its feasibility boundary.
AI.method: The authors formalize Last-Chance Policy Identification (LCPI), where correctness is evaluated at the state the agent reaches rather than at the initial state, and define the Last Identifiable Margin (LIM) as the feasibility boundary between distinguishing and homogenizing. For deterministic diagnostic graphs they derive the Exact-LIM recursion. For noisy finite-horizon recovery they propose Risk-Budgeted Compatibility Planning (RBCP), which searches a compatibility-aware frontier under a hard worst-case failure constraint.
AI.result: Across incident recovery on abstract microservice topologies and latent-damage navigation in MiniGrid, RBCP improves risk-feasible recovery while satisfying the failure budget. A sham control using cost-matched actions that preserve model incompatibility eliminates the gain entirely, confirming the benefit arises from changing which policies are acceptable for which models, not from extra search or additional budget.
AI.conclusion: The distinguish-or-homogenize principle, formalized via LCPI and bounded by the LIM, offers a path that prior identification, planning, and diagnosis frameworks leave implicit. RBCP operationalizes this for noisy finite-horizon recovery under hard failure constraints, and ablation via the sham control isolates the mechanism, showing that reshaping model-policy compatibility drives the improvement.

title: Video2STL: Grounding VLM-Generated Temporal Specifications for Robot Learning
summary: Video-based policy learning is particularly promising, as it illustrates target behaviors without requiring action annotations or embodiment-matched demonstrations. A central challenge is deciding what information should be transferred from the video to the robot. Existing approaches commonly convert visual observations into scalar similarity or value signals, or ask foundation models to directly generate reward code. These approaches can make the temporal structure of a task difficult to inspect, ground, and reuse. We present Video2STL, a framework that converts observation-only videos into parametric Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications and uses the resulting formal representation for robot learning. A vision-language model extracts an embodiment-independent semantic event trace and constructs a bank of symbolic temporal specifications. The model determines the task structure, while numerical predicate thresholds and temporal bounds are grounded from successful robot trajectories. For policy learning, we separate short- and long-timescale temporal information: short-horizon specifications provide dense rewards through rolling-window quantitative robustness, while a causal monitor over a retained long-horizon specification provides one-time progress rewards for valid temporal prefixes. The same representation supports cross-embodiment transfer from human or animal videos to robot control. Across four manipulation tasks, Video2STL achieves $85.8\%$ average success-once and $67.0\%$ success-at-end, compared with $81.5\%/59.5\%$ for native dense PPO and $65.0\%/42.3\%$ for Text2Reward; in quadruped locomotion, Qwen-3.8 and GPT-5.6-based Video2STL policies achieve $100\%$ success across velocities from $0.3$ to $2.1\,\mathrm{m/s}$ while remaining competitive in high-speed energy efficiency. Project webpage: \href{https://video2stl.github.io/}{video2stl}.

AI.tldr: Video2STL converts observation-only videos into parametric Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications, using a VLM-extracted semantic event trace and robot-grounded predicates to separate short-horizon dense rewards from long-horizon progress rewards for cross-embodiment robot policy learning.
AI.motivation: Video-based policy learning avoids action annotations and embodiment-matched demonstrations, but a central challenge is deciding what to transfer from video to robot. Existing methods collapse observations into scalar similarity/value signals or let foundation models generate reward code directly, making task temporal structure hard to inspect, ground, and reuse.
AI.method: A vision-language model extracts an embodiment-independent semantic event trace and constructs a bank of symbolic temporal specifications; the model determines task structure while numerical predicate thresholds and temporal bounds are grounded from successful robot trajectories. For policy learning, short-horizon specifications provide dense rewards via rolling-window quantitative robustness, while a causal monitor over a retained long-horizon specification provides one-time progress rewards for valid temporal prefixes.
AI.result: Across four manipulation tasks, Video2STL achieves 85.8% average success-once and 67.0% success-at-end, versus 81.5%/59.5% for native dense PPO and 65.0%/42.3% for Text2Reward. In quadruped locomotion, Qwen-3.8 and GPT-5.6-based Video2STL policies achieve 100% success across velocities from 0.3 to 2.1 m/s while remaining competitive in high-speed energy efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Parametric STL offers an inspectable, groundable, and reusable formal interface for transferring temporal task structure from observation-only videos to robot control, supporting cross-embodiment transfer from human or animal videos and outperforming scalar-reward and code-generation baselines.

title: SIPO: Unifying Reinforcement Learning with On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard paradigm for improving large language models (LLMs) on various tasks, yet its sparse outcome rewards lack token-level credit assignment for intermediate steps. To address this, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a self-teacher with privileged context to provide additional dense learning signals. However, because the self-teacher is often overconfident and imposes excessive penalties on long reasoning trajectories, OPSD frequently struggles in practice. To mitigate this, we propose self-instructing policy optimization (SIPO) with a contrastive self-teacher to provide dense credit. At each iteration, SIPO samples multiple rollouts per prompt from the current policy, scores them with environment rewards, and constructs two teacher contexts for each rollout by pairing the reference answer with mistakes made within the group. The model then re-evaluates its own responses under both contexts, using the difference between the two teacher log-probabilities as token-level feedback, so that biases shared by both contexts are expected to largely cancel. The resulting objective yields a token-level advantage for every rollout: the reward still sets the main direction of each update while the self-teacher redistributes credit across tokens. Even in groups where every rollout fails and group-relative advantages vanish, SIPO still provides a learning signal. By preserving direct optimization of the task reward while providing dense, token-level feedback, this approach bridges reinforcement learning and on-policy self-distillation. Extensive experiments across multiple reasoning and code-generation benchmarks demonstrate that SIPO outperforms both RLVR and OPSD baselines without an external teacher or additional generation.

AI.tldr: SIPO augments RLVR with a contrastive self-teacher that yields dense token-level credit assignment while keeping the task reward as the main optimization direction.
AI.motivation: RLVR's sparse outcome rewards lack token-level credit assignment for intermediate reasoning steps. OPSD addresses this via a privileged self-teacher, but the self-teacher is overconfident and over-penalizes long reasoning trajectories, limiting its practical effectiveness.
AI.method: SIPO samples multiple rollouts per prompt, scores them with environment rewards, and builds two teacher contexts per rollout by pairing the reference answer with within-group mistakes. It re-evaluates each response under both contexts and uses the difference in teacher log-probabilities as token-level feedback, so shared biases cancel. The resulting objective yields a token-level advantage for every rollout, combining the environment reward (main update direction) with self-teacher credit redistribution, and still provides signal when group-relative advantages vanish.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning and code-generation benchmarks show SIPO outperforms both RLVR and OPSD baselines, without an external teacher or additional generation.
AI.conclusion: SIPO bridges reinforcement learning and on-policy self-distillation by preserving direct task-reward optimization while supplying dense token-level feedback.

title: RawVLA: Embodied Neural Image Signal Processor For Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically operate on RGB images produced by a fixed camera image signal processor (ISP), leaving the imaging pipeline outside the learning and evaluation loop. We systematically examine the consequences of this overlooked design choice across five fundamental ISP dimensions: gain, sensor noise, chromatic response, tonal response, and bit depth. Our analysis reveals that RAW-to-RGB processing materially shapes both action prediction and manipulation success, with different ISP dimensions exerting substantially different effects. Guided by these findings, we introduce RawVLA, a streaming neural ISP that adaptively renders RAW observations for frozen VLA policies while concentrating its capacity on the imaging factors relevant to embodied behavior. We further present RawVLA-Bench, a RAW-domain manipulation benchmark to expose image processing as an explicit evaluation variable across clean and adverse acquisition conditions. Experiments on RawVLA-Bench show that RawVLA preserves performance under standard conditions while substantially improving robustness under degraded imaging, establishing adaptive RAW processing as an effective interface between physical cameras and embodied policies.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the fixed camera ISP is a critical, overlooked variable for VLA models. It systematically studies five ISP dimensions, then proposes RawVLA, a streaming neural ISP that adaptively renders RAW for frozen VLA policies, plus RawVLA-Bench, and demonstrates improved robustness under degraded imaging.
AI.motivation: VLA models consume RGB images from a fixed ISP, so the imaging pipeline sits outside the learning and evaluation loop. This design choice is rarely questioned, yet it may materially affect action prediction and manipulation success, motivating a systematic study of how RAW-to-RGB processing shapes embodied behavior.
AI.method: The authors analyze five ISP dimensions: gain, sensor noise, chromatic response, tonal response, and bit depth. Based on these findings, they introduce RawVLA, a streaming neural ISP that adaptively renders RAW observations for frozen VLA policies and concentrates capacity on imaging factors relevant to embodied behavior. They also build RawVLA-Bench, a RAW-domain manipulation benchmark exposing image processing as an explicit evaluation variable under clean and adverse acquisition conditions.
AI.result: The analysis shows RAW-to-RGB processing materially shapes both action prediction and manipulation success, with different ISP dimensions exerting substantially different effects. On RawVLA-Bench, RawVLA preserves performance under standard conditions while substantially improving robustness under degraded imaging.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive RAW processing is established as an effective interface between physical cameras and embodied policies, and image processing should be treated as an explicit evaluation and design variable rather than a fixed preprocessing step.

title: EASE: Behavior-Adaptive Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Agent skills provide a lightweight mechanism for self-evolving agents to accumulate reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. However, existing learned skill curators typically optimize curation without explicitly modeling downstream executor behavior. We show that this can cause systematic cross-executor degradation: curators trained with different executors perform best when paired with their own training executor, indicating that effective skill curation is executor-dependent. We formulate behavior-adaptive skill curation and introduce EASE, a framework that learns a single curator that adapts its decisions to different executor behaviors. EASE maintains an online behavioral profile of recent execution patterns and conditions the curator on this profile, the current trajectory, and retrieved skills to add, modify, or remove skills from an evolving repository. We train the shared curator jointly across multiple frozen executors with reinforcement learning, using retrieval-aware and behavior-aware temporal attribution to focus optimization on curation actions with observable downstream influence. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, with executors ranging from Qwen3-8B/32B and GPT-OSS-120B to unseen Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Gemini 3.5 Flash, EASE outperforms strong skill- and memory-based baselines without per-executor finetuning. EASE also maintains 34.5--41.0% fewer skills, improves skill retrieval by 36.3--38.7% and measured edit utility by 51.8--60.0%, and reduces deployment-time inference tokens by 9.1--14.5%. These results establish behavior-adaptive skill curation as an effective principle for building self-evolving agents.

AI.tldr: EASE is a framework for behavior-adaptive skill curation in self-evolving agents, learning a single curator that conditions its add/modify/remove decisions on an online profile of executor behavior, jointly trained across multiple frozen executors via RL.
AI.motivation: Existing learned skill curators optimize curation without explicitly modeling downstream executor behavior, which causes systematic cross-executor degradation: curators perform best only with their own training executor. This reveals that effective skill curation is executor-dependent, motivating a curator that adapts to different executor behaviors.
AI.method: The authors formulate behavior-adaptive skill curation and introduce EASE. EASE maintains an online behavioral profile of recent execution patterns and conditions the curator on this profile, the current trajectory, and retrieved skills to add, modify, or remove skills in an evolving repository. The shared curator is trained jointly across multiple frozen executors with reinforcement learning, using retrieval-aware and behavior-aware temporal attribution to focus optimization on curation actions with observable downstream influence.
AI.result: Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, with executors ranging from Qwen3-8B/32B and GPT-OSS-120B to unseen Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Gemini 3.5 Flash, EASE outperforms strong skill- and memory-based baselines without per-executor finetuning. It also maintains 34.5–41.0% fewer skills, improves skill retrieval by 36.3–38.7% and measured edit utility by 51.8–60.0%, and reduces deployment-time inference tokens by 9.1–14.5%.
AI.conclusion: Behavior-adaptive skill curation is established as an effective principle for building self-evolving agents. EASE achieves cross-executor generalization and efficiency gains without per-executor finetuning.

title: Wrench-ACT: Enhancing Robot Policies for Contact Rich Behavior Using Direct Wrench Control
summary: While contact-rich manipulation requires deliberate regulation of interaction forces, recent approaches to robot manipulation learning predominantly represent actions as target positions or poses. Even methods that incorporate force sensing either use it solely as an observation or, when predicting forces as part of the output, rely on a hybrid force controller. In this paper, we propose an imitation learning policy that predicts wrenches as its sole action output for direct use by a pure force controller. Our studies suggest that force-domain imitation learning depends critically on data collection, with force-feedback teleoperation improving policy performance by capturing the operator's deliberate force regulation. Using Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) as the base architecture, we train single-task models on bilateral wrench demonstrations and evaluate them on five contact-rich manipulation tasks. The wrench policy matches or outperforms position-based baselines across all tasks, with gains varying according to the degree of deliberate force regulation each task requires. Cross-condition ablations show that the bilateral data collection interface and the wrench action space each contribute independently to performance. To support further research, we will release over 1000 wrench-action demonstrations spanning these tasks on a companion website upon publication.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an imitation learning policy that predicts wrenches as its sole action output for direct use by a pure force controller, showing that wrench-based policies match or outperform position-based baselines on contact-rich manipulation tasks, with gains tied to the degree of deliberate force regulation required.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich manipulation requires deliberate regulation of interaction forces, yet most robot manipulation learning approaches represent actions as target positions or poses. Methods incorporating force sensing either use it only as an observation or, when predicting forces, rely on a hybrid force controller. The authors argue this leaves force regulation under-exploited and motivate a policy that directly outputs wrenches.
AI.method: The authors propose an imitation learning policy that predicts wrenches as its sole action output, used directly by a pure force controller. They use Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) as the base architecture and train single-task models on bilateral wrench demonstrations collected via force-feedback teleoperation. Evaluation is conducted on five contact-rich manipulation tasks, including ablations over the bilateral data collection interface and the wrench action space.
AI.result: The wrench policy matches or outperforms position-based baselines across all five tasks, with gains varying according to each task's required degree of deliberate force regulation. Cross-condition ablations show the bilateral data collection interface and the wrench action space each contribute independently to performance. The authors will release over 1000 wrench-action demonstrations on a companion website.
AI.conclusion: Force-domain imitation learning depends critically on data collection, with force-feedback teleoperation capturing the operator's deliberate force regulation and improving policy performance. Predicting wrenches as the sole action output for a pure force controller is an effective alternative to position-centric and hybrid-force approaches for contact-rich manipulation.

title: Generalizable Lifelong Model Editing via Preference Optimization
summary: Knowledge editing enables rapid updates of specific factual knowledge in large language models (LLMs) without full retraining. However, more realistic scenarios call for a lifelong framework that handles continual updates rather than one-off modifications. In such settings, existing editing methods often overfit to target prompts, significantly degrading both the generalization of the edited knowledge and the model's general capabilities. To address this issue, we propose GLIME (Generalizable Lifelong Model Editing), which combines knowledge editing with preference optimization over generation behavior. GLIME further incorporates replay-based editing and a gradient constraint to preserve previously edited knowledge. Experimental results show that GLIME significantly improves knowledge generalization in lifelong editing settings while maintaining both editing performance and general capabilities.

AI.tldr: GLIME is a lifelong model editing framework that combines knowledge editing with preference optimization over generation behavior, plus replay-based editing and gradient constraints, to improve generalization of edited knowledge while preserving prior edits and general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge editing methods handle one-off modifications but fail in realistic lifelong settings, where continual updates cause overfitting to target prompts, degrading generalization of edited knowledge and the model's general capabilities.
AI.method: GLIME (Generalizable Lifelong Model Editing) integrates knowledge editing with preference optimization over generation behavior. It further incorporates replay-based editing and a gradient constraint to preserve previously edited knowledge across sequential updates.
AI.result: Experimental results show that GLIME significantly improves knowledge generalization in lifelong editing settings while maintaining both editing performance and general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Combining preference optimization with replay-based editing and gradient constraints effectively addresses overfitting in lifelong model editing, offering a more realistic and robust editing framework for LLMs.

title: Risk-Aware Semantic Grounding for Trustworthy LLM-Based Robot Planning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as high-level planners in robot navigation, but their outputs may become unreliable when instructions are ambiguous, unsupported by the environment, or semantically inconsistent. This paper presents a Risk-Aware Semantic Grounding framework for trustworthy LLM-based robot planning. Unlike existing LLM-based planners that primarily optimize plan generation, we formulate semantic grounding reliability as a multi-dimensional risk estimation problem. The proposed architecture explicitly models grounding uncertainty through ambiguity, hallucination and semantic-conflict risks before planning occurs, enabling the system to decide whether to execute the instruction, request clarification, or reject it. To evaluate the approach, we introduce TRUST-NAV, a benchmark containing both standard navigation tasks and risk-inducing instruction scenarios. Experimental results show that while conventional LLM planners achieve strong performance on valid navigation tasks, the proposed framework substantially improves ambiguity detection and semantic conflict rejection. These findings suggest that trustworthy robot planning should be evaluated not only by task completion, but also by the ability to recognize when execution should not occur.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Risk-Aware Semantic Grounding framework that treats semantic grounding reliability as a multidimensional risk estimation problem (ambiguity, hallucination, semantic-conflict risks) for LLM-based robot navigation, and introduces the TRUST-NAV benchmark to evaluate both standard and risk-inducing instruction scenarios.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as high-level planners in robot navigation, but their outputs become unreliable when instructions are ambiguous, unsupported by the environment, or semantically inconsistent. Existing LLM-based planners mainly optimize plan generation, ignoring the question of whether an instruction should be grounded or executed at all.
AI.method: The authors formulate semantic grounding reliability as a multi-dimensional risk estimation problem. Their architecture explicitly models grounding uncertainty through ambiguity, hallucination, and semantic-conflict risks before planning occurs, enabling the system to decide whether to execute the instruction, request clarification, or reject it. They also introduce TRUST-NAV, a benchmark containing both standard navigation tasks and risk-inducing instruction scenarios.
AI.result: Conventional LLM planners achieve strong performance on valid navigation tasks, but the proposed framework substantially improves ambiguity detection and semantic conflict rejection.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy robot planning should be evaluated not only by task completion, but also by the ability to recognize when execution should not occur.

title: Emergent Specialization in Populations of Self-Supervised Collaborative Vision Experts Without a Shared Gate or Cross-Agent Gradients
summary: Can a population of neural networks develop a useful division of labor without a shared gate or gradients between agents? We study a setting where each network has its own weights, trains independently on the same heterogeneous data, and can ask another agent for help through a forward pass. Unlike mixtures of experts, where a jointly trained gate assigns inputs to experts, specialization here must emerge without central control. We test this in a small scale proxy for predictive visual pretraining. Initially identical agents are finetuned on an unlabeled mixture of six visual domains using masked prediction of frozen DINOv3 features. We measure specialization by asking whether the best agent for an input aligns with its latent domain, and utilization by asking whether responsibility is distributed across agents. We progressively remove central control, ending with DISCO (DIStributed COllaboration) where each agent locally selects a helper, reads its internal state through a gradient free channel, and rewards its router only for the improvement that help provides. Specialization emerges and is useful. Randomly routed populations underperform a single generalist, while semantically routed populations outperform it, showing that specialization rather than population size drives the gain. Specialization persists without a central router, and gradient free communication lets nonexperts exploit emergent expertise. In DISCO, a random agent helped by the expert matches the solo generalist, while experts surpass it, including on data outside the specialization mixture. Local routers select the emergent expert for 98% of inputs. These effects persist across population size, model capacity, data imbalance, and finetuning seeds, providing measurable evidence for the dynamics needed by decentralized predictive pretraining.

AI.tldr: Identical neural networks trained independently on heterogeneous data can develop useful division of labor without a shared gate or gradients between agents, with semantically routed populations outperforming a single generalist and local routers recovering the emergent expert for 98% of inputs.
AI.motivation: Mixtures of experts rely on a jointly trained gate to assign inputs to experts, requiring central control. The paper asks whether specialization and division of labor can emerge and remain useful in a fully decentralized population of independently trained networks without a shared gate or inter-agent gradients.
AI.method: A small-scale proxy for predictive visual pretraining: initially identical agents are finetuned independently on an unlabeled mixture of six visual domains via masked prediction of frozen DINOv3 features. Central control is progressively removed, ending with DISCO (DIStributed COllaboration), where each agent locally selects a helper, reads its internal state through a gradient-free channel, and rewards its router only for the improvement the help provides.
AI.result: Specialization emerges and is useful. Randomly routed populations underperform a single generalist, while semantically routed populations outperform it, indicating specialization rather than population size drives the gain. In DISCO, a random agent helped by the expert matches the solo generalist, experts surpass it (even on out-of-mixture data), and local routers select the emergent expert for 98% of inputs. Effects persist across population size, model capacity, data imbalance, and finetuning seeds.
AI.conclusion: Useful division of labor can arise in decentralized populations without a central router or inter-agent gradients. Gradient-free communication lets nonexperts exploit emergent expertise, providing measurable evidence for the decentralized dynamics needed in predictive pretraining.

title: RoboFin3D: A Sim-to-Real Platform for Robotic Surface Finishing
comment: Accepted for poster presentation at the IROS 2026 Workshop on Sim2Real and Classical Control: From Rigorous Theory to Data-Driven Robotics
summary: Grinding and sanding are fundamental processes in industrial robotic surface finishing. However, physical trials are expensive and consume workpieces, making reproducible experiments difficult. We present RoboFin3D, a sim-to-real platform built on Isaac Sim and the Newton physics engine, that provides physics-based grinding and sanding simulation for cheap and repeatable robotic surface finishing experiments. RoboFin3D utilizes a signed distance field (SDF) to model the changing geometry of the workpiece, enabling contact computation, live updates and rendering without an intermediate mesh. It additionally uses a separate surface field to model progressive surface appearance change during sanding. We also introduce WeldGen, a weld sampling module, to generate weld beads on 8,918 real-world workpiece meshes for providing diverse simulation assets. The simulation parameters are calibrated on real experimental results and our evaluation demonstrates our simulation's fidelity against the real world. We also demonstrate that simulation-generated data can be used to improve the performance of perception models. Simulation-only fine-tuning of SAM2 improves IoU for segmentation of unsanded regions from 77.15% to 84.47%, while combined synthetic and real training reaches 97.41%.

AI.tldr: RoboFin3D is a sim-to-real platform built on Isaac Sim and the Newton physics engine that provides physics-based grinding and sanding simulation, using SDF-based workpiece geometry and a separate surface field for appearance change; it also introduces WeldGen to generate welds on 8,918 meshes, and demonstrates simulation-generated data can improve perception models (SAM2 IoU from 77.15% to 84.47% via sim-only fine-tuning, 97.41% combined).
AI.motivation: Grinding and sanding are fundamental industrial robotic surface finishing processes, but physical trials are expensive, consume workpieces, and are hard to reproduce; a faithful and cheap simulation platform is needed.
AI.method: RoboFin3D is built on Isaac Sim and the Newton physics engine. It uses a signed distance field (SDF) to model changing workpiece geometry, enabling contact computation, live updates, and rendering without an intermediate mesh. A separate surface field models progressive surface appearance change during sanding. WeldGen samples and generates weld beads on 8,918 real-world workpiece meshes to provide diverse simulation assets. Simulation parameters are calibrated on real experimental results.
AI.result: Evaluation demonstrates the simulation's fidelity against the real world, and simulation-generated data improves perception model performance: simulation-only fine-tuning of SAM2 raises segmentation IoU for unsanded regions from 77.15% to 84.47%, while combined synthetic and real training reaches 97.41%.
AI.conclusion: RoboFin3D enables cheap, repeatable robotic surface finishing experiments with demonstrated real-world fidelity, and its generated data can effectively boost perception models such as SAM2 for segmentation tasks.

title: Code4Scene: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Constructing and Editing 3D Scenes
summary: Frontier coding agents can now write and execute code that authors 3D environments, but whether they reliably understand 3D structure and precisely control scene state remains unclear. The generated 3D scene is a persistent, executable artifact: a convincing render can hide incorrect spatial relations, intersecting objects, or unintended modifications. We introduce Code4Scene, a benchmark of 190 Unreal Engine cases built from human-assembled scenes that evaluates coding agents on two complementary settings under a shared execution interface. Construction tests scene-level spatial reasoning from open-ended language specifications, where many realizations are valid; editing tests precise control of scene state, where the agent must recover the target scene from reference images while preserving everything else. Rather than scoring code or rendered views, Code4Scene evaluates the generated engine-native scene for task fulfillment, artifact integrity, and static physical validity, with edits additionally compared against withheld ground truth. Across 14 coding-agent configurations on the 95-case public set, construction and editing performance are strongly correlated but not interchangeable (Spearman $ρ= 0.78$): Claude Fable 5.1 leads construction, Gemini 3.8 Flash leads editing, and GPT-6 Astra narrowly leads overall. Spatial Composition is the weakest construction category for every agent, while editing remains imprecise: the best Repair F1 is only 0.527, and 35.8% of edits that fully recover the target still introduce unintended changes elsewhere in the scene. These results expose a gap between plausible 3D generation and reliable spatial reasoning and state control.

AI.tldr: Code4Scene is a 190-case Unreal Engine benchmark showing that frontier coding agents can generate plausible 3D scenes but still lack reliable spatial reasoning and precise scene-state control.
AI.motivation: Coding agents can now author executable 3D environments, but it is unclear whether they genuinely understand 3D structure and can precisely control scene state. A convincing render may mask incorrect spatial relations, intersecting objects, or unintended scene modifications, motivating evaluation of the generated engine-native scene rather than code or rendered views.
AI.method: Code4Scene comprises 190 Unreal Engine cases built from human-assembled scenes, evaluated under a shared execution interface in two settings: Construction, testing scene-level spatial reasoning from open-ended language specifications with many valid realizations; and Editing, testing precise state control by recovering a target scene from reference images while preserving all else. Scoring targets the generated engine-native scene on task fulfillment, artifact integrity, and static physical validity, with edits compared against withheld ground truth.
AI.result: Across 14 coding-agent configurations on the 95-case public set, construction and editing performance are strongly correlated but not interchangeable (Spearman ρ = 0.78). Claude Fable 5.1 leads construction, Gemini 3.8 Flash leads editing, and GPT-6 Astra narrowly leads overall. Spatial Composition is the weakest construction category for every agent, and editing remains imprecise: best Repair F1 is only 0.527, with 35.8% of edits that fully recover the target still introducing unintended changes elsewhere.
AI.conclusion: The results expose a gap between plausible 3D generation and reliable spatial reasoning and state control, framing Code4Scene as a diagnostic benchmark for measuring progress toward trustworthy 3D-authoring coding agents.

title: RoboHarn-Evo: Evolving Hierarchical Physical Knowledge for Self-Improving Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language models can coordinate long-horizon robot manipulation, yet successful task reasoning still depends on whether local physical interactions produce the intended effects. We study how repeated interaction can improve this capability without updating the base model. We introduce RoboHarn-Evo, a dual-loop harness that evolves Hierarchical Physical Knowledge (HPK) from physical experience. HPK couples two levels of reusable knowledge: Task Knowledge captures which subtask should be executed and when it is complete, while Action Knowledge captures object-relative geometric strategies and their physical effects. During execution, the agent retrieves knowledge at the corresponding decision level and grounds it in the current scene under the task goal. Across episodes, physical feedback is used to revise historical knowledge, update its applicability, and organize reusable entries for subsequent retrieval. Experiments on RMBench show that HPK improves average success by up to 24.2 percentage points across different agent models. With 80 interaction rollouts, held-out success rises from 48.3% to 75.0% for GPT-5.5 and from 70.0% to 88.3% for GPT-6. RoboHarn-Evo also resolves over 83% of historical knowledge errors while retaining 95.8% of valid knowledge, and transfers zero-shot from RMBench to RoboDojo with gains of 35.0 and 25.0 percentage points. These results demonstrate that physical interaction can be accumulated into reusable knowledge for improving subsequent manipulation.

AI.tldr: RoboHarn-Evo is a dual-loop harness that evolves Hierarchical Physical Knowledge (HPK) from physical experience to improve long-horizon robot manipulation without updating the base vision-language model, raising success by up to 24.2 points on RMBench.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models can coordinate long-horizon manipulation, but success still hinges on whether local physical interactions produce intended effects; the paper aims to improve this via repeated interaction without updating the base model.
AI.method: A dual-loop harness, RoboHarn-Evo, evolves Hierarchical Physical Knowledge with two coupled levels: Task Knowledge (which subtask to execute and when it is complete) and Action Knowledge (object-relative geometric strategies and their physical effects). At execution, knowledge is retrieved at the corresponding decision level and grounded in the current scene under the task goal; across episodes, physical feedback revises historical knowledge, updates applicability, and organizes reusable entries for retrieval.
AI.result: On RMBench, HPK improves average success by up to 24.2 percentage points across agent models; with 80 interaction rollouts, held-out success rises from 48.3% to 75.0% for GPT-5.5 and from 70.0% to 88.3% for GPT-6. RoboHarn-Evo also resolves over 83% of historical knowledge errors while retaining 95.8% of valid knowledge and transfers zero-shot from RMBench to RoboDojo with gains of 35.0 and 25.0 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Physical interaction can be accumulated into reusable knowledge that improves subsequent manipulation, enabling base-model-free improvement and cross-environment transfer.

title: Aperture: Merge-Consistent Rotary States for Compressed Tokens
summary: Token compression combines content from several positions, yet rotary position embeddings usually assign the merged token one coordinate. We ask what positional information must survive later merges. Aperture stores Fourier moments of the token's weighted support at the model's rotary frequencies. We prove that these moments have minimal real dimension among continuous states sufficient for the selected expected rotary interactions. Represented mass makes updates additive; attention normalisation remains a separate readout choice. Uniform intervals give a centre rotation times a sinc gain. We characterise when centres determine interval widths and construct matched examples where they do not. Numerical checks verify the weighted-support implementation. In trained temporal readers, compression transfer varies with gain calibration and feature placement. In a prespecified native video question-answering comparison, stored support reaches $65.63\%$ accuracy versus $67.12\%$ for the deployed merging rule. These results separate exact positional preservation under compression from downstream benefit.

AI.tldr: This paper asks what positional information must survive token-compression merges. It introduces Aperture, which stores Fourier moments of a token's weighted support at the model's rotary frequencies, proves these moments are minimal-dimensional for the selected expected rotary interactions, and empirically separates exact positional preservation from downstream gains (65.63% vs 67.12% on a video QA task).
AI.motivation: Token compression merges content from several positions, but rotary position embeddings typically assign the merged token a single coordinate, discarding the positional spread of its constituents. The authors ask which positional information must survive later merges to preserve expected rotary interactions.
