AI.method: Aperture stores Fourier moments of the token's weighted support evaluated at the model's rotary frequencies. Represented mass makes updates additive, while attention normalisation is treated as a separate readout choice. For uniform intervals, the representation reduces to a centre rotation times a sinc gain. The authors prove minimal real dimension among continuous states sufficient for the selected expected rotary interactions, characterise when centres determine interval widths, and construct matched counterexamples where they do not. Numerical checks validate the weighted-support implementation.
AI.result: Numerical checks verify the weighted-support implementation. In trained temporal readers, compression transfer varies with gain calibration and feature placement. In a prespecified native video question-answering comparison, stored support reaches 65.63% accuracy versus 67.12% for the deployed merging rule.
AI.conclusion: The results separate exact positional preservation under compression from downstream benefit: Aperture's moments are provably minimal and exact for the chosen rotary interactions, yet do not automatically outperform the deployed merging rule, since transfer depends on gain calibration and feature placement.

title: Credit-Guided Policy Improvement for Test-time Adaptive Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Test-time adaptation for vision-language navigation (TTA-VLN) enables pretrained policies to adapt online to unseen environments using only test-time observations and interaction history. However, distribution shifts can distort local action preferences and lead to off-course decisions. Existing methods rely on predictive uncertainty, trajectory-level feedback, or accumulated adaptation experience to correct such deviations. These signals, however, do not directly reveal whether an executed action supports instruction-guided progress toward the goal. Moreover, a plausible corrective signal does not guarantee a reliable policy update. The key challenge is thus twofold: identifying interactions that support goal-directed improvement and determining whether the resulting updates are worth retaining. We observe that each executed action induces an immediate observation transition, providing evidence of its local consequences. Based on this insight, we propose Credit-Guided Policy Improvement (CGPI), which recovers signed, reference-relative decision credit from action-induced observation transitions without external outcome feedback. With the pretrained navigation policy frozen, CGPI uses this credit to propose lightweight adaptation updates and verifies them against prior credit-supported interactions. Updates are retained only when supported and rolled back otherwise. CGPI achieves consistent gains across the evaluated VLN benchmarks and navigation backbones, while qualitative robot trials further illustrate the feasibility of zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

AI.tldr: CGPI is a test-time adaptation method for vision-language navigation that derives signed, reference-relative decision credit from action-induced observation transitions, then proposes lightweight frozen-policy updates that are retained only if verified against prior credit-supported interactions, yielding consistent benchmark gains and feasible zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Test-time adaptation for VLN (TTA-VLN) lets pretrained policies adapt online to unseen environments using only test-time observations and interaction history, but distribution shifts can distort local action preferences and cause off-course decisions. Existing correction methods rely on predictive uncertainty, trajectory-level feedback, or accumulated adaptation experience, none of which directly reveal whether an executed action supports instruction-guided progress toward the goal. Additionally, a plausible corrective signal does not guarantee a reliable policy update, creating a twofold challenge: identifying interactions that support goal-directed improvement and deciding whether resulting updates are worth retaining.
AI.method: The paper observes that each executed action induces an immediate observation transition, which provides evidence of its local consequences. Building on this insight, it proposes Credit-Guided Policy Improvement (CGPI), which recovers signed, reference-relative decision credit from action-induced observation transitions without external outcome feedback. With the pretrained navigation policy frozen, CGPI uses this credit to propose lightweight adaptation updates and verifies them against prior credit-supported interactions, retaining updates only when supported and rolling them back otherwise.
AI.result: CGPI achieves consistent gains across the evaluated VLN benchmarks and navigation backbones, and qualitative robot trials further illustrate the feasibility of zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.conclusion: By grounding adaptation in action-induced observation transitions rather than predictive uncertainty or trajectory-level feedback, and by verifying updates before retention, CGPI offers a principled approach to test-time policy improvement for vision-language navigation.

title: AI as a Compiler: Compiling Triton kernels without the Triton compiler
summary: Compiler backends are expensive to build and maintain as programming models, workloads, and accelerators evolve. We investigate whether large language models can replace the conventional optimizing and lowering pipeline, a process that we call AI lowering. We study AI lowering from Triton to NVIDIA PTX: an LLM agent translates Triton kernels directly into PTX. We build an environment that evaluates candidate PTX, and an agentic harness in which an LLM translates Triton kernels into PTX. Across twelve common kernels on Ada, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs and ten kernels from recent ML papers, AI lowering achieves 0.83x-3.34x the performance of autotuned Triton. The largest gains come from transformations that Triton's lowering pipeline does not perform, such as decoding packed binary weights directly into Tensor Core operands (3.34x on BitDelta), assigning each thread a complete softmax row in tensor memory (1.37x on FlashAttention), and reusing overlapping convolution windows (up to 2.23x). These results rely on a robust evaluation harness with comprehensive verification support. We build on Volta, an existing PTX verifier, and substantially extend it to support modern GPU architectures by introducing support for Blackwell's tcgen05 Tensor Core interface. This requires modeling three architectural features: managed tensor memory, descriptor-based operand layouts, and asynchronous execution coordinated through commits, waits, memory barriers, and proxy fences. We discuss the challenges involved in formalizing them, as well as the current limitations. Our results suggest an emerging future in which AI compilers replace custom-written intermediate representations and checkers, reducing the time and engineering effort required to bring up software for new general-purpose and custom chips.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "AI lowering": using an LLM agent to translate Triton kernels directly into NVIDIA PTX, bypassing conventional compiler lowering pipelines, and shows that this approach often outperforms autotuned Triton while requiring a robust verification harness extended for modern GPU architectures.
AI.motivation: Compiler backends are expensive to build and maintain as programming models, workloads, and accelerators rapidly evolve. Conventional lowering pipelines and their custom intermediate representations and checkers demand significant engineering effort, especially when bringing up software for new general-purpose and custom chips.
AI.method: The authors study AI lowering from Triton to NVIDIA PTX, in which an LLM agent translates Triton kernels directly into PTX. They construct an environment that evaluates candidate PTX, plus an agentic harness where an LLM performs the translation. For verification they build on Volta, an existing PTX verifier, and substantially extend it to support modern GPU architectures, notably Blackwell's tcgen05 Tensor Core interface. This required modeling managed tensor memory, descriptor-based operand layouts, and asynchronous execution via commits, waits, memory barriers, and proxy fences.
AI.result: Across twelve common kernels on Ada, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs and ten kernels from recent ML papers, AI lowering achieves 0.83x-3.34x the performance of autotuned Triton. The largest gains arise from transformations Triton's lowering pipeline does not perform: decoding packed binary weights directly into Tensor Core operands (3.34x on BitDelta), assigning each thread a complete softmax row in tensor memory (1.37x on FlashAttention), and reusing overlapping convolution windows (up to 2.23x).
AI.conclusion: The results suggest an emerging future in which AI compilers replace custom-written intermediate representations and checkers, reducing the time and engineering effort required to bring up software for new general-purpose and custom chips. The authors also discuss challenges in formalizing modern architectural features and the current limitations of their approach.

title: BlenDAgger: Blended Shared Control for Interactive Imitation Learning
summary: Robot policies are frequently trained from human corrections, yet teleoperating a robot to provide corrections is burdensome, and human demonstrators are not always optimal. We propose Blended DAgger (BlenDAgger), an approach for collecting data to train imitation learning policies by using shared control to blend the policy's and demonstrator's actions during interventions. By blending human and policy actions, we aim to improve the autonomous performance of manipulation policies. We validate our approach across five manipulation tasks, two in the real world and three in simulation. Our approach achieves higher autonomous performance by 30 or more percentage points on two real-world tasks compared to a typical human-gated correction approach (HG-DAgger). We also investigate the advantages of BlenDAgger that allow for higher autonomous performance, finding that BlenDAgger results in 57% smoother transitions between policy control and human interventions, and 14% higher trajectory similarity to the training data. In a user study (n=14) on two real-world tasks, we find that BlenDAgger results in faster data collection (BF=13.32), and we do not find a difference in subjective perceptions. These results show that blended shared control leads to higher autonomous performance compared to typical methods for fine-tuning robot policies from fully teleoperated interventions.

AI.tldr: BlenDAgger blends the policy's and demonstrator's actions during interventions via shared control, yielding higher autonomous manipulation performance than standard human-gated correction.
AI.motivation: Robot policies are often trained from human corrections, but teleoperating a robot to provide corrections is burdensome, and human demonstrators are not always optimal. Existing human-gated correction methods (e.g., HG-DAgger) rely on fully teleoperated interventions, which are inefficient and can yield suboptimal data.
AI.method: The authors propose Blended DAgger (BlenDAgger), which uses shared control to blend the policy's and the demonstrator's actions during interventions. This blending is validated on five manipulation tasks: two real-world and three in simulation. The work compares BlenDAgger to HG-DAgger and analyzes transition smoothness, trajectory similarity to training data, and a user study (n=14) on two real-world tasks.
AI.result: BlenDAgger achieves higher autonomous performance by 30 or more percentage points on two real-world tasks versus HG-DAgger. It produces 57% smoother transitions between policy control and human interventions and 14% higher trajectory similarity to training data. In the user study (n=14), BlenDAgger enables faster data collection (BF=13.32) with no difference in subjective perceptions.
AI.conclusion: Blended shared control leads to higher autonomous performance compared to typical methods for fine-tuning robot policies from fully teleoperated interventions.

title: UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents reuse external memory to guide new tasks, but effective retrieval requires learning which memory sets improve execution. Such learning relies on costly outcome feedback: ordinary retrieval observes only executed sets, while evaluating alternatives requires additional rollouts. We introduce \textsc{UpliftMem}, which learns memory retrieval from set-level execution uplift relative to the same executor without memory. A theoretical analysis of how retrieval preferences restrict feedback coverage motivates targeted probing of alternative memory sets. Probe selection follows an expected value of sample information (EVSI) criterion, derived in closed form under a correlated Gaussian model, to allocate limited training rollouts according to their expected improvement in local retrieval decisions. The shared scorer is trained with a frozen executor and selects memory sets without test-time probes. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and BigCodeBench, \textsc{UpliftMem} achieves the best success rates among evaluated baselines on the main evaluation sets. Controlled fixed-store and matched probe budget evaluations further demonstrate improved memory-use decisions and more effective use of execution feedback.

AI.tldr: UpliftMem learns memory retrieval for LLM agents from set-level execution uplift versus a no-memory executor, using an EVSI-based probing criterion to target informative alternative memory sets under a limited rollout budget.
AI.motivation: Effective memory retrieval for LLM agents requires learning which memory sets improve task execution, but this learning is hindered by costly outcome feedback: standard retrieval only observes executed sets, and evaluating alternatives demands extra rollouts. This creates a feedback coverage problem that limits learning of retrieval preferences.
AI.method: The paper introduces UpliftMem, which learns memory retrieval from set-level execution uplift relative to the same executor without memory. A theoretical analysis of how retrieval preferences restrict feedback coverage motivates targeted probing of alternative memory sets. Probe selection uses an expected value of sample information (EVSI) criterion derived in closed form under a correlated Gaussian model, allocating limited training rollouts by their expected improvement in local retrieval decisions. The shared scorer is trained with a frozen executor and performs memory-set selection without test-time probes.
AI.result: On ALFWorld, WebShop, and BigCodeBench, UpliftMem achieves the best success rates among evaluated baselines on the main evaluation sets. Controlled fixed-store and matched probe budget experiments further show improved memory-use decisions and more effective use of execution feedback.
AI.conclusion: Learning memory retrieval from execution uplift, combined with EVSI-guided targeted probing, enables more effective and feedback-efficient memory-set selection for LLM agents, outperforming evaluated baselines across multiple benchmarks without requiring test-time probes.

title: When to Adapt: Multi-Signal Domain Shift Detection for Efficient Training-Free Adaptation in Open-Vocabulary Segmentation
summary: Robust and reliable perception is essential for autonomous robots operating in real-world environments, particularly in long-term missions where environmental conditions may change significantly over time. Although recent advances in Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) have improved open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, these models can still suffer from domain shift, which can significantly degrade performance if they are not adapted to the current environment. Training-free domain adaptation is a relevant paradigm for adaptation, consisting of adjusting the model online using lightweight adapters. Recent approaches apply this on a per-frame basis, which is impractical for deployments on resource-constrained robotic hardware. To tackle this, we propose a multi-signal domain shift detection method for training-free continual test-time adaptation (TF-CTTA) in open-vocabulary segmentation. Our method leverages temporal coherence across consecutive frames by monitoring and combining complementary aspects of domain shift (visual change, adapter mismatch, and semantic drift) to trigger adaptation only when needed. We validate our approach on a benchmark including indoor and outdoor environments and using real robotic data. We demonstrate that our approach maintains segmentation accuracy while substantially reducing adaptations, making training-free adaptation practical and feasible for long-term, real-world robotic deployments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-signal domain shift detection method for training-free continual test-time adaptation in open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, triggering adaptation only when needed by monitoring visual change, adapter mismatch, and semantic drift.
AI.motivation: Robust perception is essential for autonomous robots in long-term missions where environmental conditions change. Although Visual Foundation Models improve open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, they suffer from domain shift. Training-free domain adaptation via lightweight online adapters is relevant, but existing per-frame adaptation approaches are impractical for resource-constrained robotic hardware.
AI.method: A multi-signal domain shift detection method for training-free continual test-time adaptation (TF-CTTA) in open-vocabulary segmentation. It leverages temporal coherence across consecutive frames by monitoring and combining complementary aspects of domain shift—visual change, adapter mismatch, and semantic drift—to trigger adaptation only when needed.
AI.result: Validated on a benchmark including indoor and outdoor environments and using real robotic data. The approach maintains segmentation accuracy while substantially reducing the number of adaptations.
AI.conclusion: The method makes training-free adaptation practical and feasible for long-term, real-world robotic deployments by reducing unnecessary adaptations while preserving accuracy.

title: CAD-Native Transformer Operators for AI-Aided Engineering
summary: Modern engineering systems, from automobiles to aircraft, are designed by using precise, continuous parametric computer-aided design (CAD) models. Evaluating design changes through numerical simulation requires meshing the continuous geometry, a computationally expensive and often brittle process that can require manual intervention and replaces the continuous representation with a discrete approximation. Most neural surrogates accelerate the simulation, but inherit this representation gap by relying on meshes, point clouds, voxels, or other sampled approximations of geometry. We introduce CANTO, a transformer neural operator that maps directly from continuous CAD geometry to physical fields, without meshing the input geometry. We develop a theoretical framework for learning operators from geometric manifolds to function spaces of physical fields, representing geometry through sequences of parametric patches. CANTO instantiates this framework by directly tokenizing non-uniform rational B-spline (NURBS) patches from their control points, knot vectors, and weights, and predicts continuous surface and volume fields at arbitrary query locations. We evaluate CANTO on four automotive and aircraft aerodynamics industry benchmarks: AhmedML, WindsorML, DrivAerML, and HiLiftAeroML. CANTO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on most evaluated surface and volume prediction tasks, including a 19.8% reduction in surface-pressure relative $L_2$ error compared with AB-UPT on HiLiftAeroML. Differentiability with respect to CAD parameters further enables gradient-based inverse design of designs. On AhmedML, CANTO identifies designs with 4.4 to 20.4% lower drag than the best dataset designs satisfying the same volume and lift constraints, with the improvements verified using the same CFD setup used to generate the original dataset.

AI.tldr: CANTO is a transformer neural operator that maps continuous CAD geometry (NURBS patches) directly to physical fields without meshing, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on automotive and aircraft aerodynamics benchmarks and enabling gradient-based inverse design.
AI.motivation: Conventional CAD-to-simulation pipelines require meshing continuous geometry, which is computationally expensive, brittle, and often needs manual intervention. Existing neural surrogates speed up simulation but inherit this representation gap by operating on meshes, point clouds, or voxels—discrete approximations of the true continuous geometry.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical framework for learning operators from geometric manifolds to function spaces of physical fields, representing geometry as sequences of parametric patches. CANTO instantiates this by tokenizing non-uniform rational B-spline (NURBS) patches directly from their control points, knot vectors, and weights, and predicts continuous surface and volume fields at arbitrary query locations.
AI.result: Evaluated on four industry aerodynamics benchmarks (AhmedML, WindsorML, DrivAerML, HiLiftAeroML), CANTO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on most surface and volume prediction tasks, including a 19.8% reduction in surface-pressure relative L2 error versus AB-UPT on HiLiftAeroML. On AhmedML, gradient-based inverse design finds designs with 4.4–20.4% lower drag than the best dataset designs under the same volume and lift constraints, verified with the original CFD setup.
AI.conclusion: CANTO closes the representation gap between continuous CAD geometry and neural surrogates by mapping directly from CAD to physical fields without meshing. Its differentiability with respect to CAD parameters enables gradient-based inverse design, yielding verified drag improvements.

title: Cascaded consensus splitting for multi-branch contingency games
summary: Contingency games enable agents to anticipate and plan for other agents' hypothetical intents by constructing trajectories with a shared prefix and intent-dependent branches. While contingency games capture intent uncertainty, existing formulations rely on a single branching time, oversimplifying interactions in which different agents' intentions are revealed at different times. Moreover, the computational cost of such problems grows rapidly with the number of agents and intents, as all scenario-dependent best responses must be solved jointly. We introduce a multi-branch contingency architecture in which sources of intent uncertainty can be resolved progressively at different branching times, allowing the planned trajectories to adapt to the asynchronous revelation of intents. We also develop an ADMM-based solver that exploits scenario-level parallelism. Experiments on tightly coupled three-agent interactions support that the proposed architecture outperforms the conventional single-branch while achieving a lower mean receding-horizon solve time.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multi-branch contingency architecture where intent uncertainty resolves progressively at different branching times, plus an ADMM-based solver with scenario-level parallelism, improving on single-branch formulations for tightly coupled multi-agent interactions.
AI.motivation: Existing contingency games use a single branching time, oversimplifying interactions where different agents' intentions are revealed at different times; additionally, computational cost grows rapidly with the number of agents and intents because all scenario-dependent best responses must be solved jointly.
AI.method: A multi-branch contingency architecture that allows sources of intent uncertainty to be resolved progressively at different branching times so planned trajectories adapt to asynchronous intent revelation, combined with an ADMM-based solver exploiting scenario-level parallelism.
AI.result: Experiments on tightly coupled three-agent interactions show the proposed architecture outperforms the conventional single-branch formulation while achieving a lower mean receding-horizon solve time.
AI.conclusion: Multi-branch contingency planning with asynchronous branching times and a parallel ADMM solver enables more accurate modeling of intent uncertainty and more efficient computation than single-branch contingency games.

title: Geometry-Conditioned Fixed-Scaffold Encoders for Time-Warp Robust Sequence Retrieval
summary: Embedding-based retrieval is attractive for long sequence collections because each item can be encoded once and searched by nearest-neighbor ranking. The difficulty is that the objects being indexed are often observed under a noncanonical clock: cardiac cycles stretch with rate, speech changes with tempo, and sensor traces reach comparable states at different speeds. This paper studies a specific source of instability in patch-based encoders for this regime. If patch boundaries are chosen from signal geometry, then the tokenization can change under the same temporal deformation that the representation is expected to tolerate. We propose GeoPatch, a fixed-scaffold patch encoder that keeps token support independent of geometry and uses slope, curvature, acceleration, affine-residual, and confidence descriptors only as continuous conditioning variables. The design turns boundary variation into feature modulation: geometry can change the embedding through a controlled pathway, but it cannot change the number, order, or support of local tokens. We formalize this distinction through a mechanism-level stability analysis that separates boundary drift, affine timing variation, confidence-weighted geometry perturbation, and retrieval-margin effects. The same local tokens support global embedding retrieval and late-interaction scoring, so the scoring rule can be matched to the evaluation protocol. Across ECG, speech, and multivariate time-series retrieval tasks, GeoPatch improves early-rank retrieval under timing variation while exposing a clear trade-off between local surface matching and strict non-overlap retrieval.

AI.tldr: GeoPatch is a fixed-scaffold patch encoder that decouples token support from signal geometry, improving embedding-based retrieval stability under temporal deformation.
AI.motivation: Embedding-based retrieval is effective for long sequences since each item is encoded once and searched via nearest-neighbor ranking. However, many indexed objects are observed under a noncanonical clock (cardiac cycles stretch with rate, speech changes with tempo, sensor traces reach similar states at different speeds). In patch-based encoders, if patch boundaries are derived from signal geometry, tokenization itself can change under the same temporal deformation the representation is meant to tolerate, introducing instability.
AI.method: The authors propose GeoPatch, a fixed-scaffold patch encoder that keeps token support independent of geometry. Slope, curvature, acceleration, affine-residual, and confidence descriptors are used only as continuous conditioning variables. This converts boundary variation into feature modulation: geometry can alter the embedding through a controlled pathway, but cannot change the number, order, or support of local tokens. A mechanism-level stability analysis separates boundary drift, affine timing variation, confidence-weighted geometry perturbation, and retrieval-margin effects. The same local tokens support both global embedding retrieval and late-interaction scoring, allowing the scoring rule to match the evaluation protocol.
AI.result: Across ECG, speech, and multivariate time-series retrieval tasks, GeoPatch improves early-rank retrieval under timing variation, while revealing a clear trade-off between local surface matching and strict non-overlap retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Fixing token support and treating geometry as a conditioning signal yields more stable patch-based embeddings for retrieval under temporal deformation, with a controllable separation between local surface matching and strict non-overlap retrieval.

title: Semantic Map Sharing and Capability-Aware Coverage Planning for AI-Native 6G Robotic Coordination
comment: An alternative version of this work was accepted for presentation at IEEE CSCN 2026
summary: Search and Rescue (SAR) operations increasingly deploy heterogeneous teams of aerial and ground robots. However, conventional coverage methods typically do not translate perceived terrain into platform-specific reachability, while continuous image exchange imposes a high communication cost. We propose an edge-centric, semantic-aware coverage planning framework that integrates aerial terrain perception, robot-specific traversability reasoning, and payload-efficient semantic state sharing. Aerial observations are converted into compact semantic grid maps, enabling reachability-constrained area decomposition and capability-aware coverage paths that assign only regions admitted by each robot's capability profile. The resulting perception-sharing-planning loop feeds semantic corrections into traversability reasoning and replanning, forming an application-level mechanism motivated by AI-enabled goal-oriented communication envisioned for AI-native 6G networks. For the high-update case, transmitting semantic corrections reduces the application payload by a factor of approximately $82$ relative to periodic full-map sharing. Across matched benchmark scenarios, the proposed method achieved $91.5\%$ coverage with no capability-infeasible allocations, compared with $78.8\%$ coverage and a $21.5\%$ capability-infeasible allocation rate for LS-MCPP. Semantic corrections update the shared planning state without requiring repeated transmission of the complete map.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an edge-centric semantic-aware coverage planning framework for heterogeneous aerial-ground SAR robot teams, converting aerial observations into compact semantic grid maps for reachability-constrained decomposition and payload-efficient semantic state sharing.
AI.motivation: Conventional coverage methods fail to map perceived terrain to platform-specific reachability, and continuous full-image exchange incurs prohibitive communication cost in heterogeneous SAR robot teams.
AI.method: An edge-centric, semantic-aware coverage planning framework integrates aerial terrain perception, robot-specific traversability reasoning, and compact semantic grid maps. These enable reachability-constrained area decomposition and capability-aware coverage paths assigning only feasible regions. A perception-sharing-planning loop feeds semantic corrections into traversability reasoning and replanning, framed as goal-oriented communication for AI-native 6G.
AI.result: In the high-update case, transmitting semantic corrections reduces application payload by ~82x versus periodic full-map sharing. Across matched benchmarks, the method achieved 91.5% coverage with zero capability-infeasible allocations, versus 78.8% coverage and 21.5% infeasible allocation rate for LS-MCPP.
AI.conclusion: Semantic corrections update the shared planning state without repeated transmission of the complete map, improving coverage and allocation feasibility while greatly reducing communication payload.

title: Calibrate the Decisions That Change the Future: On-Policy Post-Training Quantization for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) lowers deployment cost for multimodal large language models, but calibration typically reconstructs fixed sequences with local objectives. This overlooks autoregressive feedback: a quantization-induced token change redirects the prefix and changes future states. Yet on-policy coverage alone is insufficient because many decision mismatches barely affect future generation. We propose OnPTQ, an on-policy framework that calibrates on trajectories visited by the current quantized policy. On shared prefixes, OnPTQ identifies quantization-eroded boundaries, evaluates competing tokens through short counterfactual rollouts, and combines current discrepancy with branch consequence into a Decision--Consequence risk. The risk prioritizes critical states, while context anchoring and trajectory refresh preserve multimodal behavior and keep calibration aligned with the updated policy. We further derive a Decision--Consequence bound linking behavioral deviation to current policy discrepancy and action-conditioned future-value span. Across vision--language and omni-modal Qwen models under multiple low-bit settings, OnPTQ improves downstream performance and yields fewer correctness flips against the corresponding Dense/FP16 references, without changing the deployed inference graph.

AI.tldr: OnPTQ is an on-policy post-training quantization framework that calibrates on trajectories visited by the current quantized policy, using counterfactual rollouts to prioritize decision-critical states, improving multimodal LLM performance under low-bit settings without changing the inference graph.
AI.motivation: Existing PTQ methods reconstruct fixed sequences with local objectives, overlooking autoregressive feedback where a quantization-induced token change redirects the prefix and alters future states. However, on-policy coverage alone is insufficient because many decision mismatches barely affect future generation.
AI.method: OnPTQ calibrates on trajectories visited by the current quantized policy. On shared prefixes, it identifies quantization-eroded boundaries, evaluates competing tokens via short counterfactual rollouts, and combines current discrepancy with branch consequence into a Decision–Consequence risk. Context anchoring and trajectory refresh preserve multimodal behavior and keep calibration aligned with the updated policy. The authors also derive a Decision–Consequence bound linking behavioral deviation to current policy discrepancy and action-conditioned future-value span.
AI.result: Across vision–language and omni-modal Qwen models under multiple low-bit settings, OnPTQ improves downstream performance and yields fewer correctness flips against Dense/FP16 references, without changing the deployed inference graph.
AI.conclusion: OnPTQ effectively addresses autoregressive feedback in PTQ for multimodal LLMs, prioritizing critical states for calibration and delivering measurable gains without altering deployment.

title: Learning Expressive and Compositional Motion Representation via Spectral Skills
summary: Robotic foundation models offer a promising path toward general-purpose humanoid robot control, often through hierarchical architectures. However, their effectiveness depends on the command interface between the planner and the controller, which must support accurate execution while remaining easy to predict, and ideally allow new behaviors to be composed from prior ones. In this work, we introduce spectral skills, a latent representation of this interface that meets these requirements through predictive representation learning. By design, spectral skills compactly encode short motion segments and are learned by predicting subsequent motion rather than reconstructing the encoder input. On a 29-DoF humanoid, a controller conditioned on spectral skills reduces global tracking error by 62\% relative to the state of the art. The same frozen controller chains independently encoded skills without a separate transition policy. It also composes new behaviors by adding orthogonal directions to any compatible base skill, producing combinations unseen in the training data. We demonstrate tracking, chaining, and composition, as well as control through a language-conditioned planner, on Unitree G1 hardware. Project page: https://spectral-skill.github.io

AI.tldr: Spectral skills are a latent command interface for hierarchical humanoid control, learned via predictive representation learning, that enables accurate tracking, chaining, and compositional generalization of behaviors on a 29-DoF humanoid.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical robotic foundation models for general-purpose humanoid control depend critically on the command interface between planner and controller. Such an interface must support accurate execution, be easy to predict, and ideally allow new behaviors to be composed from previously learned ones, requirements not fully met by existing representations.
AI.method: The authors propose spectral skills, a latent representation of the planner-controller interface learned through predictive representation learning. Spectral skills compactly encode short motion segments and are trained by predicting subsequent motion instead of reconstructing the encoder input. A controller is then conditioned on these spectral skills on a 29-DoF humanoid.
AI.result: Conditioning the controller on spectral skills reduces global tracking error by 62% compared to the state of the art. The same frozen controller chains independently encoded skills without a separate transition policy, and composes new behaviors by adding orthogonal directions to any compatible base skill, yielding combinations unseen in training. Tracking, chaining, composition, and language-conditioned planner control are demonstrated on Unitree G1 hardware.
AI.conclusion: Spectral skills provide a predictable, compact, and composable latent command interface that improves tracking accuracy and enables skill chaining and novel behavior composition, validating the approach on real humanoid hardware.

title: The Default Trap: Rethinking Plan Evaluation in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: An executor can respond strongly to a change in a supplied plan's priority while showing a small change in the same information-selection probability when a default-aligned whole plan is removed. We call the risk of interpreting the latter as weak responsiveness to alternative priorities the default trap. We compare paired plans that prioritize different information targets with a shared no-plan reference. An accounting identity relates these distinct behavioral contrasts. Across 3,200 decision windows on 160 selected Retail, Airline, and AgentDojo tasks, switching priorities strongly redirects two models' choices, while the two plan-versus-default contrasts differ. In 2,160 additional windows, reversing account-list order shifts default target selection by 63.3-98.3 percentage points; priority-switching effects remain 96.7-100.0 points in either order. A separate 3,240-window component study finds strong control under single priority sentences, with effects of additional text varying by group and direction. Finally, 1,080 full-task episodes yield observed success differences of -19.4 to +8.3 points relative to no plan. All Retail and Airline success intervals include zero; AgentDojo results describe four fixed application worlds. These findings support joint reporting of priority responsiveness, presentation-dependent defaults, and task success and cost.

AI.tldr: Plans can strongly redirect an executor when their priority changes, yet produce only small choice shifts when a default-aligned plan is removed—a confound the authors call the "default trap." Using an accounting identity across paired contrasts, they show priority-responsiveness and plan-versus-default effects are distinct, presentation-sensitive, and must be reported jointly with task success.
AI.motivation: Evaluations of whether an executor "responds" to a plan's priority can be misread: a large change when priority flips may coexist with a tiny change when a default-aligned whole plan is removed. Interpreting the latter as weak priority responsiveness is a systematic interpretive risk (the default trap), so the paper aims to disentangle these behavioral contrasts and establish how they should be measured and reported.
AI.method: Paired plans prioritizing different information targets are compared against a shared no-plan reference, linked by an accounting identity relating the distinct contrasts. Main study: 3,200 decision windows on 160 selected Retail, Airline, and AgentDojo tasks, two models. Order-manipulation study: 2,160 windows reversing account-list order. Component study: 3,240 windows testing single priority sentences versus additional text. Episode study: 1,080 full-task episodes comparing success to no plan.
AI.result: Priority switching strongly redirects both models' choices, but the two plan-versus-default contrasts diverge. Reversing account-list order shifts default target selection by 63.3-98.3 percentage points, while priority-switching effects stay at 96.7-100.0 points in either order. Single priority sentences yield strong control; effects of extra text vary by group and direction. Full-task success differences range from -19.4 to +8.3 points versus no plan; Retail and Airline intervals include zero, and AgentDojo covers four fixed application worlds.
AI.conclusion: Priority responsiveness, presentation-dependent defaults, and task success/cost are separable and can point in different directions, so any single contrast is insufficient. The authors advocate joint reporting of all three to avoid the default trap and to give a faithful picture of plan-following behavior.

title: ProAct-VLM: Pre-Failure Vision-Language Task Replanning with Continuous Perception Feedback
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026). Project page: https://github.com/moured/ProAct-VLM
summary: Long-horizon robotic tasks are vulnerable to unexpected environmental changes that can render planned actions ineffective or unsafe. To address this, robots must detect such changes as they occur, interpret their impact, and adjust their actions accordingly. Traditional rule-based decision-making pipelines are brittle in open-world conditions, as they are hand-tuned for specific scenarios and lack generalization. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) offer a promising alternative as they combine broad world knowledge with unified visual--text reasoning, enabling them to generalize across diverse scenarios and generate accurate, grounded task plans. However, for effective deployment in dynamic real-world settings, VLMs must be embedded into frameworks capable of handling uncertainty and environmental changes. Existing frameworks broadly address this reactively, triggering replanning only after execution failures or post-task checks, risking failed actions. Some methods verify conditions before actions, but these discrete checks miss changes occurring during execution. To address this, we present ProAct-VLM, an adaptive, physically grounded task planning framework that integrates VLMs within a real-time perception--feedback loop. ProAct-VLM continuously monitors the environment and re-plans as soon as relevant changes are detected, enabling adaptation before failure occurs. Evaluations against multiple baselines and across different VLM backbones show that our framework improves both success rates and efficiency in dynamic, long-horizon manipulation tasks. Project page: https://github.com/moured/ProAct-VLM

AI.tldr: ProAct-VLM is an adaptive, physically grounded task planning framework that embeds Vision-Language Models in a real-time perception-feedback loop, continuously monitoring the environment and re-planning the moment relevant changes are detected, thereby preventing failures before they occur in dynamic, long-horizon manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon robotic tasks are vulnerable to unexpected environmental changes that can render planned actions ineffective or unsafe. Robots must therefore detect such changes as they occur, interpret their impact, and adjust actions accordingly. Traditional rule-based decision-making pipelines are brittle in open-world conditions because they are hand-tuned for specific scenarios and lack generalization. While VLMs offer broad world knowledge and unified visual-text reasoning for generalizable, grounded task plans, deploying them in dynamic real-world settings requires embedding them in frameworks that handle uncertainty and environmental change. Existing frameworks address this reactively, triggering replanning only after execution failures or post-task checks (risking failed actions), and even methods that verify conditions before actions rely on discrete checks that miss changes occurring during execution.
AI.method: The authors present ProAct-VLM, an adaptive, physically grounded task planning framework that integrates VLMs within a real-time perception-feedback loop. The framework continuously monitors the environment and re-plans as soon as relevant changes are detected, enabling adaptation before failure occurs.
AI.result: Evaluations against multiple baselines and across different VLM backbones show that the framework improves both success rates and efficiency in dynamic, long-horizon manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: ProAct-VLM enables proactive, pre-failure adaptation for long-horizon robotic manipulation by combining VLM-based planning with continuous perceptual monitoring and real-time replanning, outperforming reactive baselines in success rate and efficiency.

title: Where Does Staleness Accumulate? Pool Aware Effective Staleness Control for Asynchronous RL in LLM Post-Training
summary: Fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) improves resource utilization in large language model post-training by overlapping rollout generation with policy optimization, but it also introduces policy lag as trajectories are generated and queued while the trainer continues to update. We study how this lag accumulates over a trajectory's lifetime and how it can be controlled without sacrificing the wall-clock benefits of asynchronous execution. We decompose trajectory staleness into Generation Staleness, accumulated before rollout completion, and Waiting Staleness, accumulated after a completed trajectory enters the pool. Motivated by this decomposition, we introduce PACE (Pool-Aware Control of Effective Staleness). PACE converts excess pool occupancy into an adaptive rejection budget and ranks completed trajectories using an effective-staleness score that combines Waiting Staleness with prefix-aware Generation Staleness. This avoids penalizing long or interrupted rollouts solely because they span multiple policy versions. In single-turn mathematical reasoning, PACE improves the six-benchmark average validation accuracy by 18.7\% over unfiltered asynchronous RL at the same wall-clock budget and matches synchronous RL performance with 47.1\% less GPU time. PACE also improves validation performance in multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning, outperforming both synchronous and unfiltered asynchronous RL. Further experiments with the mixture-of-experts model and an alternative RL algorithm support its applicability across model architectures and training algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PACE, a pool-aware staleness control method for fully asynchronous RL in LLM post-training that decomposes staleness into generation and waiting components and controls it via adaptive rejection to match synchronous performance with far less GPU time.
AI.motivation: Fully asynchronous RL improves wall-clock efficiency by overlapping rollout generation with policy optimization but introduces policy lag: trajectories generated under older policies accumulate staleness while the trainer keeps updating. The paper aims to understand how this lag accumulates over a trajectory's lifetime and to control it without losing the wall-clock benefits of asynchrony.
AI.method: The authors decompose trajectory staleness into Generation Staleness (accumulated before rollout completion) and Waiting Staleness (accumulated after entering the pool). Based on this, they propose PACE (Pool-Aware Control of Effective Staleness), which converts excess pool occupancy into an adaptive rejection budget and ranks completed trajectories by an effective-staleness score combining Waiting Staleness with prefix-aware Generation Staleness, avoiding penalizing long or interrupted rollouts solely for spanning multiple policy versions.
AI.result: In single-turn mathematical reasoning, PACE raises the six-benchmark average validation accuracy by 18.7% over unfiltered asynchronous RL at the same wall-clock budget and matches synchronous RL performance with 47.1% less GPU time. It also improves validation performance in multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning, outperforming both synchronous and unfiltered asynchronous RL. Additional experiments with a mixture-of-experts model and an alternative RL algorithm support its applicability across architectures and algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing staleness into generation and waiting components enables effective, principled staleness control in asynchronous RL, and PACE achieves synchronous-level or better performance with substantially reduced GPU time, demonstrating broad applicability across model architectures and RL algorithms.

title: CogWAM: Aligning Semantic Cognition with World Action Modeling via Event-Driven Interfaces
summary: Robot policies increasingly incorporate semantic reasoning and future-world prediction, yet combining these capabilities does not guarantee that local predictions and actions remain aligned with task progress. We introduce CogWAM, a cognition-guided world-action model that establishes an explicit semantic interface between task reasoning and world-action learning through a persistent Semantic State, which stores completed task events and the active subtask. CogWAM updates this state only when observations indicate semantic transitions, allowing task-level context to persist across multiple action chunks. To bridge semantic context with physical prediction and control, CogWAM employs progress-conditioned WORLD and ACTION queries that selectively extract task-relevant information for future-world prediction and action generation. During training, the Semantic State provides shared task-progress context for both branches, while inference removes the future-prediction branch and directly generates actions from observations and the maintained state. We further introduce semantic training strategies to improve transition learning and closed-loop conditioning. Without additional robot-action pretraining, CogWAM achieves 15.56 / 11.70 % Score/SR on RoboDojo and state-of-the-art performance on BiCoord, while real-world experiments demonstrate closed-loop dual-arm manipulation with 16.4 fewer Semantic State regenerations than step-wise updating.

AI.tldr: CogWAM is a cognition-guided world-action model that uses a persistent Semantic State to couple task reasoning with world-action learning, achieving strong results on RoboDojo, BiCoord, and real-world dual-arm manipulation.
AI.motivation: Robot policies increasingly combine semantic reasoning and future-world prediction, but these capabilities alone do not ensure that local predictions and actions stay aligned with overall task progress.
AI.method: CogWAM establishes an explicit semantic interface via a persistent Semantic State storing completed task events and the active subtask, updated only at semantic transitions so task context persists across action chunks. Progress-conditioned WORLD and ACTION queries selectively extract task-relevant information for future-world prediction and action generation; during training the Semantic State supplies shared task-progress context to both branches, while inference drops the future-prediction branch and generates actions directly from observations and the maintained state. Semantic training strategies further improve transition learning and closed-loop conditioning.
AI.result: Without additional robot-action pretraining, CogWAM achieves 15.56 / 11.70 % Score/SR on RoboDojo and state-of-the-art performance on BiCoord; real-world experiments show closed-loop dual-arm manipulation with 16.4 fewer Semantic State regenerations than step-wise updating.
AI.conclusion: An explicit, persistent Semantic State that gates updates on semantic transitions effectively aligns semantic reasoning with physical prediction and control, yielding competitive task performance and more efficient closed-loop manipulation.

title: ARC-KV: Amortizing Anchor Search for Reconstruction-Based KV Cache Compaction
summary: Long-context large language model inference is bottlenecked by KV caches that grow linearly with sequence length. This burden is especially severe for long, reusable context prefixes, whose cache must serve many downstream queries. Reconstruction-based methods such as Attention Matching achieve strong downstream task performance with compact KV caches. However, iterative anchor search dominates the compaction cost of OMP-based Attention Matching. This motivates our selective amortization principle of learning a reusable anchor-selection policy across contexts while retaining context-specific reconstruction. In this work, we propose ARC-KV, a novel reconstruction-based KV cache compaction method that follows this principle. To this end, we first train a value-aware indexer to select real-key anchors in a single scoring pass. ARC-KV then applies convex-hull-constrained key merging and fits an attention-mass bias and compact values against the full cache. At inference time, ARC-KV builds the compact cache once per context using the frozen indexer and reuses it for all subsequent queries. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ARC-KV outperforms reported compaction methods in most settings across QuALITY, RULER, and LongBench on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. In particular, at 10% KV retention on QuALITY, ARC-KV improves accuracy from 0.6409 to 0.6474 over Attention Matching while reducing compaction time by a factor of 25.73, from 959.8 s to 37.3 s.

AI.tldr: ARC-KV is a reconstruction-based KV cache compaction method that learns a reusable, value-aware anchor-selection policy (a frozen indexer) to build a compact cache once per context and reuse it across queries, avoiding the costly iterative OMP anchor search of Attention Matching. It improves accuracy on QuALITY, RULER, and LongBench and cuts compaction time by ~26x.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by KV caches that scale linearly with sequence length, a problem amplified for long, reusable context prefixes whose cache must serve many downstream queries. Reconstruction-based methods like Attention Matching give strong performance with compact KV caches, but their OMP-based iterative anchor search dominates compaction cost, making per-context cache construction expensive.
AI.method: ARC-KV follows a selective amortization principle: learn a reusable anchor-selection policy across contexts while keeping context-specific reconstruction. It trains a value-aware indexer that selects real-key anchors in a single scoring pass, then applies convex-hull-constrained key merging and fits an attention-mass bias plus compact values against the full cache. At inference, the compact cache is built once per context using the frozen indexer and reused for all subsequent queries.
AI.result: Experiments on QuALITY, RULER, and LongBench with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show ARC-KV outperforming reported compaction methods in most settings. On QuALITY at 10% KV retention, it raises accuracy from 0.6409 to 0.6474 over Attention Matching while reducing compaction time 25.73x, from 959.8 s to 37.3 s.
AI.conclusion: Amortizing anchor selection through a learned, frozen indexer while retaining context-specific reconstruction yields a compact KV cache that is both more accurate and dramatically cheaper to build than iterative OMP-based Attention Matching, making it well suited for reusable long-context prefixes.

title: Recompositional Robotics: Cross-Domain, Open-set, and Lifelong Modularity Beyond Morphology
comment: 2026 IEEE/RSJ IROS Workshop on Reconfigurable Modular Robots
summary: Research in modular robotics has produced capable approaches allowing a robot's morphology to change online, with recent efforts also developing approaches to decide which morphology to assume and automatically propagate that decision into the robot's motion planning and control. These approaches are powerful and increase adaptability in the field. However, an alternative objective is not to build robots whose structures can change, but robots whose fundamental capabilities can change, where capability is a joint function across several domains, including kino-dynamics, perception, compute, and high-level coordinating behaviors. A robot designed to be reconfigured across these domains has a greater capacity to alter its capability than one that can be reconfigured in a single domain. We refer to this cross-domain reconfigurability as integration span, and recognize a complementary measure of the resistance to reconfiguration, which we refer to as integration inertia. Current modular robots have reduced integration inertia in the structural domain while it remains high in the other domains that contribute to integration span. We assert that the systems that can provide the most utility through reconfiguration in practice are those maximizing span and minimizing inertia and call this general problem recompositional robotics: adaptation over a heterogeneous set of modules including hardware, software, compute, and behavior that abstracts each component by the interfaces it requires and provides such that they can be reasoned over holistically. We define the problem, ground it in two deployed systems and active research efforts, and pose open questions about the future of recompositional robotics.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes modular robotics around "recompositional robotics": maximizing cross-domain "integration span" (kino-dynamics, perception, compute, behavior) while minimizing "integration inertia," illustrated via deployed systems and open research questions.
AI.motivation: Existing modular robotics excels at online structural/morphological change, with decision-making for which morphology to adopt and propagation into planning and control. Yet this single-domain focus limits true adaptability. The authors argue the deeper goal is robots whose fundamental capabilities—jointly spanning kino-dynamics, perception, compute, and high-level coordinating behaviors—can change, since cross-domain reconfigurability yields greater capability alteration than single-domain structural reconfiguration alone.
AI.method: The paper is a conceptual/problem-definition contribution. It introduces "integration span" to denote cross-domain reconfigurability and "integration inertia" as the complementary resistance to reconfiguration. It asserts a utility principle (maximize span, minimize inertia) and formalizes "recompositional robotics" as adaptation over a heterogeneous set of modules—hardware, software, compute, and behavior—abstracted by the interfaces each component requires and provides so they can be reasoned over holistically. The problem is grounded in two deployed systems and active research efforts.
AI.result: Current modular robots achieve reduced integration inertia in the structural domain, but inertia remains high in the other domains contributing to integration span (perception, compute, behavior). The framing is substantiated through two deployed systems and ongoing research efforts, demonstrating the gap between structural-only reconfigurability and cross-domain recomposition.
AI.conclusion: Systems delivering the most practical utility via reconfiguration are those maximizing integration span while minimizing integration inertia. The authors define recompositional robotics as this general adaptation problem, ground it in real systems, and pose open questions about its future.

title: Automated Screw Planning for Reduced Pelvic Fractures Based on Statistical Shape Models and Deep Learning
summary: Percutaneous iliosacral screw fixation is an important minimally invasive treatment for unstable pelvic fractures. Because the sacroiliac region has complex anatomy and narrow screw corridors, the accuracy and safety of screw placement directly affect surgical outcomes. Accurate and reliable preoperative screw planning is therefore essential to improve surgical success and reduce intraoperative risks. Conventional preoperative planning typically requires surgeons to determine screw trajectories through manual measurements, a labor-intensive process that depends on subjective clinical experience. To address these challenges, we propose a fully automated pipeline for preoperative iliosacral screw planning in patients with pelvic fractures. Using patient-specific three-dimensional anatomy, the pipeline automatically identifies safe screw corridors and generates individualized insertion trajectories to support clinical preoperative planning. We evaluated the proposed pipeline on 200 clinical cases of pelvic fractures. Compared with conventional manual measurements, the safety margin of the safe insertion corridors increased by 2% across the four screw types, the mean planning time decreased by more than 90%, and the clinical acceptance rate reached 95%.

AI.tldr: A fully automated pipeline that plans iliosacral screw trajectories for pelvic fracture patients from patient-specific 3D anatomy, achieving larger safety margins, >90% time reduction, and 95% clinical acceptance over 200 cases.
AI.motivation: Percutaneous iliosacral screw fixation is a key minimally invasive treatment for unstable pelvic fractures, but the sacroiliac region has complex anatomy and narrow screw corridors, so placement accuracy and safety directly affect outcomes. Reliable preoperative planning is thus essential. Conventional planning relies on manual measurements, which is labor-intensive and subjective.
AI.method: A fully automated preoperative planning pipeline that uses patient-specific 3D anatomy to automatically identify safe screw corridors and generate individualized insertion trajectories for iliosacral screw placement.
AI.result: Evaluated on 200 clinical pelvic fracture cases: safety margin of safe insertion corridors increased by 2% across four screw types, mean planning time decreased by more than 90%, and clinical acceptance rate reached 95%, compared with conventional manual measurements.
AI.conclusion: The proposed automated pipeline supports clinical preoperative planning of iliosacral screws, improving corridor safety margins and drastically reducing planning time while attaining high clinical acceptance.

title: Faster and Better? Benchmark Bugs and Design Limitations Distort the Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Acceleration
summary: Simulated manipulation benchmarks are the standard tool for evaluating vision-language-action (VLA) policies and the acceleration methods that reduce their inference latency for on-robot deployment. On these benchmarks, we observe that some training-free acceleration methods, which approximate the baseline policy's computation, achieve higher measured success rates than the baseline itself. Success rates alone cannot establish whether such gains come from better task execution or from evaluation flaws. We therefore investigate two kinds of benchmark flaws behind these gains: bugs, where the implementation does not match the intended task or evaluation protocol, and design limitations, where success criteria and simulation settings do not fully capture how acceleration affects task execution. Starting from tasks with anomalous gains, we localize root causes by plotting object trajectories against checker acceptance regions, and classify the resulting bugs into task consistency, initialization, and reproducibility. Extending this audit to seven benchmarks, including RoboTwin, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench, we identify 22 bugs of these types and 4 design limitations. For the latter, we revise permissive success checkers, correct unrealistic object masses, and add a motion-aware score that favors smoother actions. Experiments show that bug fixes can reverse method rankings, moving the baseline from last to first on one task. Addressing design limitations can likewise remove anomalous gains: on another task, the baseline moves from 21 percentage points behind an accelerated method to 5 points ahead. Gains attributed to acceleration can therefore be artifacts of the benchmark rather than better task execution. We release our bug fixes and revised benchmark settings to support trustworthy evaluation of VLA acceleration.

AI.tldr: An audit of simulation manipulation benchmarks reveals that anomalous success-rate gains of training-free VLA acceleration methods stem from 22 implementation bugs and 4 design limitations rather than better task execution; fixing them can reverse method rankings.
AI.motivation: Training-free acceleration methods that approximate a baseline VLA policy's computation sometimes achieve higher measured success rates than the baseline on simulated manipulation benchmarks. Success rates alone cannot distinguish genuine improvements in task execution from evaluation flaws, motivating a systematic investigation into benchmark bugs and design limitations.
AI.method: Starting from tasks showing anomalous gains, the authors localize root causes by plotting object trajectories against checker acceptance regions, classifying bugs into task consistency, initialization, and reproducibility categories. The audit extends to seven benchmarks, including RoboTwin, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench. Design limitations are addressed by revising permissive success checkers, correcting unrealistic object masses, and adding a motion-aware score that favors smoother actions.
AI.result: The audit identifies 22 bugs across the three bug types and 4 design limitations. Bug fixes can reverse method rankings, moving the baseline from last to first on one task. Addressing design limitations removes anomalous gains: on another task, the baseline shifts from 21 percentage points behind an accelerated method to 5 points ahead.
AI.conclusion: Gains attributed to VLA acceleration can be artifacts of benchmark flaws rather than superior task execution. The authors release their bug fixes and revised benchmark settings to enable trustworthy evaluation of VLA acceleration.

title: When Upstream Messages Override Correct Answers: A Controlled Study of Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on message passing among specialized agents to accomplish complex tasks. However, an upstream agent may provide useful information or an incorrect answer that causes a downstream agent to override a correct answer supported by its own evidence. Prior work has not clearly separated the benefits of communication from the damage caused by incorrect messages. We study this problem with controlled experiments across five benchmarks and five receivers, keeping the downstream task and evidence fixed while comparing answers under three conditions: no message, the upstream agent's original message, or a message with the opposite conclusion. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, messages often help when the downstream agent would otherwise answer incorrectly. Second, messages can also hurt: when the downstream agent would answer correctly without a message, an incorrect upstream message changes the answer in up to 32% of cases. Third, in 94% of audited harmful cases, the downstream agent copies the upstream's specific wrong answer--a pattern we term answer substitution. Removing unreliable messages recovers part of the lost accuracy, suggesting that communication should be selective based on upstream reliability and the evidence already available to the downstream agent.

AI.tldr: This paper separates the helpful and harmful effects of inter-agent messages in multi-agent LLM systems via controlled experiments, identifying "answer substitution" as the dominant failure mode and advocating selective communication based on upstream reliability.
AI.motivation: Prior work conflates the benefits of communication with the damage caused by incorrect upstream messages, failing to clearly isolate when messages help versus hurt a downstream agent that already holds its own evidence.
AI.method: Controlled experiments across five benchmarks and five receiver agents, holding the downstream task and evidence fixed and comparing three conditions: no message, the upstream agent's original message, and a message with the opposite conclusion; plus auditing of harmful cases.
AI.result: Messages often help when the downstream agent would otherwise err; but an incorrect upstream message flips a previously correct answer in up to 32% of cases; in 94% of audited harmful cases the downstream agent copies the upstream's specific wrong answer (answer substitution); removing unreliable messages recovers part of the lost accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Communication in multi-agent LLM systems should be selective, conditioned on upstream reliability and the evidence already available to the downstream agent.

title: Urgent Actions Go First: Urgency-Aware Denoising for Real-Time VLA Control
summary: Diffusion and flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies generate action chunks through iterative denoising, incurring substantial inference latency that severely limits real-time robotic control. Existing acceleration methods treat an action chunk as a monolithic computational unit, ignoring a crucial physical reality of receding-horizon control: actions are generated jointly but consumed sequentially, resulting in inherently heterogeneous execution urgencies. We exploit this asymmetry to introduce Urgency-Aware Denoising (UAD), a novel inference-time framework that allocates denoising computation according to when each action is physically needed. UAD releases time-critical urgent actions after fewer denoising steps while overlapping the continued background refinement of tail actions with physical execution. However, heterogeneous denoising introduces two key challenges: early-release errors in urgent actions and trajectory inconsistency in tail actions. UAD elegantly resolves both through two core mechanisms: Trajectory Reconciliation, which reconstructs unified internal state evolution to restore joint denoising coherence without additional model evaluations, and Ghost Action Correction, which leverages non-executed ghost continuations to dynamically compensate for early-release errors across remaining executable actions. Extensive evaluations across multiple VLA architectures, simulation benchmarks, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that UAD achieves up to a 1.89x speedup in average action availability latency while maintaining comparable success rates to vanilla inference with optimal denoising budget, offering a more favorable success-latency trade-off than state-of-the-art VLA acceleration baselines.

AI.tldr: UAD is an inference-time framework for diffusion and flow-matching VLA policies that allocates denoising computation per action based on execution urgency, releasing time-critical actions early while refining tail actions in the background, achieving up to 1.89x speedup with comparable success rates.
AI.motivation: Diffusion and flow-matching VLA policies generate action chunks via iterative denoising, causing high inference latency that limits real-time robotic control. Existing acceleration methods treat an action chunk as a monolithic unit, ignoring that in receding-horizon control actions are generated jointly but consumed sequentially, yielding heterogeneous execution urgencies.
AI.method: UAD allocates denoising computation according to when each action is physically needed: urgent actions are released after fewer denoising steps, while tail actions undergo continued background refinement overlapped with physical execution. Two mechanisms address the resulting issues: Trajectory Reconciliation reconstructs unified internal state evolution to restore joint denoising coherence without extra model evaluations, and Ghost Action Correction uses non-executed ghost continuations to compensate for early-release errors across remaining executable actions.
AI.result: Evaluations across multiple VLA architectures, simulation benchmarks, and real-world manipulation tasks show up to 1.89x speedup in average action availability latency while maintaining success rates comparable to vanilla inference with optimal denoising budget, offering a better success-latency trade-off than state-of-the-art VLA acceleration baselines.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the asymmetry between joint generation and sequential consumption of action chunks enables urgency-aware denoising that substantially reduces action availability latency without sacrificing task success, providing a superior success-latency trade-off for real-time robotic control.

title: IronLLM: Forging Compact Edge-Native Language Models for Real-Time Embodied Intelligence
summary: We present IronLLM-0.6B, a 654M-parameter language model designed for efficient on-device inference. IronLLM-0.6B combines a hybrid attention architecture with X-MTP, a lightweight shared-KV multi-token prediction design that eliminates per-depth KV-cache replay and employs a lightweight verification head for rollback-free drafting, achieving a 1.48x decoding speedup. The model is pretrained on approximately 6.2 trillion tokens using a quality-oriented data pipeline and is further post-trained with Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation to integrate capabilities from domain-specialized teachers. To better meet the low-latency requirements of on-device scenarios, IronLLM-0.6B adopts an Instruct-Only design. Evaluations show that IronLLM-0.6B achieves competitive performance relative to larger models such as Qwen3.5-0.8B and MiniCPM5-1B, while producing more concise responses on many tasks. We further present IronLLM-0.6B-Light, which replaces RMSNorm with Dynamic Tanh and simplifies several computationally expensive components to improve inference and quantization efficiency. Together, the IronLLM models provide an effective performance-efficiency trade-off for resource-constrained deployment.

AI.tldr: IronLLM-0.6B is a 654M-parameter, Instruct-Only language model for on-device inference, combining hybrid attention with an X-MTP multi-token prediction design (1.48x decoding speedup), pretrained on ~6.2T tokens and post-trained via Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation. A lighter variant, IronLLM-0.6B-Light, swaps RMSNorm for Dynamic Tanh to boost inference/quantization efficiency.
AI.motivation: On-device scenarios demand low-latency inference under tight resource constraints, where larger models are impractical. The paper targets an effective performance-efficiency trade-off for resource-constrained deployment.
AI.method: Hybrid attention architecture plus X-MTP, a lightweight shared-KV multi-token prediction scheme eliminating per-depth KV-cache replay with a lightweight verification head for rollback-free drafting. Pretraining on ~6.2T tokens with a quality-oriented data pipeline, then Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation from domain-specialized teachers. Instruct-Only design. The -Light variant replaces RMSNorm with Dynamic Tanh and simplifies expensive components.
AI.result: Achieves 1.48x decoding speedup and competitive performance versus larger models such as Qwen3.5-0.8B and MiniCPM5-1B, with more concise responses on many tasks; the -Light variant improves inference and quantization efficiency.
AI.conclusion: IronLLM-0.6B and IronLLM-0.6B-Light jointly provide an effective performance-efficiency trade-off for resource-constrained on-device deployment.

title: Geometry-Preserving Human-to-Robot Upper-Body Motion Retargeting from Monocular Video
summary: Monocular RGB video provides an accessible source of human demonstrations for upper-body robot motion, yet video-driven human-to-robot transfer remains challenging because body and hand motion are recovered at different spatial scales, human and robot kinematics differ substantially, and fine distal motion is difficult to preserve across embodiments. We present a geometry-preserving motion-retargeting framework that integrates unified body--hand reconstruction with morphology-independent geometric transfer. Frame-wise body estimates, video-level observations, and detailed hand evidence jointly constrain a single differentiable Momentum Human Rig (MHR) state, while transient hand artifacts are repaired in parameter space. The reconstructed motion is represented by arm-segment directions, elbow configuration, relative palm orientation, and bilateral wrist relations, and is realized on the target robot through multi-stage inverse kinematics and robot-specific hand adaptation. Within the broader system, Across-VAM provides video generation, whereas Across-WAM performs human-to-robot motion mapping. The method is evaluated on 16 monocular videos comprising 1,769 source frames, including 10 signing and six reach-to-grasp sequences. Unified reconstruction reduces mean hand reprojection error from 22.36 to 7.21 pixels relative to SAM 3D Body. All 16 retargeted trajectories completed kinematic simulation playback, and representative signing and reach-to-grasp motions were further demonstrated on a physical robot. The results demonstrate a unified pipeline from monocular human video to coordinated upper-body motion on a dual-arm dexterous robot.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a geometry-preserving motion-retargeting framework that unifies body–hand reconstruction from monocular RGB video and transfers it to a dual-arm dexterous robot via morphology-independent geometric retargeting and multi-stage inverse kinematics.
AI.motivation: Monocular RGB video is an accessible source of human demonstrations for upper-body robot motion, but video-driven human-to-robot transfer is difficult because body and hand motion are recovered at different spatial scales, human and robot kinematics differ substantially, and fine distal motion is hard to preserve across embodiments.
AI.method: The framework integrates unified body–hand reconstruction with morphology-independent geometric transfer. Frame-wise body estimates, video-level observations, and detailed hand evidence jointly constrain a single differentiable Momentum Human Rig (MHR) state, while transient hand artifacts are repaired in parameter space. Reconstructed motion is encoded as arm-segment directions, elbow configuration, relative palm orientation, and bilateral wrist relations, then realized on the target robot through multi-stage inverse kinematics and robot-specific hand adaptation. Across-VAM handles video generation and Across-WAM performs the human-to-robot mapping.
AI.result: Evaluated on 16 monocular videos (1,769 source frames; 10 signing and 6 reach-to-grasp sequences), unified reconstruction reduced mean hand reprojection error from 22.36 to 7.21 pixels versus SAM 3D Body. All 16 retargeted trajectories completed kinematic simulation playback, and representative signing and reach-to-grasp motions were demonstrated on a physical robot.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a unified pipeline from monocular human video to coordinated upper-body motion on a dual-arm dexterous robot.

title: State Trace Rationale As Auxiliary Task in Reinforcement Learning
comment: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027
summary: We propose STRAT, an auxiliary task that trains deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents to predict a short textual trace of their own state.
