AI.tldr: RoVR-GSPO is a dual-channel robust optimizer that separately addresses outlier sensitivity in group-relative advantage estimation and sequence-level likelihood weighting, improving stability over GSPO.
AI.motivation: Group-relative policy optimization depends on reward-derived advantages and sequence-level likelihood weights that are sensitive to localized outliers. Extreme rewards can collapse contrast among clean responses after group normalization, while token-level log-ratio perturbations can distort sequence weights and clipping decisions.
AI.method: The method introduces a dual-channel robust optimizer. The reward channel combines robust reference estimation with bounded residual credit. The ratio channel applies differentiable SoftRoVR aggregation to construct robust sequence weights. Stability and efficiency analyses are provided for both channels.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning, long-context summarization, and tool-call annotation show consistent improvements over GSPO. Controlled perturbation studies demonstrate stronger robustness to reward contamination and token-ratio anomalies.
AI.conclusion: Separately handling reward-channel and ratio-channel outliers yields a more stable and robust group-relative policy optimization, validated across multiple tasks and under adversarial perturbations.

title: CrossBFM: Distilling a Shared Latent Behavior Space Across Humanoid Embodiments
summary: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) give humanoids a promptable policy over a latent behavior space, enabling one single vector to represent a motion to imitate, a pose to reach, or a reward to maximize. Forward-Backward representations successfully produce such spaces, but at the cost of hundreds of GPU-hours for a single robot. Moreover, when the training process is repeated for a second robot, it produces a second space unrelated to the first, resulting in embodiment-specific latents that do not unify or transfer. We address these problems with CrossBFM, treating the latent space as the transferable asset for various embodiments. As retargeting provides frame-level cross-embodiment correspondence, we propose a unified encoder architecture with no robot-specific parameters for distilling the behavior space to address all training embodiments simultaneously in less than a GPU-hour. Following this encoder, latent-conditioned trackers turn the distilled latent into whole-body control in a conventional PPO training manner in just 10 more GPU-hours. On three distilled humanoids, all three prompting modes transfer: motion tracking with latent-conditioned policy losing only $0.025$ rad to its joint-conditioned counterpart, smooth goal reaching between poses with no falls, and reward optimization for all $41$ reward prompts. Our experiments further reveal that 1) regressing the encoder on a quarter of the motion corpus costs only $5\%$ of tracking performance and 2) training the encoder on a subset of robots and evaluating on an unseen one recovers up to $89\%$ of the tracking performance of seen robots, demonstrating cross-embodiment generalization to morphologically similar robots. We also verify the pipeline on real robots across all three prompting modes and with flow-based generated latents. Project website: https://dotandung.github.io/crossbfm/

AI.tldr: CrossBFM distills a shared, embodiment-agnostic behavior foundation model latent space across multiple humanoids in under one GPU-hour, with latent-conditioned trackers adding whole-body control in ~10 more GPU-hours.
AI.motivation: Existing Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs), such as Forward-Backward representations, cost hundreds of GPU-hours per robot. Repeating training for a second robot yields a separate, unrelated latent space, so latents are embodiment-specific and neither unified nor transferable. CrossBFM aims to make the latent space itself the transferable asset across embodiments.
AI.method: Leveraging retargeting to provide frame-level cross-embodiment correspondence, CrossBFM uses a unified encoder architecture with no robot-specific parameters to distill a shared behavior space across all training embodiments simultaneously. Latent-conditioned trackers then convert the distilled latent into whole-body control via conventional PPO training. The pipeline is also verified on real robots across all three prompting modes and with flow-based generated latents.
AI.result: On three distilled humanoids, all three prompting modes transfer: motion tracking with a latent-conditioned policy loses only 0.025 rad versus a joint-conditioned counterpart; smooth goal reaching between poses occurs with no falls; and reward optimization succeeds for all 41 reward prompts. Regressing the encoder on a quarter of the motion corpus costs only 5% of tracking performance, and training the encoder on a subset of robots and evaluating on an unseen one recovers up to 89% of the tracking performance of seen robots, showing cross-embodiment generalization to morphologically similar robots.
AI.conclusion: CrossBFM unifies and transfers a promptable latent behavior space across humanoids at drastically reduced cost (distillation under one GPU-hour, control in ~10 GPU-hours), demonstrating effective cross-embodiment generalization and validating all three prompting modes on real robots.

title: REALHOP: Rethinking Multi-Hop Reasoning Evaluation via Behavioral Auditing
summary: Complex questions often require multi-hop reasoning that connects facts distributed across sources or distant regions of a long context through intermediate steps. Benchmarks commonly evaluate this ability with questions built around predefined reasoning chains, treating a correct answer as evidence that the intended composition was used. Yet answer correctness alone leaves open whether success depends on the evidence associated with each intended step: models may instead rely on memorized associations, shorter paths, or partial evidence. We examine this dependence using the Behavioral Necessity Rate (BNR), which measures how often targeted evidence removal prevents answer recovery on initially correct instances. Across five existing benchmarks, panel-mean BNR ranges from 16.6% to 48.9%, exposing a substantial gap between annotated structure and observed dependence. Guided by this diagnosis, we introduce REALHOP, a diagnose-construct-verify framework that rebinds entities, factorizes selected relations, adds complete competing paths, and places evidence at traceable locations. Structural and semantic checks precede freezing; behavioral interventions follow. On 790 paired MuSiQue questions, REALHOP raises panel-mean BNR from 27.4% to 94.4% while retaining high Full accuracy. It also yields high BNR on REALHOP-FRAMES and REALHOP-LONGBENCH. On 216 long-context questions, the matched multiple-choice spread across 16 models grows from 13.9 to 59.2 points and persists under repeated open-ended evaluation. Together, these results show that a conceptually coherent chain and a correct final answer do not by themselves establish multi-hop reasoning. Verifying that success depends on every intended hop is therefore as fundamental to multi-hop evaluation as measuring answer accuracy itself.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that correct answers on multi-hop benchmarks do not prove genuine multi-hop reasoning, introduces the Behavioral Necessity Rate (BNR) to measure dependence on each intended evidence step, and proposes REALHOP, a framework that constructs examples where every hop is behaviorally necessary.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-hop benchmarks use predefined reasoning chains and treat answer correctness as evidence that the intended composition was used. However, correctness alone cannot distinguish genuine multi-hop reasoning from memorized associations, shortcut paths, or partial evidence use. The authors aim to diagnose whether models actually depend on each intended reasoning step.
AI.method: They introduce the Behavioral Necessity Rate (BNR), which quantifies how often removing targeted evidence prevents answer recovery on initially correct instances. Testing across five existing benchmarks reveals low BNR (16.6%–48.9%). To address this, they develop REALHOP, a diagnose-construct-verify framework that rebinds entities, factorizes selected relations, adds complete competing paths, and places evidence at traceable locations. Structural and semantic checks precede freezing, followed by behavioral interventions.
AI.result: On 790 paired MuSiQue questions, REALHOP raises panel-mean BNR from 27.4% to 94.4% while preserving high Full accuracy. It also achieves high BNR on REALHOP-FRAMES and REALHOP-LONGBENCH. On 216 long-context questions, the matched multiple-choice spread across 16 models increases from 13.9 to 59.2 points and persists under repeated open-ended evaluation.
AI.conclusion: A conceptually coherent chain and a correct final answer do not by themselves establish multi-hop reasoning. Verifying that success depends on every intended hop is as fundamental to multi-hop evaluation as measuring answer accuracy itself.

title: FORM: Robot Manipulation through Direct Material Law Identification
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Project page: https://form-robots.github.io/ . Code: https://github.com/form-robots/FORM
summary: When interacting with an unfamiliar deformable material, a robot lacks prior knowledge of its physical properties and how it will respond to applied forces and motion. Rapid online identification is therefore essential for reliable manipulation. We present FORM (From Observed Response to Material laws), which identifies material properties from a single robot interaction and reuses the recovered model to plan manipulation under new actions and geometries. We use weak-form momentum balance to convert observed material motion and contact forces into linear equations in the unknown material parameters. These equations are assembled using the same material point method discretization as the forward simulator, so identification reduces to linear least-squares solves whose solutions can be used directly for prediction without refitting or conversion. Across four material classes, FORM reduces identification time from roughly 10--25 minutes for iterative baselines to 2--5 seconds, while maintaining competitive accuracy on new motions, initial conditions, and geometries. We demonstrate our approach in simulation and on hardware across four manipulation tasks: elastic rod insertion, golf putting with an elastic club, elastoplastic shaping, and target-volume pouring. In each task, the model identified from a single interaction is reused to plan new motions or manipulate a different geometry. FORM estimates elastic properties within 3.4% and elastoplastic properties within 2%, achieves 72.4--77.8% IoU in dough shaping, and keeps mean pouring error at 3.8 mL across target volumes of 60--160 mL.

AI.tldr: FORM identifies deformable material parameters from a single robot interaction using weak-form momentum balance assembled with the same MPM discretization as the forward simulator, reducing identification time from minutes to seconds while reusing the model for planning on new actions and geometries.
AI.motivation: A robot interacting with an unfamiliar deformable material has no prior knowledge of its physical properties or force/motion response, so rapid online identification is needed for reliable manipulation. Existing iterative identification baselines are slow (roughly 10–25 minutes).
AI.method: FORM converts observed material motion and contact forces into linear equations in the unknown material parameters via weak-form momentum balance. Equations are assembled using the same material point method (MPM) discretization as the forward simulator, so identification reduces to linear least-squares solves whose solutions are directly usable for prediction without refitting or conversion.
AI.result: Across four material classes, identification time drops from 10–25 minutes (iterative baselines) to 2–5 seconds with competitive accuracy on new motions, initial conditions, and geometries. Demonstrated in simulation and hardware on four tasks: elastic rod insertion, golf putting with an elastic club, elastoplastic shaping, and target-volume pouring. Elastic properties estimated within 3.4%, elastoplastic within 2%, 72.4–77.8% IoU in dough shaping, and mean pouring error 3.8 mL across 60–160 mL targets.
AI.conclusion: FORM enables fast, accurate online material identification from a single interaction and allows the recovered model to be reused to plan manipulation under new actions and geometries, spanning elastic and elastoplastic behaviors in both simulation and hardware.

title: CF-LoRA: Decoupled Factor Aggregation and Adaptation-Aware Client Clustering for Federated LoRA Fine-Tuning
summary: Federated LoRA fine-tuning enables parameter-efficient adaptation of pre-trained models without sharing private data, but suffers from two fundamental mismatches under heterogeneous client data: a structural aggregation mismatch caused by independently averaging LoRA factors, and a statistical collaboration mismatch caused by enforcing a single global adapter across divergent clients. To address these issues, we propose CF-LoRA, a clustered federated LoRA fine-tuning framework that combines decoupled factor aggregation with adaptation-aware client clustering. CF-LoRA first learns a globally shared $A$ factor while retaining personalized $B_i$ factors, then identifies clients with similar adaptation patterns based on the cosine similarity of their learned $B_i$ factors, and finally performs intra-cluster $B$-factor aggregation with a frozen $A$ factor. By decoupling LoRA factor aggregation, CF-LoRA preserves the low-rank structure and mitigates the structural aggregation mismatch, while adaptation-aware clustering promotes collaboration among clients with similar adaptation patterns and reduces negative transfer caused by statistical heterogeneity. Experiments on four language tasks and four vision datasets with RoBERTa and ViT show that CF-LoRA achieves the highest average accuracy in both modalities while communicating only one LoRA factor per optimization round.

AI.tldr: CF-LoRA is a clustered federated LoRA fine-tuning framework that decouples factor aggregation (shared A, personalized B) and clusters clients by adaptation patterns, achieving top average accuracy on language and vision tasks with minimal communication.
AI.motivation: Federated LoRA fine-tuning allows parameter-efficient adaptation of pre-trained models without sharing private data, but under heterogeneous client data it suffers from two fundamental mismatches: a structural aggregation mismatch caused by independently averaging LoRA factors, and a statistical collaboration mismatch caused by enforcing a single global adapter across divergent clients.
AI.method: CF-LoRA combines decoupled factor aggregation with adaptation-aware client clustering. It first learns a globally shared A factor while retaining personalized B_i factors, then identifies clients with similar adaptation patterns via cosine similarity of their B_i factors, and finally performs intra-cluster B-factor aggregation with a frozen A factor.
AI.result: Experiments on four language tasks and four vision datasets with RoBERTa and ViT show that CF-LoRA achieves the highest average accuracy in both modalities while communicating only one LoRA factor per optimization round.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling LoRA factor aggregation, CF-LoRA preserves the low-rank structure and mitigates the structural aggregation mismatch, while adaptation-aware clustering promotes collaboration among clients with similar adaptation patterns and reduces negative transfer caused by statistical heterogeneity.

title: Rho: A Foundation for Efficiently Adaptable VLA Models
summary: General-purpose physical AI models must combine broad visual and linguistic capabilities with precise control across robot embodiments and efficient adaptation to downstream tasks. We introduce Rho, a family of open-weights VLA models for bimanual manipulation designed for data-light task adaptation on 3 embodiments representative of dual-arm robots across research labs and the industry -- YAM Box, UR AI Trainer, and FR3 Duo. We systematically ablate Rho's action-expert architecture and training recipe, and show in controlled simulation and physical-robot experiments that embodiment midtraining improves downstream adaptation. The resulting Rho variants for YAM Box, UR AI Trainer, and FR3 Duo match or outperform existing open-weights VLAs and achieve the strongest overall performance across the tasks, embodiments, and baselines evaluated in this report. We further demonstrate the Rho model family's built-in capacity for online adaptation: an internal latent policy learns from corrective feedback to select observation-conditioned noise inputs for the frozen flow-matching action expert. With as few as 15 corrected episodes, adapting this lightweight module enables Rho to handle task situations at the fringe of its offline finetuning distribution. Together, these results position Rho as both a strong general-purpose robotic manipulation model and a practical foundation for adaptation. We release the base Rho model and the embodiment-specific checkpoints to facilitate Rho's deployment in research experiments and practical industrial use cases.

AI.tldr: Rho is a family of open-weights Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for bimanual manipulation, designed for data-light adaptation across three dual-arm embodiments (YAM Box, UR AI Trainer, FR3 Duo). It matches or outperforms existing open-weights VLAs and supports efficient online adaptation via a lightweight latent policy using as few as 15 corrected episodes.
AI.motivation: General-purpose physical AI models need to combine broad visual and linguistic capabilities with precise control across different robot embodiments, while also adapting efficiently to downstream tasks. There is a need for open-weights VLA models that enable data-light task adaptation across representative dual-arm robots used in research and industry.
AI.method: The authors introduce Rho, a family of open-weights VLA models for bimanual manipulation. They systematically ablate the action-expert architecture and training recipe, and use controlled simulation and physical-robot experiments, including embodiment midtraining, to improve downstream adaptation. For online adaptation, an internal latent policy learns from corrective feedback to select observation-conditioned noise inputs for a frozen flow-matching action expert.
AI.result: Embodiment midtraining improves downstream adaptation. Rho variants for YAM Box, UR AI Trainer, and FR3 Duo match or outperform existing open-weights VLAs and achieve the strongest overall performance across the evaluated tasks, embodiments, and baselines. With as few as 15 corrected episodes, the lightweight adaptation module enables Rho to handle task situations at the fringe of its offline finetuning distribution.
AI.conclusion: Rho positions itself as both a strong general-purpose robotic manipulation model and a practical foundation for adaptation. The base Rho model and embodiment-specific checkpoints are released to support deployment in research experiments and practical industrial use cases.

title: ImbalancE: Inference-Time Latent Search Against Degree Imbalance in Link Prediction
summary: Knowledge Graph Embedding models have been extensively used to learn representations of entities and relations in Knowledge Graphs for predicting missing links. However, the quality of the learned representations varies a lot across different areas of the graph. If previous research has loosely linked the problem to relation types or degree bias, we show that it is more widespread and it correlates with the degree imbalance of the entities in test triples. In particular, the prediction of a target entity that has a degree much smaller than the degree of the anchor entity is extremely problematic. This is critical in recommender systems and other use cases, where these triples represent important corner cases. To address this issue, we propose an inference-time latent search optimization method capable of significantly improving model predictions on the most imbalanced triples. Built on top of a pre-trained model, it explores the embedding space at evaluation time, blending known and out-of-band information to mitigate the degree imbalance bias. We show the value of our approach on imbalanced triples from common benchmark datasets, where we outperform conventional methods, opening the door to the successful adoption of Knowledge Graph Embedding models on these critical corner cases.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that poor link prediction in Knowledge Graph Embedding models correlates with the degree imbalance between anchor and target entities in test triples, and proposes an inference-time latent search optimization that improves predictions on the most imbalanced triples.
AI.motivation: Prior work loosely attributed variable embedding quality to relation types or degree bias. The authors argue this issue is more widespread and specifically tied to the degree imbalance between entities in test triples; triples where a low-degree target must be predicted from a high-degree anchor are extremely problematic yet represent important corner cases in applications like recommender systems.
AI.method: An inference-time latent search optimization method built on a pre-trained Knowledge Graph Embedding model. At evaluation time, it explores the embedding space and blends known and out-of-band information to mitigate degree imbalance bias, without retraining the underlying model.
AI.result: On imbalanced triples from common benchmark datasets, the approach outperforms conventional methods, substantially improving predictions on the most imbalanced triples.
AI.conclusion: Degree imbalance in test triples is a key driver of degraded link prediction, and inference-time latent search effectively addresses it, enabling reliable use of Knowledge Graph Embedding models on critical corner cases.

title: Counterfactual Video Generation Enables Scalable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
comment: published at CoRL 2026. Project page: https://prism-real2sim2real.github.io/
summary: Teaching humanoids loco-manipulation skills, such as carrying diverse objects, via visual imitation is a promising path toward generalist robots. However, collecting diverse, high-quality interaction videos, such as clips that clearly show a person's full body and unoccluded interactions with objects, poses a practical barrier to scaling this approach. We propose PRISM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that overcomes this limitation by amplifying a handful of real videos into a large, diverse training set. PRISM first generates hundreds of diverse "counterfactual" human-object interaction videos via video-to-video (V2V) generation from a few exemplar real videos. Our contact-anchored real-to-sim pipeline then reconstructs both human and object motions, retargeting this imperfect video data into physically plausible trajectories. The intra-class variability across these counterfactual videos lets us train a single policy that generalizes to unseen objects within each category. We demonstrate the full pipeline by deploying this policy on a real robot without any real-world fine-tuning. Using only onboard depth observations, our humanoid picks up, carries, and drops objects, including boxes, barrels, bins, and balls, across novel instances, sizes, and initial configurations.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a real-to-sim-to-real framework that amplifies a few real human-object interaction videos into a large, diverse training set to teach humanoids loco-manipulation skills like carrying objects, enabling zero-shot deployment on a real robot.
AI.motivation: Visual imitation is a promising path toward generalist humanoid robots, but collecting diverse, high-quality interaction videos (clearly showing full body and unoccluded object interactions) is a practical barrier to scaling this approach.
AI.method: PRISM first generates hundreds of diverse "counterfactual" human-object interaction videos via video-to-video (V2V) generation from a few exemplar real videos. A contact-anchored real-to-sim pipeline then reconstructs both human and object motions, retargeting the imperfect video data into physically plausible trajectories. Intra-class variability across counterfactual videos trains a single policy generalizing to unseen objects within each category.
AI.result: The policy was deployed on a real robot without any real-world fine-tuning. Using only onboard depth observations, the humanoid picks up, carries, and drops objects including boxes, barrels, bins, and balls, across novel instances, sizes, and initial configurations.
AI.conclusion: A real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that amplifies limited real videos into diverse training data can train humanoid loco-manipulation policies that transfer zero-shot to real robots and generalize to unseen objects within categories.

title: CADOC: Cache-Aware Dynamic Object Context for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: For a long-horizon agent, context is the bottleneck: the history is resent with every request, the window caps task length, and reasoning degrades as the history grows. Replacing structured objects with compact retrieval Cards shortens the prompt and keeps the exact originals retrievable, but editing the history can break prefix-cache reuse, and prior recoverable methods time their edits by forecasts of future reuse or by preset intervals. We propose CADOC (Cache-Aware Dynamic Object Context), an online algorithm that replaces structured objects with compact Cards while preserving exact, on-demand retrieval of their original contents. CADOC schedules replacements in batches by balancing accumulated waiting cost against shared cache-reconstruction cost. Its scheduling rule follows from an economic order quantity trade-off, recovers the optimal integer batch under stationary assumptions. Across evaluation, CADOC consistently achieves the lowest aggregate input cost among the compared configurations, which reduces input cost by approximately 40\% on average while maintaining task performance close to full context. CADOC thus provides a cost-derived approach to compressible context management, demonstrating that efficient compression depends not only on shortening prompts but also on scheduling edits to preserve cache reuse.

AI.tldr: CADOC is an online algorithm that replaces structured objects in an agent's context with compact retrieval "Cards," batching these replacements to balance waiting cost against cache-reconstruction cost, cutting input cost ~40% on average while keeping task performance near full-context levels.
AI.motivation: For long-horizon agents, context is the bottleneck: history is resent with every request, the window caps task length, and reasoning degrades as history grows. Compact retrieval Cards can shorten prompts while keeping originals retrievable, but editing history can break prefix-cache reuse, and prior recoverable methods time edits by forecasts of future reuse or preset intervals—leaving cache-reuse and compression uncoordinated.
AI.method: CADOC (Cache-Aware Dynamic Object Context) is an online algorithm that replaces structured objects with compact Cards while preserving exact, on-demand retrieval of their original contents. It schedules replacements in batches, balancing accumulated waiting cost against shared cache-reconstruction cost. The scheduling rule derives from an economic order quantity trade-off and recovers the optimal integer batch under stationary assumptions.
AI.result: Across evaluation, CADOC consistently achieves the lowest aggregate input cost among compared configurations, reducing input cost by approximately 40% on average while maintaining task performance close to full context.
AI.conclusion: CADOC provides a cost-derived approach to compressible context management, showing that efficient compression depends not only on shortening prompts but also on scheduling edits to preserve cache reuse.

title: In-context Robot Learning Made Simple: A Democratized Recipe for Manipulation Tasks
summary: We study robotic in-context learning (ICL), an emerging paradigm that enables robots to infer and execute tasks from visual demonstrations. Despite its growing promise, the problem itself remains under-defined: a visual demonstration simultaneously conveys action trajectories, object semantics, manipulation affordances, spatial relations, and task goals, making it unclear what information the robot is actually expected to follow. In this work, we first provide a clear problem definition of robot ICL that explicitly defines its learning target and resolves this fundamental prompt ambiguity. Building on this definition, we develop a minimalist and reproducible ICL framework (SimpleICL) with a visual prompt encoder and a low-cost data collection protocol. Without massive pre-training or specialized data infrastructure, our framework achieves strong performance in both simulation and real-world environments. Extensive experiments further reveal several key properties of robot ICL, including action, semantic, composition, and affordance discrimination. We will fully open-source our data and training pipeline to facilitate systematic and reproducible research on robot ICL. The project page can be found at https://simpleicl.github.io/simpleicl.

AI.tldr: This paper clarifies the under-defined problem of robotic in-context learning (ICL) by providing an explicit definition that resolves prompt ambiguity, and introduces SimpleICL, a minimalist, reproducible framework achieving strong simulation and real-world performance without large-scale pre-training.
AI.motivation: Robotic ICL enables robots to infer and execute tasks from visual demonstrations, but the problem is under-defined: a single visual demonstration conveys action trajectories, object semantics, manipulation affordances, spatial relations, and task goals simultaneously, leaving unclear what information the robot should follow. This prompt ambiguity hinders systematic progress.
AI.method: The authors first formalize robot ICL by explicitly defining its learning target to resolve the prompt ambiguity. Building on this definition, they propose SimpleICL, a minimalist and reproducible framework consisting of a visual prompt encoder and a low-cost data collection protocol, avoiding massive pre-training or specialized data infrastructure.
AI.result: SimpleICL achieves strong performance in both simulated and real-world environments. Experiments reveal key properties of robot ICL, including discrimination along action, semantic, composition, and affordance dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a clear problem definition and a lightweight, reproducible baseline for robot ICL, and the authors will fully open-source data and training pipelines to support systematic, reproducible research. Project page: https://simpleicl.github.io/simpleicl.

title: Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination for Hospital Patient Flow Optimization
comment: Accepted to PRIMA 2026 (Full paper). 16 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Efficient patient flow coordination across autonomous hospital departments is critical for mitigating overcrowding and balancing resource utilization. While classical queueing theory, specifically open Baskett--Chandy--Muntz--Palacios (BCMP) networks, provides an interpretable mathematical topology for healthcare operations, analytical models rely on stationary assumptions and fixed routing matrices that degrade under state-dependent real-world dynamics. Conversely, centralized reinforcement learning approaches struggle to accommodate the decentralized structure of hospital governance, where individual clinical departments function with localized observations, heterogeneous resources, and divergent operational objectives. In this paper, we present a Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) framework titled \emph{Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination}, which embeds empirically calibrated BCMP queueing topologies as physical priors within a decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture. Formulated as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under coupled resource constraints, our method enables autonomous departmental agents to cooperatively negotiate patient routing and dynamic service scaling. To mitigate environmental non-stationarity without inducing excessive communication overhead, agents exchange localized action fingerprints along network edges and optimize a spatially decomposed reward structure. Empirical evaluations driven by real-world MIMIC-IV patient trajectories indicate that this cooperative multi-agent approach substantially reduces cumulative system delay compared to static Markovian approximations, heuristic dispatching, and independent multi-agent baselines, while maintaining clinical safety constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination, a decentralized multi-agent RL framework that embeds calibrated BCMP queueing topologies as physical priors into a Dec-POMDP to coordinate patient routing and service scaling across autonomous hospital departments.
AI.motivation: Hospital overcrowding and imbalanced resource use require coordination across autonomous departments. Classical queueing models (open BCMP networks) are interpretable but rely on stationary assumptions and fixed routing, degrading under state-dependent dynamics; centralized RL cannot accommodate decentralized hospital governance with localized observations, heterogeneous resources, and divergent objectives.
AI.method: The authors formulate the problem as a Dec-POMDP under coupled resource constraints and embed empirically calibrated BCMP queueing topologies as physical priors within a decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture. Agents exchange localized action fingerprints along network edges and optimize a spatially decomposed reward structure to counter non-stationarity while limiting communication overhead.
AI.result: Evaluations using real-world MIMIC-IV patient trajectories show the cooperative multi-agent approach substantially reduces cumulative system delay relative to static Markovian approximations, heuristic dispatching, and independent multi-agent baselines, while preserving clinical safety constraints.
AI.conclusion: Combining physics-informed queueing priors with decentralized multi-agent RL offers an effective, communication-efficient means of coordinating patient flow across autonomous hospital departments, outperforming static and non-cooperative baselines under realistic, non-stationary dynamics.

title: Skill-Space Shooting for Autonomous Robot Policy Improvement
summary: Robots deployed in the physical world must be able to improve beyond their initial training as they encounter new situations and failures. For this improvement to scale across tasks, it must make effective use of experience without requiring human demonstration of each correction. Recent agentic systems offer a way to reduce this reliance on human effort by using foundation models to autonomously compose learned behaviors to complete tasks. Yet completing tasks this way does not itself teach a task policy to overcome its own failures; that requires turning these behaviors into learnable corrections for the policy. Our insight is that many such corrections are familiar short behaviors, or skills: they recur across tasks and describe actions that foundation models can reason about from a scene. We introduce skill-space shooting, which uses foundation model guidance to explore corrections through these reusable skills and turn successful trials into policy improvement. Real-world experiments show repeated improvement in policies acting autonomously, while skills can also be shared to reduce the teaching needed to improve on new tasks. By making reusable skills a source of corrective supervision, skill-space shooting enables scalable and generalizable policy improvement within and across tasks. Additional results and videos at https://skill-space-shooting.github.io.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces skill-space shooting, a method that uses foundation-model-guided exploration of reusable skills to generate corrective supervision, enabling autonomous and scalable policy improvement for real-world robots within and across tasks.
AI.motivation: Robots deployed in the physical world must improve beyond initial training as they encounter new situations and failures. For this improvement to scale across tasks, it must leverage experience without requiring human demonstration of each correction. Existing agentic systems reduce human effort by using foundation models to autonomously compose learned behaviors, but composing behaviors to complete tasks does not itself teach a task policy to overcome its own failures; behavior composition must be converted into learnable corrections for the policy.
AI.method: The authors exploit the insight that many corrections are familiar short, reusable behaviors ("skills") that recur across tasks and that foundation models can reason about from a scene. They propose skill-space shooting, which uses foundation-model guidance to explore corrections through these reusable skills and then converts successful trials into policy improvement.
AI.result: Real-world experiments show repeated improvement in policies acting autonomously (iterative self-improvement without human demonstrations), and skills can be shared to reduce the teaching needed to improve on new tasks.
AI.conclusion: By making reusable skills a source of corrective supervision, skill-space shooting enables scalable and generalizable policy improvement both within and across tasks.

title: Language as the Interface: Foundation-Model Contrastive Learning Links Transcriptomes and Electrophysiology
summary: Integrating transcriptomic and electrophysiological data is essential for building multimodal foundation models for neuroscience. Patch-seq provides paired measurements of gene expression and intrinsic electrophysiology from the same neuron, establishing a basis for training cross-modal models. Here we introduce LangPatch, a foundation-model-based contrastive learning framework that uses paired Patch-seq data to align pretrained GenePT representations with electrophysiological phenotypes through a language-based interface. Gene descriptions and verbalized electrophysiological profiles are embedded by the same frozen text encoder. A context adapter and projection modules connect the modalities through paired contrastive learning. Across mouse visual, mouse motor, and human cortical cohorts, LangPatch achieves the highest mean transcriptome-to-electrophysiology prediction correlation among the evaluated foundation-model and representation-learning methods. It also improves held-out cross-modal alignment in the two mouse cohorts (FOSCTTM 0.107/0.135 vs. 0.208/0.222 for JAMIE, an existing cross-modal Patch-seq imputation method). It predicts transcriptomic family, type, cortical layer, and marker-gene expression from electrophysiology, exceeding other baselines on most endpoints. More importantly, the method transfers across brain areas and species: a model trained on mouse visual cortex predicts electrophysiology in motor cortex with approximately 70% correlation retention and in human cortex with 47% (58% on acute-slice recordings). Together, these results demonstrate alignment between molecular and functional representations of neurons, providing a building block for multimodal foundation models in neuroscience.

AI.tldr: LangPatch is a contrastive learning framework that aligns pretrained GenePT transcriptomic representations with verbalized electrophysiological profiles via a shared frozen text encoder, achieving top cross-modal prediction and cross-species/brain-area transfer.
AI.motivation: Integrating transcriptomic and electrophysiological data is key to multimodal neuroscience foundation models. Patch-seq provides paired gene-expression and electrophysiology recordings from the same neuron, offering a basis to train cross-modal models that bridge molecular and functional representations.
AI.method: A foundation-model-based contrastive learning framework using paired Patch-seq data. Both gene descriptions and verbalized electrophysiological profiles are embedded by the same frozen text encoder, creating a language-based interface. A context adapter and projection modules connect the modalities through paired contrastive learning, aligning pretrained GenePT representations with electrophysiological phenotypes.
AI.result: Across mouse visual, mouse motor, and human cortical cohorts, LangPatch attains the highest mean transcriptome-to-electrophysiology prediction correlation among evaluated foundation-model and representation-learning methods. It improves held-out cross-modal alignment in both mouse cohorts (FOSCTTM 0.107/0.135 vs. 0.208/0.222 for JAMIE). It predicts transcriptomic family, type, cortical layer, and marker-gene expression from electrophysiology, exceeding baselines on most endpoints. It transfers across areas and species: training on mouse visual cortex retains ~70% correlation in motor cortex and 47% in human cortex (58% on acute-slice recordings).
AI.conclusion: LangPatch demonstrates alignment between molecular and functional neuronal representations, providing a building block for multimodal foundation models in neuroscience.

title: AnyAct: Universal Action for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: As large language models (LLMs) advance, AI agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments to tackle complex sequential tasks (e.g., document processing, cross-application collaboration), relying heavily on actions ranging from GUI operations to semantic APIs. However, three core challenges persist: the "scale dilemma" of massive tool ecosystems exceeding LLM context windows, the "non-stationarity" of tool quality due to updates or outages, and the "heterogeneity" of feedback formats (pixels, text, structured data) creating information silos. To address these, we propose AnyAct, a universal action layer that unifies available capabilities into a self-evolving action space, enabling agents to operate efficiently and reliably in large-scale, dynamic tool ecosystems. AnyAct's core design focuses on two objectives: constructing this action space via hierarchical progressive retrieval (filtering task-relevant actions) and test-time reliability evolution (pruning unreliable actions), and enabling reliability-aware action orchestration through a heterogeneous observation grounding module that unifies multi-modal feedback. Additionally, it defines a hybrid action space (primitive + semantic actions) and optimizes for a balance between task success rate and execution cost. Evaluations on LiveMCPBench and OSMCP (a new benchmark we developed for multi-granularity action collaboration) demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. AnyAct delivers substantial performance gains over baseline methods across various LLM base models on LiveMCPBench and improvements are particularly notable for models with constrained native capabilities. On OSMCP, it achieves 77.27% overall success with only 50 steps, which is half the steps required by most competitors.

AI.tldr: AnyAct is a universal action layer that unifies capabilities into a self-evolving action space, addressing the scale dilemma, tool non-stationarity, and feedback heterogeneity in LLM agents operating in large-scale dynamic tool ecosystems.
AI.motivation: As LLMs advance, AI agents are deployed in open-world environments for complex sequential tasks relying on diverse actions from GUI operations to semantic APIs. Three core challenges persist: the "scale dilemma" of massive tool ecosystems exceeding LLM context windows, the "non-stationarity" of tool quality due to updates/outages, and the "heterogeneity" of feedback formats (pixels, text, structured data) creating information silos.
AI.method: AnyAct constructs a self-evolving action space via two objectives: hierarchical progressive retrieval (filtering task-relevant actions) and test-time reliability evolution (pruning unreliable actions). It enables reliability-aware action orchestration through a heterogeneous observation grounding module unifying multi-modal feedback. It defines a hybrid action space (primitive + semantic actions) and optimizes for balance between task success rate and execution cost.
AI.result: Evaluations on LiveMCPBench and OSMCP (a new benchmark developed for multi-granularity action collaboration) demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. AnyAct delivers substantial gains over baselines across various LLM base models on LiveMCPBench, particularly for models with constrained native capabilities. On OSMCP, it achieves 77.27% overall success with only 50 steps—half the steps required by most competitors.
AI.conclusion: AnyAct serves as a universal action layer enabling AI agents to operate efficiently and reliably in large-scale, dynamic tool ecosystems by unifying capabilities into a self-evolving action space, achieving SOTA performance with reduced execution cost.

title: Beyond Low-Rank Parameterization: Narrowing the Gap Between LoRA and Full Fine-Tuning via Gradient Decomposition
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet a performance gap can remain relative to full fine-tuning (FFT). Many LoRA variants improve the initialization or optimization of low-rank factors. At each training step, however, their first-order weight-space directions are constrained by the current parameterization. We characterize the corresponding LoRA-accessible gradient space and show that it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. This characterization yields an orthogonal decomposition of the full weight gradient at the current model parameters. We term the component orthogonal to this space the normal gradient. Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation). GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backward signals, extracts its normal component, and directly updates the base weights with this component, while retaining standard AdamW optimization for the LoRA factors. GDLoRA incorporates complementary normal gradients without increasing standard LoRA's optimizer-state memory budget under matched adapter and optimizer configurations. Experiments on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification show that GDLoRA consistently improves over LoRA and narrows the performance gap to FFT. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GDLoRA.

AI.tldr: LoRA's first-order update directions are confined to the tangent space of its low-rank parameterization, leaving a "normal gradient" component unexploited. GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient, extracts this orthogonal component, and updates base weights with it while keeping standard AdamW for LoRA factors, improving performance at no extra optimizer-state memory cost.
AI.motivation: LoRA is a widely used PEFT method, but a performance gap remains relative to full fine-tuning (FFT). While many LoRA variants improve initialization or optimization of low-rank factors, at each training step their first-order weight-space update directions are constrained by the current parameterization, limiting the achievable optimization trajectory. The paper aims to characterize this limitation and exploit the unusable gradient directions to close the gap to FFT.
AI.method: The authors characterize the LoRA-accessible gradient space and prove it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. This yields an orthogonal decomposition of the full weight gradient at the current parameters, with the component orthogonal to this space termed the "normal gradient." Based on this decomposition, they propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation): it reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backward signals, extracts its normal component, and directly updates the base weights with this component, while retaining standard AdamW optimization for the LoRA factors. GDLoRA adds complementary normal gradients without increasing standard LoRA's optimizer-state memory budget under matched adapter and optimizer configurations.
AI.result: Experiments on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification show that GDLoRA consistently improves over LoRA and narrows the performance gap to full fine-tuning. The gains are achieved with no increase in optimizer-state memory budget relative to standard LoRA under matched adapter and optimizer configurations.
AI.conclusion: GDLoRA demonstrates that explicitly incorporating the normal gradient component—orthogonal to LoRA's accessible tangent space—is an effective and memory-efficient way to enhance parameter-efficient fine-tuning, consistently surpassing LoRA and approaching FFT performance across diverse tasks.

title: Direct Experience World-Model Optimization: Learning the World Beyond Action Imitation
comment: World Action Model; post-deployment training; dexterous manipulation
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of how physical interactions unfold. However, current post-deployment learning paradigms typically improve behavior without requiring better world predictions. Especially in dexterous manipulation, small execution errors can compound in high-dimensional action spaces, hindering policy improvement and pushing interactions beyond the world model's training distribution. Motivated by this, we propose Direct Experience World-Model Optimization (DEWO), a post-deployment learning paradigm for WAMs that, alongside action imitation, refines world representations through visual experience to better condition action generation. Specifically, it identifies interaction turning points and learns from successful and failed futures to support classifier-free guidance. An additional value head estimates task progress from video representations and activates guidance when progress stalls during inference. Across five DexJoCo tasks, DEWO improves average success across all three WAM formulations. Ablations show that visual supervision from successful and failed continuations improves both prediction and control beyond action supervision alone. On four real-world tasks across Wuji and Sharpa, 3 x 3 grid evaluations show that two rounds of deployment learning increase success from 51.0% to 71.7% in cells with at least one initial success, a gain of 20.7 percentage points. These findings support continued predictive learning for improving control through deployment experience, making world modeling an active part of WAM adaptation.

AI.tldr: DEWO is a post-deployment learning paradigm for World-Action Models that refines world representations via visual experience from successful and failed futures, improving dexterous manipulation control.
AI.motivation: Current post-deployment learning paradigms typically improve behavior without requiring better world predictions. In dexterous manipulation, small execution errors compound in high-dimensional action spaces, hindering policy improvement and pushing interactions beyond the world model's training distribution. This motivates making world modeling an active part of WAM adaptation.
AI.method: DEWO combines action imitation with refinement of world representations through visual experience. It identifies interaction turning points and learns from successful and failed futures to support classifier-free guidance. A value head estimates task progress from video representations and activates guidance when progress stalls during inference.
AI.result: Across five DexJoCo tasks, DEWO improves average success across all three WAM formulations. Ablations show visual supervision from successful and failed continuations improves both prediction and control beyond action supervision alone. On four real-world tasks across Wuji and Sharpa, 3x3 grid evaluations show two rounds of deployment learning increase success from 51.0% to 71.7% in cells with at least one initial success (a 20.7 percentage point gain).
AI.conclusion: These findings support continued predictive learning for improving control through deployment experience, making world modeling an active part of WAM adaptation.

title: FedLAFP: Low-Rank Aggregation Meets Full-Rank Personalization in Federated Fine-Tuning
summary: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables clients to adapt pre-trained models without sharing raw data or communicating the full model, but statistical heterogeneity makes a single global adapter insufficient for personalized prediction. Existing personalized methods typically use the same low-rank structure for both shared and private adaptation, overlooking their distinct requirements for aggregation and personalization. We propose FedLAFP, a role-aware framework that couples a compact, globally aggregated LoRA branch with a client-private, full-rank-capable RandLoRA branch. The shared branch provides an efficient interface for transferring common knowledge, whereas the private branch combines fixed random low-rank bases with learned scaling coefficients to provide expressive client-specific adaptation without additional communication. Client- and layer-specific mixing coefficients jointly fuse the two branches, and only the shared LoRA parameters are exchanged. A controlled linear study supports this role assignment: LoRA yields more aligned client updates and lower aggregation error, while RandLoRA more accurately recovers client-specific residuals. Experiments across four visual recognition benchmarks show that FedLAFP consistently outperforms local-only and federated LoRA baselines, achieving an average personalized accuracy of $86.93\%$ and exceeding the best baseline average by $1.30$ percentage points.

AI.tldr: FedLAFP is a role-aware federated PEFT framework that couples a globally aggregated low-rank LoRA branch with a client-private, full-rank-capable RandLoRA branch, using client- and layer-specific mixing coefficients, to improve personalized prediction under statistical heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning lets clients adapt pre-trained models without sharing raw data or the full model, but statistical heterogeneity makes a single global adapter insufficient for personalized prediction. Existing personalized methods typically use the same low-rank structure for both shared and private adaptation, overlooking their distinct requirements for aggregation and personalization.
AI.method: FedLAFP is a role-aware framework coupling a compact, globally aggregated LoRA branch with a client-private, full-rank-capable RandLoRA branch. The shared branch transfers common knowledge efficiently, while the private branch combines fixed random low-rank bases with learned scaling coefficients for expressive client-specific adaptation without extra communication. Client- and layer-specific mixing coefficients jointly fuse the two branches, and only the shared LoRA parameters are exchanged.
AI.result: A controlled linear study supports the role assignment: LoRA yields more aligned client updates and lower aggregation error, while RandLoRA more accurately recovers client-specific residuals. Across four visual recognition benchmarks, FedLAFP consistently outperforms local-only and federated LoRA baselines, achieving an average personalized accuracy of 86.93%, exceeding the best baseline average by 1.30 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: FedLAFP shows that separating the roles of shared and private branches—efficient low-rank aggregation versus expressive private adaptation—improves personalized federated fine-tuning under statistical heterogeneity, with consistent gains over local-only and federated LoRA baselines.

title: Learning from Shared-Control Overrides: Context-Driven Acceleration Profile Prediction for Personalized Overtaking
summary: Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) systems are typically calibrated for an average driver, often resulting in a mismatch between vehicle behavior and individual expectations during time-critical maneuvers such as highway overtaking. When the ACC is perceived as too conservative and inconsistent, drivers intervene through throttle overrides, providing implicit feedback on the system's behavior. This paper reframes these override actions as human-in-theloop supervisory signals and proposes a data-driven framework for personalized vehicle adaptation, termed Context-driven Personalized ACC (CoP-ACC). Rather than relying solely on end-to-end regression, which tends to over-smooth dynamic responses, we introduce a hybrid pipeline combining: (i) unsupervised hierarchical clustering to extract representative acceleration profiles from override events; (ii) a context classifier that maps pre-maneuver driving conditions to the appropriate profile; and (iii) a residual regressor that refines the selected profile into a smooth, personalized acceleration profile tailored to the immediate context. Evaluated on real-world public-road data against a withheld forced-ACC baseline, the approach demonstrates high reconstruction fidelity and generates acceleration profiles that tend toward the driver's expected behavior in potential override contexts. The results highlight the potential of learning from shared-control overrides to enable anticipatory, personalized ACC behavior, reducing manual interventions and improving ride comfort.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CoP-ACC, a data-driven framework that reframes driver throttle overrides in ACC systems as human-in-the-loop supervisory signals to learn personalized, context-adaptive acceleration profiles.
AI.motivation: ACC systems are calibrated for an average driver, causing mismatches with individual expectations in time-critical maneuvers like highway overtaking. When ACC feels too conservative, drivers override via throttle, and these implicit feedback signals are currently unexploited for personalization.
AI.method: A hybrid pipeline with three stages: (i) unsupervised hierarchical clustering to extract representative acceleration profiles from override events; (ii) a context classifier mapping pre-maneuver driving conditions to the appropriate profile; (iii) a residual regressor refining the selected profile into a smooth, personalized acceleration trajectory. This avoids the over-smoothing of pure end-to-end regression.
AI.result: Evaluated on real-world public-road data against a withheld forced-ACC baseline, the approach achieves high reconstruction fidelity and produces acceleration profiles tending toward the driver's expected behavior in potential override contexts.
AI.conclusion: Learning from shared-control override signals enables anticipatory, personalized ACC behavior, reducing manual interventions and improving ride comfort.

title: Watch-Think-Interact: Bootstrapping Long-Horizon Multi-Turn Streaming Video Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Streaming video assistance requires models to answer asynchronous questions from an observed prefix under a fixed context budget. Existing approaches model response timing or compress history, but an online state formed before future questions are known can omit visual details before later questions reveal their relevance; the retained state alone cannot recover them. We introduce Watch-Think-Interact (WTI), a closed-loop framework for multi-question streaming video reasoning. WTI maintains compact natural-language memory entries tagged with source-video time ranges; these entries support direct reasoning when sufficient and otherwise anchor selective recall of finer visual evidence. For each question, WTI answers when current context and memory suffice, continues watching when required evidence has not appeared, or recalls a relevant past interval and decides again after incorporating the returned chunks, without replaying the full observed history. To train this behavior, we construct WTI-82K, comprising 82,335 timed questions across 4,812 causally aligned trajectories, and develop Stream-GDPO to optimize complete multi-question streaming rollouts using trajectory-level feedback for response timing, source-video recall, and memory updates. WTI achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance among the compared open-source streaming baselines, reaching 83.3% on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted overall accuracy on OVO-Bench.

AI.tldr: WTI is a closed-loop framework for multi-question streaming video reasoning that maintains time-tagged natural-language memory and selectively recalls visual evidence on demand, trained via WTI-82K and Stream-GDPO, achieving SOTA among open-source streaming baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing streaming video approaches model response timing or compress history, but an online state formed before future questions are known may omit visual details that later questions reveal as relevant; the retained compressed state alone cannot recover them.
AI.method: WTI maintains compact natural-language memory entries tagged with source-video time ranges, supporting direct reasoning when sufficient and otherwise anchoring selective recall of finer visual evidence. Per question it either answers (context+memory suffice), continues watching (evidence not yet appeared), or recalls a relevant past interval and re-decides after incorporating returned chunks, without replaying full history. Trained on WTI-82K (82,335 timed questions, 4,812 causally aligned trajectories) with Stream-GDPO, which optimizes complete multi-question streaming rollouts via trajectory-level feedback for response timing, source-video recall, and memory updates.
AI.result: State-of-the-art aggregate performance among compared open-source streaming baselines: 83.3% on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted overall accuracy on OVO-Bench.
AI.conclusion: A closed-loop, memory-anchored recall design combined with trajectory-level RL training enables effective multi-question streaming video reasoning under fixed context budgets, outperforming comparable open-source streaming baselines.

title: Brain-SAD: A Brain-Inspired Safe Autonomous Driving Control Framework with Dynamic Fear-Oriented Constraint on Dual-Policy
summary: Constrained Reinforcement Learning has recently gained increasing attention in the field of Safe Autonomous Driving, where the general mechanism is to maximize the expected reward while keeping the overall action risk bounded. In this way, the safety issues arising in AD can be mitigated through constrained actions. However, existing Constrained RL methods still lack dynamics on the imposed constraints. For instance, the action cost adopted by the existing Primal-Dual/soft-constrained methods is often defined as static state-to-cost mapping, and the safe-action projection in hard-constrained methods relies on the static projection with the fixed feasible region boundary estimated from offline demonstrations. The above drawback tightly couples the imposed constraints to the training scenarios, leaving the AD policy hard to handle different interaction scenarios, due to the improper state-level action-cost and the static projection boundary. Consequently, in this paper, we propose Brain-SAD, a brain-inspired safe autonomous driving control framework with dynamic fear-oriented constraints. By perceiving the current vehicle-interaction scene, Brain-SAD generates dynamic fear signal as fear reaction to online decide long-term policy for regular interaction or short-term policy for urgent-collision defense. In such two policy, the above fear-reaction will be constructed as the dynamic fear constraints, respectively reflecting the overall fear cost directly coupled with action-impact, and the dynamic fear boundary of the feasible region derived from different risky neighbors, both of which will in turn serve for the online policy optimization. Experimental results show that Brain-SAD outperforms existing methods, achieving higher success rate in shorter task-completion and collision-recovery time, and exhibits stronger reliability across continuous intersections of fluctuating complexity.

AI.tldr: Brain-SAD is a brain-inspired safe autonomous driving framework that replaces static constraints in constrained RL with dynamic fear-oriented constraints, achieved via a fear signal that adaptively selects long-term or short-term policies and constructs dynamic fear cost and dynamic feasible-region boundaries for online policy optimization.
AI.motivation: Constrained RL is widely used in Safe Autonomous Driving to maximize expected reward while bounding overall action risk, mitigating safety issues via constrained actions. However, existing constrained RL methods lack dynamics in the imposed constraints: primal-dual/soft-constrained methods use a static state-to-cost mapping, and hard-constrained methods rely on static safe-action projection with a fixed feasible region boundary estimated from offline demonstrations. This tightly couples constraints to training scenarios, making the AD policy unable to handle diverse interaction scenarios due to improper state-level action costs and static projection boundaries.
AI.method: The authors propose Brain-SAD, a brain-inspired safe autonomous driving control framework with dynamic fear-oriented constraints. By perceiving the current vehicle-interaction scene, Brain-SAD generates a dynamic fear signal as a fear reaction to online decide a long-term policy for regular interaction or a short-term policy for urgent-collision defense. In these two policies, the fear reaction is constructed as dynamic fear constraints: (1) an overall fear cost directly coupled with action-impact, and (2) a dynamic fear boundary of the feasible region derived from different risky neighbors. Both constraints in turn serve online policy optimization.
AI.result: Brain-SAD outperforms existing methods, achieving a higher success rate with shorter task-completion and collision-recovery time, and exhibits stronger reliability across continuous intersections of fluctuating complexity.
AI.conclusion: Introducing dynamic, fear-oriented constraints that adapt the cost mapping and feasible-region boundary to the online interaction scene improves safe autonomous driving performance and reliability over static-constraint constrained RL baselines.

title: MatToolBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents in Real-World Materials Science Workflows
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures. Mei Wu and Rui Xie contributed equally. Bo Chen and Lu Chen are corresponding authors. Project page: https://mattoolbench.github.io/ ; code: https://github.com/meiwu5/MatToolBench
summary: Multimodal GUI agents have achieved impressive results on general software benchmarks, yet their ability to operate professional scientific software remains largely unexplored. In materials science, sparse domain-specific web data, specialized interfaces, and tacit workflow conventions create blind spots that general-purpose pretraining cannot readily bridge. We present MatToolBench, the first real-environment benchmark for evaluating multimodal GUI agents on professional materials science software, comprising 204 tasks across 10 tools in three modalities: GUI operation, OriginPro scripting, and code-based database queries, all executed inside a Windows 11 VM. Each task is decomposed into fine-grained sub-criteria by domain experts, enabling interpretable partial-credit scoring; the GUI component of our multi-level evaluation pipeline achieves an average F1 of 0.98. For OriginPro figure-generation tasks, we further conduct a human-LLM agreement study to validate the use of a multimodal judge for secondary aesthetic assessment. Our experiments show that strong performance on general benchmarks does not transfer to professional scientific workflows, and that this gap is not a visual-grounding problem alone: failures arise from domain-specific operational knowledge, sparse pretraining coverage of scientific software, weak cross-tool artifact handoff, and critical states exposed only visually. Even the best model reaches only 25% success rate on GUI tasks and 45% on code tasks. MatToolBench therefore serves as a challenging diagnostic benchmark and real-environment testbed for data-scarce, knowledge-intensive scientific workflows.

AI.tldr: MatToolBench is the first real-environment benchmark for evaluating multimodal GUI agents on professional materials science software, revealing a large transfer gap from general benchmarks to scientific workflows.
AI.motivation: Multimodal GUI agents perform well on general software benchmarks, but their ability to operate professional scientific software is unexplored. In materials science, sparse domain-specific web data, specialized interfaces, and tacit workflow conventions create blind spots that general-purpose pretraining cannot bridge, and no benchmark existed to measure this gap.
AI.method: The authors built MatToolBench with 204 tasks across 10 tools in three modalities—GUI operation, OriginPro scripting, and code-based database queries—all executed inside a Windows 11 VM. Domain experts decomposed each task into fine-grained sub-criteria to enable interpretable partial-credit scoring; the GUI component of the multi-level evaluation pipeline achieves an average F1 of 0.98. For OriginPro figure-generation tasks, a human-LLM agreement study validated a multimodal judge for secondary aesthetic assessment.
AI.result: Strong general-benchmark performance does not transfer to professional scientific workflows. The gap is not merely a visual-grounding problem; failures stem from domain-specific operational knowledge, sparse pretraining coverage of scientific software, weak cross-tool artifact handoff, and critical states exposed only visually. Even the best model reaches only 25% success on GUI tasks and 45% on code tasks.
AI.conclusion: MatToolBench serves as a challenging diagnostic benchmark and real-environment testbed for data-scarce, knowledge-intensive scientific workflows, exposing transfer failures that current agents cannot overcome.

title: actr: aligning thoughts and responses for multilingual safety in reasoning llms
summary: Ensuring the safety of reasoning large language models (LLMs) across languages is essential for their reliable deployment. However, when exposed to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages, these models may generate unsafe responses even when their reasoning traces identify safety risks. To address this issue, we propose aligning cross-lingual thoughts and responses (ACTR), a framework that improves multilingual safety alignment by strengthening the use of existing safety reasoning. Specifically, we first present the think gap score (TGS) to compare the normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, and use reasoning- trace substitution to measure the cross-lingual safety gap. Next, using a corpus of jailbreak queries, we assess neuron importance through changes in response representations caused by neuron masking and compare the high-importance neuron sets obtained with reasoning enabled and disabled to identify safety think neurons that support the use of safety reasoning. Finally, we devise neuron-selective consistency optimization (NSCO), which uses a frozen judge model to reward agreement between the safety categories of reasoning traces and responses while updating only the parameters associated with the selected neurons, requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data. Across two reasoning models, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, with safety gains extending to unseen languages, while preserving or improving average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks and limiting false refusals of benign requests. Warning: this paper contains examples with unsafe content.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ACTR, a framework for improving multilingual safety alignment in reasoning LLMs by strengthening their use of existing safety reasoning traces. It introduces the Think Gap Score to quantify cross-lingual safety gaps, identifies "safety think neurons" via neuron masking, and optimizes them through neuron-selective consistency optimization using a frozen judge model. ACTR reduces attack success rates on AdvBench-X and MultiJail across two reasoning models while preserving general task performance and limiting false refusals.
AI.motivation: Reasoning LLMs can generate unsafe responses to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages even when their internal reasoning traces correctly identify safety risks. This cross-lingual safety gap threatens reliable multilingual deployment, motivating a method that leverages rather than overrides existing safety reasoning.
AI.method: ACTR comprises three components. (1) A Think Gap Score (TGS) measures normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, using reasoning-trace substitution to quantify the cross-lingual safety gap. (2) Neuron importance is assessed via changes in response representations under neuron masking, comparing high-importance neuron sets with reasoning enabled versus disabled to isolate safety think neurons. (3) Neuron-Selective Consistency Optimization (NSCO) uses a frozen judge model to reward consistency between safety categories of reasoning traces and responses, updating only selected neuron parameters and requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data.
AI.result: On AdvBench-X and MultiJail, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than evaluated state-of-the-art methods across two reasoning models. Safety gains generalize to unseen languages, while average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks is preserved or improved, and false refusals of benign requests remain limited.
AI.conclusion: ACTR provides an effective multilingual safety alignment approach for reasoning LLMs by reinforcing the influence of existing safety reasoning traces, mitigating cross-lingual jailbreak vulnerabilities without degrading general capabilities or over-refusing benign inputs. The paper contains unsafe content examples.

title: Breaking the Illusion of Review Reliability under Static Evaluation: SCOPE Fuzzing for LLM-based Scientific Reviewers
summary: The rapid growth of submissions and reviewing workload has accelerated the use of large language models (LLMs) in peer review. Prior studies suggest that LLM-based reviewers can penalize content perturbations, such as overclaiming, indicating a certain degree of reliability. Yet these conclusions are largely based on a narrow set of perturbation strategies instantiated with static templates, providing limited evidence of actual reliability. In this paper, we construct a three-level evaluation framework covering perturbations to surface presentation, argumentative logic, and value judgment. Experiments on representative LLM-based reviewers reveal two limitations of static evaluation: stratified vulnerability, where perturbation effects depend on whether the paper's original review score is high or low, and perturbation undercoverage, where a single template misses vulnerabilities exposed by diverse realizations. To address these limitations, we propose SCOPE-Fuzzer, a strategy-aware fuzzer that combines feedback-driven strategy selection with adaptive mutation of paper content. By iteratively probing reviewers with dynamic perturbations, SCOPE-Fuzzer consistently uncovers vulnerabilities overlooked by static evaluation and other baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a three-level perturbation framework (surface, argumentative, value) to test LLM-based reviewers and exposes two flaws of static evaluation—stratified vulnerability and perturbation undercoverage—then proposes SCOPE-Fuzzer, a strategy-aware fuzzer with feedback-driven strategy selection and adaptive mutation that uncovers more reviewer vulnerabilities than static baselines.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based reviewers become widely used due to rising submission and reviewing workloads, evidence of their actual reliability is needed. Prior conclusions that they penalize perturbations like overclaiming rely on narrow, static-template perturbations, offering limited proof of robustness.
AI.method: A three-level evaluation framework covering perturbations to surface presentation, argumentative logic, and value judgment. Experiments on representative LLM-based reviewers identify limitations of static evaluation, motivating SCOPE-Fuzzer, a strategy-aware fuzzer combining feedback-driven strategy selection with adaptive mutation of paper content that iteratively probes reviewers with dynamic perturbations.
AI.result: Static evaluation exhibits stratified vulnerability (perturbation effects depend on whether the original review score is high or low) and perturbation undercoverage (a single template misses vulnerabilities exposed by diverse realizations). SCOPE-Fuzzer consistently uncovers vulnerabilities overlooked by static evaluation and other baselines.
AI.conclusion: Static-template evaluation is insufficient for assessing LLM reviewer reliability. A feedback-driven, adaptive fuzzing approach such as SCOPE-Fuzzer provides stronger and more consistent vulnerability discovery.

title: Learning from Viable Failure Prefixes: Milestone Viability Potential Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents require reinforcement learning methods that can assign credit to intermediate decisions under sparse and delayed rewards. Existing group-based methods such as GRPO and GiGPO alleviate this issue by comparing rollout returns or repeated anchor states, but they still fail when the compared returns have no variation. We identify this failure mode as zero-credit failure: during early training, many failed rollouts contain useful prefixes, yet existing methods assign them no task-discriminative advantage. To address this issue, we propose Milestone Viability Potential Policy Optimization (MVPO), a potential-routed policy optimization algorithm that learns from viable failure prefixes. MVPO estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions, repairs zero-credit groups with potential-difference advantages, and attenuates the potential branch according to relative performance progress. Experiments with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct show that MVPO outperforms eight strong baselines, including GRPO and GiGPO. Under the same training length, MVPO improves over the GiGPO baseline by +4.4 success points on ALFWorld and +5.3 on WebShop, while adding only 0.16%-0.20% advantage-construction overhead.

AI.tldr: MVPO is a potential-routed policy optimization method that addresses the zero-credit failure of group-based RL methods by learning from viable failure prefixes via Union-Find viability regions and potential-difference advantages.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents need RL methods for credit assignment under sparse, delayed rewards. Group-based methods like GRPO and GiGPO compare rollout returns or anchor states, but fail when compared returns show no variation.
