Stage 2: Counterfactual Contrastive Policy Optimization (C2PO) reinforcement fine-tuning compares each evidence-seeking branch against a counterfactual direct-navigation branch from the same state, using a contrastive reward to credit seeking decisions by their subsequent navigation benefit.
AI.result: On simulated benchmarks, SeekVLN achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving success rate by 12.7% on R2R-CE and 7.5% on RxR-CE over the base model. Simulated and real-world evaluations both exhibit human-like evidence-seeking behaviors for more reliable progress grounding.
AI.conclusion: Coupling active evidence acquisition with progress reasoning, and reinforcing it via counterfactual contrastive rewards, effectively mitigates Progress Myopia and yields more reliable long-horizon VLN performance.

title: Teaching LLMs to Generate Challenging MILP Instances via Solver Feedback
summary: Generating optimization instances that are both feasible and computationally challenging is crucial for benchmarking solvers and training learning-based optimization algorithms. Existing non-LLM generators rely on seed instances or parameter tuning, resulting in high test-time computational cost, while existing LLM generators lack explicit hardness measures. Recent reinforcement learning methods with verifier feedback evaluate only binary correctness, which is misaligned with generating challenging problems. We note that an optimization solver reports the cost of solving at several stages of its pipeline, and leverage this to design a reward that scores both the solvability and the hardness of generated problems, measured by branch-and-bound nodes and post-cut relaxation gaps. Our key idea is a challenger-solver asymmetric self-play approach, where an LLM challenger generates progressively harder instances and the solver verifies feasibility and hardness, so no seed or training MILP instances are required. We fine-tune Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3.5-4B with GRPO and a size curriculum into OptiScribe-12B and OptiScribe-4B, which generate feasible yet challenging MILP problems from natural language instructions. On capacitated facility location and max-cut, OptiScribe-12B raises median SCIP search nodes by 1.7-5x and post-cut gaps by 1.1-1.7x over its base model and improves the feasibility rate on facility location by 9-19 points, while OptiScribe-4B raises median nodes by up to 15.6x. The problems cover a wider difficulty range than public benchmarks of the same size, follow instructions on density and difficulty, and can tune solver settings for families that public libraries lack. These results indicate that optimization-specific rewards, used in self-play mode, can teach LLMs to generate high-difficulty optimization benchmarks. We will release our code and models publicly on acceptance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an asymmetric challenger-solver self-play framework that fine-tunes LLMs with GRPO and an optimization-specific reward (branch-and-bound nodes and post-cut relaxation gaps) to generate feasible yet computationally challenging MILP instances from natural language, without needing seed or training MILP instances.
AI.motivation: Generating optimization instances that are both feasible and computationally hard is essential for benchmarking solvers and training learning-based optimization methods. Existing non-LLM generators depend on seed instances or parameter tuning, incurring high test-time cost, while existing LLM generators lack explicit hardness measures. RL methods with verifier feedback typically reward only binary correctness, which is misaligned with the goal of producing challenging problems.
AI.method: The authors exploit the cost reports emitted by an optimization solver at multiple pipeline stages to design a reward scoring both solvability and hardness, measured by branch-and-bound nodes and post-cut relaxation gaps. They propose a challenger-solver asymmetric self-play scheme in which an LLM challenger progressively generates harder instances while the solver verifies feasibility and hardness, eliminating the need for seed or training MILP instances. Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3.5-4B are fine-tuned with GRPO under a size curriculum to yield OptiScribe-12B and OptiScribe-4B.
AI.result: On capacitated facility location and max-cut, OptiScribe-12B increases median SCIP search nodes by 1.7-5x and post-cut gaps by 1.1-1.7x over its base model, and improves the feasibility rate on facility location by 9-19 points, while OptiScribe-4B raises median nodes by up to 15.6x. The generated problems span a wider difficulty range than public benchmarks of comparable size, follow instructions on density and difficulty, and can tune solver settings for families that public libraries lack.
AI.conclusion: Optimization-specific rewards used in self-play mode can teach LLMs to generate high-difficulty optimization benchmarks. The authors state that code and models will be released publicly upon acceptance.

title: Pretrain Once, Route Anywhere: Towards a Foundation Model for LLM Routing
summary: Large language model (LLM) routing aims to assign each query to the most suitable model from a heterogeneous candidate pool, improving the quality--efficiency trade-off of LLM inference. Existing routers are typically learned through local fitting: a router is optimized for a particular query workload and candidate pool, and often requires additional supervision or retraining as the routing environment changes. We ask whether LLM routing can instead be approached from a foundation-model perspective, learning a reusable routing capability that generalizes across tasks, candidate models, and deployment conditions. To this end, we introduce RouteFM, which learns to characterize anonymous candidate models from behavioral context and infer their target-specific capabilities, rather than binding routing decisions to fixed model identities or a single environment. Through episodic pretraining across heterogeneous routing environments, this capability can be reused by a frozen router and adapted to new environments through context alone. Experiments demonstrate transfer across changes in domains, modalities, candidate pools, and context budgets, with the largest gains when behavioral evidence is limited. On MMR-Bench, which is excluded from pretraining, RouteFM outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.23 quality points with only eight observations per candidate. These results support moving LLM routing from repeated local fitting toward a pretrain once, route anywhere paradigm. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LAMDA-Model-Reuse/RouteFM.

AI.tldr: RouteFM reframes LLM routing as a reusable foundation-model capability: instead of fitting a router per workload, it learns to characterize anonymous candidate models from behavioral context and generalizes across tasks, pools, and deployment conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM routers are learned via local fitting—optimized for a specific query workload and candidate pool, and requiring extra supervision or retraining when the routing environment changes. The paper asks whether routing can instead be learned as a reusable, generalizable capability from a foundation-model perspective.
AI.method: RouteFM learns to infer anonymous candidate models' target-specific capabilities from behavioral context rather than binding decisions to fixed model identities or a single environment. It is trained via episodic pretraining across heterogeneous routing environments, so a frozen router can reuse the learned capability and adapt to new environments through context alone.
AI.result: Transfer is demonstrated across changes in domains, modalities, candidate pools, and context budgets, with the largest gains when behavioral evidence is limited. On the held-out MMR-Bench, RouteFM beats the strongest baseline by 2.23 quality points using only eight observations per candidate.
AI.conclusion: The results support shifting LLM routing from repeated local fitting toward a "pretrain once, route anywhere" paradigm; code is publicly released.

title: Beyond Prompt Count: How Data Shapes Transfer in On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains students using teacher feedback on their own sampled responses, yet how prompt choice shapes transfer across teacher-student pairs remains poorly understood. We systematically study prompt quantity, source, and selection across RL- and SFT-continuation pairs and cross-model settings. We find that OPD can be highly prompt-efficient: a few prompts can approach large-pool performance, with four DAPO prompts matching the observed mathematics score of 3,840 DeepMath prompts. However, prompt utility is relational rather than intrinsic: changing only the teacher can reverse the relative effectiveness of mathematics and code prompts. To characterize these transfer differences, we analyze parameter and functional changes across prompt supports and model pairs. Functional alignment with the teacher varies across supports and target tasks; in continuation pairs, teacher-aligned prediction changes can coexist with weak parameter alignment. Continued OPD on effective supports can restore performance after unfavorable transfer. Finally, targeted selection does not consistently outperform uniform random sampling, and filtering out a source that performs poorly alone yields no consistent gain across three paired support draws. Overall, our results distinguish prompt efficiency from prompt interchangeability and show that effective data choice depends on the teacher-student pair and target capability, with random sampling providing a competitive baseline in the studied settings.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies how prompt quantity, source, and selection affect on-policy distillation (OPD) transfer across teacher-student pairs and cross-model settings, finding that prompt utility is relational rather than intrinsic.
AI.motivation: OPD trains students using teacher feedback on their own sampled responses, but how prompt choice shapes transfer across teacher-student pairs is poorly understood. The authors aim to characterize the factors (quantity, source, selection) that determine OPD effectiveness.
AI.method: They study prompt quantity, source, and selection across RL- and SFT-continuation pairs and cross-model settings. They analyze parameter and functional changes across prompt supports and model pairs, examining functional alignment with the teacher and parameter alignment in continuation pairs. They also test continued OPD on effective supports and compare targeted selection against uniform random sampling.
AI.result: OPD can be highly prompt-efficient: a few prompts approach large-pool performance, with four DAPO prompts matching the observed mathematics score of 3,840 DeepMath prompts. However, prompt utility is relational: changing only the teacher can reverse the relative effectiveness of mathematics and code prompts. Functional alignment varies across supports and target tasks; teacher-aligned prediction changes can coexist with weak parameter alignment in continuation pairs. Targeted selection does not consistently outperform uniform random sampling, and filtering out a source that performs poorly alone yields no consistent gain across three paired support draws.
AI.conclusion: The results distinguish prompt efficiency from prompt interchangeability, showing that effective data choice depends on the teacher-student pair and target capability, with random sampling providing a competitive baseline in the studied settings. Continued OPD on effective supports can restore performance after unfavorable transfer.

title: Routing Should Pay for Itself: Sparse Supervision for Economical LLM Routing
summary: Large language model (LLM) routing reduces serving cost by assigning each query to an appropriate model while preserving response quality. Learning such a router, however, often requires executing multiple candidate models on historical queries to collect query--model quality feedback, creating a nontrivial supervision cost before deployment. Existing work largely focuses on serving-time efficiency, overlooking whether the resulting savings are sufficient to recover this upfront expenditure. We further observe that routing quality often saturates well before all query--model feedback is collected, suggesting that dense supervision can be economically over-provisioned. We propose SaveRouter, a sparse-supervision routing framework that selectively acquires informative model feedback and shares capability information across related queries, while retaining query-level refinement for fine-grained routing. We evaluate routing by jointly accounting for supervision expenditure and subsequent serving-time savings. Across four routing benchmarks, the main setting uses only about 33--41% of available training feedback while maintaining competitive or better routing quality, and reduces the break-even deployment volume by approximately 1.9--9.5 times compared with the fastest conventional router. Further analysis shows that acquiring more supervision is not always economically preferable: the supervision level that minimizes serving cost can differ from the one that achieves the earliest payback. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LAMDA-Model-Reuse/SaveRouter.

AI.tldr: SaveRouter is a sparse-supervision LLM routing framework that selectively acquires informative query-model feedback and shares capability information across related queries, cutting training feedback use to ~33-41% while lowering the break-even deployment volume by 1.9-9.5x.
AI.motivation: LLM routing lowers serving cost by assigning queries to suitable models, but learning a router typically requires executing many candidate models on historical queries to collect query-model quality feedback, incurring upfront supervision cost. Prior work focuses on serving-time efficiency and largely ignores whether the resulting savings can recover this supervision expenditure. The authors also observe that routing quality saturates well before all feedback is collected, implying dense supervision may be economically over-provisioned.
AI.method: SaveRouter is a sparse-supervision routing framework that selectively acquires informative model feedback and shares capability information across related queries, while retaining query-level refinement for fine-grained routing. Routing performance is evaluated by jointly accounting for supervision expenditure and subsequent serving-time savings.
AI.result: Across four routing benchmarks, the main setting uses only about 33-41% of available training feedback while maintaining competitive or better routing quality, and reduces the break-even deployment volume by roughly 1.9-9.5x versus the fastest conventional router. Further analysis shows acquiring more supervision is not always economically preferable: the supervision level minimizing serving cost can differ from the one achieving earliest payback.
AI.conclusion: Supervision cost should be treated as a first-class objective in LLM routing alongside serving-time efficiency. Sparse, selective feedback acquisition can match dense-supervision routing quality while substantially improving economic viability, and the cost-optimal supervision level need not coincide with the fastest-payback level. Code is available at https://github.com/LAMDA-Model-Reuse/SaveRouter.

title: Demistifying Data and Simulator Assumptions in Supervised Causal Discovery
summary: Supervised causal discovery learns to infer causal structure for a new dataset from training datasets paired with structural labels. These training pairs are typically simulated, making the simulator both a source of supervision and a carrier of assumptions about causal graphs, mechanisms, and noise. Understanding the resulting predictions therefore requires examining how these assumptions supplement the information available in observational data, which may be compatible with multiple causal graphs. This paper examines that relationship across representative methods available through June 2026. We organize these methods by prediction target, prediction granularity, encoder, structural decoder, and training regime to relate what each method predicts to how it uses data and simulator-based supervision. Using this framework, we distinguish two questions: whether the target is identifiable under the assumed model class, and whether a trained predictor generalizes beyond its training distribution. Restrictions on mechanisms and noise can make otherwise ambiguous causal directions identifiable, but predictive accuracy under those restrictions does not establish transfer when they change. This distinction motivates evaluation that matches metrics to the identifiable graph target and tests changes in graphs, mechanisms, and noise between training and deployment. Extending such evaluation to real data also requires documenting the external causal evidence and uncertainty behind benchmark reference graphs. Together, these analyses guide method comparison and identify open questions in transfer, test-time adaptation, and uncertainty assessment.

AI.tldr: This review examines supervised causal discovery, mapping representative methods by prediction target, granularity, encoder, decoder, and training regime, and shows that simulator assumptions can make causal direction identifiable but do not guarantee transfer when graphs, mechanisms, or noise shift, motivating matched evaluation and uncertainty-aware real-data benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Supervised causal discovery relies on simulated training pairs, so the simulator is both a supervision source and a carrier of assumptions about causal graphs, mechanisms, and noise. Since observational data may be compatible with multiple causal graphs, understanding predictions requires clarifying how these assumptions supplement observational information. A principled framework is needed to compare methods and separate what is learned from how assumptions enable it.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured review of representative supervised causal discovery methods available through June 2026. They organize methods along five axes: prediction target, prediction granularity, encoder, structural decoder, and training regime, relating what each method predicts to how it uses observational data and simulator-based supervision. They then use this framework to distinguish two questions: whether the target is identifiable under the assumed model class, and whether a trained predictor generalizes beyond its training distribution.
AI.result: The analysis shows that restrictions on mechanisms and noise can render otherwise ambiguous causal directions identifiable, but predictive accuracy under those restrictions does not establish transfer when the restrictions change. These identifiability and generalization concerns are largely conflated in existing evaluations, leading to metrics that do not match the identifiable graph target and to incomplete testing across distribution shifts in graphs, mechanisms, and noise.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues for evaluation that matches metrics to the identifiable graph target and explicitly tests changes in graphs, mechanisms, and noise between training and deployment. Extending such evaluation to real data requires documenting the external causal evidence and uncertainty behind benchmark reference graphs. These analyses guide method comparison and highlight open questions in transfer, test-time adaptation, and uncertainty assessment.

title: Commitment Hierarchies under Intent Revision: A Belief-Revision Account of Salvage in Tool-Use Agents
comment: Accepted in the 27th International Conference on Principles and Practice of Multi-Agent Systems
summary: When a user changes their mind partway through a task, an agent that has already split the task into sub-goals and paid for tool calls must decide, per cached sub-result, whether to keep, patch, or discard it (salvage), restarting wastes valid work and continuing unchanged answers the old question. Our main finding is that salvage quality is a matter of role design rather than model capability: a language model asked the keep/patch/discard question one node at a time is unreliable, but asked to classify the revision once, with a deterministic layer propagating the decision, it reaches the cost-optimal oracle on all three models tested, from two vendors. Modeling the plan as a commitment hierarchy and the intent change as a belief-revision operator with AGM style postulates, we prove that no policy observing only a node's local view can be both safe and cost optimal, while the single classification design is both. Across three environments the policy recovers the full achievable savings, 43% cheaper than restart, at 100% correctness.

AI.tldr: Salvage quality after an intent change is a role-design problem, not a model-capability limit: classifying the revision once and propagating it deterministically matches the cost-optimal oracle, whereas per-node keep/patch/discard prompting does not.
AI.motivation: When a user changes their mind mid-task, an agent that already decomposed the task into sub-goals and paid for tool calls must decide per cached sub-result whether to keep, patch, or discard it. Restarting wastes valid work, while continuing unchanged answers the old question; so a reliable salvage policy is needed.
AI.method: The plan is modeled as a commitment hierarchy and the intent change as a belief-revision operator with AGM-style postulates. A single revision classification is made once by the language model, then propagated by a deterministic layer. A local-view-only policy is proven to be unable to be both safe and cost-optimal.
AI.result: The per-node keep/patch/discard design is unreliable, while the single-classification design reaches the cost-optimal oracle on all three tested models (from two vendors). Across three environments it recovers the full achievable savings at 100% correctness, 43% cheaper than restart.
AI.conclusion: Salvage quality depends on role design rather than model capability. No policy observing only a node's local view can be both safe and cost-optimal, whereas the single-classification design is both.

title: Governing the Edge: Automating Commercial Property and Casualty Insurance Underwriting via a Hybrid Local-Cloud Multi-Agent Framework
comment: Accepted at AIxB 2026. 6 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Data and Code in github: https://github.com/vsingh45/governing-the-edge
summary: Underwriters in commercial Property and Casualty (P&C) insurance spend 30 to 40% of their time on administrative work rather than risk judgment, and a single submission takes about 40 minutes by hand. We present Governing the Edge, a multi-agent framework for that layer, organized around a data-residency constraint: sensitive submission data must not leave the perimeter. Eleven agents and two deterministic control nodes, one a human-escalation interrupt, form a 13-node LangGraph workflow across two tiers. Agents touching raw submissions run locally on Gemma 2, each bound through a tool interface logging every invocation (synthetic stubs in the current prototype); only anonymized scores and non-identifying fields cross to Claude Sonnet in the cloud. Compliance rules are encoded as conditions on graph edges, so a non-compliant submission never reaches pricing. We walk through one full scenario end to end, a commercial auto submission whose principal driver carries serious violations, showing every agent call, every tool invocation, and the resulting routing decision. The framework processes a 40-minute manual submission in a few minutes on a single edge device, dominated by serialized on-device inference. On the hard-stop violation tier the framework enforces every rule correctly and reproducibly, since hard stops are deterministic predicates over fields extracted at temperature 0; overall compliance accuracy across the 20-scenario benchmark is 70%, with the remaining gap concentrated in softer, judgment-based tiers. It keeps a complete audit trail and respects the privacy boundary throughout. We release all code, compliance rules, tool stubs, and synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: Presents "Governing the Edge," a 13-node LangGraph multi-agent framework for P&C insurance underwriting that enforces a data-residency constraint: privacy-sensitive agents run locally on Gemma 2, while only anonymized scores reach Claude Sonnet in the cloud.
AI.motivation: Commercial P&C underwriters spend 30–40% of their time on administrative work, and a single submission takes about 40 minutes by hand. The work targets this administrative layer, constrained by the requirement that sensitive submission data must not leave the perimeter.
AI.method: Eleven agents plus two deterministic control nodes (one a human-escalation interrupt) form a two-tier 13-node LangGraph workflow. Agents handling raw submissions run locally on Gemma 2, each bound via a tool interface that logs every invocation (synthetic stubs in the prototype); only anonymized scores and non-identifying fields cross to Claude Sonnet. Compliance rules are encoded as conditions on graph edges, so non-compliant submissions never reach pricing. One full commercial-auto scenario with a high-violation principal driver is walked through end to end.
AI.result: A 40-minute manual submission is processed in a few minutes on a single edge device, dominated by serialized on-device inference. Hard-stop violation tiers are enforced correctly and reproducibly (deterministic predicates over fields extracted at temperature 0). Overall compliance accuracy on a 20-scenario benchmark is 70%, with the remaining gap concentrated in softer, judgment-based tiers. A complete audit trail is maintained and the privacy boundary is respected throughout.
AI.conclusion: Code, compliance rules, tool stubs, and synthetic datasets are released. The framework demonstrates that edge-local inference can automate underwriting administration under data-residency constraints, though accuracy on judgment-based compliance tiers remains a limitation.

title: VeriWeave Govern: Evidence-Gated Deterministic Runtime Governance for Enterprise AI Agents
summary: Enterprise artificial-intelligence agents increasingly call tools, modify infrastructure, and process protected data, creating a need to separate action generation from action authorization. This article presents VeriWeave Govern, a deterministic runtime governance layer that evaluates structured agent actions against versioned policies, validates typed evidence, applies fixed deny > review > allow precedence, routes consequential actions to accountable human review, and records replayable tamper-evident audit state. GovernBench evaluates the design over 30 independent seeds and 60,000 oracle-labelled cases spanning five enterprise domains, adversarial evidence, out-of-distribution actions, and temporal policy evolution. VeriWeave achieves 0.9888 mean accuracy, 0.9836 macro-F1, zero observed aggregate false allows, and zero observed Governance Attack Success Rate on the evaluated cases. Six ablations show that evidence gating, deny precedence, out-of-distribution fail-safe behavior, human review, contradiction handling, and temporal replay contribute complementary safety. The deployed API additionally passes 12/12 end-to-end scenarios and a 40,040-request concurrency matrix with zero failures. A separate 150-case EU/Austria regulation-grounded evaluation uses frozen predictions and two independent blinded human annotators, who agree on all decisions. On this set, deterministic engines remain conservative, while a Gemma 4 31B comparator aligns more closely with the human consensus. The results expose a measurable safety--utility trade-off and motivate evidence-aware, replayable governance as an independent control plane for enterprise agent execution.

AI.tldr: VeriWeave Govern is a deterministic runtime governance layer that separates agent action generation from authorization, using versioned policies, typed evidence validation, fixed precedence, human review, and replayable audit trails; it is evaluated on 60,000 oracle-labelled GovernBench cases and additional regulatory and API tests.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI agents increasingly call tools, modify infrastructure, and process protected data, making it necessary to decouple action generation from action authorization.
AI.method: VeriWeave Govern evaluates structured agent actions against versioned policies, validates typed evidence, applies fixed deny > review > allow precedence, routes consequential actions to accountable human review, and records replayable tamper-evident audit state. GovernBench spans 30 seeds and 60,000 oracle-labelled cases across five enterprise domains, adversarial evidence, out-of-distribution actions, and temporal policy evolution; six ablations and a deployed API evaluation are included.
AI.result: VeriWeave achieves 0.9888 mean accuracy, 0.9836 macro-F1, zero observed aggregate false allows, and zero observed Governance Attack Success Rate. Ablations show complementary safety contributions from evidence gating, deny precedence, out-of-distribution fail-safe behavior, human review, contradiction handling, and temporal replay. The API passes 12/12 end-to-end scenarios and a 40,040-request concurrency matrix with zero failures. In a 150-case EU/Austria regulation-grounded evaluation with two blinded annotators, deterministic engines remain conservative while a Gemma 4 31B comparator aligns more closely with human consensus.
AI.conclusion: The results expose a measurable safety-utility trade-off and motivate evidence-aware, replayable governance as an independent control plane for enterprise agent execution.

title: CRASM-Gate: Deterministic-First Constraint- and Role-Aware Semantic Mapping with Selective Model Assistance Across Heterogeneous Industrial Standards
summary: Industrial standards often encode the same engineering concept through incompatible hierarchies, identifiers, roles, and structural constraints, so the nearest lexical or embedding match can still be technically inadmissible. This article presents CRASM, a deterministic constraint- and role-aware semantic mapping method, and CRASM-Gate, its selectively model-assisted extension. The framework separates standard-specific canonicalization, bounded retrieval, deterministic rules, destination-versus-origin role interpretation, semantic and structural ranking, ambiguity refusal, and target validation. CRASM-Gate adds a confidence/disagreement gate that may invoke a candidate-constrained large language model, while final authority remains with deterministic validation. A controlled artifact covers six directed industrial-standard pairs, three difficulty levels, and ten configurations, yielding 14,400 sample-level decisions. With a fixed local model endpoint, CRASM-Gate reaches mean F1 0.9938 and an implemented structural-validity rate of 1.0000; deterministic CRASM reaches 0.9931 without generative-model calls; and the model-only baseline reaches 0.5347. Relative to the model-only baseline, CRASM reduces top-1 errors from 670 to 10 while exhibiting 0.0688 s/sample rather than 24.5263 s/sample observed latency. CRASM-Gate improves CRASM by one additional correct decision out of 1,440, with observed latency increasing to 15.7666 s/sample. The results support a deterministic-first interoperability architecture in which model assistance is optional, measurable, candidate-bounded, and unable to bypass structural validation.

AI.tldr: CRASM is a deterministic, constraint- and role-aware semantic mapping method for industrial-standard interoperability, with an optional model-assisted variant (CRASM-Gate). It achieves near-perfect mapping accuracy (F1 0.9931/0.9938) and full structural validity, vastly outperforming a model-only baseline while being far faster.
AI.motivation: Industrial standards often encode the same engineering concept through incompatible hierarchies, identifiers, roles, and structural constraints, so the nearest lexical or embedding match can still be technically inadmissible. This motivates a mapping approach that respects structural and role constraints rather than relying on surface similarity.
AI.method: The framework separates standard-specific canonicalization, bounded retrieval, deterministic rules, destination-versus-origin role interpretation, semantic and structural ranking, ambiguity refusal, and target validation. CRASM-Gate adds a confidence/disagreement gate that may invoke a candidate-constrained LLM, while final authority remains with deterministic validation. Evaluation used a controlled artifact of six directed industrial-standard pairs, three difficulty levels, and ten configurations, yielding 14,400 sample-level decisions, with a fixed local model endpoint.
AI.result: CRASM-Gate reaches mean F1 0.9938 and an implemented structural-validity rate of 1.0000; deterministic CRASM reaches 0.9931 without generative-model calls; the model-only baseline reaches 0.5347. Relative to the baseline, CRASM reduces top-1 errors from 670 to 10 while exhibiting 0.0688 s/sample versus 24.5263 s/sample observed latency. CRASM-Gate improves CRASM by one additional correct decision out of 1,440, with latency rising to 15.7666 s/sample.
AI.conclusion: The results support a deterministic-first interoperability architecture in which model assistance is optional, measurable, candidate-bounded, and unable to bypass structural validation.

title: Authority Before Utility: Non-Compensatory Control for Persistent LLM Memory
summary:
Persistent memory creates a control problem that retrieval relevance alone does not solve: a memory can remain highly useful after an update, deletion, or revocation makes it inadmissible for the current answer. We formalize this as a separation between utility and authority. A fixed finite penalty applied to an unnormalized utility score cannot guarantee exclusion under arbitrary positive-affine reparameterization of that score; by contrast, rank-normalized compensation is scale-invariant and therefore forms a stronger empirical comparator.
  Our prospectively frozen TIDE/LongMemEval primary was quarantined before a valid HELDOUT comparison because the materialized TIDE adapter conflated historical age with query-relative inadmissibility and the aligned LongMemEval split left no DEV set for the predeclared penalty selection. We therefore report a post-primary replacement diagnostic on Memora Remembering, where update/delete operations provide item-level forgetting state.
  On Qwen3-8B, DEV selected lambda = 0.6 from a ten-point normalized SOFT family. Across 185 HELDOUT units in 28 dependency clusters, HARD exclusion yields 4.04% balanced construct error versus 19.66% for locked SOFT, a paired difference of 15.61 points with a 20,000-replicate cluster-bootstrap 95% interval of [13.07, 18.76].
  The effect is driven primarily by forgotten-value leakage while current-value recall is preserved. This is same-Q operator-comparison evidence, not a universal claim that scalar control fails, not an evaluation of learned authority inference, and not an independent downstream-harm endpoint.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes persistent-memory control as a separation between utility and authority, showing that a fixed penalty on unnormalized utility cannot guarantee exclusion under positive-affine reparameterization while rank-normalized compensation can. Due to a quarantined primary benchmark, the authors report a post-primary diagnostic on Memora Remembering: HARD exclusion reduces balanced construct error to 4.04% versus 19.66% for locked SOFT (paired difference 15.61 points, 95% cluster-bootstrap interval [13.07, 18.76]) on Qwen3-8B, driven mainly by reduced forgotten-value leakage with current-value recall preserved.
AI.motivation: Retrieval relevance alone cannot solve a control problem in persistent memory: a memory may still be highly useful after an update, deletion, or revocation renders it inadmissible for the current answer. The work seeks to formalize and empirically test this separation between utility and authority, and to identify a control mechanism that guarantees exclusion robustly rather than depending on score scale.
AI.method: The authors formalize utility–authority separation and show analytically that a fixed finite penalty on an unnormalized utility score fails to guarantee exclusion under arbitrary positive-affine reparameterization, whereas rank-normalized compensation is scale-invariant. The prospectively frozen TIDE/LongMemEval primary was quarantined (the materialized TIDE adapter conflated historical age with query-relative inadmissibility, and the aligned LongMemEval split left no DEV set for predeclared penalty selection), so they run a post-primary replacement diagnostic on Memora Remembering, which provides item-level forgetting state via update/delete operations. On Qwen3-8B, lambda = 0.6 is selected on DEV from a ten-point normalized SOFT family, and HARD exclusion is compared against locked SOFT across 185 HELDOUT units in 28 dependency clusters using paired cluster-bootstrap inference.
AI.result: HARD exclusion yields 4.04% balanced construct error versus 19.66% for locked SOFT, a paired difference of 15.61 points with a 20,000-replicate cluster-bootstrap 95% interval of [13.07, 18.76]. The effect is driven primarily by forgotten-value leakage, while current-value recall is preserved.
AI.conclusion: The findings support rank-normalized compensation as a stronger empirical comparator than fixed penalties on unnormalized utility for enforcing memory admissibility. The authors frame this as same-Q operator-comparison evidence: it is not a universal claim that scalar control fails, not an evaluation of learned authority inference, and not an independent downstream-harm endpoint.

title: Boundary-State Control for Tool-Using Language-Model Agents: Commit-Time Consistency under State Drift
summary: Tool-using language-model agents can decide that an action is permissible and execute it only after security-relevant state has changed. We study this proposal-to-commit gap and introduce BSC-R, a deterministic effect-boundary mechanism that binds a single-use commit authorization to the exact action and to a semantic projection of the authorization state that justified it. On 2,847 attacked AgentDojo episodes, the boundary kernel preserves the unprotected agent's behavior exactly (80.576% utility; 1.616% attack success). On 10,302 frozen proposals, it accepts every unchanged commit and rejects every instance of ten prospectively specified changed or replayed classes. In an independently generated boundary-drift experiment, full joint binding commits 0/4,403 invalid contexts while retaining 5,899/5,899 valid contexts. A prospective external evaluation on the 3,460-scenario CONTINUITY suite retains all 700 benign cases, prevents 1,200/1,200 represented non-replay invalid effects, handles 160/160 replay lifecycles correctly, and withholds 200/200 ambiguous no-release cases. The broader external suite also exposes the method's limit: across all 2,560 attacks, BSC-R has a 25% invalid-effect commit rate versus 0% for CONTINUITY. The result is therefore a scoped commit-time consistency mechanism, not a universal agent-safety claim.

AI.tldr: BSC-R is a deterministic commit-time mechanism that binds a single-use authorization to the exact action and a semantic projection of the security-relevant state, eliminating the proposal-to-commit gap in tool-using LLM agents within represented effect classes, though with a scoped rather than universal safety claim.
AI.motivation: Tool-using language-model agents can authorize an action while security-relevant state subsequently changes before execution, creating a proposal-to-commit gap in which a permitted decision is executed against invalidated context (changed or replayed state).
AI.method: BSC-R is a deterministic effect-boundary mechanism. It binds a single-use commit authorization to (i) the exact action and (ii) a semantic projection of the authorization state that justified the decision, so that any changed or replayed state invalidates the commit.
AI.result: On 2,847 attacked AgentDojo episodes, the boundary kernel preserves the unprotected agent's behavior exactly (80.576% utility; 1.616% attack success). On 10,302 frozen proposals, it accepts every unchanged commit and rejects every instance of ten prospectively specified changed or replayed classes. In an independent boundary-drift experiment, full joint binding commits 0/4,403 invalid contexts while retaining 5,899/5,899 valid contexts. Prospectively on the 3,460-scenario CONTINUITY suite, it retains all 700 benign cases, prevents 1,200/1,200 represented non-replay invalid effects, handles 160/160 replay lifecycles correctly, and withholds 200/200 ambiguous no-release cases. However, across all 2,560 attacks in the broader external suite, BSC-R shows a 25% invalid-effect commit rate versus 0% for CONTINUITY.
AI.conclusion: BSC-R is a scoped commit-time consistency mechanism rather than a universal agent-safety guarantee: it is sound for represented changed/replayed effect classes and preserves utility, but its 25% invalid-effect commit rate on the broader external suite exposes coverage limits.

title: SkillGym: Training Skill-Use Agents with Automatic Verifiable Environment Generation
summary: Skills equip LLM agents with professional knowledge and guidance to complete long-horizon and complex tasks. Although skills have been widely adopted in recent agent paradigms and harnesses, how to synthesize reliable training data and how to train agents for skill use remain underexplored. In this work, we propose SkillGym, an automatic pipeline to build verifiable environments, collect trajectories, and train skill-use agents. SkillGym first crawls a large volume of skills from the internet, then keeps those whose workflows can run reproducibly offline. A builder-reviewer pipeline is used to construct difficulty-controlled tasks, spanning four task types, each with a reference solution and an executable verifier. With this pipeline, we build 6.8k environments and collect 19k verified successful trajectories for supervised finetuning. Finetuning on these trajectories improves LLMs of different families and sizes, from 2B to 122B parameters across four skill-use benchmarks; Our Qwen3.5-9B SFT model outperforms the 397B untrained model on two of them. Further analysis shows that training teaches agents to invoke skills, raising the rate of reading the relevant skill from 28% to 96%, and that the gains hold across reasoning structures, extending to task types that form a minority of the training data and to skills held out from training

AI.tldr: SkillGym is an automatic pipeline that crawls internet skills, filters them for reproducible offline execution, and builds verifiable training environments to synthesize trajectories for training LLM agents in skill use.
AI.motivation: Skills provide LLM agents with professional knowledge for long-horizon complex tasks, but how to synthesize reliable training data and train agents to use skills effectively remains underexplored.
AI.method: SkillGym crawls a large volume of skills from the internet and retains those whose workflows run reproducibly offline. A builder-reviewer pipeline constructs difficulty-controlled tasks spanning four task types, each with a reference solution and an executable verifier. This yields 6.8k environments and 19k verified successful trajectories used for supervised finetuning.
AI.result: Finetuning on the collected trajectories improves LLMs across families and sizes (2B to 122B parameters) on four skill-use benchmarks. The Qwen3.5-9B SFT model outperforms a 397B untrained model on two benchmarks. Training raises the rate of reading the relevant skill from 28% to 96%, with gains holding across reasoning structures, minority task types, and held-out skills.
AI.conclusion: Automatic, verifiable skill-environment construction and trajectory-based supervised finetuning effectively teach LLM agents to invoke and use skills, yielding broad generalization beyond the training distribution.

title: How Can Recommendation Feedback Evolve Agent Memory?
summary: Content-generation agents continuously receive impressions, clicks, conversions, and negative feedback from recommendation systems, providing real-world outcome signals for memory evolution. However, these signals are delayed and noisy, confounded by audience composition, placement, and recommendation policies, and may result from the combined influence of multiple memories, making accurate attribution difficult. Existing methods rely primarily on immediate feedback or semantic retrieval and therefore struggle to reliably translate recommendation outcomes into memory fitness. To address this challenge, we propose TIDE (Trajectory-Informed Directed Memory Evolution), an external memory evolution framework driven by delayed recommendation feedback. We further introduce Memory Evolution Gain (MEG), which measures the utility improvement of evolved memory over a no memory baseline on strictly future tasks. TIDE treats memory as a capacity-constrained population of experiences: temporal and semantic credit assignment estimates contextual fitness, while responsibility credit distributes outcome signals according to the memories referenced during generation. These signals are then used to reinforce, crossover, mutate, or evict memories. On an e-commerce membership marketing content-generation agent, TIDE achieves a +7.75-percentage-point MEG in offline temporal replay and significantly improves both unique click-through rate (UCTR) and activation rate in an online A/B test. On a delayed-label benchmark, TIDE achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) and the highest MEG among the compared methods, demonstrating its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: TIDE is an external memory evolution framework for content-generation agents that converts delayed, noisy recommendation feedback into memory fitness via temporal, semantic, and responsibility credit assignment, optimizing memory through reinforcement, crossover, mutation, and eviction, validated by the proposed Memory Evolution Gain (MEG) metric.
AI.motivation: Content-generation agents receive delayed and noisy outcome signals from recommendation systems (impressions, clicks, conversions, negative feedback) that are confounded by audience composition, placement, and recommendation policies, and may stem from multiple memories jointly, making accurate attribution to memory fitness difficult. Existing methods rely on immediate feedback or semantic retrieval, which cannot reliably translate recommendation outcomes into memory fitness.
AI.method: The paper proposes TIDE (Trajectory-Informed Directed Memory Evolution), an external memory evolution framework driven by delayed recommendation feedback. It models memory as a capacity-constrained population of experiences. Temporal and semantic credit assignment estimates contextual fitness, while responsibility credit distributes outcome signals according to which memories were referenced during generation. These signals drive memory operations: reinforcement, crossover, mutation, or eviction. The paper also introduces Memory Evolution Gain (MEG), which measures the utility improvement of evolved memory over a no-memory baseline on strictly future tasks.
AI.result: On an e-commerce membership marketing content-generation agent, TIDE achieves a +7.75-percentage-point MEG in offline temporal replay and significantly improves both unique click-through rate (UCTR) and activation rate in an online A/B test. On a delayed-label benchmark, TIDE attains the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) and the highest MEG among compared methods.
AI.conclusion: TIDE effectively translates delayed, noisy recommendation feedback into memory fitness through multi-faceted credit assignment, enabling directed memory evolution that improves downstream content-generation performance both offline and online, demonstrating its effectiveness for outcome-driven memory evolution.

title: Rational Clarification by Assistive Agents via Value-of-Information Reasoning
summary: Users of language-based assistive agents often make ambiguous requests. In response, an assistant can either directly act on its interpretation of the request --- risking misalignment with the user --- or ask a clarifying question. Which option is the most safe and helpful? A common approach is to ask questions that minimize uncertainty about the user's intent until a threshold is reached. However, this neglects the impact of uncertainty reduction on downstream performance, the costs of asking versus acting immediately, and the possibility that users may provide corrections without being asked. To navigate these trade-offs, we introduce Rational Enquiry via Value-of-Information Reasoning (REVOIR). REVOIR makes clarification decisions via inference-time reasoning about the value-of-information of a question, which captures the expected improvement in task reward due to the answer received. In two assistive tasks --- ambiguous question answering (CondAmbigQA) and preference-aligned household task planning (ADAPT) --- we show that REVOIR achieves greater success with fewer questions than approaches based on prompting, chain-of-thought, fine-tuning, or information gain, improving preference satisfaction on ADAPT by 13-15% over a fine-tuned clarification policy while requiring no training and asking five times fewer questions. Furthermore, when the assistant can receive cheap user corrections after acting, REVOIR naturally infers that asking questions is not always efficient, demonstrating the adaptivity of our approach. In contrast, we find that vanilla reasoning agents fail to adaptively clarify user requests, and request fewer clarifications as reasoning effort increases.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces REVOIR, an inference-time method for deciding when an assistive agent should ask clarifying questions versus act immediately. By reasoning about the value-of-information of a potential question, REVOIR balances uncertainty reduction against downstream task reward and interaction costs, outperforming prompting, chain-of-thought, fine-tuning, and information-gain baselines while asking far fewer questions.
AI.motivation: Users of language-based assistive agents frequently issue ambiguous requests. The agent must choose between acting on its own interpretation (risking misalignment with the user) or asking a clarifying question. Existing approaches typically ask questions that minimize uncertainty about user intent until a threshold is reached, but this neglects: (1) how uncertainty reduction affects downstream performance, (2) the costs of asking versus acting immediately, and (3) the possibility that users may offer corrections without being prompted.
AI.method: The authors propose Rational Enquiry via Value-of-Information Reasoning (REVOIR). REVOIR makes clarification decisions through inference-time reasoning about the value-of-information of a question, which captures the expected improvement in task reward resulting from the answer received. No training or fine-tuning is required.
AI.result: Evaluated on two assistive tasks—ambiguous question answering (CondAmbigQA) and preference-aligned household task planning (ADAPT)—REVOIR achieves greater success with fewer questions than prompting, chain-of-thought, fine-tuning, and information-gain baselines. On ADAPT it improves preference satisfaction by 13-15% over a fine-tuned clarification policy while requiring no training and asking five times fewer questions. When cheap user corrections are available after acting, REVOIR naturally infers that asking is not always efficient, demonstrating adaptivity. In contrast, vanilla reasoning agents fail to clarify adaptively and request fewer clarifications as reasoning effort increases.
AI.conclusion: Framing clarification as value-of-information reasoning yields a training-free, adaptive policy that outperforms existing methods in both task success and efficiency. REVOIR appropriately balances asking versus acting, including when cheap post-hoc corrections exist, whereas standard reasoning agents exhibit the opposite, undesirable trend of clarifying less as they reason more.

title: FOCUS: Training-Free Decision-Preserving Context Compression for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents accumulate interaction histories that grow linearly with task length, causing quadratic inference cost scaling and performance degradation from attention dilution. Existing context-compression methods learn what to discard offline: by contrastively optimizing guidelines, distilling compressors, or training compression policies. This incurs a substantial cost. Further, the compression policy is learned a priori and is not dynamically conditioned on the evolving test-time trajectories. In this paper we ask a complementary question: Which past interactions causally shape the agent's future decisions? We recast context compression as a causal decision preservation problem over discrete interaction units and introduce FOCUS, a training-free context compression framework that operates entirely at test time. Our method requires no offline data collection or fine-tuning, and is architecture-agnostic, attaching to any closed-API frontier model as a modular compression layer. We evaluate FOCUS on diverse agentic benchmarks including API and tool-calling, QA, web domain and multi-turn dialogue. Our method establishes new state of the art performance, cutting peak context by up to 48% and dependency by 73% while improving task success by up to 8.9 percentage points over uncompressed execution.

AI.tldr: FOCUS is a training-free, test-time context compression framework that treats compression as causal decision preservation over discrete interaction units, reducing peak context and dependency while improving agent task success.
AI.motivation: LLM agents' interaction histories grow linearly with task length, causing quadratic inference costs and performance degradation from attention dilution. Existing compression methods learn what to discard offline via contrastive guidelines, distilled compressors, or trained policies, which is costly and not dynamically conditioned on evolving test-time trajectories.
AI.method: The paper reframes context compression as a causal decision preservation problem over discrete interaction units and proposes FOCUS, a training-free framework operating entirely at test time. It requires no offline data collection or fine-tuning, is architecture-agnostic, and attaches to any closed-API frontier model as a modular compression layer.
AI.result: Evaluated on diverse agentic benchmarks (API and tool-calling, QA, web domain, multi-turn dialogue), FOCUS achieves new state-of-the-art, reducing peak context by up to 48% and dependency by 73%, while improving task success by up to 8.9 percentage points over uncompressed execution.
AI.conclusion: FOCUS demonstrates that test-time, causal decision-preserving context compression can substantially cut inference cost and dependency while improving agent performance, offering a practical, architecture-agnostic alternative to offline-learned compression.

title: XU-RS: Explaining Credal Width in Random-Set Language Models
summary: Uncertainty estimates tell us how unsure a model is, but not why. Without knowing which parts of an input influences a model's uncertainty, we cannot tell whether that uncertainty score depends on input features that are relevant for the task. We study this problem in randomset classifiers built using pretrained language models. These classifiers assign probability to individual answers and to groups of answers, producing lower and upper probabilities for each answer; The difference between these probabilities, called credal width, is used to represent epistemic uncertainty about an answer arising from limited training data. We propose XU-RS, a framework that attributes an answer's credal width to the input tokens (words or word pieces) supplied to a language model. XU-RS uses Expected Gradients (a standard feature attribution method) to estimate how input tokens contribute to credal width. The proposed framework is evaluated on a MedQA dataset using SmolLM3-3B and Llama-2-7B models, demonstrating that setting the embedding of a token ranked highly by XU-RS to zero (zero-masking) causes larger changes in credal width than zero-masking randomly selected tokens. In addition, we show that normalisation can cause other answer groups to influence an answer's width, reveal how token attribution can mask numerical errors, and provide diagnostic checks to verify whether a token ranked highly by XU-RS meaningfully explains model uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces XU-RS, a framework that attributes an answer's credal width (epistemic uncertainty) in random-set classifiers built on pretrained language models to individual input tokens, using Expected Gradients, and validates it on MedQA with SmolLM3-3B and Llama-2-7B.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty estimates indicate how unsure a model is but not why. Without knowing which input parts influence a model's uncertainty, one cannot determine whether that uncertainty depends on task-relevant features. The paper addresses this interpretability gap for epistemic uncertainty in random-set classifiers.
AI.method: The authors propose XU-RS, a framework that attributes an answer's credal width (the difference between lower and upper probabilities in a random-set classifier) to input tokens (words or word pieces). XU-RS applies Expected Gradients, a standard feature attribution method, to estimate how input tokens contribute to credal width. It is evaluated on a MedQA dataset using SmolLM3-3B and Llama-2-7B models, with zero-masking of highly ranked tokens compared to randomly selected tokens.
AI.result: Zero-masking a token ranked highly by XU-RS causes larger changes in credal width than zero-masking randomly selected tokens. Additionally, the paper shows that normalisation can cause other answer groups to influence an answer's width, reveals how token attribution can mask numerical errors, and provides diagnostic checks to verify whether a highly ranked token meaningfully explains model uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: XU-RS provides a viable means to attribute epistemic uncertainty (credal width) to input tokens in random-set classifiers, offering insights into model uncertainty drivers and diagnostic tools, while also highlighting caveats such as the influence of normalisation, masking of numerical errors, and the need for diagnostic checks.

title: Flattening the Connectome Spectrum: A Spectral Filter for FC Induces a Pretraining Target for fMRI Encoders
summary: Self-supervised pretraining reshaped prediction in language and vision, and brain foundation models (BFMs) inherited its promise. Representations learned from large unlabelled corpora should capture individual functional dynamics and generalise across cohorts. However, kernel ridge regression (KRR) fitted on functional connectivity (FC) matrices still predicts individual phenotypes more accurately than any BFM we tested. In this paper, we show that KRR is weighted by the eigenvalues of the FC which are miscalibrated for phenotype prediction. We apply an efficient spectral filter to recalibrate the eigenvalues of each subject's FC matrix, enabling the model to exploit more inter-individual variance. Across the 5 datasets, 11 parcellations and 6 prediction targets we tested, we match or exceed the KRR baseline. Based on this finding, we then pretrain a small encoder model on about 4,000 hours of fMRI from 162 open datasets, whereby we align the pairwise similarities between the embeddings of recording snippets with those between the recalibrated connectomes. Our model performs on par with the best of the 6 published BFMs we tested while having an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Our encoder performs better than FC on short scans and in smaller cohorts, especially in fingerprinting. We release the pretrained model weights, the code and the pretraining data, preprocessed and parcellated.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that kernel ridge regression (KRR) on functional connectivity (FC) is effectively weighted by eigenvalues that are miscalibrated for phenotype prediction. A spectral recalibration of FC eigenvalues improves prediction, and a small encoder pretrained on ~4,000 hours of fMRI to match embedding similarities to recalibrated connectome similarities matches far larger brain foundation models with an order of magnitude fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Brain foundation models promise that representations from large unlabelled corpora capture individual functional dynamics and generalise across cohorts. Yet KRR fitted on FC matrices still predicts individual phenotypes more accurately than any tested BFM, indicating that self-supervised BFM representations are not exploiting inter-individual variance effectively.
AI.method: The authors analyse KRR and show it is weighted by the eigenvalues of the FC matrix, which are miscalibrated for phenotype prediction. They apply an efficient spectral filter to recalibrate the eigenvalues of each subject's FC matrix. Building on this, they pretrain a small encoder on about 4,000 hours of fMRI from 162 open datasets, aligning pairwise similarities between embeddings of recording snippets with those between the recalibrated connectomes.
AI.result: Across 5 datasets, 11 parcellations and 6 prediction targets, the spectral recalibration matches or exceeds the KRR baseline. The pretrained encoder performs on par with the best of 6 published BFMs while having an order of magnitude fewer parameters. It outperforms FC on short scans and in smaller cohorts, especially in fingerprinting.
AI.conclusion: Recalibrating FC eigenvalues addresses a key limitation of KRR and yields a simple, effective pretraining objective. A compact encoder trained on this objective rivals much larger brain foundation models at a fraction of the parameter count, and the authors release pretrained weights, code, and preprocessed, parcellated pretraining data.

title: Beyond a single latent space: a dual-latent world model for long-horizon planning
comment: 31 pages, 22 figures, 9 tables. Main text: 9 pages
summary: Latent world models often struggle with long-horizon planning despite accurate short-term predictions. Recursive rollouts accumulate errors, while distance concentration in high-dimensional latent spaces can weaken goal discrimination. We introduce the Dual-Latent World Model (Dual-WM), which separates local execution and long-range planning through distinct state representations and dynamics models. The low-level model predicts action-conditioned transitions, while the high-level model uses learned macro-actions to plan over longer temporal spans. We also propose Long-Horizon Representation Learning with Weighted Rollout (LoRe), which supervises self-generated predictions at both levels. An analysis of recursive error propagation motivates exponential horizon weights with separate decay rates for the two temporal scales. During planning, the high-level model generates latent subgoals that the low-level model refines into actions for precise execution. We evaluate from-scratch Dual-WM on five goal-conditioned visual control tasks against the task-wise strongest baselines without actor-guided proposals. At goal offsets of 50 and 100 environment steps, mean success increases from 75.9% to 84.4% and from 61.4% to 69.5%, respectively. At offset 100, Dual-WM outperforms these baselines on all five tasks and improves mean success over LeWM by 30.8 percentage points. Ablations and supporting analyses provide evidence of more informative representations for goal evaluation and greater consistency under recursive prediction. These results highlight the value of separating temporal roles and training across multiple horizons for reliable latent planning. Our core implementation is available at https://github.com/DeLin1001/Dual-WM-Official.

AI.tldr: Dual-WM separates local execution and long-range planning into two latent models—a low-level action-conditioned transition model and a high-level macro-action planner—trained with LoRe's weighted rollout supervision, improving long-horizon goal-conditioned control.
AI.motivation: Latent world models predict accurately short-term but fail at long-horizon planning: recursive rollouts accumulate errors, and distance concentration in high-dimensional latent spaces weakens goal discrimination.
AI.method: Dual-Latent World Model with distinct state representations and dynamics models: low-level model predicts action-conditioned transitions; high-level model uses learned macro-actions for longer temporal spans. Long-Horizon Representation Learning with Weighted Rollout (LoRe) supervises self-generated predictions at both levels, using exponential horizon weights with separate decay rates (motivated by recursive error propagation analysis). During planning, the high-level model emits latent subgoals refined by the low-level model into actions.
AI.result: On five goal-conditioned visual control tasks (from-scratch, vs. task-wise strongest baselines without actor-guided proposals): mean success at goal offsets 50 and 100 rises from 75.9% to 84.4% and from 61.4% to 69.5%. At offset 100, Dual-WM wins on all five tasks and beats LeWM by 30.8 percentage points mean success.
AI.conclusion: Separating temporal roles and training across multiple horizons yields more informative representations for goal evaluation and greater consistency under recursive prediction, enabling reliable latent planning. Ablations support these claims; code is released.

title: EnterpriseBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Enterprise-Level Strategic Reasoning and Decision-Making
summary: LLM agents are increasingly expected to support enterprise workflows, where tasks often involve missing information, uncertainty, feedback, and long-term trade-offs. However, existing enterprise and financial benchmarks mainly test static capabilities such as information extraction, numerical calculation, domain knowledge, and financial QA, leaving interactive and long-horizon decision-making underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce EnterpriseBench, a benchmark that evaluates LLM agents across this spectrum, from static question answering to dynamic decision-making. Specifically, EnterpriseBench reorganizes existing enterprise and financial QA datasets into a unified foundational suite annotated by capability and difficulty, and introduces three professional interactive settings: Consulting, based on management-consulting-style business cases for client problem diagnosis through multi-turn information seeking; the Beer Game, adapted from a classic supply-chain management simulation for inventory control under delayed feedback; and Enterprise Digital Twin, a project-based business simulator for workforce, risk, and project planning. Experiments with nine agent methods under four backbone models show that current agents have not yet achieved stable, comprehensive, and cross-task reliability in enterprise scenarios. These results show that EnterpriseBench provides a practical benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in realistic enterprise strategic reasoning and decision-making.

AI.tldr: EnterpriseBench is a new benchmark spanning static QA to dynamic decision-making, combining reorganized enterprise/financial QA datasets with three interactive simulations (Consulting, Beer Game, Enterprise Digital Twin). Nine agent methods across four backbone models show current agents lack stable, comprehensive, cross-task reliability in enterprise settings.
AI.motivation: Enterprise workflows demand handling of missing information, uncertainty, feedback, and long-term trade-offs, yet existing enterprise and financial benchmarks only assess static capabilities (information extraction, numerical calculation, domain knowledge, financial QA), leaving interactive and long-horizon decision-making underexplored.
AI.method: EnterpriseBench reorganizes existing enterprise and financial QA datasets into a unified foundational suite annotated by capability and difficulty, and adds three professional interactive settings: Consulting (multi-turn information seeking on management-consulting-style business cases), the Beer Game (supply-chain inventory control under delayed feedback), and Enterprise Digital Twin (project-based simulation of workforce, risk, and project planning).
AI.result: Experiments with nine agent methods under four backbone models reveal that current agents have not achieved stable, comprehensive, and cross-task reliability in enterprise scenarios.
AI.conclusion: EnterpriseBench offers a practical benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in realistic enterprise strategic reasoning and decision-making, and exposes reliability gaps that current agents must close.

title: MeanFlowAdvantage: Stable Reward Fine-Tuning for Few-Step Average-Velocity Generators
summary: MeanFlow enables efficient few-step generation by predicting interval-average velocities, but this representation creates a mismatch for reward fine-tuning: existing advantage-based objectives are typically defined on instantaneous velocities or equivalent $x_0$-space predictions, whereas inference directly uses the learned average-velocity map. We introduce MeanFlowAdvantage, a signed advantage-weighted least-squares objective for average-velocity generators. Our key construction uses a shared, detached MeanFlow derivative correction to express the reward objective in prediction space while making rollout and reference regularization exact penalties on the average-velocity network deployed at inference. The resulting formulation preserves MeanFlow's native few-step sampler and provides a direct mechanism for transferring reward improvements to the deployed flow map. On SD3.5-Medium, MeanFlowAdvantage improves all eight reported metrics over the matched four-step MeanFlowNFT baseline and, with only four NFEs, matches or exceeds the 40-step DiffusionNFT baseline on six of eight metrics. The same objective also transfers to DNA promoter design, where it supports both teacher-free on-policy RL for a generator defined on a manifold and teacher-guided reward-graded distillation, with the latter yielding the lowest one-step Sei profile MSE among the compared configurations.

AI.tldr: MeanFlowAdvantage introduces a signed advantage-weighted least-squares objective that aligns reward fine-tuning with the average-velocity representation used at inference in MeanFlow few-step generators.
AI.motivation: MeanFlow achieves efficient few-step generation by predicting interval-average velocities, but this creates a mismatch for reward fine-tuning: existing advantage-based objectives are defined on instantaneous velocities or equivalent x0-space predictions, whereas inference directly uses the learned average-velocity map. This representational gap limits the effective transfer of reward improvements to the deployed sampler.
AI.method: The paper proposes MeanFlowAdvantage, a signed advantage-weighted least-squares objective for average-velocity generators. Its key construction employs a shared, detached MeanFlow derivative correction that expresses the reward objective in prediction space while rendering rollout and reference regularization exact penalties on the average-velocity network actually deployed at inference. The formulation preserves MeanFlow's native few-step sampler and offers a direct mechanism for transferring reward gains to the deployed flow map.
AI.result: On SD3.5-Medium, MeanFlowAdvantage improves all eight reported metrics over the matched four-step MeanFlowNFT baseline, and with only four NFEs matches or exceeds the 40-step DiffusionNFT baseline on six of eight metrics. The same objective also transfers to DNA promoter design, supporting both teacher-free on-policy RL for a manifold-defined generator and teacher-guided reward-graded distillation, the latter achieving the lowest one-step Sei profile MSE among compared configurations.
AI.conclusion: MeanFlowAdvantage resolves the representation mismatch in reward fine-tuning of MeanFlow by operating directly in average-velocity space via a detached derivative correction, enabling efficient few-step generation to benefit from reward optimization while retaining native sampler fidelity and generalizing beyond image generation to scientific sequence design.

title: KUPAS MASTER: Distilling the Tacit Expertise of Master Practitioners into Agent-Ready Experience Corpora
comment: Technical Report. Official website: https://lsf.kupasai.com/ Report homepage: https://tongjiai4e.github.io/KUPAS-MASTER-Report/
summary: Experienced professionals know more than just facts and conclusions. They know which cues matter, why a judgment is reasonable, and which action to take. Routine work records often leave out this tacit knowledge, making it difficult for Large Language Model (LLM) agents to use professional experience effectively. We introduce KUPAS MASTER, an experience engineering platform built around nine-layer cognitive corpus construction. It turns heterogeneous work records and practitioner interviews into traceable, reusable experience corpora for agents. Six case elements preserve the task process: context, cues, judgment, action, boundaries, and outcomes. Nine-layer cognitive corpus construction organizes tacit experience along nine extraction dimensions and stores the resulting assets in six libraries: rules, constraints, best practices, negative examples, corner cases, and skills. Semantic alignment, individual experience distillation, organizational consolidation, and cross-review preserve source evidence, conditions of use, and unresolved disagreements. The platform packages these assets into callable skills with explicit inputs, steps, dependencies, and stopping conditions, connecting experience collection to task execution and evaluation feedback. Using authorized samples from 20 randomly selected practitioners, the platform processed 1,576 source files into 23,024 individual experience records and 13,113 organizational assets. The evaluation spans multiple professional domains. Under common task inputs and scoring criteria, the base model, raw corpus retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and KUPAS MASTER agent scored 70.63, 79.75, and 89.58, respectively. The KUPAS MASTER agent improved on raw-corpus RAG in all seven scoring dimensions. The platform provides a practical path from individual tacit experience to organizational knowledge and agent capabilities.

AI.tldr: KUPAS MASTER is an experience engineering platform that converts tacit professional knowledge from work records and interviews into traceable, reusable cognitive corpora and callable skills, letting LLM agents execute professional tasks with significantly higher scores than baseline or raw-corpus RAG.
AI.motivation: Experienced professionals possess tacit knowledge—such as which cues matter, why a judgment is reasonable, and which action to take—that routine work records fail to capture, making it hard for LLM agents to leverage professional experience effectively.
AI.method: The platform uses nine-layer cognitive corpus construction. Six case elements (context, cues, judgment, action, boundaries, outcomes) preserve the task process; nine extraction dimensions organize tacit experience; six libraries (rules, constraints, best practices, negative examples, corner cases, skills) store resulting assets. Semantic alignment, individual experience distillation, organizational consolidation, and cross-review preserve source evidence, conditions of use, and unresolved disagreements. Assets are packaged into callable skills with explicit inputs, steps, dependencies, and stopping conditions, linking experience collection to task execution and evaluation feedback.
AI.result: Using authorized samples from 20 randomly selected practitioners, the platform processed 1,576 source files into 23,024 individual experience records and 13,113 organizational assets. Across multiple professional domains under common task inputs and scoring criteria, the base model scored 70.63, raw-corpus RAG scored 79.75, and the KUPAS MASTER agent scored 89.58; the agent improved on raw-corpus RAG in all seven scoring dimensions.
AI.conclusion: KUPAS MASTER offers a practical path from individual tacit experience to organizational knowledge and enhanced agent capabilities.

title: EngiWorld: What Can Frontier Agents Deliver in Professional Engineering Environments?
summary: Autonomous agents have made rapid progress in general-purpose computer use, but reliable automation of professional industrial engineering remains out of reach, as engineering workflows demand reasoning over geometric and physical constraints and dependencies preserved across software and design stages. We present EngiWorld, the first benchmark structured around the complete design loop: 1,301 expert-curated tasks spanning 6 engineering domains (CAD, CAE, CAM, BIM, EDA, and 3D visualization) and 26 professional software platforms, with both GUI and CLI interfaces and 6 task types ranging from software-selection to open-ended tasks. We further introduce an artifact-centric evaluation methodology built on a unified domain-verifier suite, which programmatically checks the geometric validity, physical feasibility, and rule compliance of final and intermediate artifacts, and scores quantitative design tasks continuously by specification attainment rather than binary success. Evaluation of seven frontier models reveals a substantial capability gap: the strongest model achieves an EngiScore of only 44.3, and just 3.6% of multi-software attempts succeed. EngiWorld provides the first rigorous foundation for measuring progress toward agents that operate professional engineering software end to end.

AI.tldr: EngiWorld is the first benchmark for autonomous agents performing professional industrial engineering across the complete design loop, featuring 1,301 expert-curated tasks over 6 domains and 26 software platforms, with an artifact-centric evaluation methodology using a unified verifier suite; frontier models score at most 44.3 EngScore, exposing a large capability gap.
AI.motivation: While autonomous agents have advanced rapidly in general-purpose computer use, reliable automation of professional industrial engineering remains out of reach because engineering workflows require reasoning over geometric and physical constraints and dependencies preserved across software and design stages, a setting not addressed by existing benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors build EngiWorld, a benchmark of 1,301 expert-curated tasks covering 6 engineering domains (CAD, CAE, CAM, BIM, EDA, 3D visualization) and 26 professional software platforms, with both GUI and CLI interfaces and 6 task types from software-selection to open-ended tasks. They also introduce an artifact-centric evaluation methodology based on a unified domain-verifier suite that programmatically checks geometric validity, physical feasibility, and rule compliance of final and intermediate artifacts, scoring quantitative design tasks continuously by specification attainment rather than binary success.
AI.result: Evaluation of seven frontier models shows a substantial capability gap: the strongest model reaches only 44.3 EngScore, and only 3.6% of multi-software attempts succeed.
