AI.conclusion: EngiWorld provides the first rigorous foundation for measuring progress toward agents that operate professional engineering software end to end.

title: WISE-ATTA: When to Ask for Labels in Budgeted Active Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Active test-time adaptation (ATTA) improves robustness under distribution shift by updating a deployed model during inference while selectively querying supervision. However, most existing ATTA methods implicitly assume that supervision can be requested for every incoming test batch, which can incur substantial annotation cost over long test streams. In this work, we introduce \emph{budgeted ATTA} in which labels are available for only a fraction of test batches. This formulation shifts the central challenge from deciding \emph{what} to label within a batch to deciding \emph{when} supervision should be applied over time. To address this challenge, we propose a budget-aware approach \emph{WISE-ATTA} that allocates supervision over the test stream based on lightweight signals computed online, prioritizing periods where supervision is likely to be most useful. When a batch is selected for supervision, we further employ a drift-based sample selection criterion that targets samples exhibiting ongoing, unconverged adaptation dynamics, enabling effective updates from a single labeled example. We evaluate this approach on synthetic corruptions (ImageNet-C) and natural distribution shifts (ImageNet-R/K/A). Across settings, WISE-ATTA achieves competitive or improved performance compared to recent ATTA methods while requiring substantially fewer labels. Overall, we find that the timing of supervision is a key, yet underexplored, aspect of active test-time adaptation. Code: https://github.com/Muhammad-Huzaifaa/WISE-ATTA

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "budgeted ATTA," where labels are available only for a fraction of test batches, shifting the challenge from what to label within a batch to when to apply supervision over the test stream. It proposes WISE-ATTA, a budget-aware method using lightweight online signals to schedule supervision, plus a drift-based sample selection that targets samples with ongoing, unconverged adaptation dynamics for effective single-example updates. Evaluated on ImageNet-C/R/K/A, it matches or exceeds recent ATTA methods with substantially fewer labels.
AI.motivation: Existing active test-time adaptation (ATTA) methods implicitly assume supervision can be requested for every incoming test batch, which incurs substantial annotation cost over long test streams. This assumption is unrealistic under tight annotation budgets, motivating a formulation where only a fraction of test batches can be labeled.
AI.method: The authors formulate budgeted ATTA and propose WISE-ATTA, a budget-aware approach that allocates supervision across the test stream using lightweight signals computed online, prioritizing periods where supervision is most useful. When a batch is selected, a drift-based sample selection criterion targets samples exhibiting ongoing, unconverged adaptation dynamics, enabling effective updates from a single labeled example.
AI.result: On synthetic corruptions (ImageNet-C) and natural distribution shifts (ImageNet-R/K/A), WISE-ATTA achieves competitive or improved performance versus recent ATTA methods while requiring substantially fewer labels.
AI.conclusion: The timing of supervision is a key yet underexplored aspect of active test-time adaptation.

title: Locating Answer-Correctness Signals in Frozen Large Language Models
summary: Language models expose internal signals that predict whether an answer is correct, readable from a single forward pass of a frozen model without additional generations. Yet existing probes often commit to one signal family or layer and can be brittle under distribution shift; in retrieval-augmented settings, many specialized detectors instead target passage faithfulness, which can diverge from correctness when retrieved evidence is unhelpful or conflicting. We therefore ask where answer correctness is readable, which internal signal families carry it, and how they should be combined. We search over hidden states, token probabilities, residual-stream features, attention, and their fusion, treating the selected readouts as a predictive measurement rather than a mechanistic localization. We run this analysis separately in closed-book and with-context settings, since context can change which readouts are informative. A consistent anatomy emerges: correctness concentrates in the answer span, recovered from the answer tokens even under retrieval, and the families carry it complementarily, so fusing them helps most out of distribution, where a single signal is weakest. The protocol is effective across two backbones and gates a retrieval controller as one downstream use.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically maps where and how answer correctness is readable inside frozen language models, comparing hidden states, token probabilities, residual-stream features, and attention, and finds that correctness concentrates in the answer span and that fusing complementary signal families improves out-of-distribution detection.
AI.motivation: Existing correctness probes tend to fixate on a single signal family or layer, making them brittle under distribution shift, while retrieval-augmented detectors typically target passage faithfulness—which can diverge from correctness when retrieved evidence is unhelpful or conflicting. The paper therefore asks where correctness is readable, which internal signal families carry it, and how they should be combined.
AI.method: The authors search over hidden states, token probabilities, residual-stream features, attention, and their fusion, treating the selected readouts as a predictive measurement rather than a mechanistic localization. They run the analysis separately in closed-book and with-context settings, since context can change which readouts are informative, and evaluate across two backbones.
AI.result: A consistent anatomy emerges: correctness concentrates in the answer span and is recoverable from answer tokens even under retrieval. The signal families carry correctness complementarily, so fusing them helps most out of distribution, where any single signal is weakest.
AI.conclusion: The protocol is effective across two backbones and can gate a retrieval controller as one downstream use, showing that fused internal readouts provide a robust, generalizable way to measure answer correctness.

title: Generative Interactions: Weaving Multiparty Human Motion with Bilevel Latent Dynamics
summary: Human social behaviour is not a collection of independent motions, but a jointly organised process in which group dynamics and individual variation continuously shape one another. Yet existing social motion models often prioritise plausible trajectories while leaving interaction state implicit, limiting their ability to transfer across groups, tasks, and partial-observation regimes. To address this gap, we introduce Bilevel Representations for Agent Interaction Dynamics (BRAID), a hierarchical sequential latent-variable model for generative multi-person interaction. BRAID explicitly formulates social motion generation as a meta-transfer learning problem: shared interaction priors are learned across datasets and adapted through arbitrary context sets of observed people and joints. The model represents each scene through a group-level latent state that captures shared interaction dynamics and person-level latent states that capture individual behaviour conditioned on the evolving group context. This modelling choice enables coherent generation under full, sparse, or partial observations while exposing compact social-state vectors that can serve as an interface for downstream embodied-agent systems. We evaluate BRAID under a unified SMPL-based representation on social forecasting, tracking and in-filling, and response generation, using metrics that assess not only reconstruction accuracy but also realism, diversity, temporal alignment, and interpersonal coordination. We further analyse the hierarchical latent space, showing that it captures separable group- and individual-level structure.

AI.tldr: BRAID is a hierarchical sequential latent-variable model that casts multi-person social motion generation as meta-transfer learning, using group- and person-level latent states to enable coherent generation under full, sparse, or partial observations.
AI.motivation: Human social behaviour is a jointly organised process where group dynamics and individual variation shape each other. Existing social motion models often prioritise plausible trajectories while leaving interaction state implicit, which limits transfer across groups, tasks, and partial-observation regimes.
AI.method: BRAID formulates social motion generation as a meta-transfer learning problem: shared interaction priors are learned across datasets and adapted via arbitrary context sets of observed people and joints. It represents each scene with a group-level latent state capturing shared interaction dynamics and person-level latent states capturing individual behaviour conditioned on the evolving group context. Evaluation uses a unified SMPL-based representation.
AI.result: Evaluated on social forecasting, tracking and in-filling, and response generation, with metrics covering reconstruction accuracy, realism, diversity, temporal alignment, and interpersonal coordination. Latent-space analysis shows the hierarchy captures separable group- and individual-level structure.
AI.conclusion: BRAID enables coherent generation under full, sparse, or partial observations and yields compact social-state vectors usable as an interface for downstream embodied-agent systems.

title: Context Language Models
summary: We introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), language models that natively manage their own context. We implement this by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file. This allows the model to learn what is most important to maintain in context, and naturally extends to multi-agent systems where multiple agent contexts coexist as files. Building CLMs zero-shot with existing models outperforms SOTA context management strategies across a variety of tasks: 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus, 5% higher scores with 59% fewer FLOPs on 12-hour EdgeBench, and 65% greater improvement with the same compute on a 24-hour multi-repository agent-swarm task. Moreover, by shifting context management from external harness control to intrinsic model behavior, CLMs naturally enable both in-context and parametric learning of context-management strategies. We show that CLMs can be steered with natural-language instructions evolved through a standard skill-optimization loop, improving held-out accuracy by up to 35.9 points on a context-management task while reducing compute. We also introduce an online reinforcement learning method for CLMs, improving Qwen3.5-9B performance on BrowseComp-Plus by 47.6% while using 12% fewer FLOPs. Finally, we co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, further reducing server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Context Language Models (CLMs), which treat context as a model-managed file updated by the model itself, outperforming prior context-management strategies while reducing compute.
AI.motivation: Existing context management is controlled by external harnesses rather than intrinsic model behavior, limiting the model's ability to decide what is important to retain and constraining extension to multi-agent settings.
AI.method: Context is represented as a file that the model can update without restriction, enabling native self-management; this extends to multi-agent systems where agent contexts coexist as files. CLMs are built zero-shot with existing models, steered via natural-language instructions evolved through a skill-optimization loop, trained with an online reinforcement learning method, and served via a co-designed Suffix Cache Reuse scheme.
AI.result: Zero-shot CLMs beat SOTA context management: +11.4% accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus, +5% score with 59% fewer FLOPs on 12-hour EdgeBench, and 65% greater improvement at equal compute on a 24-hour multi-repository agent-swarm task. Instruction steering improved held-out accuracy by up to 35.9 points; online RL raised Qwen3.5-9B on BrowseComp-Plus by 47.6% with 12% fewer FLOPs; Suffix Cache Reuse cut server compute 35% versus standard SGLang at matched performance.
AI.conclusion: Treating context as a model-managed file shifts context management from external harness control to intrinsic model behavior, enabling both in-context and parametric learning of context-management strategies and yielding accuracy gains with substantial compute savings.

title: Spatiotemporal Hyperedges for EEG Seizure Detection and Prediction
summary: Seizure detection and prediction from EEG are clinically important but challenging because seizures are rare, temporally localized, and propagate as coordinated events across multiple channels. Recent dynamic graph neural networks model this by running a temporal model over a sequence of per-time-step pairwise channel edges. However, this pairwise construction misses the spatiotemporal coupling that constitutes a seizure, at substantial training cost. We propose HyBrain, which summarizes spatiotemporal EEG evidence through a small set of soft hyperedges rather than pairwise edges. A per-channel Mamba backbone produces one token per (channel, second), and a spatiotemporal hyperedge block pools these tokens into E_h shared group embeddings through soft memberships and broadcasts them back. The same encoder serves three downstream tasks: window-based detection, one-second point-wise detection, and preictal seizure prediction. On TUSZ and CHB-MIT, HyBrain achieves the best AUROC on every reported setting against ten baselines, with the largest gap on long-clip preictal prediction. It also matches the most efficient baselines in training time and peak GPU memory. A qualitative analysis shows that even a single learned hyperedge cleanly captures the preictal -> ictal -> postictal trajectory on a real seizure clip.

AI.tldr: HyBrain replaces pairwise channel-edge dynamic graph models with a small set of soft spatiotemporal hyperedges: a per-channel Mamba encoder produces (channel, second) tokens, and a hyperedge block pools/broadcasts them via soft memberships. This shared encoder handles window detection, point-wise detection, and preictal prediction, achieving best AUROC against ten baselines on TUSZ and CHB-MIT at comparable training time and memory.
AI.motivation: Seizure detection and prediction from EEG are clinically important yet hard: seizures are rare, temporally localized, and manifest as coordinated activity propagating across multiple channels. Existing dynamic graph neural networks capture inter-channel relations by modeling a sequence of per-time-step pairwise channel edges, but this pairwise construction fails to represent the higher-order spatiotemporal coupling that constitutes a seizure and incurs substantial training cost.
AI.method: HyBrain summarizes spatiotemporal EEG evidence using a small set of soft hyperedges instead of pairwise edges. A per-channel Mamba backbone yields one token per (channel, second); a spatiotemporal hyperedge block then pools these tokens into E_h shared group embeddings through soft memberships and broadcasts them back to the tokens. The same encoder is reused across three downstream tasks: window-based detection, one-second point-wise detection, and preictal seizure prediction.
AI.result: On TUSZ and CHB-MIT, HyBrain attains the best AUROC on every reported setting against ten baselines, with the largest margin on long-clip preictal prediction. It matches the most efficient baselines in training time and peak GPU memory. A qualitative analysis shows that a single learned hyperedge cleanly captures the preictal -> ictal -> postictal trajectory on a real seizure clip.
AI.conclusion: Modeling EEG seizure dynamics via a compact set of soft hyperedges provides a more faithful and efficient alternative to pairwise dynamic graphs. HyBrain unifies detection and prediction under one encoder, delivers consistent AUROC gains at no extra computational cost, and yields interpretable hyperedges that trace the ictal trajectory.

title: ContextRender: From Execution Dependencies to Agent Context
summary: LLM agents performing long-horizon tasks accumulate tool results that later steps may need. Passing the full history to every invocation is costly even when it fits within the context window, while reducing it risks omitting needed information. Existing context management methods can overlook how earlier tool results are used in subsequent execution, leaving needed information out of context. We introduce ContextRender, which manages context through a persistent graph of execution dependencies. We develop Tool-Flow Analysis to track how later operations reuse information from earlier tool results, providing a signal called observed reuse. A renderer combines this signal with recency and semantic relevance to select results within a fixed history budget, retaining omitted results for later use. Across AppWorld and 8-objective QA with three execution models, ContextRender outperforms the evaluated context management baselines using a 6K history budget, well below the models' maximum context windows. Within this budget, it achieves task performance close to or above that of passing the full history while reducing mean inference cost by 10.2%-32.2% relative to Full history. Ablations show that observed reuse improves task performance and retention of results reused later.

AI.tldr: ContextRender manages LLM agent context via a persistent execution-dependency graph, using Tool-Flow Analysis to track "observed reuse" of earlier tool results, then renders context within a fixed history budget to cut cost while preserving task performance.
AI.motivation: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks accumulate tool results that later steps may need. Passing the full history to every invocation is costly even when it fits the context window, while reducing it risks omitting needed information. Existing context management methods overlook how earlier tool results are used in subsequent execution, leaving needed information out of context.
AI.method: ContextRender manages context through a persistent graph of execution dependencies. It develops Tool-Flow Analysis to track how later operations reuse information from earlier tool results, providing a signal called observed reuse. A renderer combines this signal with recency and semantic relevance to select results within a fixed history budget, retaining omitted results for later use.
AI.result: Across AppWorld and 8-objective QA with three execution models, ContextRender outperforms the evaluated context management baselines using a 6K history budget, well below the models' maximum context windows. Within this budget, it achieves task performance close to or above that of passing the full history while reducing mean inference cost by 10.2%-32.2% relative to Full history. Ablations show that observed reuse improves task performance and retention of results reused later.
AI.conclusion: ContextRender effectively manages LLM agent context by leveraging execution-dependency information, achieving near- or above-full-history task performance at a much smaller 6K budget and substantially lower inference cost. The observed reuse signal is shown to be a key contributor to performance and to the retention of later-reused tool results.

title: Cross-Entropy Guided Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) large language models scale model capacity by routing each token to a small subset of experts. Their routers are regularized with load balancing terms and learn affinity scores through the language-model objective. However, these objectives do not provide direct alignment between routing affinities and token-level error. We introduce token-error supervision for sparse routing in two forms. The first form predicts an error score per expert. The affinity-weighted aggregate of these scores is aligned to the next-token cross-entropy loss, while the individual scores attenuate affinity before top-$K$ selection. The second directly aligns the router's affinities to the model's objective without requiring an additional head or inference-time modification. Both formulations use the Itakura--Saito divergence or an exponential negative log-likelihood for aligning affinities and token errors. Across two sparse MoE backbones and four multiple-choice question-answering benchmarks, we evaluate both supervision mechanisms. On Granite, our method improves accuracy by approximately 2.3 percentage points on average over a parameter-matched routing baseline. With stronger supervision, the gain on ARC-Challenge reaches 2.94 points. Both mechanisms preserve the native sparse execution budget and aggregation policy. Our code is available in the supplementary materials.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces token-error supervision for sparse MoE routing, aligning router affinities with token-level error via Itakura-Saito divergence or exponential NLL, improving accuracy ~2.3 points on average without changing sparse execution budget.
AI.motivation: Sparse MoE LLMs scale capacity by routing tokens to few experts. Routers are regularized with load balancing terms and learn affinity scores via the LM objective, but these objectives do not directly align routing affinities with token-level error.
AI.method: Token-error supervision in two forms: (1) predict an error score per expert; the affinity-weighted aggregate is aligned to next-token cross-entropy while individual scores attenuate affinity before top-K selection; (2) directly align router affinities to the model objective without extra head or inference-time modification. Both use Itakura-Saito divergence or exponential negative log-likelihood for alignment.
AI.result: Across two sparse MoE backbones and four multiple-choice QA benchmarks: on Granite, ~2.3 percentage points average accuracy gain over parameter-matched routing baseline; with stronger supervision, gain on ARC-Challenge reaches 2.94 points. Both mechanisms preserve native sparse execution budget and aggregation policy.
AI.conclusion: Token-error supervision provides direct alignment between routing affinities and token-level error, consistently improving MoE routing accuracy while preserving the standard sparse execution budget and aggregation policy.

title: OmniVCBench: Benchmarking Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning Towards AI Virtual Cells
summary: Artificial Intelligence Virtual Cells (AIVCs) are envisioned as scientific agents that simulate cellular responses, explain underlying mechanisms, and support hypothesis-driven discovery. Existing AIVC benchmarks, however, operate primarily at the simulation layer, motivating complementary evaluation of how models interpret experimental evidence and formulate biological hypotheses. We introduce OmniVCBench, a figure-centric, source-traceable benchmark for the interpretation component of an AIVC. It contains 6,077 curated single- and multi-subfigure question--answer pairs derived from figures and experimental contexts in the scientific literature. Guided by Bloom's taxonomy, we instantiate interpretation-layer counterparts of the AIVC Predict--Explain--Discover agenda through three scientific reasoning tasks. We further introduce AIVC-Judge, a task-conditioned MLLM-as-a-judge framework with category-specific, reference-aware rubrics for evaluating open-ended responses. A complementary Model-Derived Hard-Negative Mining (MDHNM) strategy converts plausible errors observed during model inference into MCQ distractors for lower-cost evaluation. Within the evaluated heterogeneous model pool, MCQ accuracy correlates positively with AIVC-Judge scores, providing a complementary view of performance alongside open-response evaluation. Code and data demo are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OmniVCBench.

AI.tldr: OmniVCBench is a figure-centric, source-traceable benchmark for the interpretation layer of AI Virtual Cells, comprising 6,077 figure-derived QA pairs organized into three scientific reasoning tasks under Bloom's taxonomy, evaluated via a task-conditioned MLLM-as-a-judge framework (AIVC-Judge) and a Model-Derived Hard-Negative Mining strategy for cheaper MCQ evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing AIVC benchmarks operate primarily at the simulation layer, leaving the interpretation of experimental evidence and the formulation of biological hypotheses insufficiently evaluated. The authors argue for complementary evaluation of how models interpret experimental evidence to assess the interpretation component of an AIVC.
AI.method: The authors build OmniVCBench from figures and experimental contexts in scientific literature, producing 6,077 curated single- and multi-subfigure QA pairs. Guided by Bloom's taxonomy, they instantiate interpretation-layer counterparts of the AIVC Predict-Explain-Discover agenda as three scientific reasoning tasks. They propose AIVC-Judge, a task-conditioned MLLM-as-a-judge framework with category-specific, reference-aware rubrics for open-ended responses, plus a Model-Derived Hard-Negative Mining (MDHNM) strategy that turns plausible model errors into MCQ distractors for low-cost evaluation.
AI.result: Within a heterogeneous model pool, MCQ accuracy correlates positively with AIVC-Judge scores, indicating the two evaluation modes offer complementary views of performance rather than conflicting signals.
AI.conclusion: OmniVCBench supplies a figure-centric, source-traceable interpretation-layer benchmark for AIVCs, with AIVC-Judge and MDHNM enabling both rigorous open-ended judging and efficient MCQ-based evaluation; code and data are released.

title: Adam under Generalized Smoothness with Second-Moment-Type Stochastic Gradients
summary: Adam is widely observed to remain stable even when the objective deviates significantly from global smoothness. Under the generalized smoothness framework, however, existing analyses rely on strong tail assumptions on the stochastic gradients, such as almost-sure boundedness or sub-Gaussianity. Whether Adam converges on generalized smooth objectives under only second moment information on the stochastic gradients, without such concentration assumptions, was identified as an important open direction by Li et al. (2023). This paper gives an affirmative answer under fairly general conditions: such tail assumptions are not necessary. Building on the Adam self-normalization framework of Jin et al. (2026), developed for classical smoothness and bounded variance, we extend the stopping-time and de-preconditioning strategy to the $L_0$-$L_p$ generalized smoothness condition and a generalized second moment ABC condition. Even when the stochastic-gradient condition provides only second moment information that may grow along the trajectory, the stochastic trajectory of Adam remains in a locally well-behaved smoothness region, with stretched-exponential tail decay under bounded variance and global smoothness. Consequently, we establish high-probability convergence rate guarantees over the full range $p<2$, with confidence dependence of order $δ^{-1/2}$, while the stepsize prefactor depends on $δ$ only through a single logarithmic factor. We further construct a hard instance showing that, under only second-moment information, this $δ^{-1/2}$-type confidence dependence is sharp. Finally, in the regime $p<1$, we combine the trajectory control with polynomial-growth estimates on rare events to obtain convergence rate guarantees in expectation.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that Adam converges on generalized smooth objectives using only second moment information on stochastic gradients, removing the tail assumptions previously required, and shows the resulting confidence dependence is sharp.
AI.motivation: Adam is empirically stable even when objectives deviate from global smoothness, but under the generalized smoothness framework existing analyses rely on strong tail assumptions on stochastic gradients (e.g., almost-sure boundedness or sub-Gaussianity). Whether Adam converges under only second moment information, without such concentration assumptions, was identified as an important open direction by Li et al. (2023).
AI.method: Building on the Adam self-normalization framework of Jin et al. (2026) for classical smoothness and bounded variance, the authors extend the stopping-time and de-preconditioning strategy to the L0-Lp generalized smoothness condition and a generalized second moment ABC condition.
AI.result: Even when the stochastic-gradient condition provides only second moment information that may grow along the trajectory, Adam's stochastic trajectory remains in a locally well-behaved smoothness region with stretched-exponential tail decay under bounded variance and global smoothness. This yields high-probability convergence rate guarantees over the full range p<2, with confidence dependence of order delta^{-1/2} and a stepsize prefactor depending on delta only through a single logarithmic factor. A hard instance shows this delta^{-1/2}-type confidence dependence is sharp under only second-moment information. For p<1, combining trajectory control with polynomial-growth estimates on rare events gives convergence rate guarantees in expectation.
AI.conclusion: Tail assumptions on stochastic gradients are not necessary for Adam's convergence on generalized smooth objectives; second moment information suffices, with sharp confidence dependence and both high-probability and in-expectation guarantees.

title: A neural network that maintains and retrieves memories based on context
summary: Every day, people continuously infer situational context and adjust the way they understand and remember the world. Context, signaled by the prefrontal cortex, is known to modulate working memory and episodic memory, but the algorithmic understanding of this modulation remains limited. Here, we train a recurrent neural network (RNN), augmented with an episodic memory buffer, to infer context using Bayesian inference as it continuously makes predictions of upcoming scenes while watching naturalistic movies. When the inferred context modulates the RNN's recurrent connectivity (the basis of working memory) in a low-rank manner, the model's activity patterns best match neural responses in human participants who watched the same movies during fMRI. Context also modulates episodic memory retrieval, such that the model retrieves memories based on not only content similarity but also context similarity. This is implemented as a key-value system with self-attention, designed to additionally encode context and retrieve context-congruent memories. The resulting model not only better resembles human brain representations but also learns to retrieve memories like humans much faster than a model without context modulation. Together, our findings suggest a computational mechanism by which context modulates information maintenance and long-term memory retrieval in naturalistic environments.

AI.tldr: A recurrent neural network with an episodic memory buffer infers context via Bayesian inference while predicting naturalistic movie scenes; low-rank context modulation of recurrent connectivity (working memory) and context-congruent key-value retrieval (episodic memory) yield better matches to human fMRI responses and faster human-like memory retrieval.
AI.motivation: Context, signaled by the prefrontal cortex, is known to modulate working memory and episodic memory, but the algorithmic understanding of this modulation remains limited. The paper aims to uncover the computational mechanism by which context modulates information maintenance and long-term memory retrieval in naturalistic environments.
AI.method: The authors trained an RNN augmented with an episodic memory buffer to infer context using Bayesian inference while continuously predicting upcoming scenes during naturalistic movies. Context modulated the RNN's recurrent connectivity (working memory) in a low-rank manner. Context also modulated episodic memory retrieval via a key-value system with self-attention that additionally encodes context to retrieve context-congruent memories, based on both content and context similarity.
AI.result: With low-rank context modulation of recurrent connectivity, the model's activity patterns best matched neural responses in human participants who watched the same movies during fMRI. The retrieval model better resembled human brain representations and learned to retrieve memories like humans much faster than a model without context modulation.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest a computational mechanism by which context modulates information maintenance and long-term memory retrieval in naturalistic environments.

title: DIET: Deletion-response Expert Trimming for Video Diffusion Transformers
summary: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) increasingly adopt mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures to reduce active computation, but their full expert storage remains costly. Existing one-shot pruning criteria mainly rely on static activation or routing statistics and cannot capture layer-level re-routing after expert deletion. We introduce DIET, a training-free expert pruning framework based on deletion responses. A single all-expert calibration pass records expert outputs and router states for matched conditional and unconditional tokens. Candidate deletions are then replayed from cached tensors, requiring no additional model forward passes. The resulting deletion-response signatures characterize each expert by the changes induced when it is removed. DIET selects retained experts by minimizing Overall Diversity Loss (ODL), which preserves directional coverage in signature space, and combines intra-layer local search with an inter-layer regression-guided budget search to allocate experts across layers. On LingBot-Video 30B-A3B, pruning 50% of experts (6,144 to 3,072) reduces the checkpoint from 57 GB to 30 GB and enables single-card deployment on a 48 GB GPU without fine-tuning. Under a fixed 284-case VBench protocol, the VBench Total increases from 0.7941 to 0.8115. Across tested retention budgets, DIET consistently outperforms competitive pruning baselines adapted from large language models.

AI.tldr: DIET is a training-free MoE expert pruning framework for video DiTs that uses deletion-response signatures from a single calibration pass to select experts, cutting a 30B-A3B model's checkpoint from 57GB to 30GB while improving VBench Total from 0.7941 to 0.8115.
AI.motivation: Video DiTs adopt MoE to reduce active computation, but storing all experts remains costly. Existing one-shot pruning criteria rely on static activation or routing statistics and fail to capture layer-level re-routing that occurs after expert deletion.
AI.method: DIET is training-free and based on deletion responses. A single all-expert calibration pass records expert outputs and router states for matched conditional and unconditional tokens. Candidate deletions are replayed from cached tensors without extra forward passes, yielding deletion-response signatures that characterize each expert by the changes induced upon removal. Experts are selected by minimizing Overall Diversity Loss (ODL) to preserve directional coverage in signature space, with intra-layer local search plus inter-layer regression-guided budget search for cross-layer allocation.
AI.result: On LingBot-Video 30B-A3B, pruning 50% of experts (6,144 to 3,072) reduces the checkpoint from 57 GB to 30 GB, enabling single-card deployment on a 48 GB GPU without fine-tuning. Under a fixed 284-case VBench protocol, VBench Total rises from 0.7941 to 0.8115, and DIET consistently outperforms competitive pruning baselines adapted from LLMs across tested retention budgets.
AI.conclusion: Deletion-response-based pruning offers an effective, training-free way to compress MoE video DiTs, achieving substantial storage reduction and improved quality while outperforming LLM-derived pruning baselines.

title: Can a Cacheable Decision Model Follow Rules?
summary:
Certo is a small non-generative decision model (Qwen3-4B): it scores candidate actions from their text and returns a probability, instead of generating an answer. The accurate design reads the state, the rules, and each candidate together (a joint scorer), so cost grows with the menu. Independent encoding lets each candidate be encoded once and reused across states (about 5x cheaper at 77 candidates), but separates state from candidate. We ask how much rule-sensitivity survives that move, and whether it can be trained back.
  Four experiments on Certo: (1) the tested conversion to cacheable scoring loses rule-sensitivity (recall@1 1.00 -> 0.24) while the joint scorer holds 1.00, and a shortlist+rerank rescue fails; (2) targeted counterfactual supervision restores strong performance on held-out synthetic rule tasks (paraphrase, counterfactual, composition; reproducible across seeds), though we do not isolate whether predictions depend on the supplied rule; (3) on real rules the added benefit is not established -- after fixing a truncation confound, the joint scorer wins significantly on the short tier (0.861 vs 0.500) and directionally on the hard tier (0.655 vs 0.483, n=29); (4) a matched cross-domain real-prose mixture did not help and reduced contract accuracy (-9.3, -16.2 points). A cacheable encoder can be made rule-sensitive on its training distribution, but transfer to unseen-source real rules is not established; the joint scorer keeps an edge at the cost of caching.

AI.tldr: Certo, a small non-generative scorer (Qwen3-4B), can be made rule-sensitive when candidates are encoded independently for caching, but only on its training distribution; transfer to unseen real rules is unestablished, and the joint scorer retains an advantage at the cost of caching.
AI.motivation: A cacheable independent encoder (encoding each candidate once, reused across states) is ~5x cheaper at 77 candidates, but it separates state from candidate. The paper asks how much rule-sensitivity survives this move and whether it can be trained back.
AI.method: Four experiments on Certo: (1) test whether the cacheable conversion loses rule-sensitivity versus the joint scorer, plus a shortlist+rerank rescue; (2) apply targeted counterfactual supervision to restore performance on held-out synthetic rule tasks (paraphrase, counterfactual, composition, across seeds); (3) evaluate on real rules after fixing a truncation confound; (4) test a matched cross-domain real-prose mixture.
AI.result: (1) Cacheable scoring drops recall@1 from 1.00 to 0.24 while the joint scorer holds 1.00; shortlist+rerank rescue fails. (2) Counterfactual supervision restores strong performance on held-out synthetic tasks, reproducible across seeds, though rule-dependence is not isolated. (3) On real rules, after fixing truncation, the joint scorer wins significantly on the short tier (0.861 vs 0.500) and directionally on the hard tier (0.655 vs 0.483, n=29). (4) The matched cross-domain real-prose mixture did not help and reduced contract accuracy (-9.3, -16.2 points).
AI.conclusion: A cacheable encoder can be made rule-sensitive on its training distribution, but transfer to unseen-source real rules is not established; the joint scorer keeps an edge at the cost of caching.

title: Mixture of Self-Improving Branches For Agent Harness Optimization
summary: Harness optimization provides a practical setting for recursive self-improvement (RSI), where agent-generated modifications inform subsequent changes through execution feedback. Recent work such as Meta-Harness implements this process through iterative code generation and evaluation, but retains a fixed development set and proposal policy. These constraints channel evolution along a single search trajectory, increasing the risk of converging to a local optimum. We make the improvement process itself adaptive by organizing search into branches with evolving development subsets and proposal policies. Each branch retains development cases solved by more of its leading harnesses than by those of other branches, drops cases solved by every leading harness across all branches, and revises its proposal policy using its own search history. To deploy the resulting complementary harnesses, we propose a router to select one development-selected branch head for each new input before execution. Across mathematical reasoning and agentic coding benchmarks, our system achieves relative improvements over Meta-Harness of 34.8% on Olympiad-level mathematical reasoning, 11.6% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, and 3.8% on SWE-bench Lite, with harness selection and router configuration based solely on development data. These results show that evolving branch objectives and proposal policies can yield complementary harnesses whose strengths a router combines without access to test outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive branch-based harness optimization method for recursive self-improvement, using evolving development subsets, proposal policies, and a router to combine complementary harnesses, outperforming Meta-Harness on math and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Meta-Harness-style recursive self-improvement relies on a fixed development set and a fixed proposal policy, which channels evolution along a single search trajectory and risks converging to a local optimum. The authors aim to make the improvement process itself adaptive to escape this limitation.
AI.method: Search is organized into branches with evolving development subsets and proposal policies. Each branch retains development cases solved by more of its leading harnesses than by other branches' harnesses, drops cases solved by all leading harnesses across branches, and revises its proposal policy using its own search history. A router then selects one development-selected branch head per new input before execution.
AI.result: Relative improvements over Meta-Harness: 34.8% on Olympiad-level mathematical reasoning, 11.6% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, and 3.8% on SWE-bench Lite, with harness selection and router configuration based solely on development data.
AI.conclusion: Evolving branch objectives and proposal policies yields complementary harnesses whose combined strengths a router can exploit without access to test outcomes, improving recursive self-improvement over fixed-set, fixed-policy baselines.

title: Active Budget Can Kill Sensitivity: Diagnosing and Repairing TopK Sparse Autoencoder Reliability
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are increasingly scaled to wider dictionaries to recover fine-grained structure from large language model activations. However, a feature is useful for interpretation only if it remains a stable unit of analysis when the same meaning is expressed in different surface forms. We study this reliability question for TopK SAEs via feature sensitivity. Experiments demonstrate that scaling selectively reduces the sensitivity of rare features, while common features remain comparatively stable. A controlled width\(\times k\) factorial experiment identifies the active budget k as the root cause: the degradation arises from the selection boundary rather than dictionary width alone. We attribute this failure to the geometry of TopK selection. The active margin, the distance to the cutoff, predicts feature loss without thresholds. Guided by this margin diagnosis, we introduce pairwise rank stabilization. Our method targets ordering failures at the cutoff and improves rare-feature sensitivity by \(8.83\) percentage points, while keeping reconstruction and alive-feature coverage near the baseline. Overall, our results suggest that wide TopK SAEs should be evaluated not only by reconstruction, sparsity, and feature count, but also by feature reliability under semantic variation and boundary geometry for stable interpretability.

AI.tldr: The paper studies feature reliability in TopK sparse autoencoders via feature sensitivity, showing that scaling dictionaries selectively destabilizes rare features. A width×k factorial experiment identifies the active budget k (selection boundary) as the root cause, and the authors introduce pairwise rank stabilization, improving rare-feature sensitivity by 8.83 percentage points.
AI.motivation: SAEs are increasingly scaled to wider dictionaries to recover fine-grained structure from LLM activations. Yet a feature is useful for interpretation only if it is a stable unit of analysis across different surface forms expressing the same meaning. The paper investigates this reliability question for TopK SAEs.
AI.method: The authors analyze feature sensitivity in TopK SAEs and run a controlled width×k factorial experiment. They attribute degradation to the geometry of TopK selection, using the active margin (distance to the cutoff) as a threshold-free predictor of feature loss. Guided by this diagnosis, they introduce pairwise rank stabilization targeting ordering failures at the cutoff.
AI.result: Scaling selectively reduces sensitivity of rare features while common features remain comparatively stable. The active budget k, not dictionary width alone, is the root cause, with failure arising from the selection boundary. Pairwise rank stabilization improves rare-feature sensitivity by 8.83 percentage points while keeping reconstruction and alive-feature coverage near baseline.
AI.conclusion: Wide TopK SAEs should be evaluated not only by reconstruction, sparsity, and feature count, but also by feature reliability under semantic variation and boundary geometry for stable interpretability.

title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design
summary: Inverse design of physical systems (molecules, devices, microstructures) often reduces to optimizing a high-dimensional structure against an expensive black-box simulator. Direct search is difficult because the space is non-Euclidean, feasibility is hard to encode, and each evaluation is expensive. We present Co-PiLOT, a latent optimization approach that maps candidates through a generative encoder-decoder, uses the decoder as a learned validity prior, and searches the latent space with physics-informed black-box optimization. The framework is applied on the inverse design of magnesium alloy microstructure/texture. We develop a vision transformer based-encoder; paired with latent diffusion, diffusion transformer and rectified-flow transformer-based decoders on $\sim80{,}000$ EBSD-derived microstructure dataset to learn a minimal bottleneck, $z$. The ViT-FMDiT model ($z$=$768$) reconstructs high-fidelity microstructure images (FID $27.86$, MS-SSIM $0.178$), which our self-segmenting orientation codec converts into input grids for crystal plasticity solver. Finally, we introduce MERIDIAN, an active latent optimizer driven by deep-kernel Gaussian-process uncertainty, failure-aware feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition. Within a budget of $160$ simulations, the ViT-FMDiT and MERIDIAN combination yields the best target-driven objective score, reducing the relative target error by $3$--$22\%$ against seven baselines (DANTE, TuRBO, BAxUS, CMA-ES, DDOM, SEIKO, DDPO) on the same decoder.

AI.tldr: Co-PiLOT is a latent optimization framework for inverse design of physical systems that combines a generative encoder-decoder as a validity prior with physics-informed black-box optimization; applied to magnesium alloy microstructure design, its ViT-FMDiT variant plus the MERIDIAN active latent optimizer reduces relative target error by 3–22% versus seven baselines within 160 simulations.
AI.motivation: Inverse design of physical systems such as molecules, devices, and microstructures requires optimizing high-dimensional structures against expensive black-box simulators. Direct search is challenging because the design space is non-Euclidean, feasibility constraints are hard to encode, and each simulator evaluation is costly, motivating a learned latent representation with feasibility-aware, sample-efficient search.
AI.method: Co-PiLOT maps candidates through a generative encoder-decoder, uses the decoder as a learned validity prior, and searches the latent space with physics-informed black-box optimization. For magnesium alloy microstructure/texture inverse design, a vision transformer (ViT) encoder is paired with latent diffusion, diffusion transformer, and rectified-flow transformer decoders trained on ~80,000 EBSD-derived microstructure images to learn a minimal bottleneck z. The ViT-FMDiT model (z=768) reconstructs high-fidelity microstructures, and a self-segmenting orientation codec converts them into input grids for a crystal plasticity solver. MERIDIAN, an active latent optimizer, uses deep-kernel Gaussian-process uncertainty, failure-aware feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition.
AI.result: ViT-FMDiT (z=768) reconstructs high-fidelity microstructure images with FID 27.86 and MS-SSIM 0.178. Within a 160-simulation budget, the ViT-FMDiT + MERIDIAN combination achieves the best target-driven objective score, reducing relative target error by 3–22% against seven baselines (DANTE, TuRBO, BAxUS, CMA-ES, DDOM, SEIKO, DDPO) on the same decoder.
AI.conclusion: Latent generative modeling with a learned validity prior, combined with uncertainty- and feasibility-aware active latent optimization, enables effective and sample-efficient inverse design of physical microstructures; the ViT-FMDiT + MERIDIAN approach outperforms strong black-box and latent optimization baselines under a tight simulation budget.

title: Guide, Then Let Go: Gap-Adaptive Teacher Scheduling for Sparse-Reward Agentic RL
summary: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents typically relies on sparse outcome-based rewards. This leads to a severe cold-start problem, as early-stage policies often fail to solve sampled tasks, leaving little useful reward signal for learning. To mitigate this problem, we use on-policy distillation (OPD) to provide token-level guidance on the student's own rollouts. We find that the benefit of this guidance depends on the performance gap between the teacher and the student. When the teacher substantially outperforms the student, distillation helps guide the student through the early training stage where outcome rewards provide little learning signal. As the gap narrows and eventually reverses, however, continued distillation becomes less beneficial and may hinder further improvement. Motivated by this observation, we propose Gap-Adaptive Teacher Scheduling (GATS), which augments the student's RL objective with an OPD term whose weight adapts to the teacher-student performance gap. Specifically, GATS gradually reduces teacher guidance as the student approaches the teacher's reference performance and withdraws it once that reference is reached. This enables GATS to leverage task-trained teachers smaller than the student, since teacher guidance is primarily needed during early training. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with three Qwen2.5 teacher-student configurations, GATS achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods in all three configurations, improving over reward-only GRPO by 4.37%-11.87% under matched student rollout budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/Ricardo-H/guide-then-let-go.

AI.tldr: GATS adaptively schedules on-policy distillation from a teacher to a student RL agent, reducing teacher guidance as the teacher-student performance gap narrows and withdrawing it once the student matches the teacher, yielding the best average success rates across three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon RL agents trained with sparse outcome-based rewards suffer a cold-start problem: early policies rarely solve sampled tasks, so outcome rewards provide little learning signal. On-policy distillation can supply token-level guidance, but its usefulness depends on the teacher-student performance gap, which the authors seek to exploit rather than apply uniformly.
AI.method: The paper analyzes on-policy distillation (OPD) and finds that guidance helps mainly when the teacher substantially outperforms the student, becoming less beneficial or harmful as the gap narrows or reverses. Based on this, they propose Gap-Adaptive Teacher Scheduling (GATS), which augments the student's RL objective with an OPD term whose weight adapts to the teacher-student performance gap — gradually reducing guidance as the student approaches the teacher's reference performance and withdrawing it once that reference is reached. This allows using task-trained teachers smaller than the student.
AI.result: Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with three Qwen2.5 teacher-student configurations, GATS achieves the highest average success rate among compared methods in all three configurations, improving over reward-only GRPO by 4.37%–11.87% under matched student rollout budgets.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive schedules of teacher guidance based on the teacher-student performance gap are effective: distillation should be leveraged early and withdrawn as the student catches up, enabling smaller teachers and consistently improving long-horizon RL performance over reward-only baselines.

title: You Cannot Pick a Provider From the Price List: Market-Aware Routing for Open-Weight LLM Inference
summary: Existing LLM routers choose among models using static per-model costs. We show that open-weight inference markets introduce a second, largely ignored decision axis: after choosing a model, a client must still choose which provider serves it. Measuring live endpoints across [nummodels] open models, competing providers, multiple task types, and three measurement waves, we find that provider choice cannot be inferred from the price list. The same model can vary sharply in quality, latency, availability, and price across providers; higher-priced providers are consistently faster, but price does not reliably predict quality or availability; and provider feasibility is task-selective, with one deployment nearly normal on knowledge tasks but catastrophically degraded on multi-step reasoning. We formulate same-model provider selection as a price-taker market-aware routing problem. A simple measured-map policy routes to the cheapest provider that is both quality-equivalent and healthy, yielding matched-quality savings while avoiding degraded endpoints. Because the map drifts, we introduce FACET, an online provider router that certifies per-(provider x task) feasibility facets and fails safe to an anchor before serving uncertified arms. Across relaxed deployment assumptions, FACET tolerates imperfect task assignment and sparse feedback, while systematic evaluator bias exposes a quality-signal trust boundary that can be mitigated with ground-truth probes or audits. Live provider runs further confirm that certification can move real traffic from a premium anchor to a substantially cheaper certified endpoint. Our results suggest that market-aware LLM routing must measure not only which model to use, but also who serves it.

AI.tldr: LLM routing must select not only which model to use but also which provider serves it; provider quality, latency, availability, and price vary within the same model, so the authors propose FACET, an online provider router that certifies per-(provider × task) feasibility and fails safe to an anchor.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM routers treat per-model costs as static and choose only among models. In open-weight inference markets, a second decision axis is overlooked: after model selection, the client must choose a provider. Provider choice cannot be inferred from price lists, since the same model varies across providers in quality, latency, availability, and price, and provider feasibility is task-selective.
AI.method: The authors measure live endpoints across [nummodels] open models, competing providers, multiple task types, and three measurement waves. They formulate same-model provider selection as a price-taker, market-aware routing problem and develop a measured-map policy that routes to the cheapest provider that is both quality-equivalent and healthy. To handle map drift, they introduce FACET, an online provider router that certifies per-(provider × task) feasibility facets and fails safe to an anchor before serving uncertified arms. They test under relaxed deployment assumptions (imperfect task assignment, sparse feedback) and analyze evaluator bias.
AI.result: Provider choice cannot be inferred from price lists. Higher-priced providers are consistently faster, but price does not reliably predict quality or availability. Provider feasibility is task-selective: one deployment was nearly normal on knowledge tasks but catastrophically degraded on multi-step reasoning. The measured-map policy yields matched-quality savings while avoiding degraded endpoints. FACET tolerates imperfect task assignment and sparse feedback, and systematic evaluator bias exposes a quality-signal trust boundary that can be mitigated with ground-truth probes or audits. Live provider runs confirm certification can move real traffic from a premium anchor to a substantially cheaper certified endpoint.
AI.conclusion: Market-aware LLM routing must measure not only which model to use but also who serves it.

title: Pixels to Keys: Exploring Spatial and Motion Cues in Gameplay Inverse Dynamics
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Multimodal Digital Agents (ECCV 2026): https://mda-workshop.allen.ai/
summary: Video games offer scalable environments for studying perception and control in embodied agents.Abundant online gameplay videos could supply demonstrations, but they rarely include player inputs for training. Inverse Dynamics Models (IDMs) have thus been proposed to infer inputs from frames. Large (up to 1B parameters) IDMs trained on $\sim$1K-2K gameplay hours demonstrate feasibility and cross-environment generalization at this scale, but researchers do not clarify what the key components are to recover individual actions and often report only aggregate accuracy that can mask rare-action failures. We study the problem in a data-constrained scenario to evaluate how spatial motion features, model architectures, and training objectives affect an IDM's outcome and we analyse our models on per-key and balanced metrics such as $F_1^{macro}$. Our experiments on Trackmania highlight the importance of factors like the model architecture and motion flow extraction in preprocessing, while also showing the limits of evaluation through unbalanced metrics. The application of the same architecture and training recipe to Cyberpunk 2077 reveals uneven performance across game mechanics. Our per-action evaluation and failure analysis highlight ambiguities from camera motion, delayed effects and imbalanced key-press frequencies that call for explicit modeling of 3D scene structure, long-term state and the adoption of proper losses in future implementations.

AI.tldr: This paper studies Inverse Dynamics Models (IDMs) for inferring player inputs from gameplay frames in a data-constrained setting, using per-key and balanced metrics to expose failure modes that aggregate accuracy hides.
AI.motivation: Online gameplay videos are abundant but lack player input labels, limiting their use as demonstrations for training embodied agents. IDMs were proposed to recover inputs from frames, and large-scale IDMs (up to 1B parameters, ~1K-2K hours) showed feasibility and cross-environment generalization, yet the field lacks clarity on which components are essential for recovering individual actions, and typically reports only aggregate accuracy that masks rare-action failures.
AI.method: The authors conduct controlled experiments in a data-constrained regime to isolate the effect of spatial motion features, model architectures, and training objectives on IDM performance. They evaluate on Trackmania and transfer the same architecture and training recipe to Cyberpunk 2077, assessing models with per-key and balanced metrics such as F1-macro alongside a failure analysis.
AI.result: On Trackmania, factors such as model architecture and motion flow extraction in preprocessing prove important, and unbalanced metrics are shown to be insufficient for evaluation. Applying the same architecture and training recipe to Cyberpunk 2077 yields uneven performance across game mechanics, with per-action evaluation and failure analysis revealing ambiguities caused by camera motion, delayed effects, and imbalanced key-press frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Recovering player inputs from frames is limited by ambiguities that aggregate metrics conceal. The authors call for explicit modeling of 3D scene structure and long-term state, together with the adoption of proper (balanced) losses in future IDM implementations.

title: GRFBrain: Graph-Structured Rectified Flows for EEG Dynamic Modeling
summary: Forecasting time-varying functional connectivity from electroencephalography (EEG) requires modeling both history-dependent trends and structured variability across channels. Conditional flow matching provides a framework for distributional forecasting, yet it remains unclear whether graph-informed source distributions offer practical advantages over isotropic noise and strong deterministic predictors. We introduce a graph-structured residual flow framework that separates conditional mean prediction from stochastic residual transport. A history-only predictor estimates the future connectivity graph, while a graph Gaussian source encodes dependencies derived from past connectivity through a Laplacian-based covariance. A conditional velocity field transports source samples to future graph residuals, with transport time explicitly distinguished from physical EEG time. Our study identifies the conditions and controls needed to distinguish useful residual transport from improvements attributable to deterministic prediction, learned representations, and sampling effects.

AI.tldr: A graph-structured residual flow framework for forecasting time-varying EEG functional connectivity, separating deterministic mean prediction from stochastic residual transport.
AI.motivation: Forecasting time-varying functional connectivity from EEG requires modeling both history-dependent trends and structured variability across channels. It remains unclear whether graph-informed source distributions (vs. isotropic noise and strong deterministic predictors) offer practical advantages in conditional flow matching.
AI.method: The framework separates conditional mean prediction from stochastic residual transport. A history-only predictor estimates the future connectivity graph; a graph Gaussian source encodes dependencies from past connectivity via a Laplacian-based covariance; a conditional velocity field transports source samples to future graph residuals, with transport time explicitly distinguished from physical EEG time.
AI.result: The study identifies the conditions and controls needed to distinguish useful residual transport from improvements attributable to deterministic prediction, learned representations, and sampling effects.
AI.conclusion: Graph-informed source distributions offer benefits only under specific conditions; careful controls are required to isolate genuine gains from residual transport versus confounds such as deterministic prediction and sampling effects.

title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution
summary: Video understanding agents acquire evidence through an executable harness that controls what they observe and how they use those observations. However, execution traces contain only the evidence acquired by the current harness, leaving competing explanations for failure unresolved and limiting the basis for self-improvement. We introduce Video-RSI, a framework for recursive self-improvement in which a video understanding agent uses its own language model to revise its harness. Through active video investigation, the model revisits the original training videos to test competing failure explanations with additional observations, grounding proposed changes in evidence beyond the existing trace. Cost-aware harness evolution turns these diagnoses into reusable revisions and determines which revisions to retain by considering both answer accuracy and visual cost. Across our evaluation settings on video understanding benchmarks, the evolved agent improves accuracy while processing fewer frames and achieves competitive accuracy-efficiency trade-offs against existing video understanding agents. These results demonstrate the potential for video understanding agents to improve their own evidence acquisition and use through harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/Video-RSI .

AI.tldr: Video-RSI enables a video understanding agent to recursively self-improve by letting its own language model revise the execution harness that governs evidence acquisition, using active video investigation and cost-aware evolution.
AI.motivation: Existing video understanding agents rely on an executable harness controlling observation and usage, but execution traces capture only evidence from the current harness. This leaves competing failure explanations unresolved and limits self-improvement.
AI.method: The framework performs recursive self-improvement: the agent's language model revises its harness. Active video investigation revisits original training videos to test competing failure explanations with additional observations, grounding changes beyond the existing trace. Cost-aware harness evolution converts diagnoses into reusable revisions, retaining those that balance answer accuracy and visual cost.
AI.result: On video understanding benchmarks, the evolved agent improves accuracy while processing fewer frames, achieving competitive accuracy-efficiency trade-offs versus existing video understanding agents.
AI.conclusion: Video understanding agents can improve their own evidence acquisition and use through harness evolution. Code available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/Video-RSI.

title: Topological Coherence for Self-evolving Multi-agent Systems
summary: Complex tasks inherently couple workflow structure, agent responsibility, collaboration, and memory access: task regions delimit responsibility and tool scope, cross-region dependencies give rise to handoffs, and ownership boundaries delimit private and selectively shared memory. Existing methods can jointly optimize agent and communication structures, yet such optimization does not by itself require responsibility, handoff, and memory boundaries to remain consistent with task dependencies. We term this requirement topological coherence. We introduce TOCOMAS, a Topology-Coherent Multi-Agent System. TOCOMAS grounds a task graph in tool interfaces, organizes compatible task nodes into reusable responsibility domains, and derives dependency-induced and profile-conditioned collaboration together with boundary-regulated memory visibility. During online self-evolution, TOCOMAS proposes coupled changes to agent, collaboration, and memory policies, retaining for subsequent tasks only candidates that satisfy structural constraints and improve evaluated reward. Across BBEH, WorkBench, SWE-Bench-Verified, and CoMemBench, TOCOMAS improves task success over baselines across backbones. CoMemBench also shows gains over the self-evolving baseline in verified progress, handoffs, and memory isolation.

AI.tldr: TOCOMAS is a topology-coherent multi-agent system that aligns agent responsibility, collaboration (handoffs), and memory access boundaries with task dependencies, achieving gains across BBEH, WorkBench, SWE-Bench-Verified, and CoMemBench.
AI.motivation: Complex tasks tightly couple workflow structure, agent responsibility, collaboration, and memory access: task regions define responsibility/tool scope, cross-region dependencies create handoffs, and ownership boundaries separate private from shared memory. Prior methods can jointly optimize agent and communication structures, but this optimization alone does not guarantee that responsibility, handoff, and memory boundaries stay consistent with task dependencies—a property the authors call topological coherence.
AI.method: TOCOMAS grounds a task graph in tool interfaces, groups compatible task nodes into reusable responsibility domains, and derives dependency-induced and profile-conditioned collaboration plus boundary-regulated memory visibility. In online self-evolution, it proposes coupled updates to agent, collaboration, and memory policies and retains only candidates satisfying structural constraints and improving evaluated reward for later tasks.
AI.result: On BBEH, WorkBench, SWE-Bench-Verified, and CoMemBench, TOCOMAS improves task success over baselines across backbones. On CoMemBench it also outperforms the self-evolving baseline on verified progress, handoffs, and memory isolation.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing topological coherence via coupled optimization of agent, collaboration, and memory policies yields consistent multi-agent performance and structural advantages.

title: BrainNet Studio: A Unified Toolkit for Brain Network Construction, Intelligent Analysis, and Visualization
summary: Brain networks characterize structural and functional relationships among brain regions and support research on cognition, brain disorders, and brain-computer interfaces. Their time-varying topology and higher-order spatiotemporal dependencies are not adequately represented by conventional static networks. Existing tools primarily focus on static connectomes and provide limited integration of dynamic network modeling with modern graph and sequence learning methods. We present BrainNet Studio, an integrated toolkit for static and dynamic brain network analysis. It provides a unified workflow encompassing network construction, feature extraction, predictive modeling, candidate biomarker identification, visualization, and assisted interpretation. The toolkit integrates 27 algorithms, including deep learning, graph neural networks, and spatiotemporal sequence models, to support classification and the identification of discriminative brain regions and connections. A large language model generates researcher-verifiable summaries of functional connectivity, structural connectivity, and structure-function coupling at individual and group levels. Within a consistent computational framework, users can configure analytical tasks, compare methods, inspect outputs, and extend functionality without repeatedly assembling application-specific pipelines. BrainNet Studio provides a practical and extensible platform for connectome analysis in cognitive neuroscience, exploratory studies of brain disorders, and brain-computer interfaces. The toolkit is publicly available at https://github.com/xbrainnet/Brainnet-Studio.

AI.tldr: BrainNet Studio is an integrated toolkit unifying static and dynamic brain network analysis, combining 27 algorithms (deep learning, GNNs, spatiotemporal models) with an LLM-based interpretation module within a single workflow.
AI.motivation: Brain networks capture structural and functional relationships among brain regions, supporting research on cognition, brain disorders, and brain-computer interfaces. However, their time-varying topology and higher-order spatiotemporal dependencies are poorly represented by conventional static networks. Existing tools are largely limited to static connectomes and offer limited integration of dynamic network modeling with modern graph and sequence learning methods.
AI.method: BrainNet Studio provides a unified workflow covering network construction, feature extraction, predictive modeling, candidate biomarker identification, visualization, and assisted interpretation. It integrates 27 algorithms spanning deep learning, graph neural networks, and spatiotemporal sequence models for classification and identification of discriminative brain regions and connections. A large language model generates researcher-verifiable summaries of functional connectivity, structural connectivity, and structure-function coupling at individual and group levels, all within a consistent computational framework.
AI.result: The toolkit enables users to configure analytical tasks, compare methods, inspect outputs, and extend functionality without repeatedly assembling application-specific pipelines, supporting classification and the identification of discriminative brain regions and connections.
AI.conclusion: BrainNet Studio offers a practical, extensible platform for connectome analysis in cognitive neuroscience, exploratory brain disorder studies, and brain-computer interfaces, and is publicly available at https://github.com/xbrainnet/Brainnet-Studio.

title: SelfSearch: Reward-Free Search for Self-Improving Agents
summary: Advances in the coding capabilities of LLM agents allow them to inspect and modify their own instructions, tools, and execution procedures. Existing approaches use this ability to search for improved agents through repeated downstream evaluation, which incurs substantial costs and ties the search to the evaluated tasks. We introduce \textbf{SelfSearch}, a reward-free search procedure in which agents modify themselves using records of previous self-improvement episodes. These records capture the reasoning, tool actions, and outcomes of earlier modification attempts, providing concrete experience for improving both task solving and self-modification. Without downstream reward signals during search, SelfSearch improves population-mean success over the initial agent in all six model--benchmark settings, with individual agents gaining up to 11.2 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On SWE-bench Multilingual, an agent improves success by \textbf{5.0} percentage points while reducing execution cost by \textbf{38.5}\% on tasks solved by both the initial and evolved agents. SelfSearch achieves competitive task success with evaluation-guided search baselines at lower search cost. With only \textbf{\$4.03} in search cost, it produces a harness that solves \textbf{82.0}\% of Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks with DeepSeek V4 Flash under the settings of a public nine-harness comparison, matching the top-scoring harness, Codex. These results suggest that experience gained through self-modification can improve agents' downstream capabilities and efficiency.

AI.tldr: SelfSearch is a reward-free self-improvement procedure where LLM agents evolve themselves using records of prior self-modification episodes, improving success and efficiency across six model–benchmark settings at low search cost.
AI.motivation: Existing self-improvement approaches rely on repeated downstream evaluation to search for better agents, incurring substantial costs and tying the search to the specific evaluated tasks. The paper aims to remove this dependence on downstream reward signals while still enabling effective self-modification.
AI.method: Agents modify their own instructions, tools, and execution procedures using records of previous self-improvement episodes. These records capture reasoning, tool actions, and outcomes of earlier modification attempts, serving as concrete experience for improving both task solving and self-modification. The search proceeds without downstream reward signals, using this accumulated experience to guide further self-modification.
AI.result: SelfSearch improves population-mean success over the initial agent in all six model–benchmark settings, with individual agents gaining up to 11.2 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On SWE-bench Multilingual, an agent improves success by 5.0 percentage points while reducing execution cost by 38.5% on tasks solved by both the initial and evolved agents. It achieves competitive task success versus evaluation-guided search baselines at lower search cost. With $4.03 in search cost, it produces a harness solving 82.0% of Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks with DeepSeek V4 Flash in a public nine-harness comparison, matching the top-scoring harness, Codex.
AI.conclusion: Experience gained through self-modification can improve agents' downstream capabilities and efficiency, and competitive performance can be achieved without downstream reward signals during search and at low search cost.

title: KV-Kaizen: Learning Context-Adaptive Cache Compression Choices
summary: As the context size of text processed with an LLM grows, the size of KV caches can outstrip the memory allocated for the original model weights. This impacts LLM throughput negatively, since decoding is memory-bound and decode cost grows with cache size. Recent work alleviates this bottleneck by discarding the least relevant tokens. Eviction introduces a tension, since a one-off decision to discard content may prove detrimental later. Instead, we focus on alternative choices that can lead to cache compression without evicting tokens. We achieve this by learning a selector that is able to produce, based on context, a per-layer cache configuration towards an overall compression budget. The selector operates along three axes: sharing one cache across layers (depth), caching at fewer bits (precision), or truncating the low-rank latent cache representations (rank). We call the resulting method KV-Kaizen, for the many small per-layer choices it compounds. We observe that these interventions taken independently and uniformly over all layers limit achievable compression because they degrade accuracy. Crucially, composing them locally and adaptively to the context can instead preserve accuracy while achieving large memory savings. At inference, the selector runs once, before pre-fill. In evaluations on instruction following and reasoning tasks, our selectors reach the Pareto frontier of accuracy against cache size, against learning-free and post-hoc baselines. On long-context tasks, KV-Kaizen improves on eviction and can be composed with it, reaching a 32x smaller decode-time cache on a 14B model while preserving accuracy. A 4x cache size reduction incurs no accuracy degradation from 7B parameters up, and a compressed model is more accurate than a smaller uncompressed one with the same cache size. Together, these findings support pre-training large models and compressing them only afterwards.

AI.tldr: KV-Kaizen learns a context-dependent, per-layer selector that compresses the KV cache along three axes—cross-layer sharing, precision, and rank—avoiding token eviction and reaching up to 32x smaller decode-time caches while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: As LLM context grows, KV cache size can exceed model weight memory, hurting throughput because decoding is memory-bound. Prior work discards least relevant tokens (eviction), but a one-off eviction decision may be detrimental later, creating a tension. This motivates cache compression without evicting tokens.
AI.method: KV-Kaizen trains a selector that, based on context, produces a per-layer cache configuration under an overall compression budget. It operates along three axes: sharing one cache across layers (depth), caching at fewer bits (precision), and truncating low-rank latent cache representations (rank).
