It composes these interventions locally and adaptively, and the selector runs once before pre-fill at inference.
AI.result: On instruction following and reasoning tasks, selectors reach the Pareto frontier of accuracy vs. cache size, beating learning-free and post-hoc baselines. On long-context tasks, KV-Kaizen improves on eviction and composes with it, reaching a 32x smaller decode-time cache on a 14B model while preserving accuracy. A 4x reduction incurs no accuracy degradation from 7B up, and a compressed model outperforms a smaller uncompressed one with the same cache size.
AI.conclusion: Composing per-layer compression choices locally and adaptively preserves accuracy while achieving large memory savings, supporting pre-training large models and compressing them only afterwards.

title: Which Attention Heads are like the Human Head? Not the Ones that Compute
summary: Brain-AI alignment is often interpreted as a sign that model and brain perform similar computations. Whether the aligned units are causally involved in model computation is rarely checked. On an abstract pattern-completion task (AAABAAA $\rightarrow$ B), we compare LLM attention-head representations with human EEG and test how ablating those heads affects task performance. Alignment and causation dissociate: brain-aligned heads contribute to performance, but their removal is substantially less disruptive than removal of heads selected via attribution patching. We compare two head sets that prior interpretability work defines without reference to the brain: concept vectors (CVs), which represent abstract patterns across formats, and function vectors (FVs), selected for their contribution to correct-answer prediction. Brain alignment shows little association with FV scores, while its association with CV scores varies across models. Among brain-aligned heads, we find recurring attention profiles: one emphasizes distinctive elements (novelty heads), the other repeating elements (repetition heads). The novelty family tracks salience and attends to the same elements that humans look at, yet its removal is less damaging than random ablation on average. Repetition heads contribute modestly to performance and are associated with abstract-pattern representation (CVs). Across 17 models spanning 3B-72B parameters, FV-ranked removal is substantially more disruptive than brain-ranked removal. Brain alignment thus captures how the model reads the stimulus, and only faintly captures how it represents the pattern and solves the task.

AI.tldr: Brain-AI alignment dissociates from causal contribution: brain-aligned attention heads contribute to task performance but are far less disruptive when ablated than heads selected by attribution patching or function vectors.
AI.motivation: Alignment between brain activity and model representations is frequently taken as evidence that model and brain perform similar computations, yet the causal role of aligned units is rarely tested. This paper asks whether brain-aligned units are actually causally involved in model computation.
AI.method: On an abstract pattern-completion task (AAABAAA → B), the authors compare LLM attention-head representations with human EEG and measure how ablating those heads affects task performance. They contrast brain-aligned heads with two head sets defined without reference to the brain—concept vectors (CVs) for abstract pattern representation across formats and function vectors (FVs) selected for correct-answer prediction—and characterize recurring attention profiles among brain-aligned heads across 17 models (3B–72B parameters).
AI.result: Alignment and causation dissociate: brain-aligned heads contribute to performance, but their removal is substantially less disruptive than removal of heads selected via attribution patching. Brain alignment shows little association with FV scores, while its association with CV scores varies across models. Among brain-aligned heads, two recurring profiles emerge: novelty heads emphasizing distinctive elements and repetition heads emphasizing repeating elements. The novelty family tracks salience and attends to the same elements as humans, yet its removal is less damaging than random ablation on average. Repetition heads contribute modestly to performance and are associated with abstract-pattern representation (CVs). Across all models, FV-ranked removal is substantially more disruptive than brain-ranked removal.
AI.conclusion: Brain alignment captures how the model reads the stimulus, but only faintly captures how it represents the pattern and solves the task. Alignment should therefore not be equated with shared computation or causal relevance.

title: Diagnosing and Improving Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as decision assistants who must reason probabilistically from available evidence under explicit decision costs. We propose a decision-theoretic framework that decomposes LLMs' decision loss into two components: forming accurate beliefs from provided evidence and translating those beliefs into actions that optimize a provided utility function. Using a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth, we apply the decomposition to characterize probabilistic reasoning in frontier and open-sourced models. We further evaluate whether RL interventions targeting beliefs, decisions, or both improve these components across three domains, whether improvements transfer across components and elicitation formats, and whether decision performance can improve without improvement in belief formation. We find that targeting one component of probabilistic reasoning redistributes decision loss, improving the target without necessarily transferring to others, and that jointly targeting belief formation and decision-making improves both but hinges on matched formats between training and evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a decision-theoretic decomposition of LLM decision loss into belief formation and action selection, then uses RL interventions to show that targeting one component does not reliably transfer to the other, while joint training helps only when train/eval formats match.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as decision assistants that must reason probabilistically from evidence under explicit decision costs, yet prior evaluations conflate two distinct capabilities: forming accurate beliefs and translating beliefs into utility-optimal actions. The paper motivates the need to disentangle these components to properly diagnose and improve probabilistic reasoning.
AI.method: The authors propose a decision-theoretic framework decomposing LLM decision loss into (1) belief formation from provided evidence and (2) belief-to-action translation optimizing a given utility. They build a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth to characterize frontier and open-source models, then apply RL interventions that target beliefs, decisions, or both across three domains, testing cross-component transfer, cross-format transfer, and whether decision performance can improve without belief improvement.
AI.result: Targeting one component of probabilistic reasoning redistributes decision loss: it improves the targeted component without necessarily transferring to the other. Jointly targeting belief formation and decision-making improves both components, but this benefit depends on matched formats between training and evaluation. Decision performance can improve without improved belief formation.
AI.conclusion: The decomposition provides a principled lens for diagnosing LLM probabilistic reasoning and shows that improving decision quality requires care: single-component RL interventions yield partial, non-transferable gains, and effective joint training hinges on format alignment between training and evaluation.

title: HARISSA: Inference-Time Self-Checks for Efficient and Safe Local Language Model Deployment
summary: Running a language model locally offers advantages in privacy, latency, and cost, but local hardware fits only small models, which are less capable than frontier models. The usual remedy for a hard query, escalating it to a cloud model, gives up the privacy and cost advantages of running locally. A deployment that stays local faces two decisions for hard queries instead. First, it can spend more computation on a query, e.g., reasoning before answering, which raises accuracy at a cost in latency, so it must decide which queries are worth the extra computation (efficiency). Second, some queries are beyond the local model, and delivering a wrong answer is worse than deferring the query to a human in the loop, so it must decide which answers are safe to deliver (safety). We show that both decisions can be made from the model's own hidden states. The prefill state, computed before any token is generated, predicts whether the model will answer correctly, and the answer state, at the end of the generated answer, predicts whether that answer is correct. HARISSA fine-tunes the model so that both states predict correctness, then makes both decisions with one policy that cascades through the ways of answering from cheapest to most expensive, skipping a way the prefill state predicts will fail and deferring the query when the answer it stops with is predicted wrong. On a device running a single model, HARISSA is within one accuracy point of chain-of-thought at 2.7 times lower latency. On a server holding four sizes of one model, HARISSA is more accurate than the FrugalGPT and Self-REF cascades at the same latency, and at the same deferral rate the answer state leaves fewer wrong answers than the standard confidence signals in five of six task and setting pairs.

AI.tldr: HARISSA uses a local model's hidden states (prefill and answer states) to decide which queries need extra computation and which answers are safe to deliver, achieving near-CoT accuracy at much lower latency.
AI.motivation: Local language models offer privacy, latency, and cost benefits but are weaker than frontier cloud models. Escalating hard queries to the cloud sacrifices these benefits. A fully local deployment instead faces two problems: (1) efficiency, deciding which queries justify extra computation (e.g., reasoning) versus latency cost, and (2) safety, deciding which answers are reliable enough to deliver versus deferring to a human.
AI.method: HARISSA fine-tunes the model so that two hidden states predict correctness: the prefill state (computed before any token is generated, predicting whether the model will answer correctly) and the answer state (at the end of generation, predicting whether the answer is correct). A single policy then cascades through answering strategies from cheapest to most expensive, skipping any strategy the prefill state predicts will fail and deferring the query when the final answer is predicted incorrect.
AI.result: On a single-model device, HARISSA is within one accuracy point of chain-of-thought while achieving 2.7x lower latency. On a server with four model sizes, it outperforms the FrugalGPT and Self-REF cascades at equal latency, and at equal deferral rate the answer state yields fewer wrong answers than standard confidence signals in five of six task/setting pairs.
AI.conclusion: Both computation-allocation and answer-safety decisions can be derived from a model's own hidden states, enabling efficient and reliable fully local deployment without cloud escalation.

title: PE-EK-PINN: Physics Embedding with Evolving Kernel for Scalable Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) embed governing equations into deep learning, but enforce them only through loss residuals, leaving highly oscillatory wave behavior to be discovered by optimization. As a result, methods that achieve relative $L_2$ errors below $10^{-3}$ on standard manufactured Helmholtz benchmarks can fail on practical radiation problems involving singular excitations, absorbing boundaries, and wave fields spanning tens of wavelengths. Architectural physics embedding addresses this limitation by factorizing the field into analytically derived oscillatory kernels and learnable envelopes. However, the kernel dictionary must be manually constructed and scales with the number of elementary units, growing exponentially with the depth of hierarchically structured systems such as antenna arrays and metasurfaces. We propose PE-EK-PINN (Physics Embedded with Evolving Kernels), which treats physics kernels as reusable learned representations rather than fixed analytical inputs. A converged subsystem field is frozen and promoted to an evolved kernel, whose transformed copies are reused to represent higher-level configurations without deriving new governing equations. The resulting hierarchy makes the peak number of active kernels independent of system size and reduces cumulative training cost from $O(N)$ to $O(\log N)$. Experiments on dipole arrays, composite line-source geometries, and cross arrays demonstrate the dramatic training cost reduction, while achieving a reduced or comparable relative $L_2$ error. One notable example is PE-EK-PINN solves a $256$-dipole array more than 30 times faster than direct PE-PINN.

AI.tldr: PE-EK-PINN replaces fixed analytical physics kernels with reusable learned "evolved kernels" that can be frozen and transformed, enabling hierarchical reuse for large-scale wave problems and reducing training cost from O(N) to O(log N).
AI.motivation: Standard PINNs enforce governing equations only via loss residuals, so highly oscillatory wave behavior must be discovered by optimization; they can achieve low relative L2 error on manufactured Helmholtz benchmarks yet fail on practical radiation problems with singular excitations, absorbing boundaries, and fields spanning tens of wavelengths. Architectural physics embedding helps by factorizing fields into analytical oscillatory kernels and learnable envelopes, but its kernel dictionary is manually constructed and scales with the number of elementary units, growing exponentially with hierarchical depth in antenna arrays and metasurfaces.
AI.method: PE-EK-PINN treats physics kernels as reusable learned representations rather than fixed analytical inputs. A converged subsystem field is frozen and promoted to an evolved kernel, and transformed copies of this kernel are reused to represent higher-level configurations without deriving new governing equations, forming a hierarchy where peak active kernels are independent of system size.
AI.result: Experiments on dipole arrays, composite line-source geometries, and cross arrays show dramatic training cost reduction with reduced or comparable relative L2 error; PE-EK-PINN solves a 256-dipole array more than 30 times faster than direct PE-PINN.
AI.conclusion: Promoting converged subsystem fields into reusable transformed kernels enables scalable physics-embedded learning, making the peak number of active kernels independent of system size and cutting cumulative training cost from O(N) to O(log N) while preserving accuracy.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization via Cross-Harness Adaptation
summary: An agent skill is a reusable, actionable natural-language artifact that guides an agent to perform a task effectively under a given harness. Recent studies have explored the optimization of agent skills, contributing to a growing collection of publicly available skills spanning diverse tasks, domains, and harnesses. Despite millions of publicly shared skills, existing skill optimization methods largely overlook this accumulated knowledge, instead relying solely on expensive agent rollouts to iteratively refine skills for a target task. To address this, we propose \textbf{Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization (RASO)}, a framework that leverages an external skill corpus as prior knowledge throughout skill optimization. RASO retrieves relevant knowledge from existing skills and adapts it to the target task and harness via Cross-Harness Adaptation, accounting for mismatches in both domain and harness. RASO comprises two complementary stages: \textbf{Retrieval-Augmented Skill Initialization (RASI)} constructs a knowledge-grounded initial skill without requiring agent rollouts, while \textbf{Retrieval-Augmented Skill Update (RASU)} iteratively refines the skill by retrieving external knowledge guided by execution feedback. Across four agent benchmarks and two models, extensive experiments show that RASO consistently outperforms baselines without retrieval-augmented skill initialization and updating.

AI.tldr: RASO is a framework that leverages an external skill corpus as prior knowledge to optimize agent skills, using retrieval, cross-harness adaptation, and two stages (RASI initialization and RASU iterative update), outperforming baselines that lack retrieval augmentation.
AI.motivation: Existing agent skill optimization methods overlook the millions of publicly available skills and rely solely on expensive agent rollouts to iteratively refine skills for a target task. This wastes accumulated knowledge and is costly.
AI.method: Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization (RASO) retrieves relevant knowledge from existing skills and adapts it to the target task and harness via Cross-Harness Adaptation, handling mismatches in domain and harness. It has two stages: Retrieval-Augmented Skill Initialization (RASI), which builds a knowledge-grounded initial skill without agent rollouts, and Retrieval-Augmented Skill Update (RASU), which iteratively refines the skill using execution-feedback-guided retrieval of external knowledge.
AI.result: Across four agent benchmarks and two models, RASO consistently outperforms baselines without retrieval-augmented skill initialization and updating.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging an external skill corpus as prior knowledge throughout skill optimization is effective and improves agent skill performance over rollout-only refinement approaches.

title: UserProxyBench: Evaluating LLM User Simulators for Agent Benchmarks and Training
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks Workshop (AABA4ET) at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Interactive agent benchmarks and multi-turn reinforcement learning increasingly place a second language model in the role of the user. This simulated user controls what information the agent receives and when, yet current benchmarks score only the agent and do not directly measure whether the user correctly executed its assigned role. We introduce UserProxyBench, an evaluation layer over the tau-bench family, and the User Fidelity Score (UFS), which measures adherence to the benchmark's private user instructions using task-grounded rubric criteria scored independently of agent success. Holding the agent fixed at GPT-5.5 and varying only the user proxy across 375 enterprise tasks changes mean task reward by 15.2 points, while 24.4% of successful episodes contain a user-specification violation. The dominant failure is premature disclosure: users provide information before it is requested. This behavior has little effect on task reward, yet among successful episodes it causes the agent to make 1.06 fewer tool calls on average, changing the interaction being evaluated while preserving the reward. Finally, across seven proxies we identify an empirical cost-fidelity frontier, enabling practitioners to select the least expensive simulator that satisfies a required fidelity level.

AI.tldr: UserProxyBench and the User Fidelity Score (UFS) measure whether the simulated user in interactive agent benchmarks correctly executes its assigned role, independent of agent success. Varying only the user proxy across 375 enterprise tasks shifts mean task reward by 15.2 points, and 24.4% of successful episodes contain user-specification violations, dominated by premature disclosure.
AI.motivation: Interactive agent benchmarks and multi-turn RL increasingly use a second language model as the simulated user, controlling what information the agent receives and when. However, current benchmarks score only the agent and never directly verify whether the user proxy faithfully performed its assigned role, leaving a blind spot in evaluation validity.
AI.method: The authors introduce UserProxyBench, an evaluation layer over the tau-bench family, and the User Fidelity Score (UFS). UFS measures adherence to the benchmark's private user instructions via task-grounded rubric criteria scored independently of agent success. They hold the agent fixed at GPT-5.5 and vary only the user proxy across 375 enterprise tasks, analyzing reward variance, violation rates, and interaction-level effects.
AI.result: Changing the user proxy alone alters mean task reward by 15.2 points, while 24.4% of successful episodes contain a user-specification violation. The dominant failure mode is premature disclosure, where users volunteer information before it is requested; this has little effect on task reward but causes 1.06 fewer tool calls on average among successful episodes. Across seven proxies, the authors identify an empirical cost-fidelity frontier.
AI.conclusion: Current benchmarks conflate agent competence with user simulator fidelity, since reward can remain stable while the evaluated interaction changes materially. UFS and UserProxyBench expose this gap, and the cost-fidelity frontier lets practitioners select the least expensive simulator that satisfies a required fidelity level.

title: Probability is Not Enough: Exploring and Counting Divergent Tokens for Reasoning Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
comment: 25 pages, 16 figures, 8 tables. Under peer review
summary: As the chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities of large language models improve, evaluating and calibrating their reasoning confidence is becoming increasingly important for quantifying the uncertainty of their answers. Current methods for estimating the confidence of large language models are generally based on probabilities of selected key tokens, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Our pilot study finds that replacing selected token probabilities with coarse substitutes can also improve calibration, motivating us to further explore effective signals of model confidence. We introduce Divergent Token Confidence (DTC), a framework that estimates confidence by counting tokens at which two models strongly disagree during decoding. DTC identifies these divergent tokens using the Jensen-Shannon divergence between next-token distributions evaluated along the same reasoning trajectory. We find that their count is almost negatively associated with answer accuracy, thereby serving as a simple yet effective signal for uncertainty quantification. DTC supports both white-box and black-box evaluation using auxiliary models, without explicit training and affecting the generation process. Experiments across multiple model families and six mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved calibration over probability-based and verbalized baselines. Under white-box evaluation, the count-only estimator achieves an average expected calibration error of 13.0%, compared with 32.7%-42.4% for standard full-sequence confidence methods. In black-box settings, it also improves calibration over the original verbalized scores. For example, mean expected calibration error falls from 32.1%-40.2% to 13.7%-16.3% on DeepSeek-V3.2. These findings provide new insights for improving reasoning uncertainty quantification in large language models. The code is released at https://github.com/szu-tera/DTC.git.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Divergent Token Confidence (DTC), a training-free framework that quantifies LLM reasoning confidence by counting tokens where two models strongly disagree (via Jensen-Shannon divergence), yielding better calibration than probability-based and verbalized baselines.
AI.motivation: As chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs improves, calibrating reasoning confidence is increasingly important for quantifying answer uncertainty. Existing confidence estimation methods rely on probabilities of selected key tokens, yet their underlying mechanism is unclear, and a pilot study shows coarse substitutes can also improve calibration, motivating exploration of better confidence signals.
AI.method: DTC estimates confidence by counting divergent tokens where two models strongly disagree during decoding, identified via Jensen-Shannon divergence between next-token distributions along the same reasoning trajectory. It supports white-box and black-box evaluation using auxiliary models, requiring no explicit training and not affecting generation.
AI.result: The divergent token count is almost negatively correlated with answer accuracy. Across multiple model families and six mathematical benchmarks, DTC improves calibration: the count-only estimator achieves average expected calibration error of 13.0% under white-box evaluation, versus 32.7%-42.4% for standard full-sequence confidence methods; in black-box settings it reduces mean ECE from 32.1%-40.2% to 13.7%-16.3% on DeepSeek-V3.2.
AI.conclusion: DTC offers a simple yet effective signal for uncertainty quantification, improving reasoning confidence calibration over probability-based and verbalized baselines, providing new insights for uncertainty quantification in LLMs.

title: Character Training for Risk-Averse Agents
summary: Risk aversion in resources could prevent misaligned AI agents from causing catastrophic harm. Misaligned but risk-averse agents would tend to favor safer strategies like making deals with humans over riskier strategies like rebelling. We train agents to be risk averse through character training, finding that persona traits provide a robust mechanism for instilling risk preferences. To do this, we construct a model constitution describing constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) over an agent's resources and instill it through on-policy distillation. Despite never seeing the benchmark's decision format during training, character-trained models are competitive with baselines trained directly on it, and generalise better than them out of distribution on two of our four models. We also modulate different aspects of the constitution, finding that token budget and model choice are the most influential aspect of character training to instill risk aversion. We conclude from these results that character training is a promising and scalable way to instil broad dispositions, which we can use to our advantage in mitigating risk from misaligned AI agents.

AI.tldr: Character training via a CARA-based constitution and on-policy distillation instills robust risk aversion in AI agents, matching decision-format baselines and generalizing OOD on two of four models, offering a scalable disposition-shaping approach for misalignment mitigation.
AI.motivation: Risk aversion over resources could steer misaligned AI agents away from catastrophic actions (e.g., rebelling) toward safer strategies (e.g., negotiating with humans). The authors seek a robust, scalable mechanism to instill such risk preferences rather than relying on task-specific training, and to understand which design factors most influence its effectiveness.
AI.method: The authors perform character training by constructing a model constitution that specifies constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) over an agent's resources, then instilling this persona trait via on-policy distillation. They train and evaluate across four models, comparing against baselines trained directly on the benchmark's decision format. They also ablate components of the constitution (e.g., token budget, model choice) to identify the most influential factors.
AI.result: Character-trained models, despite never seeing the benchmark's decision format in training, are competitive with baselines trained directly on it, and outperform those baselines out-of-distribution on two of the four models. Ablations show token budget and model choice are the most influential aspects of character training for instilling risk aversion.
AI.conclusion: Character training is a promising and scalable method for instilling broad dispositions such as risk aversion, and can be leveraged to mitigate risks posed by misaligned AI agents. Token budget and model choice are key levers in this process.

title: NeuronEye: Query-Guided Visual Concept Activation for Vision-Language Reasoning
summary: Current vision-language models (VLMs) encode visual information in dense hidden states where object identity, spatial layout, and local attributes are implicitly entangled rather than explicitly disentangled, limiting their ability to isolate and modulate the specific visual evidence required by a given language query. Inspired by sparse population coding and top-down modulation in biological vision, we introduce NeuronEye, a plug-in framework that constructs a sparse, concept-level neuron vocabulary from intermediate VLM representations and selectively activates query-relevant visual concepts during inference. NeuronEye decomposes vision-token states into an overcomplete sparse basis organized by concept-level clusters, uses the language query to activate relevant clusters and localize the patches where selected concepts are expressed, and injects the focused evidence back into vision tokens. A complementary suppression mechanism attenuates dominant perceptual directions to preserve weaker but relevant cues. All operations run in a single forward pass over a frozen VLM backbone. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, NeuronEye raises CV-Bench overall accuracy by +3.1 with gains of +9.5 on Distance, and improves BLINK Multi-view by +8.3, with similar trends on LLaVA-1.6-7B. These results suggest that sparse neuron vocabularies can serve not only as post-hoc interpretability tools but also as active interfaces for concept-level visual reasoning.

AI.tldr: NeuronEye is a plug-in framework that builds a sparse, concept-level neuron vocabulary from intermediate VLM representations and selectively activates query-relevant visual concepts during inference, improving visual reasoning on frozen backbones.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs encode visual information in dense hidden states where object identity, spatial layout, and local attributes are implicitly entangled rather than explicitly disentangled, limiting the ability to isolate and modulate specific visual evidence required by a language query.
AI.method: Inspired by sparse population coding and top-down modulation in biological vision, NeuronEye constructs a sparse, concept-level neuron vocabulary from intermediate VLM representations. It decomposes vision-token states into an overcomplete sparse basis organized by concept-level clusters, uses the language query to activate relevant clusters and localize patches where selected concepts are expressed, and injects focused evidence back into vision tokens. A suppression mechanism attenuates dominant perceptual directions to preserve weaker relevant cues. All operations run in a single forward pass over a frozen VLM backbone.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, NeuronEye raises CV-Bench overall accuracy by +3.1 with gains of +9.5 on Distance, and improves BLINK Multi-view by +8.3, with similar trends on LLaVA-1.6-7B.
AI.conclusion: Sparse neuron vocabularies can serve not only as post-hoc interpretability tools but also as active interfaces for concept-level visual reasoning.

title: Do LLM Agents Execute the Plans They Declare? From Planning-Mode Declaration to Pattern-Specific Execution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) enable agents to solve long-horizon tasks by generating a plan and then executing it in an environment. However, successful planning requires two distinct capabilities: selecting an appropriate plan for the task and executing it faithfully. Existing planner--executor systems can fail at either stage, while final task success alone cannot distinguish selection from execution failures. We therefore study the Plan Declaration--Execution Gap and introduce Planning-as-Routing, where an LLM declares one of four planning modes: Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search, and a deterministic router dispatches the task to the corresponding pattern-specific executor. Across four benchmarks and three LLMs, we find three consistent patterns. First, generic Plan+ReAct often fails to preserve declared planning structure, especially for longer plans: across three benchmarks, only (22)--(45%) of trajectories preserve it, whereas pattern-specific executors enforce the intended structure. Second, planning-mode effectiveness varies across environments and models: Search performs best on ALFWorld, Hierarchical on SWE-bench, and the strongest pattern can vary across models within the same benchmark. Third, the largest gains come from execution: pattern-specific executors improve task success from (0.48) to (0.92) on ALFWorld and from (0.36) to (0.44) on SWE-bench Verified over Plan+ReAct. Current LLMs, however, do not reliably select the strongest mode for each task, although few-shot examples improve selection in some benchmark--model combinations. Overall, reliable agent planning requires both effective mode selection and faithful execution: routing substantially closes the execution gap, while task-specific mode selection remains open.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a "Plan Declaration–Execution Gap" in LLM agents, proposing "Planning-as-Routing" where an LLM declares one of four planning modes and a router dispatches to pattern-specific executors; it finds execution fidelity is the dominant bottleneck, while mode selection remains unreliable.
AI.motivation: Successful planning requires two distinct capabilities—selecting an appropriate plan and executing it faithfully—yet existing planner–executor systems can fail at either stage, and final task success alone cannot disentangle selection failures from execution failures. This motivates explicitly separating and measuring these two failure sources.
AI.method: The authors formalize the Plan Declaration–Execution Gap and introduce Planning-as-Routing. An LLM declares one of four planning modes (Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, Search), and a deterministic router dispatches the task to the corresponding pattern-specific executor. Evaluation spans four benchmarks and three LLMs, comparing pattern-specific executors against a generic Plan+ReAct baseline, with structure-preservation analysis and few-shot selection experiments.
AI.result: First, generic Plan+ReAct often fails to preserve declared planning structure, especially for longer plans: only 22–45% of trajectories preserve it across three benchmarks, whereas pattern-specific executors enforce the intended structure. Second, planning-mode effectiveness varies across environments and models: Search is best on ALFWorld, Hierarchical on SWE-bench, and the strongest pattern can vary across models within the same benchmark. Third, the largest gains come from execution: pattern-specific executors raise task success from 0.48 to 0.92 on ALFWorld and from 0.36 to 0.44 on SWE-bench Verified over Plan+ReAct. However, current LLMs do not reliably select the strongest mode per task, though few-shot examples improve selection in some benchmark–model combinations.
AI.conclusion: Reliable agent planning requires both effective mode selection and faithful execution. Routing substantially closes the execution gap, while task-specific mode selection remains an open problem.

title: Stochastic World Models for Verifying Vision-Based Neural Feedback Systems
summary: Verifying a vision-based neural feedback system requires a model of the observations its controller acts upon. Such a model must capture the variation the sensor produces, while remaining tractable for closed-loop analysis. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have served as perception surrogates, but they are large, reproduce complex scenes poorly, and are hard to verify. We explore stochastic world models as a richer class of perception surrogates. We train a world model with physically grounded latents, built from operations that standard verifiers bound. It reproduces held-out frames more faithfully than GAN surrogates with up to 130 times as many parameters. To verify these surrogates, we develop a procedure that combines falsification, adaptive refinement, symbolic, and backward analyses. On an emergency braking benchmark with a GAN surrogate, our procedure resolves the entire state space, 38% of which the state-of-the-art verifier left unresolved. On the RGB version of the benchmark, where no verification results have previously been reported, our procedure resolves over 80% of the state space with a world model surrogate.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes stochastic world models with physically grounded latents as perception surrogates for verifying vision-based neural feedback systems, and a combined verification procedure that substantially outperforms prior GAN-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Verifying vision-based neural feedback systems requires an observation model that captures sensor variation while remaining tractable for closed-loop analysis. Existing GAN-based perception surrogates are large, reproduce complex scenes poorly, and are difficult to verify, limiting verification coverage.
AI.method: The authors train a world model with physically grounded latents built from operations that standard verifiers can bound, and develop a verification procedure combining falsification, adaptive refinement, symbolic analysis, and backward analysis.
AI.result: The world model reproduces held-out frames more faithfully than GAN surrogates with up to 130 times as many parameters. On an emergency braking benchmark with a GAN surrogate, the procedure resolves the entire state space, 38% of which the state-of-the-art verifier left unresolved. On the RGB version, it resolves over 80% of the state space with a world model surrogate, where no prior verification results existed.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic world models serve as richer, more faithful, and more verifiable perception surrogates than GANs, and the proposed hybrid verification procedure achieves substantially greater state-space resolution than existing methods, including on previously unverified RGB benchmarks.

title: AdviSD: Learning to Advise Frontier LLMs via Targeted Multi-Turn Self-Distillation
summary: A small trainable advisor can steer a frozen language-model executor using natural-language advice. In addition to learning from task rewards, the advisor can use feedback from completed interactions to improve its advice. However, a plausible correction need not change execution, yet learning from such corrections can still affect the advisor's future decisions in other contexts. In a shared-parameter model, we prove that such corrections can limit learning if their targets favor useful advice less strongly than those of other corrections. Keeping them less often than the rest improves the model's eventual performance compared to learning from every correction. Motivated by this, our method, Advisor Self-Distillation (AdviSD), pairs outcome-based reinforcement learning with self-distillation from a feedback-conditioned copy of the advisor selectively. Reflection proposes corrections, and the advisor scores the same recorded executor response with and without its issued advice, using the magnitude of the difference to select decisions for supervision. This approach does not require executor likelihoods or additional executor rollouts. Experiments with Qwen3-8B advisors for Gemini and Claude show that AdviSD outperforms advisor-GRPO by 4.2-6.4 percentage points on BFCL-v3 and by 3.9-5.1 score points on EnvScaler. The trained advisors generalize to out-of-domain tasks and transfer across different executor versions and model families. AdviSD also beats matched-count random selection, supporting the value of its selection rule.

AI.tldr: AdviSD pairs outcome-based RL with selective self-distillation from a feedback-conditioned advisor copy, selecting corrections whose advice causally changes executor responses, improving advisor-guided frozen-executor performance.
AI.motivation: A trainable advisor can steer a frozen executor via natural-language advice and improve using feedback from completed interactions. However, plausible corrections may not actually change execution, and learning from such ineffective corrections can still shift the advisor's future decisions in other contexts. In shared-parameter models, these corrections can limit learning when their targets favor useful advice less strongly than other corrections do.
AI.method: The paper proves that learning from such corrections less often than from others improves eventual performance. Based on this, AdviSD combines outcome-based reinforcement learning with selective self-distillation from a feedback-conditioned copy of the advisor. Reflection proposes corrections, and the advisor scores the same recorded executor response both with and without its issued advice; the magnitude of the difference is used to select decisions for supervision. The method requires no executor likelihoods or additional executor rollouts.
AI.result: With Qwen3-8B advisors for Gemini and Claude, AdviSD outperforms advisor-GRPO by 4.2–6.4 percentage points on BFCL-v3 and 3.9–5.1 score points on EnvScaler. The trained advisors generalize to out-of-domain tasks and transfer across executor versions and model families, and AdviSD also beats matched-count random selection.
AI.conclusion: Selectively learning from corrections that demonstrably influence executor behavior yields better advisor training than learning from all corrections, validating AdviSD's selection rule and its practical effectiveness and transferability.

title: Learning Meta-Skills for Agent Harness Design in Test-Time AI4AI
summary: Agent performance depends on both reasoning ability and the environment in which it acts. We study test-time AI-for-AI, asking how a Builder can learn to construct better execution environments for a Target while both models' weights remain fixed. To make the Builder's experience reusable, we introduce Meta-Skill: principles specifying when support is needed and what resources to provide. The Builder learns these principles from Target's execution feedback on the development set, then uses the frozen skill bank to construct harnesses for unseen tasks. Across Harness-Bench and NewtonBench, full-bank meta-skills improve macro-average performance by 8.95 percentage points over no-skill construction, and 12.02 points over direct delivery of the same bank to the Target. These results highlight the value of translating experience into executable support. Gains when the same model serves both roles further suggest a path to system level self-improvement through learning to build better environments.

AI.tldr: A Builder model learns transferable "Meta-Skill" principles from a Target's execution feedback to construct better execution environments (harnesses) for unseen tasks, all with frozen weights. Full-bank meta-skills improve macro-average performance by 8.95 points over no-skill construction and 12.02 points over directly handing the skill bank to the Target across Harness-Bench and NewtonBench, suggesting a route to system-level self-improvement.
AI.motivation: Agent performance is shaped not only by reasoning ability but also by the environment in which the agent acts. The paper asks how a Builder can learn, at test time, to construct better execution environments for a Target while both models' weights stay fixed, and how to make the Builder's experience reusable rather than task-specific.
AI.method: Test-time AI-for-AI setup with frozen weights. The Builder distills its experience into Meta-Skill: principles specifying when support is needed and what resources to provide. It learns these principles from the Target's execution feedback on a development set, then applies the frozen skill bank to construct harnesses for unseen tasks. Evaluated on Harness-Bench and NewtonBench, with ablations comparing full-bank meta-skills, no-skill construction, and direct delivery of the same bank to the Target, including cases where one model serves both roles.
AI.result: Full-bank meta-skills improve macro-average performance by 8.95 percentage points over no-skill construction and by 12.02 percentage points over directly delivering the same skill bank to the Target. Gains persist when the same model serves both Builder and Target roles.
AI.conclusion: Reusable, principle-based meta-skills that translate the Builder's experience into executable support yield better environments and higher Target performance than either bare construction or raw skill delivery. The findings, including gains under self-role sharing, point toward system-level self-improvement through learning to build better environments.

title: Thinking Before Thinking: Scaling Agentic Inference Through Meta-Reasoning
summary: As agents take on longer and more complex problems, controlling the execution becomes a task in its own right. Each step in the run brings new control choices, like which partial work to build on, whether to start fresh, or when to stop. We introduce agentic meta-reasoning, an inference-time harness that makes these choices an explicit and structured reasoning process. Workers carry out the task-level computation, while a controller consolidates what the run has established, explores next options, assesses what each option is worth under the remaining budget, and dispatches the chosen work with context drawn from persistent memory. Between decisions the controller carries only a compact account of the run rather than replaying its full history. Our baselines span production coding agents and research harnesses, together with a Direct Control Agent using the same workers and compute budget allowance. On ProgramBench, which tests long-horizon agentic capability through program reconstruction, meta-reasoning achieves 71.5% with GPT-5.5 against 58.0% for Codex; with Opus 4.8 it achieves 67.2% against 65.5% for Claude Code. On the other benchmarks, spanning abstract reasoning, multi-domain long-horizon reasoning, and proof generation, it gains between 3.6 and 4.2 points over direct control, averaged across three frontier models. It keeps improving over the tested budget ranges where direct control plateaus, though its overhead can hurt at small budgets. Artifact-graph analysis reveals more reuse of earlier work, higher coverage of correct solutions in most settings, and nonuniform gains in final selection. These results indicate that spending computation on structured control becomes more important as agents scale to longer runs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "agentic meta-reasoning," an inference-time harness that makes control decisions during long agent runs an explicit, structured reasoning process. It separates task-level execution (workers) from a controller that consolidates progress, explores options, evaluates them under budget, and dispatches work using persistent memory. On ProgramBench it reaches 71.5% with GPT-5.5 vs 58.0% for Codex, and 67.2% with Opus 4.8 vs 65.5% for Claude Code, with 3.6–4.2 point gains over direct control on other benchmarks.
AI.motivation: As agents tackle longer and more complex problems, execution control itself becomes a distinct challenge. Each step introduces new control choices—which partial work to build on, whether to restart, when to stop—and these decisions become increasingly consequential as runs lengthen. The paper motivates treating control as an explicit reasoning problem rather than an implicit byproduct of task execution.
AI.method: The proposed agentic meta-reasoning is an inference-time harness that structures control decisions. Workers perform task-level computation, while a controller consolidates the run's established results, explores next options, assesses each option's value under the remaining budget, and dispatches chosen work with context drawn from persistent memory. Between decisions, the controller retains only a compact account of the run rather than replaying full history, reducing overhead. Baselines include production coding agents, research harnesses, and a Direct Control Agent sharing the same workers and compute budget.
AI.result: On ProgramBench, meta-reasoning achieves 71.5% with GPT-5.5 versus 58.0% for Codex, and 67.2% with Opus 4.8 versus 65.5% for Claude Code. On abstract reasoning, multi-domain long-horizon reasoning, and proof generation benchmarks, it gains 3.6–4.2 points over direct control averaged across three frontier models. It continues improving across tested budget ranges where direct control plateaus, though overhead can hurt at small budgets. Artifact-graph analysis shows more reuse of earlier work, higher coverage of correct solutions in most settings, and nonuniform gains in final selection.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate that spending computation on structured control becomes increasingly important as agents scale to longer runs. Explicit meta-reasoning improves long-horizon performance, though its overhead imposes a trade-off at small budgets. The findings position control as a first-class object of inference-time computation in agentic systems.
